Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet include a typed styling layer with compile-time CSS property and unit checks?
decisions.gist: A typed styling layer would let UI components declare styles using Jet types rather than CSS strings — catching wrong units (px vs em vs %), unknown properties, and invalid values at compile time. This rides the #Unit system and the reactive-UI stack. It is a new idea with no card.
decisions.explainer: Typed styles only make sense if Jet has a UI kit and a reactive component model. Both are still in the proposal stage. Designing the style layer now risks building against a component API that changes. The dependency order is: reactive-UI-stack → component model → typed styles. The #Unit system (already ratified) would provide the unit type machinery; the style layer would add CSS property names as a constrained type. No new syntax is needed beyond what #Unit already provides — this is a library design question, not a language design question. The crux is sequencing, not whether to do it.
decisions.story: I set a font-size to 14 when I meant 14px. The browser silently ignored it. I want the compiler to tell me 'font-size expects a length unit; you gave a bare number.'

options.name: Part of the reactive-UI stack; sequence after component model is ratified
options.detail: Commit to typed styles as a first-class part of the UI kit. Design it after the component model is stable so the style API fits the component API. The #Unit system already provides the unit machinery; the style layer adds property typing as a library concern. No new language surface needed.

options.name: Standalone styling library; no component model dependency
options.detail: Ship a typed-styles library independent of the component model. Users can apply it to any output target (HTML strings, native renderers, etc.). More flexible but harder to integrate cleanly with the component system later; risks two style APIs.

options.name: Defer — no card until reactive-UI stack is ratified
options.detail: Do not open a typed-styles card until the reactive-UI stack and component model decisions are settled. Avoids designing against a moving target.
options.code:
// Status quo: no styled components; users write CSS strings
let style = "font-size: 14px; margin: 1.5rem;"

comparisons.note: Elm’s typed UI ecosystem catches many invalid attributes and values at compile time.
CSS authored in TypeScript with full type checking on property names and values. Generated at build time as plain CSS. Property names are typed; values are strings (no unit types).
CSS properties are typed functions returning typed values; unit functions (px, rem, pct) enforce dimensional correctness at compile time. Closest model to what Jet proposes.

decisions.bestCurrent: Elm: Elm’s typed UI ecosystem catches many invalid attributes and values at compile time.
decisions.recommendation: Sequence typed styles inside the reactive UI stack. Jet should match Elm’s safety while sharing one component/layout model.
decisions.comment: I want this also ratified: How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.

decisions.title: Should Jet's UI kit bake accessibility in by default, with a11y lints that gate release?
decisions.gist: The idea is that Jet's UI components ship ARIA roles, focus management, and keyboard navigation built in — not as opt-in add-ons — and that the compiler/linter can emit a11y diagnostics that block a release build. This is a new idea with no card. It depends on the reactive-UI stack existing.
decisions.explainer: If Jet is building a UI kit, the 'safe by default' ethos (I1) applies to accessibility as much as memory safety. A component that can receive focus but has no keyboard handler is a bug, not a choice. Baking a11y in by default means component authors get correct ARIA behavior without thinking about it; opting out requires an explicit escape. The diagnostic-gate angle is a release-profile feature: a11y lints are warnings in dev builds and errors in release builds, analogous to how safety rules work. This depends on: the component model being designed, the diagnostic system (I4), and the reactive-UI-stack card. The sequencing is clear: decide the UI stack first, then design a11y as a first-class layer of it. Splitting the component behavior from the diagnostic gate into two sub-decisions is possible but unnecessary — they are the same idea.
decisions.story: I built a custom dropdown menu. A screen-reader user reported they couldn't use it. The component library should have given me ARIA and keyboard handling by default — I shouldn't have had to know to add them.

options.name: A11y by default in component kit + release-gating lints
options.detail: Components ship with correct ARIA roles, focus management, and keyboard handling. Opting out requires an explicit @no_a11y annotation with a justification string. A11y lints are warnings in dev, errors in release. Fits safe-by-default and I4 (every lint has a code and a snapshot test).
options.code:
// Missing label on interactive element — release-gating lint
error[A001]: interactive element has no accessible label
  --> src/ui/search.jet:12
   |
12 | component SearchBar { ... }
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   | help: add a label: parameter or aria_label: to the component

options.name: Opt-in a11y — components ship without ARIA by default
options.detail: Components are unstyled/inaccessible by default; authors add ARIA and keyboard handling explicitly. More flexible for non-browser targets (native, terminal) but makes inaccessibility the default. Violates the safe-by-default ethos when targeting web.

options.name: Defer — decide after reactive-UI stack and component model are ratified
options.detail: A11y design depends on what components look like. Defer this card until the reactive-UI-stack and ownable-components decisions are settled. Open this card as the first a11y decision at that point, not later.
options.code:
// No current surface. Status quo: no UI kit, no a11y story.
// Revisit: after reactive-UI-stack + ownable-components ratified.

comparisons.note: Separate library that adds ARIA and keyboard behavior to unstyled component hooks. Accessible behavior is opt-in; most React apps don't use it. Jet's proposal inverts this default.
svelte-check runs axe-based a11y lints as warnings at build time. Not a hard error; not baked into components. Closer to Jet's lint-gate idea but opt-in tooling, not framework default.

decisions.comment: But we should support some kind of magical default that allows us to do some level of automatic fill in for defaults so it doesnt piss off jet users by requiring tiny fixes to every little thing they do

decisions.bestCurrent: No ratified decision yet.
decisions.recommendation: Use built-in inference plus explicit typed override: beginner-safe defaults, expert control, no raw stringly ARIA as the main path.

log.text: Reopened: agent incorrectly ratified after answering owner question; owner had not selected an option.
Question answered; Option A updated to combine built-in magic/inference with explicit expert override.
Ballot added because implementation plan had a decision blocker.

decisions.title: How are component accessibility roles inferred, specified, and overridden?
decisions.gist: A11y-by-default should combine beginner magic with expert control: built-in components infer roles automatically, custom interactive components must declare or derive a typed role, and experts can override deliberately.
decisions.story: Walter ships a form. Standard Button/Dialog/Menu controls should be keyboard-correct with no ceremony. When he builds a custom icon-only control, Jet should infer what it safely can, require an explicit role when inference is ambiguous, and give experts a typed override path instead of raw string ARIA.
decisions.inWild:
Button.{ label: "Save", on_click: save }              // built-in role: button
IconButton.{ icon: .Trash, on_click: delete }       // inferred interactive, may need label
#Role(.Button)
component ToolbarToggle { ... }                     // explicit expert override

options.name: Built-in inference + explicit typed override (recommended)
options.detail: Combine A and B: core components carry fixed role/keyboard behavior; simple custom components get conservative inference from typed properties/events; ambiguous custom interactive components must use a typed role/keyboard marker. Experts can override through audited typed APIs, not raw ARIA strings. Release lint blocks missing accessible names, focus behavior, or invalid role/property combinations.
options.code:
Button.{ label: "Save", on_click: save }          // role inferred from core Button
IconButton.{ icon: .Trash, label: "Delete", on_click: delete } // inferred button + required accessible name

#Role(.Switch)
#Keyboard(.Toggle)
component ThemeToggle {
    checked: Bool
    on_toggle: fn(Bool)
}

options.name: Name/property inference only
options.detail: Jet guesses roles from component names and fields. Low ceremony, but fragile: renaming or unusual component shapes can silently change a11y behavior.
options.code:
component SaveButton { on_click: fn() }
component Pill { on_click: fn() } // role guess unclear

options.name: Manual ARIA fields only
options.detail: Expose raw ARIA properties and require users to set them. Maximum control, poor beginner safety, and stringly typed mistakes reach release builds.
options.code: Element.{ aria_role: "button", tab_index: 0, on_key_down: handle_key }

comparisons.note: Components have built-in accessibility traits with override APIs.

decisions.explainer: A11y-by-default should combine beginner magic with expert control: built-in components infer roles automatically, custom interactive components must declare or derive a typed role, and experts can override deliberately.

decisions.title: Native app UI: FFI to platform widgets first, own renderer later?
decisions.gist: Jet has C FFI but no native UI strategy. The question is whether to build platform widget bridges (Win32/AppKit/GTK) as a first phase and defer an own renderer, or pick a different sequencing. This is the proceed/kill gate and phase-ordering decision for native app support.
decisions.explainer: Native UI is the widest blast radius of any backend target — it touches codegen targets, FFI bridge patterns, the stdlib surface, and the package ecosystem. An FFI bridge to platform widgets reuses the existing C FFI and the ffi-bridge stdlib pattern; it ships value immediately without owning a renderer. An own renderer (canvas/GPU) is a separate, later phase that replaces the widget bridges over time. Choosing C alone defers native-UI indefinitely. This decision gates the native-backend card; the render-target-abstraction, reactive-ui, and web-backend cards are parallel but interact at the view-model boundary.
decisions.story: I want to write a native macOS/Windows app in Jet and ship it today. I don't care if it renders via AppKit internally — I just want real native controls without reaching for Electron.

options.name: Phase 1 widget FFI, phase 2 own renderer
options.detail: Ship a thin core library layer over platform widget APIs (AppKit on macOS, Win32/WinUI on Windows, GTK on Linux) using the existing C FFI bridge pattern. Defer an own renderer to a later epoch. Fast first value; borrows platform look-and-feel for free; renderer work does not block.

options.name: Own renderer from the start
options.detail: Skip platform widget bridges; build a GPU/canvas renderer (wgpu or similar) that draws every widget from scratch. Pixel-perfect control, no platform style variation. Massive upfront cost; no native look-and-feel; blocks any native app use until the renderer ships.

options.name: Web-only; defer native
options.detail: No native widget work; ship the web backend (D-WEBBACKEND1) first and use Electron or a webview as the path to 'native' apps. Simplifies the target matrix; native look-and-feel is impossible; blocks desktop-first use cases indefinitely.

comparisons.note: Apple ships SwiftUI as a declarative layer over AppKit/UIKit platform widgets — the same phase-1 strategy: lean on existing platform renderers first.
Flutter chose own renderer (Skia/Impeller) from day one. High pixel-perfect control, but no native widget look-and-feel and a multi-year investment before shipping.

decisions.gist: D-NATIVEUI1 approved Phase 1: thin Jet wrapper over native platform widgets. This decides which platform to build first and whether to build all three simultaneously.
decisions.story: Derek is building a Jet desktop app. He's on macOS. He wants to ship to Windows users too. He needs the native UI backend to exist so his app can render native widgets on both platforms from the same Jet code.
decisions.comparisons: Qt: cross-platform C++ widget toolkit, all platforms simultaneously. GTK: Linux-first, cross-platform with backends. wxWidgets: wraps native APIs per platform, all platforms. Electron: web tech, all platforms simultaneously. Flutter desktop: all platforms (macOS/Win/Linux) in one unified release. Tauri: web + native, all platforms.

options.name: macOS (AppKit) first, then Windows and Linux
options.detail: Build the macOS AppKit wrapper first (narrowest FFI surface, best macOS support). The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is defined and proven against AppKit before tackling Win32/GTK. Ship macOS, then add platforms. Risk: Windows users wait; API may be too AppKit-shaped.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: macOS only
use core.ui.native  // backed by AppKit on macOS

options.name: All three platforms simultaneously (recommended)
options.detail: Build AppKit, Win32/WinUI, and GTK backends in parallel. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is kept platform-agnostic from day one. Jet's platform detection at compile time routes to the right backend. Flutter's desktop approach — commitment to parity from the start prevents API drift. Higher up-front cost but the right shape from the start.

options.name: Linux (GTK) first for CI/headless testing
options.detail: GTK is available in CI headless environments (Xvfb). Build GTK first to establish the testing infrastructure and Backend trait API with automated tests. Then port to AppKit and Win32. Best for testing rigor; not ideal for the majority macOS/Windows developer audience.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: GTK on Linux (CI-first)
use core.ui.native  // backed by GTK on Linux

decisions.recReason: Flutter's lesson: committing to cross-platform from the start produces a better API than porting a single-platform API later. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) provides the seam; parallel implementation keeps all three honest against the same contract.

decisions.title: JS/npm and Swift interop: sequence JS first, Swift via C-ABI later?
decisions.gist: Jet can call C today. JS/npm interop and Swift interop are separate tracks beyond C/Rust FFI. This is the proceed/kill gate and sequencing decision: approve both, sequence them, or defer.
decisions.explainer: JS/npm interop is a natural output of the web backend (D-WEBBACKEND1): when Jet compiles to WASM+JS, it needs a way to import JS modules and call npm packages. This is not a separate FFI mechanism — it's a web-target import protocol. Swift interop is a different beast: Swift's ABI is unstable and platform-specific, so the only safe bridge is the C ABI (marked `@_cdecl` on the Swift side). Approving both simultaneously risks underdelivering both. Sequencing JS first ties it to D-WEBBACKEND1 and avoids a standalone Swift FFI effort before a native backend exists. Neither track needs a new invariant carve-out; both use the ffi-bridge pattern.
decisions.story: I want to call an existing npm charting library from my Jet web app, and later call an existing Swift networking library from my macOS Jet app — without rewriting them.

options.name: JS/npm first (gated on web backend), Swift via C-ABI later
options.detail: JS import syntax ships as part of D-WEBBACKEND1: a Jet web module can `import npm:"chart.js"` and the web codegen handles the binding. Swift interop is deferred until the native backend (D-NATIVEUI1) exists; then bridge via `@_cdecl`/C-ABI. Avoids a standalone Swift FFI track with no native target to attach it to.

options.name: Both tracks now
options.detail: Open both JS/npm and Swift interop as active work items in parallel. Spreads effort thin; Swift ABI is unstable without a native target; JS import is meaningless without a web target. High risk of both landing half-done.

options.name: Defer both
options.detail: No JS or Swift interop until respective backends ship and prove out. Keeps the surface small; blocks any ecosystem reuse in web or native apps until those backends mature.
options.code:
// no npm or swift imports
// users must wrap in a C shim to call any JS/Swift library

comparisons.note: wasm-bindgen's `#[wasm_bindgen]` attribute lets Rust call JS functions and import npm types — the same pattern Jet's web target would adopt.
Swift exports C-ABI functions with @_cdecl, which is the only stable Swift↔other-language bridge. A Jet↔Swift bridge would use this as the seam.

decisions.bestCurrent: No ratified decision yet.
decisions.recommendation: Use first-party typed Jet stub packages (Option A).

log.text: Ballot added because implementation plan had a decision blocker.

decisions.title: How are npm package types authored for Jet JS interop?
decisions.gist: JS/npm interop needs a typed stub story before importing npm packages from Jet.
decisions.story: Doris imports a charting npm package. She needs typed Jet calls without hand-writing unsafe glue in every project.
decisions.inWild: use npm."chart.js" as chart

options.name: First-party Jet stub packages (recommended)
options.detail: Typed npm bindings are Jet packages maintained like Core wrappers. Safe default, reviewable, and compatible with package manager.
options.code: use npm.chart_js as chart

options.name: Read TypeScript declarations directly
options.detail: Parse `.d.ts` files into Jet types. Broad coverage, but TypeScript semantics leak into Jet and diagnostics get worse.
options.code: use npm."chart.js" as chart

options.name: Dynamic untyped npm import
options.detail: Allow untyped dynamic JS values. Fastest to reach packages, but violates static safety for ordinary users.
options.code: use npm."chart.js" as chart // Any

comparisons.note: Prefer typed wrappers around foreign ecosystems.

decisions.title: JS/npm binder depth: two hosts (browser + native), one `use js.<lib>` surface
decisions.gist: JS is unique: the web target already has a JS engine (the browser), but a native Jet CLI/server has none. Pick how npm is mounted on each host, and reconcile the `jet bind js` binder with D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored-stub floor.
decisions.explainer: On the web target (D-WEBBACKEND1=A) the browser is the JS engine, boundary types are fixed by D-JSBIND1=A, the WASM triple by D-WEBKIND1=A, the partition by D-WASM1=A — so `use js.plotly` there is a solved binding into the browser JS host. The open question is native targets: to let a native binary call an npm package there is no ambient JS engine, so JS must be mounted as a WASM component on the already-approved wasmtime runtime (D-DEP-WASM1=A, the #5 substrate) via a QuickJS/componentize-js interpreter — sandboxed, I1-clean, and zero new runtime dependency. Recommended is one `use js.X` surface whose host is chosen by the compile target. Second, the depth ballot must reconcile D-NPMTYPE1=A (typed npm surfaces are first-party hand-authored Jet stubs, no .d.ts parsing) with the frame's `jet bind js` binder: the recommendation is that `jet bind js` generates a committable, Jet-checked stub from the package's .d.ts (inspectable binder output, not runtime .d.ts semantics), which supersedes D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored-only floor — this is what tapping all npm immediately requires. Long-tail packages with no .d.ts fall back to a #Unsafe-gated dynamic Any surface.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. In the browser her chart view calls plotly.js; on the server her CLI wants lodash and a markdown npm package. She wants the same `use js.<lib>` line to work in both places, typed, without hand-writing a stub for every package she touches.
decisions.detail: Honors D-FFI-UNIFY1 (namespace, three tiers, `jet bind js` -> `.jet/bindings/js/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers, `#Unsafe` for raw). Marshalling is governed by D-JSBIND1=A on BOTH hosts: number<->Int/Float, string<->String, array<->[T], object<->Codable struct or Map; JS throw -> Jet Result + E-code; JS Promise <-> Jet async (`await js.fn(...)`); a Jet closure crosses as a JS callback only via the explicit wrap D-JSBIND1 requires. Distribution: npm ref in pkg.jet, fetched from the npm registry, vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); the JS-on-wasm runtime is the already-approved wasmtime (no new I6 dep); registry-provider policy rides D-JPK-EXTPROV1. Sequencing honors D-JSWIFTFFI1=A (JS first). The D-NPMTYPE1 reconciliation is the one place this ballot amends a prior ratification and must be stated in the outcome.

options.name: Target-dispatched host (browser + JS-on-wasm) with generated stubs (recommended)
options.detail: `use js.X` binds on both hosts: on the web target it wires into the browser JS engine (D-WEBBACKEND1); on native targets it runs the package inside a QuickJS/componentize-js WASM component on the existing wasmtime runtime — sandboxed, no new runtime dep. `jet bind js` generates a committable typed stub from the package's .d.ts (superseding D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored floor); no-.d.ts packages get a #Unsafe-gated dynamic Any fallback. A Node-subprocess broker is an opt-in tier for packages needing full Node APIs or native addons.
options.code:
$ jet bind js: plotly.js@2
  -> .jet/bindings/js/plotly.jet (from plotly.d.ts, 118 typed fns)

use js.plotly as plot      // browser on web target
use js.lodash as _          // JS-on-wasm on native target, same line

// long-tail, no .d.ts:
use js.obscure_pkg as ob    // error unless wrapped:
#Unsafe("untyped npm package") { ob.frobnicate(x) }

options.name: Web-target-only binding
options.detail: `use js.X` is valid only inside web-target modules; the browser is the sole JS host. Smallest surface and rides D-WEBBACKEND1 directly. A native CLI or server can never call an npm package, so the entire server-side npm ecosystem stays out of reach.

options.name: In-process V8/Node embed for native
options.detail: Native targets embed a full V8/Node engine in-process. Fastest native JS and full Node API coverage; pulls a large in-process engine as a new runtime dependency separate from the approved wasmtime, and an in-process engine is a weaker isolation boundary than the sandbox for untrusted npm code.
options.code: use js.lodash as _         // in-process V8 in the native binary

options.name: Node subprocess broker for native
options.detail: Native targets spawn a supervised `node` worker and marshal JSON; the browser still hosts the web target. Full Node ecosystem including native addons, process-isolated; requires a node install present, marshals every value (no zero-copy), and grows a process tree in production binaries. Best kept as the opt-in tier under A rather than the default.
options.code: use js.sharp as sharp      // supervised node worker, marshaled

comparisons.note: Compiles logic to WASM and generates JS bindings for the browser host — the web-host half of A, and the pattern D-WEBBACKEND1 already adopted.
Runs JS as a WASM component on wasmtime — the native-host half of A, reusing the #5 runtime with no new dependency and full sandbox isolation.
comparisons.code: // npm package -> wasm component -> loaded by the same PluginHost

comparisons.note: Embed V8 in-process (option C) for a full Node-compatible runtime — great API coverage, but a heavy in-process engine and a weaker boundary for untrusted code.
comparisons.code: // V8 embedded in the host process

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Swift binder depth over the fixed C-ABI seam
decisions.gist: D-JSWIFTFFI1=A already fixed the transport (Swift via the stable C-ABI, since Swift's own ABI is unstable). This picks how much typed projection sits on top: shallow hand-exported C-ABI, a swift-bridge-style generated bridge, or a full Clang-importer projection.
decisions.explainer: The Swift use case (card #122) is calling platform framework libraries — Foundation, AppKit, networking — from a native macOS/iOS Jet app, so the real Swift runtime and its frameworks are required; a WASM path forfeits the frameworks and is out. D-JSWIFTFFI1=A fixed the transport at the C-ABI (@_cdecl is Swift's only stable cross-language seam). The remaining choice is projection depth. Shallow means the user (or a hand-written shim) marks each Swift function @_cdecl and Jet binds the resulting C ABI via the existing S59 C binder — real but low-level, no classes/generics/String ergonomics. A swift-bridge-style generated bridge runs swiftc from a bridge description to auto-emit the @_cdecl shims and generate typed Jet wrappers: classes/actors become opaque ref-counted handles, String/Array/Optional/throws/async marshal, and it feels native while the C-ABI stays the stable transport underneath. Full Clang-importer projection of .swiftinterface is the aspirational ceiling but a moving target against Swift's evolving module format. Recommended is the generated bridge: it delivers the frame's 'feels native for static languages' depth without reopening D-JSWIFTFFI1's C-ABI transport.
decisions.story: Marco is writing a macOS menubar app in Jet. He wants to call Alamofire for networking and a Foundation date formatter without hand-writing a C shim for every function, and without a NSObject handle leaking or a Swift `throws` turning into a crash.
decisions.detail: Honors D-FFI-UNIFY1 (swift.<lib> namespace, three tiers, `jet bind swift` -> `.jet/bindings/swift/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers, `#Unsafe` for raw pointers) and D-JSWIFTFFI1=A (C-ABI transport, sequenced after JS + the native backend). Marshalling: Swift String<->String (UTF-8), Array<T><->[T], Optional<->optional, structs by-value, classes/actors as opaque ref-counted handles (retain/release compiler-vetted, I1), throws->Result, async->Jet async via @_cdecl continuation shims; no raw pointer crosses outside #Unsafe. Distribution: SwiftPM/git ref pinned in pkg.jet, vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); swiftc is a build-time native toolchain (like cc for S59), provisioned via jetpack/nixpkgs/Xcode, not an I6 compiler dep; registry fetch rides D-JPK-EXTPROV1. Platform-gated: macOS/iOS + Linux-Swift only; elsewhere `use swift.X` is an honest gated E-code. swiftc/linker errors laundered to Jet E-codes (I2/I4).

options.name: swift-bridge-style generated projection over the C-ABI (recommended)
options.detail: `jet bind swift` runs swiftc to emit @_cdecl shims for the declared surface, compiles them to a static lib, and generates typed Jet wrappers reusing the S59 C-binding lowering. Classes/actors become opaque ref-counted handles, String/Array/Optional/throws/async all marshal. The C-ABI stays the stable transport underneath (honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1); the projection is the depth. Feels native without hand-written shims.
options.code:
$ jet bind swift: Alamofire@5.8
  -> generates @_cdecl shims + .jet/bindings/swift/Alamofire.jet

use swift.Alamofire as af
let r = af.request(url).await   // handle, async, error all projected

options.name: Hand-exported C-ABI only (shallow)
options.detail: The user marks Swift functions @_cdecl themselves (or wraps a library in a hand-written C-compatible shim) and Jet binds the resulting C header via the existing S59 C binder. No new binder machinery. But every function needs a hand-written export, classes/generics/String ergonomics do not come across, and wrapping a real framework is a wall of manual shims — the opposite of the frame's near-trivial bar.

options.name: Full Clang-importer projection of .swiftinterface
options.detail: Parse .swiftinterface/.swiftmodule and project whole Swift modules into typed Jet, the way Swift's own Clang importer projects C — the deepest 'feels native' ceiling and the right static-language end-state. Swift's module format and ABI instability make it a moving target that would chase every toolchain release; better as an aspirational upgrade on top of A than the first landing.
options.code: use swift.Alamofire as af   // whole module projected, no bridge description

options.name: Swift-to-WASM component
options.detail: Compile Swift with the swiftwasm toolchain to a WASM component on wasmtime (reuse #5). Sandboxed and I1-clean — but swiftwasm loses the platform frameworks (AppKit/Foundation/UIKit), which are the entire reason for Swift interop. Wrong for the native-app use case.
options.code: use swift.PureSwiftLib as p  // frameworks unavailable

comparisons.note: Generates @_cdecl shims + typed Rust wrappers from a bridge description over the C-ABI — exactly option A's mechanism, proven in production.
Full typed projection of C/ObjC modules so foreign APIs feel native — the ceiling option C aims at, and why A keeps C as the transport it can later deepen onto.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Generates typed bindings from a def file over the C-ABI for Apple frameworks — the same generated-bridge-over-C-ABI shape as A, for the same platform-framework reason.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Reopen S18: flip to public-by-default or add a file-scope marker?
decisions.gist: S18 ratified private-by-default with per-item `pub`. The proposal is to reopen that decision and either flip the default (public-by-default + opt-in private) or add a positional file-scope marker. The owner already considered and declined grouped visibility (Jai-style blocks, section markers, export lists) when ratifying S18.
decisions.explainer: S18 was ratified 2026-06-11 and the owner explicitly declined grouped visibility at that time. The owner's stated reasons: a file mostly in a `pub` block hollows out private-by-default, and positional grouping dictates file structure. Public-by-default has the same hollowing-out problem: every item is public unless explicitly hidden, so beginners accidentally expose implementation details. The `#scope_file` marker is a Jai-ism that is a positional grouping by another name. Reopening adds no new tradeoff the owner hasn't seen; the only new argument is beginner-ergonomics boilerplate pain from writing `pub` on every exported item. This decision does not gate any other card; it is cosmetic to the safety model.
decisions.story: I write a module with 20 functions, 18 of which are public. I'm tired of writing `pub` on every one. I want to flip the default so I only mark the two private ones.
decisions.inWild:
// current S18 — private by default, pub per item:
pub fn send(msg: String) { ... }  // exported
pub fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // exported
fn internal_retry() { ... }  // private — no annotation needed

options.name: Keep S18: private-by-default + per-item pub
options.detail: No change. Beginners never accidentally expose internals. Boilerplate grows proportionally with exports, not inversely. The safety argument is unchanged from the original ratification. The correct response to a module with 18 public items is to ask whether it has too many exports, not to flip the default.

options.name: Public-by-default + explicit private
options.detail: Every item is exported unless marked `priv` or `private`. Lowers the pub-count for export-heavy modules. Beginners accidentally expose internals; the 'safe by default' principle (I1 analog for encapsulation) is broken. The owner declined this in the S18 ratification notes.
options.code:
// proposed public-by-default:
fn send(msg: String) { ... }      // public — no annotation
fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // public — no annotation
priv fn retry() { ... }           // must opt into private

options.name: Add a file-scope marker (#scope_file / pub:)
options.detail: Keep private-by-default but allow a section marker that flips the default for everything below it in the file. Owner explicitly declined this form at S18 (positional grouping dictates file structure). It is Jai-style grouped visibility under a different name.
options.code:
// proposed section marker (owner declined this form at S18):
pub:
fn send(msg: String) { ... }      // public by position
fn connect(host: String) { ... }  // public by position
priv:
fn retry() { ... }                // private by position

comparisons.note: Go uses public-by-default via capitalization: exported identifiers start with an uppercase letter. Simple but tied to naming; no keyword for visibility.
comparisons.code:
func Send(msg string) {}     // exported (capital S)
func retry() {}              // unexported (lowercase)

comparisons.note: Rust uses private-by-default + `pub`, same as S18. The `pub(crate)` and `pub(super)` scopes are considered a strength, not a boilerplate problem.
comparisons.code:
pub fn send(msg: &str) {}
fn retry() {}  // private — no annotation

decisions.comment: We will keep private by default, per item pub, BUT allow public/private scope markers. I want a new decision open to compare syntax options for the marker though

decisions.gist: D-VISDEFAULT1 already approved a file-scope marker. This card decides the marker spelling and whether the exception is a new private keyword or the existing per-item `pub` model inverted. It is one syntax choice; it does not reopen private-by-default as the language baseline.
decisions.story: Maya owns `core.http.server`. Almost every function in the file is public API. She wants one line at the top so the file reads like an API surface, while `parse_header_fast_path` stays private without being moved to another file.

comparisons.note: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
`public`/`internal`/`private` are per declaration; no file-wide flip. Clear, but noisy for API-heavy files.
comparisons.code:
public func listen(_ port: Int) -> Server { ... }
private func parseHeaderFastPath(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Visibility is per item (`pub`, `pub(crate)`); modules give structural grouping. No file-wide public default.
comparisons.code:
pub fn listen(port: i64) -> Server { ... }
fn parse_header_fast_path(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Section labels (`@public`, `@private`) exist, but item position changes visibility. Jet already rejected that kind of positional surprise.

options.name: #PubFile + `priv` exceptions (recommended)
options.detail: One marker at the top flips this file to public-by-default. `priv` is the single exception keyword inside that file. Reads literally and keeps the exception local. Follow-up needed only to register `priv` in Syntax.rs and teaching errors.
options.code:
#PubFile

fn listen(port: Int) -> Server { ... }      // public
fn route(path: String) -> Route { ... }     // public
priv fn normalize_path(p: String) -> String { ... }

options.name: #PublicFile + `private` exceptions
options.detail: Same semantics, more English. `private` is longer and introduces a second visibility word beside `pub`, but it is self-explanatory for beginners.

options.name: Section labels `pub:` / `priv:`
options.detail: Lets one file mix public and private sections. Rejected as recommendation because item position becomes semantic: moving a helper above or below a label changes exports. That is the exact readability trap the file marker avoids.

decisions.recReason: `#PubFile` is short, direct, and consistent with Jet marker casing. `priv` is the smallest readable opposite of existing `pub`. Section labels are too position-sensitive.
decisions.title: What is the file-scope public-by-default marker, and how do private exceptions read?
decisions.explainer: S18 stays private-by-default. The approved marker is an opt-in escape for files that are mostly public API. The owner needs to pick two visible words: the file marker and the explicit-private exception inside that file. Avoid section markers here: S18 already rejected grouped visibility because moving an item across a line silently changes its export status. Also avoid `@` markers: D-ATTR1 retired `@` as an attribute prefix; Jet markers use `#PascalCase`/`#Name(...)`.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
decisions.recommendation: Use `#PubFile` with `priv` exceptions. Jet keeps private-by-default globally while giving API-heavy files a clear opt-in.

decisions.title: Stdlib-only DSL blocks: what does a checked SQL/HTML/etc. syntax island look like?
decisions.gist: Pick the spelling and limits for stdlib-owned DSL blocks.
decisions.story: Alice writes database code. Plain strings let SQL mistakes ship to runtime, but full reader macros would let any package change Jet grammar. She wants `core.db` to check SQL at build time while the language stays one fixed grammar.

options.name: PascalCase directive expression (recommended)
options.detail: A fixed stdlib whitelist in Syntax.rs: `#Sql<Row> { ... }`, `#Html { ... }`, etc. The block produces a typed value and diagnostics owned by the stdlib module.

options.name: Function call with triple-quoted text
options.detail: No new syntax; DSLs are ordinary strings checked by library functions. Simple grammar, but weaker visual affordance and less natural multi-language editing.
options.code:
query :: db.sql<UserRow>("""
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = :id
""")

options.name: Rust-style bang block
options.detail: `sql!{...}` is familiar to Rust users, but introduces a macro-looking syntax Jet otherwise rejects.

options.name: No DSL blocks
options.detail: Keep DSL validation in ordinary APIs only. Avoids syntax expansion, but gives up a high-value stdlib safety feature.
options.code: query :: db.Query<UserRow>.new("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?")?

comparisons.note: Macros commonly host SQL and HTML DSLs.
comparisons.code: sqlx::query!("SELECT id FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)

comparisons.note: String interpolation plus result builders cover some DSLs.
Type-safe builders avoid grammar mutation but are less direct for SQL.

decisions.title: Reflection read API: what does a type expose to comptime code?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need to inspect types at comptime. This decision specifies what a type exposes: field names, field types, markers, ordering, and privacy. It is the read side of the metaprogramming system; the write side (output mechanism) is D-METADERIVE1. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: The reflection API must be read-only (no mutation of type structure at comptime), privacy-respecting (private fields not visible to derives from other packages), and typed (fields expose their Jet types, not strings). The minimum to author a Serialize derive is: iterate fields, get each field's name (String) and type (Type), and read its markers. Methods, generics, and inheritance reflection can come in a later phase. The API surface must be expressible inside the existing `comptime { }` block and `$` splice system. New syntax is not required — it is a stdlib comptime API, not a new language construct. I8 is satisfied: this is the only mechanism to inspect a type at comptime.
decisions.story: In my derive_Serialize comptime function, I call `T.fields()` and get back an array of field descriptors. I loop over them, read each field's name and type, and splice in the encode call for that field. I never see private fields from other packages.

options.name: Read-only typed API: fields + types + markers (v1 minimum)
options.detail: Expose `T.fields() -> [FieldDesc]` where each FieldDesc has `.name() -> String`, `.type() -> Type`, `.markers() -> [Marker]`, and `.is_pub() -> Bool`. Private fields from other packages are invisible. No method reflection, no generic-param reflection in v1. Minimum surface to ship Serialize, Codable, ORM mapping.

options.name: Opaque types: no reflection API
options.detail: Types are opaque to comptime code; no field introspection. Derives must be hardcoded in the compiler. Blocks D-USERDERIVE1; makes this ballot moot. Listed for completeness.
options.code:
// no T.fields() available
// derive_Serialize cannot be written by a library author

options.name: Rich reflection: fields + methods + generics + annotations
options.detail: Expose method reflection (`T.methods()`), generic parameter reflection (`T.type_params()`), and arbitrary annotation inspection in v1. More powerful but much larger API surface to stabilize. Methods are not needed for any known derive use case; adds complexity before the simpler path proves out.

comparisons.note: Zig's `@typeInfo` returns a tagged union describing a type's fields, decls, and layout. Read-only; used by comptime functions to drive codegen. Close to option A.
Java's reflection is runtime-based, not comptime. It exposes fields, methods, annotations, and generics — option C's scope — but at a runtime cost and without type safety at the call site.

decisions.gist: Rich reflection is already approved. This card decides whether `T.reflect()` returns one typed handle with methods, a variant description you pattern-match, or trait-gated reflection. The goal is derive authors reading fields, methods, generics, and markers without raw AST access.
decisions.story: Victor writes a `Codable` derive. For each field he needs the Jet field name, type, visibility, default marker, and rename marker. He should not parse source text or inspect generated Rust; he should ask the reflected type handle.

comparisons.note: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.

options.name: One `TypeInfo` handle with typed metadata values (recommended)
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns `TypeInfo`. It has methods like `.fields() -> [FieldInfo]`, `.methods() -> [MethodInfo]`, `.type_params()`, `.markers()`, `.implements(Trait)`. Each info value exposes typed methods, not open dictionaries.

options.name: Variant description tree
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns a `TypeDescription` enum. Users dispatch on `.Struct`, `.Enum`, `.Primitive`, etc. This is precise, but every simple field loop starts with boilerplate.

options.name: Reflection as a trait
options.detail: Only types implementing `Reflect` expose metadata. This fits trait vocabulary, but makes reflection availability another derive/trait condition and conflicts with the goal that compiler-known type facts are always available to comptime derives.

decisions.recReason: One typed handle matches the ratified reflection direction and gives derive authors the shortest correct path. It exposes sema facts, not AST internals.
decisions.title: What shape does the typed reflection API return to comptime code?
decisions.explainer: D-METAREFLECT1 chose one reflected type handle, not AST injection. D-CTCODEGEN1 says generated code re-enters lexer/parser/sema, so reflection must expose sema-approved facts only. That means no raw parser nodes, no Rust types, and no untyped `Any` blob that makes derive authors guess. Examples use ratified Jet spellings: `comptime`, `::` bindings, `if subject == { }` style dispatch when needed.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.
decisions.recommendation: Return one typed `TypeInfo` handle. Jet can make Swift-style reflection compile-time-only and strongly typed for derives.

decisions.title: Should core reactivity (auto-updating dependents) be baked into Jet's evaluation model, or remain a library?
decisions.gist: D-REACT1 already decided: reactivity is a library/signal mechanism, not a language primitive. This reopens that decision. The question is whether dependent values should re-evaluate automatically at the language level (spreadsheet-style) or whether the reactive graph lives entirely in user space via a library. This gates every other reactive-UI card in this batch.
decisions.explainer: Amends D-REACT1. If core-semantic reactivity is adopted, it changes how assignments and data-flow work throughout the language — every cell/value becomes potentially reactive, which has massive implications for mental model, predictability, and interop with the rest of the type system. If it stays a library, reactivity is opt-in and explicit, matching I1 (safe/predictable defaults) and I8 (one canonical mechanism — the signal library). The following cards all gate on this decision: D-REACTUI1 (reactive-ui-stack), D-MOTION1 (motion-as-state), typed-styles, ownable-components. Decide this first before any of those can proceed.
decisions.story: I want to write a UI where changing a value automatically updates everything that depends on it — like a spreadsheet, but in compiled code. The question is whether that auto-update behavior is built into the language itself or comes from a library I import.

options.name: Library / signals (keep D-REACT1)
options.detail: Reactivity lives in a stdlib signals library. Dependents re-evaluate only when explicitly using signal APIs. Predictable evaluation order, no hidden re-runs, I1-safe — the reactive graph is always visible. This is the current decision.

options.name: Core evaluation semantics (reactive cells)
options.detail: Assignment to a 'cell' in a reactive scope automatically propagates to all dependents, like a spreadsheet. Elegant for UI but hides re-evaluation, makes reasoning about when code runs harder, and complicates the ownership/borrow model. Large blast radius — touches assignment semantics, closures, and codegen.

options.name: Defer
options.detail: Block all reactive-UI cards until a later milestone. Avoids committing to a design before the UI stack architecture is clearer. Delays the entire reactive-UI roadmap.

options.name: #Reactive scope marker (new — owner question 2026-06-26)
options.detail: Add a `#Reactive` compiler-blessed scope marker. Inside `#Reactive { ... }` or `#Reactive fn`, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions — the library handles the graph. Outside the marker, code is purely imperative. Desugars to a library call: `reactive_scope(|| { ... })`. Exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works. I8-safe: one way to opt into reactive behavior. No new evaluation semantics — `core.reactive` provides all the machinery. Both spellings work: `#Reactive fn update(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (function always re-runs when sources change) and `fn update { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (block-level scope). Closer to Option A (library) than Option B (core semantics) — only a scope marker is added to the language.

comparisons.note: Compiler-level reactivity: `$:` labels make assignments reactive at compile time. Elegant but it is a compiler transform, not runtime semantics — and it only applies inside Svelte components.
Library-level signals via property wrappers. Reactive but explicit opt-in — closer to option A.

decisions.gist: `#Reactive` is already the opt-in scope marker. This card decides the library vocabulary underneath it: mutable sources, derived values, and side-effect scopes. It should be one small API, not a second language.
decisions.story: Fiona writes a counter widget. `count` changes on click, `doubled` updates from `count`, and the label rerenders when either value changes. She should see exactly which values are mutable and which are derived.

comparisons.note: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.

options.name: `Signal<T>` + `Computed<T>` + `Effect` (recommended)
options.detail: Three names for three jobs. `Signal` is mutable, `Computed` is read-only derived state, `Effect` is the runtime value created by `#Reactive`. Familiar from Preact/Solid/Vue while staying explicit.

options.name: `Cell<T>` + `derived` + `watch`
options.detail: More plain-English, spreadsheet-flavored names. Good beginner readability, but `Cell` already has meanings in Rust/interior mutability and spreadsheets; `watch` is less clearly a retained effect value.
options.code:
count :: Cell(0)
doubled :: derived(() => count.get() * 2)
watch(() => label.set_text(doubled.get().to_string()))

options.name: One `Reactive<T>` value with `.map()` / `.effect()`
options.detail: Fewer type names, but blurs mutable source, derived value, and effect lifetime. Harder diagnostics because every misuse is on one overloaded concept.
options.code:
count :: Reactive(0)
doubled :: count.map((n: Int) => n * 2)
doubled.effect((n: Int) => label.set_text(n.to_string()))

decisions.recReason: Three concrete types make dependency graph roles visible and keep diagnostics simple. `#Reactive` remains the only reactive syntax; the library handles graph mechanics.
decisions.title: What are the primitive `core.reactive` types under `#Reactive`?
decisions.explainer: Reactive code has three jobs: hold changing state, compute a value from other reactive reads, and rerun an effect when dependencies change. `#Reactive { }` should desugar to the effect job only; ordinary library types do the rest. Avoid syntax-shaped examples like `let` or operator lambdas that Jet has not ratified. This card is API naming, not new syntax.
decisions.bestCurrent: SolidJS: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.
decisions.recommendation: Use `Signal<T>`, `Computed<T>`, and `Effect`. Jet should adopt the clearest fine-grained reactive triad and let `#Reactive` wire capture.

decisions.title: Should Jet define a render-target backend-trait seam now, before any concrete UI backend exists?
decisions.gist: A render-target abstraction would let one UI description compile to web, native, embedded, or TUI by swapping a backend trait. The question is whether to define that seam now (before backends exist), build one target first and generalize later, or defer entirely. Research recommends deciding the seam early to avoid lock-in.
decisions.explainer: This is prerequisite architecture for D-REACTUI1. If the seam is wrong, migrating later forces breaking changes to every UI-layer API. Defining the trait shape now does not require implementing any backend — just agreeing on what a backend must provide (layout, paint, event dispatch). Gated on D-REACTCORE1 for the reactive-event model. Touches the typed-styles card (styles must be expressible in backend-agnostic terms). Bundle-risk: each target (web/WASM, native/GPU, embedded/framebuffer, TUI/ANSI) has very different constraints — the seam must be thin enough to not over-specify.
decisions.story: I want to write a UI once and ship it to the web, desktop, and terminal without rewriting the view layer. That means the core UI logic can't assume any one rendering backend.

options.name: Define the backend-trait seam now
options.detail: Agree on the minimum backend trait (layout, paint, event) in the stdlib. No backend needs to be implemented yet. Locks in the abstraction boundary early so all higher-level UI work builds against it. Cost: requires a design round before any UI code ships.

options.name: Build one target first, generalize later
options.detail: Pick the most important target (web/WASM), ship it, then extract the abstraction. Faster initial progress but likely forces breaking changes when generalizing. Proven pattern for early-stage projects; risky if the first target's constraints contaminate the API.

options.name: Defer — UI backends post-v1
options.detail: No render-target decision until after v1. Keeps scope tight. Entire reactive-UI stack deferred.
options.code: // No UI framework in Jet v1; users bring their own.

comparisons.note: Defines a thin `RenderObject` seam early; backends (Skia, Impeller, web-canvas) swap beneath it. The seam was designed before all targets existed and held up well.
TUI-only; no backend abstraction. Works for terminals but cannot generalize to GUI without a full rewrite.

decisions.gist: D-RENDERTGT1 approved a backend seam. This card decides the minimum trait between Jet UI and platform renderers: layout phases, event delivery, and paint calls. It is internal API shape, not user syntax.
decisions.story: Sophie is implementing the web backend for Jet's UI. She needs to implement the Backend trait. She wants to know: what methods does she have to implement, what data types do they pass around, and how do events flow back to Jet code?

comparisons.note: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.

options.name: Three-phase measure-layout-paint trait (recommended)
options.detail: Backend trait has three required methods: measure(node, constraint) -> Size (phase 1), layout(node, frame) (phase 2, sets final positions), paint(node, painter) (phase 3, draws to backend surface). Events flow in via a separate on_event(event) method. This is the universal model used by Flutter, SwiftUI internals, and Yoga.

options.name: Two-phase layout-paint trait (simplified)
options.detail: Combine measure+layout into a single layout(node, available: Size) -> Rect phase. Simpler to implement but less powerful: intrinsic size information is lost after layout, making some responsive layouts impossible. Better for simple backends (TUI, fixed-size targets), worse for CSS-flexbox-style adaptive layouts.

options.name: Event-driven reactive trait
options.detail: Backend is fully event-driven: the UI framework pushes layout/paint requests as events to the backend, and the backend responds. No synchronous method calls. Aligns with async runtime and signal model but introduces significant complexity in the protocol — backends must process events in order and cannot ask the framework questions synchronously.

decisions.recReason: Three-phase is the proven industry model (Flutter, Yoga, SwiftUI internals). Backends can implement C (simplified) on top of A by merging measure+layout, but A cannot be recovered from B. The measure phase is essential for intrinsic-size-aware layout (text reflow, content-sized containers).
decisions.explainer: Group this with layout/reactive UI. The owner is choosing architectural contract, not syntax. The trait must support native widgets, browser DOM, and future custom renderers without leaking one platform into the Jet UI model.
decisions.bestCurrent: Flutter: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.
decisions.recommendation: Use a three-phase measure-layout-paint trait. Jet gets Flutter-grade backend portability while keeping layout decisions explicit and testable.

decisions.title: How should Jet unify motion and authored animation while preserving beginner magic and expert timeline control?
decisions.gist: D-MOTION1 conflates two design decisions with different epoch timelines, different users, and unresolved architectural questions between them: (1) the signal/time/value primitive (`core.motion`, ready for E3 design) and (2) the authored scene/timeline layer (`core.animation`, blocked on execution-model and export-pipeline questions). The ballot should either split these or explicitly resolve the three open design holes before implementation: the `SpringSignal<T>` type gap with D-SIGNAL1, the reactive-vs-deterministic execution boundary, and the VideoBackend export hook absent from the ratified Backend trait.
decisions.explainer: Owner questions answered: motion and animation should be one layered system, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the signal/time/value primitive connected to reactivity and the M:N task clock. `core.animation` is a Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer on top: objects, transformations, keyframes, camera/render concepts, updaters, and timeline sequencing. Adversarial pass: two layers can drift. Patch: one clock, one scheduler integration, one render-target seam; `core.animation` only produces motion tracks/render commands that `core.motion` drives.
decisions.story: Maya builds a dashboard and gets a spring transition by changing state. Later she records a product explainer: the same values become timeline tracks with named beats, camera moves, transforms, and frame-accurate export. She does not switch languages or abandon the reactive UI model.
decisions.inWild:
state :: Signal.new(false)
opacity :: motion.spring(state.map((on) => on ? 1.0 : 0.0))

scene :: animation.scene {
    title :: Text("Jet")
    play title.write(duration: 0.6)
    play title.move_to(x: 0, y: 2).ease(.out_cubic)
    wait(seconds: 0.25)
}
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: How does this interplay with the planned async/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
Agent answer: Two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing — animations are derived signals over a Clock signal, run on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems — a programmatic generator of core.motion values. `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes.

Owner Q: Please update to support a cohesive vision of both animation & motion with magic out of the box to beginners and full control for experts.
Agent answer: Updated. New recommendation A: core.motion as signal/time/value primitive, core.animation as Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer on top. One clock, one scheduler integration, one render-target seam; core.animation only produces motion tracks and render commands.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): Type gap: `motion.spring()` cannot be `Computed<T>` (pure/stateless; springs carry velocity across frames) nor plain `Signal<T>` — it is a new reactive primitive (SpringSignal<T>) requiring a named decision or I8 risk. Execution boundary: reactive evaluation is lazy/pull; deterministic video rendering is push-based — the "one clock" patch requires specifying the Clock type, how animation scenes tick it forward in export vs real-time mode, and how the layout engine's synchronous cycle is triggered by async motion-value updates. Backend: the ratified Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2=A) has no export/frame-capture hook; `core.animation` export implies a VideoBackend, two rendering paths. `Signal.new()` in examples conflicts with D-SIGNAL1's ratified constructor form `Signal(0)`.

options.name: `core.motion` in E3 (signal/time layer); raise D-ANIMATION1 for scene/timeline (recommended)
options.detail: Ship core.motion in Epoch 3 alongside the reactive UI stack: springs (SpringSignal<T> — a new reactive primitive with internal physics state subscribed to a source signal), tweens, easing, interpolation, a Clock signal (advanced by the M:N scheduler each frame), and reactive delivery to layout properties. Beginners get spring transitions out of the box. The designed design of `core.animation` (scenes, timelines, keyframes, camera, video export) is deferred to a separate D-ANIMATION1 ballot raised immediately, gated on: (a) real renderer experience from D-RENDERTGT2, (b) the reactive-vs-deterministic execution boundary resolved (reactive is lazy/pull; video rendering is push-based), (c) VideoBackend export hook added to the ratified Backend trait. Note: fix `Signal.new()` in all examples to `Signal(0)` per D-SIGNAL1's ratified constructor form.

options.name: Full layered motion + animation together (blocked on two sub-ballots)
options.detail: core.motion as signal/time layer AND core.animation as Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer in one decision. Blocked: requires D-SPRINGVAL1 (SpringSignal<T> reactive type definition) and D-SCENEBLOCK1 (animation scene DSL surface — `play`/`wait` as library functions vs keywords) to exist as ballot cards before implementation. The VideoBackend export hook is absent from the ratified Backend trait. Choose this only if those two sub-ballots are raised and ratified first.

options.name: Defer both core.motion and core.animation to Epoch 6
options.detail: No motion primitives in the current UI stack. Static/reactive UI only; revisit a unified motion/animation system in Epoch 6 with real renderer experience. Only appropriate if the UI stack is lower priority than other E3 work. Beginners need manual reactive workarounds for UI transitions until E6.

comparisons.note: Best educational-animation ergonomics: scene/object/animation building blocks, rich transformations, timeline control, and updaters.
Best app-motion mental model: state changes drive animation with minimal ceremony, but deep timeline authoring is not the core strength.
Great declarative motion values and transforms for app UI, less complete as a deterministic educational/video scene system.

decisions.bestCurrent: SwiftUI: SwiftUI treats animation as state changes over time, so views derive frames from reactive state.
decisions.recommendation: Ship `core.motion` in E3 as the signal/time/value layer; raise D-ANIMATION1 as a separate ballot for scene/timeline/export (Option A). Option B (full layered system) is blocked on D-SPRINGVAL1 and D-SCENEBLOCK1 sub-ballots that don't exist yet.
