decisions.title: U18 follow-up — canonical module body: module env.dev { fields } or ns.path: Type contributions?
decisions.gist: Vision and every U11–U19 ballot example write module env.dev { packages: [...] } — namespace in the declaration name, fields bare. Shipped code parses module dev { env.dev: Env.{ ... } } — plain name, namespaced typed contributions inside. TWONAMES1 ratified filenames/commands, not this grammar. Pick the one canonical form (I8).
decisions.explainer: Two grammars exist for the same semantic job. The shipped form (module <name> { ns.path: Type.{ fields } }) lets one module contribute to several namespaces and carries the U5 merge machinery; it is what ModuleEval evaluates today. The vision form (module env.dev { fields }) is what the owner ratified examples in six ballots show: the namespace IS the module path, fields sit bare, and discovery-by-declaration (the U18 amendment's find() acceptance test) reads the role straight off the declaration name. I8 says one way to mean it: both forms surviving as equals is the rejected outcome. Note the U18 amendment ('role modules … discovered by declaration') reads most naturally against form A, where the declaration name itself is the role.
decisions.story: Priya reads the U12 ballot, copies module env.dev { services: { postgres: Service.{} } } into her repo, and runs jet dev. Under A it works verbatim. Under B she gets a teaching error showing the module dev { env.dev: Env.{ ... } } wrapping — and learns the docs' own examples don't parse.
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md, 'Module body sugar' ambiguity flagged at hand-off; evaluator at crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/ModuleEval/ (form B is what tests exercise today), discovery at PackageManifest/Discovery.rs. Adversarial notes: (A) matches every owner-ratified worked example verbatim and makes the U18 find()-by-declaration test read the role off the module name; migration = parser accepts dotted module names as namespace roles + a teaching error rewrites form B; multi-namespace authors write two modules (module env.dev + module system.laptop) — arguably clearer, loses one-module-many-contributions. Contribution machinery survives underneath: env.dev: Env.{} becomes the desugared form of module env.dev {}. (B) zero code motion, keeps one module contributing to many namespaces, but every ratified U11–U19 example is then wrong-as-written and needs an owner-visible errata sweep — the docs teaching a spelling the parser rejects is the worst beginner outcome available here. (C) both-legal is listed for completeness and fails I8's bar on its face: two spellings for the same semantic job, doubled docs, doubled formatter/round-trip surface, and every future example forced to pick a dialect. Formatter round-trip + fmt STABILITY test required for whichever wins (house rule).

options.name: Canonical: module env.dev { fields } (vision/ballot form)
options.detail: Namespace is the declaration name; fields sit bare; form B becomes a teaching error that names the rewrite. Matches all ratified examples and the U18 discovery-by-declaration amendment; multi-namespace files write one module per role.

options.name: Canonical: ns.path: Type.{ } contributions (shipped form)
options.detail: Keep the evaluator as-is; one module may contribute to several namespaces; U5 merge machinery untouched. Every ratified U11–U19 worked example must be errata'd to the wrapped spelling — docs and ballots currently teach a form the parser would reject.

options.name: Both legal (sugar + desugared) — fails the I8 bar
options.detail: module env.dev { fields } desugars to the contribution form; both parse forever. Listed for completeness: two spellings for one semantic job, doubled formatter/docs/teaching surface — exactly the second-feature-same-job shape I8 exists to reject.

comparisons.note: One attrset grammar for every module — but roles live in option paths, not declaration names; the discovery-by-name idea A ratifies is the thing Nix lacks.
mod a::b { } is illegal — a module declares one path segment; Rust chose the B-shaped restriction and nobody writes dotted module names.
Block label carries the role (resource "aws_instance" "web") — the A shape: the declaration head states what the block is.

decisions.title: U18 follow-up — engine dispatch scope for this card: in-process crate or git-style exec now?
decisions.gist: TWONAMES1 prose says jet 'dispatches unknown verbs to jetpack/jetos by name, git-style, zero coupling — the compiler stays fully standalone'. Today Jetpack is a linked crate (jet::Jetpack::run, in-process). Decide whether U11–U19 ride the linked path with separation as a later rung, or binary separation lands first.
decisions.explainer: The user-facing contract (one command, verbs resolve against declared modules) is identical either way — this is an architecture-sequencing call, not syntax. Today Source/main.rs already has both mechanisms: jet env calls the linked crate in-process, and a git-style external jet-<cmd> PATH fallback exists (find_external, D-DX5). Full separation means the compiler binary stops linking jet-driver's Jetpack module and execs a jetpack binary for every engine verb: a real seam move (error-rendering, exit codes, --json plumbing, test harness all cross a process boundary) that touches every verb this card adds. The ratified text names the end state; it does not date it.
decisions.story: Nate types jet dev. Under A, nothing observable changes now — the verb runs in-process, fast, one binary to ship — and a later card moves the seam. Under B, jet execs jetpack dev; the compiler binary provably contains no package-manager code, and deleting the jetpack binary leaves a still-working compiler — the standalone claim is checkable today.
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U18 — the two-names rename', step 5 ('full … separation is a larger architectural item — do NOT block U11–U19 on binary separation'), and the third hand-off ambiguity. Adversarial notes: (A) matches the plan as written; all new verbs (services/secrets/image/switch/push/bridge/lock/config) route through the existing in-process dispatch; diagnostics stay one rendering path; the one-way arrow jetos->jetpack->jet holds at the module level even while linked; cost — 'the compiler stays fully standalone' remains a promise, not a property, and every verb added now is a verb to move later. (B) makes the ratified claim true immediately and forces the process-boundary contract (exit codes, --json diagnostics over the seam, engine-version skew handling) to be designed once, before eight new verbs pile onto the wrong side; cost — it front-loads a seam move onto the critical path of every U11–U19 gate, and the trust gate (U19) + service supervisor (U12) then need their first implementations written against the cross-process contract. Repo already builds two binaries (jet + jetpack per Cargo [[bin]]), so B is a wiring+contract change, not a new build system. Difficulty is not a factor (house rule); the question is purely which order produces the better seam.

options.name: In-process linked crate now; binary separation as its own later card
options.detail: All U11–U19 verbs ride jet::Jetpack::run as jet env does today; the D-DX5 jet-<cmd> PATH fallback stays for third parties. Separation becomes a named follow-on card with its own contract design. One diagnostics path, no cross-process plumbing in this card.
options.code:
// Source/main.rs — extend the existing arm:
"services" | "secrets" | "image" | "switch" | "push" | "bridge" =>
    exit(jet::Jetpack::run(raw[1..].to_vec())),

$ jet services logs postgres   # in-process, one binary shipped

options.name: Git-style exec separation now, before new verbs land
options.detail: Compiler drops the Jetpack linkage; engine verbs exec the jetpack binary by name (both binaries already build). The standalone claim becomes checkable; the process-boundary contract (exit codes, --json diagnostics, version skew) is designed once, first — on the critical path of every gate in this card.

comparisons.note: External subcommand dispatch by binary name — the mechanism the ratified text names, and what D-DX5 already implements for third-party jet-<cmd>.
cargo links its ops crates in-process and still fronts rustc as a separate binary — the A shape: one UX, seam moved where it pays.
Plugin verbs exec kubectl-<name> from PATH; core verbs stay linked — a proven hybrid identical to A + D-DX5 fallback.

decisions.explainer: Entering an environment and running project code are different intents with different risk. jet env [name] realizes the environment (base env.* plus an optional named overlay) and opens a shell — no project function ever runs from env entry. jet dev is the explicit execution verb: it realizes env(base + env.dev) because running needs the toolchain anyway, then runs fn dev() (fallback: fn run under watch/reload). jet test / jet build use env.test / env.build the same way. The danger direction is closed: code runs only when a verb whose MEANING is "run code" is typed.
decisions.story: Ken types jet dev. Postgres comes up seeded, the wasm toolchain is on PATH, fn dev() starts the server with hot reload — one command, and the same command works identically on his teammate's machine. In CI, jet test gets the env.test overlay with a throwaway database, no YAML.
decisions.detail: Owner direction 2026-07-01: entering a dev env is often just "give me the tools to work" — autorunning project functions from an entry verb is dangerous (clone untrusted repo, enter env, project code executes). Split ratifies the intent boundary. Residual hole closed with it: on_enter hooks and service definitions are also project-authored code — first jet env in a fresh repo shows a trust summary (hooks, services, sources) and requires confirmation, direnv-allow style; the grant is recorded and re-prompted when the env definition changes hash. jet dev inside an untrusted repo is explicitly running its code — that is the user's stated intent, no gate. Option A (auto-compose entry+run under one verb) kept below for the record; superseded by D. Owner addition 2026-07-01: --trust flag bypasses the gate in one shot (CI/scripts/known sources) and records the grant; expert/org tier: jet config trust add <pattern> pre-trusts sources by pattern so matching repos never prompt.

comparisons.note: processes + enterShell + scripts approximate this composition with three concepts; env.<verb> is one.
npm run dev — entry only, environment is your problem; the half-answer everyone has.
Solves enter-on-cd only; composition with a dev process is manual.

decisions.title: U19 — What exactly does jet dev do? (env.dev module vs fn dev entry)
decisions.gist: Owner-refined split: jet env enters the shell (tools only — NEVER executes project functions); jet dev explicitly runs fn dev() inside env(base + env.dev). Named env.<verb> overlays stay.

options.name: Compose: env overlay + entry fn, one verb
options.detail: jet dev = env(base+dev) -> services -> fn dev. env.<verb> generalizes to test/build. jet enter for shell-only.
options.code:

$ jet enter dev

options.name: Separate: jet dev runs only fn dev; environments need jet enter first
options.detail: No composition magic; every session is two commands and CI scripts chain them — the glue Jet exists to delete.
options.code:
$ jet enter
$ jet dev      # two steps, every time

options.name: Compose, but rename the env overlay (env.local/env.serve) to avoid the double "dev"
options.detail: Same semantics as A with distinct names; costs the neat env.<verb> generalization symmetry.
options.code:
module env.local { ... }
$ jet dev   # env(base+local) -> fn dev

options.name: jet env enters (no execution) / jet dev runs fn dev inside env (recommended — owner direction)
options.detail: jet env [name]: shell with base env or named overlay; never runs project fns; first-entry trust gate covers hooks/services. jet dev/test/build: explicit execution verbs, each inside env(base + env.<verb>) when declared.
options.code:

$ jet env dev            # shell with the dev overlay — still nothing runs
$ jet dev                # EXPLICIT: env(base+dev) -> services -> fn dev()
$ jet test               # env(base+test) -> #test items

$ cd fresh-clone && jet env
// trust gate: env.dev declares 2 services, 1 on_enter hook, 3 sources
//   review: jet env --show   allow: jet env --trust
$ jet env --trust        # bypass the prompt when you trust the source
$ jet config trust add github.com/acme/*   # org tier: pattern-trusted sources, no prompts

decisions.title: U20 — How does jetpack define and run refs with no pkg.jet, no flake, no nixpkgs equivalent? (ad-hoc adapters)
decisions.gist: Pick the escape hatch for using any repo, release tarball, or binary as a normal package: adapter recipes over fetched bytes, a new provider kind, or requiring upstream metadata.
decisions.explainer: Today jetpack has two clean paths: a source with pkg.jet realizes through the core provider; a source with Nix packaging realizes through the bridge. The missing path is the normal internet — a GitHub repo with only a Makefile, a release tarball with a binary, a Go/Cargo/npm project with no flake, a private tool that will never publish Jet metadata. The proposal: adapter packages — a typed recipe that turns already-fetched bytes into a normal Pkg. Providers answer "where do the bytes come from"; adapters answer "how do these bytes become a package output". U9 provider inference stays intact; no via: marker. Curated recipe families (prebuilt, copy, cargo, go, node, cmake/make) are sugar over one expert Recipe.build(fn(BuildContext)); autodetect drafts recipes from read-only probes and never executes upstream code; lock identity = source hash + recipe text hash + helper version + platform + declared tool deps + output hash.
decisions.story: Walter wants the codex CLI in his dev env. There is no pkg.jet upstream, the community flake is three versions stale, and nixpkgs lags the vendor by weeks. Nix's answer is "fork the repo and write a derivation." Walter types jet add github@openai/codex --adapt, reviews the drafted three-line recipe, and has the vendor's release from two days ago on PATH — locked, reproducible, no fork.
decisions.detail: Full proposal folded into docs/plans/epoch-5/README.md (§ Open / Proposed) from ad-hoc-adapters.md (2026-07-02). Safety contract regardless of option: probe is read-only (file names, manifests, release metadata — no upstream script runs); network during build denied except locked fetch(url, sha256:); ambient commands only through BuildContext with effect provenance in .jet/lock; outputs install only under the package output root; build tools are Pkg deps, never host /usr/bin. First build passes the U19 trust gate. Exact constructor names (Pkg.adapt, Recipe.*) are follow-up ballot surface; this ballot decides the model. New E12xx diagnostics: no usable metadata, ambiguous autodetect, missing declared bin, unpinned binary URL, undeclared build tool, ambient network/exec denied — each fix names the next command or field.

options.name: Adapter packages as Pkg values (recommended)
options.detail: One package mechanism; adapters are recipes, not providers; inline in env.* or named in pkg.jet, same IR and lock path. jet add <ref> --adapt drafts a recipe from a read-only probe.
options.code:
$ jet run github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d
Error [E1240]: `github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d` has no Jet package or Nix flake
 Why: jetpack needs package metadata or an adapter recipe before it can run a repo
 Fix: run `jet add github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d --adapt` to draft one

$ jet add github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d --adapt
  detected: CMake project, binary candidate `weirdctl`
  recipe:   cmake + ninja, install `build/weirdctl`
  save to:  module env.dev in toolchain.jet? [Y/n] y
✓ locked (source hash + recipe hash + output hash)

options.name: New provider kind (adapter@ / via: adapter)
options.detail: A provider that owns both fetching and realizing. Leaks policy back into refs — the exact thing U9 dissolved; every ref grows a second axis and inference weakens.

options.name: Require upstream metadata
options.detail: Every repo must add pkg.jet or a flake before jetpack can touch it. Kills "use anything now"; users fork repos to add metadata — the Nix wall, restated.
options.code:
$ jet add github@acme/weirdctl
Error: no pkg.jet in source
 Fix: ask upstream to adopt Jet, or fork and add pkg.jet   // <- the wall

comparisons.note: Writing a derivation + often forking the repo; the exact wall this removes.
Formula DSL in a separate tap repo; adapters keep the recipe at the call site.

class Weirdctl < Formula

decisions.title: What are the exact spellings for adapter packages and build recipes? (the naming ballot D-JPK-ADAPTER1 deferred)
decisions.gist: Name the adapter constructor and the recipe builders that turn fetched bytes into a package — the surface a user types to package any repo, tarball, or binary.
decisions.explainer: D-JPK-ADAPTER1=A ratified the mechanism (adapters are Pkg values; recipes over fetched bytes; read-only probe; sandboxed build) but explicitly left the constructor and recipe spellings as a follow-up ballot. The vision doc uses Pkg.adapt(...) and Recipe.build/prebuilt/copy; nothing binds those names yet. This is the user-facing surface for the escape hatch, so it should read naturally and stay consistent with dot-construction (D-DOTCTOR1: T.{ } / .{ } are the only struct-literal spellings).
decisions.story: Ruth, a platform engineer, needs a niche CLI (`weirdctl`) that has no pkg.jet, no flake, and isn't in nixpkgs. She reaches for the adapter. Whatever we name it is the first thing she types and the thing she'll search the docs for — it has to be obvious and hard to misspell.
decisions.detail: Two names to fix: the adapter constructor and the recipe family (curated: prebuilt, copy, cargo, go, node, cmake, make; expert: the fn(BuildContext) form). Rank on consistency with the one ratified construction mechanism (D-DOTCTOR1 dot-construction), one-path (I8), beginner learnability, and how naturally it reads at a call site.

options.name: Pkg.adapt(...) + Recipe.* (recommended — the shipped-vision spelling)
options.detail: Adapter is a named constructor on Pkg; recipes are a Recipe family. Verb-shaped (adapt, build, copy) reads as an action; consistent with core.* dot paths and dot-construction. `jet add <ref> --adapt` drafts one.
options.code:
packages: [ Pkg.adapt(name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: Recipe.cargo) ]

// typo:
packages: [ Pkg.adap(name: ...) ]
error[E12xx]: no constructor `Pkg.adap`
  fix: did you mean `Pkg.adapt`? (packages an external source with a recipe)

options.name: Adapter.{ ... } record + Recipe.*
options.detail: Adapter is a dot-construction record literal (maximally consistent with D-DOTCTOR1 — it looks exactly like every other Jet value). Recipe family unchanged. Reads as data rather than an action.
options.code:
packages: [ Adapter.{ name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: Recipe.cargo } ]

// typo:
packages: [ Adaptor.{ ... } ]
error[E12xx]: unknown type `Adaptor`
  fix: did you mean `Adapter`? (a package built from an external source)

options.name: Bare adapt(...) function + recipe.*
options.detail: A free function, no namespace prefix — shortest to type. Costs the discoverability that a Pkg./Recipe. prefix gives (no completion anchor) and reads less clearly next to typed package values.
options.code: packages: [ adapt(name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: recipe.cargo) ]

options.name: Pkg.from(...) + Build.*
options.detail: Frames it as 'a package from a source' with a Build.* recipe family. 'from' is gentle but vague (from what? already implied by source:); 'Build' collides conceptually with fn build / D-BUILDSCOPE1.
options.code: packages: [ Pkg.from(source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, build: Build.cmake) ]

comparisons.note: The adapter equivalents are named by builder function — stdenv.mkDerivation, buildRustPackage, buildGoModule. Verb-ish builder names, like Recipe.cargo/go.
A formula is a class with a declarative body and a verb-y `install do ... end` block — mirrors Pkg.adapt + Recipe.build(fn).
comparisons.code:
class Weirdctl < Formula
  def install; system "cmake", "."; end
end

comparisons.note: Rules are verb-shaped functions (rust_binary, cc_library) — reinforces that the recipe family reads best as named actions.

decisions.rec: A — Pkg.adapt reads as the action a user takes, anchors editor completion under Pkg./Recipe., stays consistent with core.* dot paths, and matches the ratified vision so no fixtures need re-spelling; the Recipe.* family names each build strategy as a verb the way Nix/Bazel builders do.
decisions.recommendation: A — Pkg.adapt reads as the action a user takes, anchors editor completion under Pkg./Recipe., stays consistent with core.* dot paths, and matches the ratified vision so no fixtures need re-spelling; the Recipe.* family names each build strategy as a verb the way Nix/Bazel builders do.

decisions.title: U21 — How does a dependency track a vendor's releases? (channel refs + jet update / jet outdated)
decisions.gist: Decide how "give me the latest from this vendor" is spelled and when it resolves: channel refs updated only by jet update, floating resolution, an update-only verb with no syntax, or a separate channels module.
decisions.explainer: Adapters and deps pin an exact rev — right for reproducibility, but nothing yet says how a ref FOLLOWS a vendor. Without a tracking story, "use the latest directly from any vendor" is a one-time snapshot: the codex adapter written today serves v0.48.2 forever until someone hand-edits the rev. The invariant every option must keep: the lockfile stays exact, so jet env / jet build never surprise-upgrade; the question is only where update INTENT lives and which verb moves the pin.
decisions.story: Doris added the codex CLI via an adapter last month at v0.48.2. The vendor ships weekly; v0.50.1 fixes the bug she reported. She should not have to visit the vendor's releases page, copy a tag, and edit a ref by hand — she types jet update codex, reviews the bump, commits the lock. Her teammates stay on v0.48.2 until that commit lands.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (jetpack-vision walkthrough, gap 2). Applies to every source-ref position: adapters, deps on git sources, jet run <ref>, script-dep use lines (U11). Channel grammar if ratified: #latest (newest release/tag), #v0.x (semver mask over tags), #main (branch head — discouraged, allowed). Resolution happens ONLY in jet update (and first add); lock records the exact rev + channel that produced it. jet outdated is read-only: compares locked revs against channels and registries, prints available bumps, changes nothing. CI never resolves channels — a channel ref with no lock entry is an error, not a silent fetch of newest.

options.name: Channel refs, resolved only by jet update (recommended)
options.detail: Intent is declared where the dep is declared: #latest / #v0.x / #main on any source ref. jet update [pkg] re-resolves channels and moves the lock; jet outdated reports; realize verbs never resolve.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#latest

$ jet update codex
  codex  v0.48.2 → v0.50.1  (github@openai/codex, released 3h ago)
  lock updated · teammates get 0.50.1 on next `jet env` after commit

$ jet outdated
  codex     v0.50.1 → v0.51.0   github releases
  textkit   1.4.2   → 1.5.0     jet registry

options.name: Floating resolution at realize time
options.detail: jet env / jet run resolve #latest on every entry. Maximally fresh, but two machines realize different envs from the same commit — breaks the reproducibility promise that is the whole point.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#latest

$ jet env        # Monday: fetches v0.50.1
$ jet env        # Friday, teammate: fetches v0.51.0  ← same commit, different env

options.name: No channel syntax; jet update bumps exact pins
options.detail: Refs are always exact. jet update <pkg> finds the newest release/tag and rewrites the pinned rev in source. Smallest surface, but tracking intent lives nowhere: update cannot know "stay on v0.x" vs "jump majors", and the tool edits the user's .jet files.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#v0.48.2   // always exact

$ jet update codex
  codex v0.48.2 → v1.0.0   ← wanted to stay on v0.x; nowhere to say so
  rewrote toolchain.jet:6

options.name: Separate channels module
options.detail: Refs stay exact; a module channels { } block maps names to policies. Splits one fact across two places — the reader of the dep cannot see it tracks the vendor without hunting for the channels block (anti-repetition pressure says no).

comparisons.note: Ranges resolve at update time; Cargo.lock pins. The model users already trust — but only for registry deps, not arbitrary vendors.
Inputs float to branch head; nix flake update moves flake.lock. No release/semver awareness — you track main or a hand-pinned tag.
"latest" dist-tag plus package-lock; the two-file split confuses beginners but the resolve-at-update-only rule is right.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U23 — What happens on a machine without Nix? (bridge fallback + the no-Nix diagnostic)
decisions.gist: Define the exact experience when a ref needs the Nix bridge on a Nix-less machine: degrade gracefully with a precise diagnostic, offer to install Nix, or require Nix outright.
decisions.explainer: U16's bridge and the owner-approved native-deps stopgap (nixpkgs for C libs/BLAS) both assume Nix is installed. Nothing defines the other machine: a Windows-adjacent laptop, a fresh VM, a locked-down CI runner. What must be true regardless: jet-registry deps, core-provider builds, and adapters with prebuilt/copy recipes need no Nix — most of the vendor-tool story works on a bare machine. This ballot decides what the nixpkgs@-shaped hole says and does, and doubles as the exit-ramp marker: every adapter written is one fewer nixpkgs dependency, and this diagnostic is where users see the seam shrink.
decisions.story: Hank clones his team's repo onto a fresh Fedora laptop — no Nix, never heard of it. jet env realizes fourteen packages fine, then hits default.postgres_16, which today rides the nixpkgs stopgap. What Hank reads next decides whether his first jetpack hour feels like a product or like a stack of shims.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 4). Owner precedent: nixpkgs approved as native-deps stopgap IF the user has Nix, with an explicit requirement that non-Nix users get a clear message — this ballot writes that message. Whatever the option, the diagnostic must (a) name exactly which packages needed the bridge, (b) never block the packages that did not, (c) point at the narrowest fix. Partial realization semantics: env enters with realized packages on PATH and lists the holes, or refuses atomically — the option code blocks show the recommended shape; atomic-vs-partial can be sub-balloted if the owner wants it separate.

options.name: Graceful degrade + precise diagnostic (recommended)
options.detail: Everything Nix-free realizes; bridge-needing packages fail with one E12xx naming them, the why, and both fixes (install Nix, or switch to an adapter/core path). CI-friendly: --json lists the holes.
options.code:
$ jet env
✓ 14 of 16 packages realized
Error [E1252]: 2 packages need the Nix bridge, and Nix is not installed
 Why: `postgres_16`, `openblas` currently realize through nixpkgs on this platform
 Fix: install Nix (https://jet.dev/nix-bridge), or replace with an adapter:
      `jet add postgres --adapt` can draft a prebuilt recipe from postgresql.org

options.name: Offer to install Nix inline
options.detail: Same detection, plus jetpack offers a pinned, single-user Nix install on the spot. One keypress from working — but jetpack now owns a root-touching installer for a third-party system, its failure modes, and its corp-policy fights.
options.code:
$ jet env
2 packages need the Nix bridge. Install Nix now (single-user, ~/.nix)? [y/N] y
downloading nix 2.24.1 (pinned, checksum verified)...
✓ bridge ready · resuming realization

options.name: Require Nix for any bridge-era project
options.detail: jetpack refuses to realize an env containing any nixpkgs-path package until Nix exists. Honest about the dependency, but punishes the 14 packages that were fine and makes jetpack read as a Nix frontend — the opposite of the pitch.
options.code:
$ jet env
Error: this project requires Nix (2 packages realize via nixpkgs)
 Fix: install Nix, then re-run `jet env`
^ the 14 Nix-free packages are hostage

comparisons.note: The null case: no Nix, no anything. Install is a curl|bash that creates /nix and a daemon — famously heavy on corp machines.
Gold standard for a toolchain that self-bootstraps without a system package manager; jetpack's core provider should feel like this.
comparisons.code: $ rustup target add wasm32-wasi   # no apt, no brew, just works

comparisons.note: Formulae simply fail on Linux-without-brew; no graceful subset. The shape to avoid.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U26 — Package & option discovery: jet search / jet info / LSP completions in env modules
decisions.gist: Decide the discovery surface: how users find package names, versions, and typed options — full CLI + in-editor completions, CLI only, or a web index.
decisions.explainer: Nix discovery is grep-shaped: `nix search` is slow and fuzzy, NixOS options live on a separate website, and the standard workflow is search.nixos.org in a browser tab next to the editor. Jet's env modules are typed — that already paid for a better answer: the checker knows every source, package, version set, and Service/option field, so discovery can live where the user is typing. This is the Blueprint north star cashed in for environments: completing default.postgres_16 from a typo, hovering a Service field for its docs and default, and a fast local jet search — no browser, no second language, no website lag behind reality.
decisions.story: Ruth needs Postgres and image tooling in her env. In Nix she has three browser tabs: search.nixos.org for the attr name, the options site for service flags, a blog post for the overlay incantation. In Jet she types default.post, the editor completes postgres_16 and postgres_17, hover shows versions and platforms, and Service.{ completes its typed fields with defaults inline. She never leaves the file.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 2). Feeds on existing machinery: E09xx nearest-name diagnostics already do fuzzy matching; the LSP is an existing epoch track; sources (default/unstable/registry) are typed values with enumerable members. Contract questions the option decides: search index is local and offline (synced with lock/provider metadata, so results match what would actually resolve — never a stale web index); `jet info <pkg>` shows versions, platforms, source, and typed options with defaults; completions and hover work in any .jet file inside module env/system/image blocks. Registry-side full-text search can ride the registry track later without changing this surface.

options.name: Full surface: jet search + jet info + LSP completions/hover (recommended)
options.detail: Fast local index for the CLI pair; LSP completes package names after source dots and typed option fields inside Service/module bodies, hover shows docs/defaults/platforms. One source of truth: the same provider metadata the resolver uses.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres
  default.postgres_16    16.4   linux, macos, windows
  default.postgres_17    17.2   linux, macos, windows
  unstable.postgres_18   18.0b  linux

$ jet info default.postgres_16
  versions: 16.0–16.4 · service options: version, port, init, ephemeral, data_dir

// in-editor: packages: [default.post▌] → completes postgres_16 / postgres_17
// hover Service.init → "SQL file run once on first service start"

options.name: CLI only (jet search / jet info)
options.detail: Terminal answers without the editor half. Solid floor, but leaves the typed-options payoff on the table — the user still context-switches to ask "what fields does Service take", which is the question they ask most.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres     # works
// editor: services: { postgres: Service.{ ▌ } }   ← still guessing fields

options.name: Web index (search.jet.dev), minimal CLI
options.detail: The Nix model with better paint. A hosted index lags providers, needs network, and keeps discovery outside both the terminal and the editor — two context switches where A has zero.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres
see https://search.jet.dev?q=postgres   ← the browser tab, again

comparisons.note: CLI search slow; options on a website; the browser-tab workflow this deletes.
comparisons.code:
$ nix search nixpkgs postgres   # …seconds pass
# then open search.nixos.org for the service options anyway

comparisons.note: cargo search + docs.rs is serviceable but out-of-editor; rust-analyzer completes code, not manifest deps.
The in-editor bar: typed config objects complete their own fields with docs on hover. Jet env modules are exactly this shape.
comparisons.code: const cfg: ServerOptions = { po| }   // completes port, with docs

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U27 — Failed-build debuggability: --shell-on-fail, jet explain, persisted build logs
decisions.gist: Decide the debugging contract when a package or adapter build fails: drop into the exact failing build env + explain resolution + persisted logs, logs only, or verbose-rerun.
decisions.explainer: When a Nix build fails, the human is locked out of the crime scene: the sandbox is gone, `nix log` shows a wall of text, and reproducing interactively means arcana (keep-failed, nix develop on the derivation) that even experts google. Jetpack builds — core packages and adapter recipes — will fail too; the question is whether the failure hands the user the exact environment and step that failed or just a log. Three parts under one ballot: (1) --shell-on-fail: on failure, open a shell inside the preserved build scratch dir with the build's exact PATH/env, positioned at the failing step; (2) jet explain <ref>: why this ref resolved to pkg.jet vs flake vs adapter, what was locked (source hash, recipe hash, platform), and which step failed; (3) jet logs <pkg>: full per-step logs persisted in .jet/, survive the failure, --json for CI.
decisions.story: Vernon's adapter build for a C tool dies at the ninja step on his machine only. In Nix he would rerun with --keep-failed, hunt /tmp for the half-built tree, and reconstruct the env by hand. Here he reruns with --shell-on-fail, lands in the preserved build dir with the build's exact toolchain on PATH, runs the failing command himself, and sees the missing header in thirty seconds.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env
Error [E1246]: adapter `weirdctl` failed at step 2 of 3 (ninja -C build)
 Why: `ninja` exited 1 — full log: `jet logs weirdctl`
 Fix: rerun with `jet env --shell-on-fail` to debug inside the build environment

$ jet env --shell-on-fail
build failed at step 2 · shell in preserved build dir (tools on PATH: cmake, ninja)
[weirdctl-build]$ ninja -C build
build/src/net.c:14: fatal error: openssl/ssl.h: No such file or directory
[weirdctl-build]$ # ah — missing dep. exit, add default.openssl to deps, done.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 3). Interlocks: preserved-on-failure scratch dirs are the one exception to U22's always-cleaned rule — kept under the hangar tmp area, tagged, and swept by the next jet gc or auto-GC age-out, so the zero-/tmp guarantee holds; jet explain generalizes the adapter proposal's `jet adapter explain` to every ref kind; the shell-on-fail shell is inert (nothing auto-runs in it — it is the user's hands, consistent with U19's intent boundary). Diagnostics: build-failure E12xx always names the step, the log verb, and the shell-on-fail flag — the fix line is the debugging tutorial.

options.name: Full contract: --shell-on-fail + jet explain + persisted logs (recommended)
options.detail: Failure hands over the crime scene: preserved scratch + exact build env shell at the failing step; explain shows the resolution/lock story per ref; logs persist per step with --json. Every build-failure diagnostic names all three.
options.code:
$ jet explain weirdctl
  ref      github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d
  path     adapter (no pkg.jet, no flake upstream)
  locked   source 8a31c9d · recipe hash 4be2… · platform linux_x64
  deps     default.cmake, default.ninja
  status   FAILED step 2/3 (ninja) · scratch preserved · `jet logs weirdctl`

options.name: Persisted logs only
options.detail: jet logs <pkg> with per-step structure; no preserved scratch, no shell. Better than Nix's wall of text, but the user still reconstructs the environment by hand for anything a log line does not explain — which is most native-build failures.
options.code:
$ jet logs weirdctl
[step 2/3 ninja] build/src/net.c:14: fatal error: openssl/ssl.h...
$ # now what? recreate the env yourself to poke at it

options.name: Verbose rerun (Nix model)
options.detail: On failure, suggest rerunning with -v for more output. No preserved state, nothing interactive; debugging stays read-only archaeology. Listed for completeness — it is the status quo this ballot exists to beat.
options.code:
$ jet env -v
…4000 lines later, the same error, now with company

comparisons.note: keep-failed + manual env reconstruction; the interactive path is folklore, not product.
comparisons.code:
$ nix build --keep-failed
$ ls /tmp/nix-build-*   # now reconstruct PATH yourself

comparisons.note: The workflow everyone actually uses: run a shell from the last good layer. Proof that "shell at the failure" is the debugging primitive people want.
Structured logs + explain exist and are loved; interactive failing-env entry still missing — half the answer.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: Highlighting source of truth
decisions.gist: Where the coloring rules live, so VS Code, Zed, GitHub, and the docs all color Jet identically and new syntax is never missed.
decisions.explainer: Today there are three hand-written grammars that each independently guess at Jet: a TextMate grammar for VS Code/GitHub (164 lines), a tree-sitter grammar for Zed and code parsing (998 lines), and Zed highlight queries (136 lines). The real token registry — Syntax.rs, where invariant I7 says every user-typeable keyword and sigil must live — has 568 entries and none of the grammars is checked against it. Semantic tokens = the LSP can also send exact, compiler-derived coloring to live editors, on top of any grammar.
decisions.story: Marco writes the v5 memory example and pushes it. In VS Code `copy` is plain white — the grammar predates S4. On GitHub the PR diff colors differently than his editor did. In Zed, a third coloring. His reviewer asks 'is `copy` even a keyword?' Every ratified decision that ships new syntax silently rots three grammars, and nothing fails when it happens.
decisions.detail: Recommend D. I7 already makes Syntax.rs the registry — generating from it is the 'one way to mean it' answer (I8), and the semantic overlay is what makes in-editor coloring compiler-exact. The CI drift gate turns 'grammar rot' from a silent decay into a red build.

options.name: Generate grammars from Syntax.rs
options.detail: A build step reads the I7 registry and emits the keyword/sigil/marker layers of all three grammars (tmLanguage JSON, tree-sitter keyword tables, Zed queries). Hand-written parts shrink to structure rules (strings, comments, blocks). A CI drift test fails the moment Syntax.rs gains a token the grammars don't color. Ratifying new syntax updates every editor in the same commit, mechanically.
options.code:
$ jet devtools grammars   # or build.rs step
  wrote editors/vscode/syntaxes/jet.tmLanguage.json   (generated section)
  wrote editors/tree-sitter/keywords.js                (generated)
  wrote editors/zed/languages/jet/highlights.scm       (generated section)
$ cargo test --test grammar
  every_syntax_token_is_highlighted ... ok   // 568/568 covered, or red

options.name: tree-sitter grammar is canon
options.detail: The tree-sitter grammar (already the richest, 998 lines, and what GitHub/Zed natively consume) becomes the single hand-maintained source; tmLanguage and Zed queries are generated or derived from it; a CI test checks it covers every Syntax.rs token. One grammar to maintain, but it is maintained by hand — new syntax still requires remembering to edit it, the test just makes forgetting loud.
options.code:
$ cargo test --test grammar
  tree_sitter_covers_syntax_rs ... FAILED
  missing: `copy` (D-CAP2), `^` move sigil (D-MEM1)
  fix: add to editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js, regenerate derived grammars

options.name: Semantic tokens carry the truth; grammars stay minimal
options.detail: Invest in the LSP's compiler-derived coloring (exact by construction — it knows a type from a variable, a live keyword from a retired one) as the primary experience in VS Code/Zed/Cursor. Grammars remain small lexical fallbacks for places the LSP can't reach (GitHub diffs, docs sites, quick views). Perfect where the LSP runs; GitHub and docs remain only roughly right.

options.name: Generated lexical base + semantic overlay (A + C)
options.detail: Both layers, each doing what only it can: Syntax.rs generates the keyword layer of all grammars (so GitHub, docs, and cold files are always current — no human step, CI-gated), and LSP semantic tokens refine live editors with compiler-exact coloring on top. New ratified syntax colors correctly everywhere in the same commit that lands it.

comparisons.note: rust-analyzer semantic tokens over a hand-kept TextMate base — the in-editor half is superb, but the TextMate grammar drifts and GitHub coloring lags new syntax for months.
comparisons.code: async closures colored wrong on GitHub long after stabilization

comparisons.note: zls semantic tokens + community grammars; same drift problem, editors disagree.
JetBrains model: the compiler IS the highlighter in-IDE (option C taken to the limit) — flawless there, but everywhere outside the IDE depends on separate grammars.

decisions.title: How Jet gets a game/graphics stack
decisions.gist: What 'making a game in Jet' looks like: bare stdlib primitives, a batteries-included flagship engine, official bindings to existing engines, or wait.
decisions.explainer: Baseline already decided: D-RAYLIB1 ratified a first-party core.raylib bridge package (FFI-bridge pattern) for cross-platform games and visual demos — that ships regardless. It is not built yet, so today Jet still cannot open a window; and a C bridge is a floor, not a strategy. This ballot decides what Jet's own stack ABOVE that floor is. Primitives = low-level building blocks (window, GPU surface, audio out, input events) on which anyone can build an engine. Engine = the batteries layer (sprites, scenes, cameras, asset loading, game loop) that lets a beginner make Pong in an afternoon. Under I6, stdlib sub-libraries may bootstrap on external crates (wgpu/winit class) through the established FFI-bridge pattern until end of Epoch 3, then go native — any new external dep is exactly the approval this ballot grants or withholds.
decisions.story: A 15-year-old picks her first language because she wants to make a game — the single most common reason beginners pick one. Python has pygame, Lua has LÖVE, C# has Unity. Jet — whose north star is Blueprint-class friendliness (#182) and which already studied UE's gameplay architecture (#181) — has to say 'we can't open a window.' Meanwhile UE6 dropping Blueprint is the market gap #182 exists to take; a visual editor with no runtime to drive is a body without legs.
decisions.detail: Recommend B, 2D first. It is the beginner-magic priority made concrete (afternoon Pong), gives #182's visual editor its runtime, and keeps the expert tier honest underneath (primitives are public, not internal). The ratified core.raylib bridge (D-RAYLIB1) ships first as the interim path and stays as a compatibility package; the flagship engine bootstraps GPU/window/audio via the I6 FFI-bridge pattern (wgpu/winit-class crates) with the native replacement owed post-E3 — approving this option approves those bridge deps.

options.name: Stdlib primitives only
options.detail: Ship core.window, core.gpu, core.audio, core.input — thin, honest, expert-shaped. Engines grow in the package ecosystem. Beginners face raw GPU concepts (pipelines, buffers) before their first sprite; the afternoon-Pong story doesn't exist until someone else builds it.

options.name: Flagship engine package on stdlib primitives
options.detail: Both layers, matching Jet's dual-facet identity: primitives (option A) beneath, plus a first-party batteries engine — window/loop/sprites/text/audio/input, 2D first, scene tree, asset pipeline — so `jet run pong.jet` opens a window with zero setup. Becomes the runtime #182's visual editor drives and the living proof of the beginner promise. Largest first-party surface to own and keep excellent.

options.name: core.raylib is the whole story for now
options.detail: Build the already-ratified D-RAYLIB1 bridge and stop there: raylib for 2D/3D, wgpu-level bindings later via next-gen FFI (#180). A real game path exists soonest, but the beginner types a foreign API with foreign docs and foreign error messages — the anti-thesis of front-end-owns-every-error — and a native Jet-shaped stack still has to be decided someday.

options.name: Defer past Epoch 3
options.detail: Nothing until the jetos/self-host era. Honest sequencing-wise, but 'replace every language' keeps a hole in the domain that recruits the most beginners, and #182 stays a body without legs.
options.code:
$ jet run pong.jet
error: no window/graphics capability exists in this epoch

comparisons.note: The beginner gold standard: one file, a draw callback, a window. Thousands learned programming through it.
comparisons.code: function love.draw() love.graphics.circle("fill", x, y, 8) end

comparisons.note: A language built BY game development — its credibility flows from shipping a real game with it. Games are how systems languages prove themselves fun.
Ecosystem-grown engine (option A's bet). Excellent — after ~5 years, and beginners still rate Rust gamedev 'hard mode'.
First-party-adjacent engine on stdlib primitives — the option B shape, earlier in its life.

decisions.title: Name of the flagship game engine package
decisions.gist: What the batteries game engine is called — the word in every beginner's first `use` line and every tutorial title.
decisions.explainer: D-GAME1=B ratified a first-party engine package on stdlib primitives. Primitives keep plain core.* names (core.window, core.gpu, core.audio, core.input — descriptive, not brandable). The engine itself needs a name: either a plain stdlib slot (core.game) or a branded first-party package in the jet/jetpack/jetos naming canon. The name appears in code (`use …`), in the install line, in docs titles, in search results ('… tutorial'), and eventually on #182's visual editor.
decisions.story: Every game made in Jet starts with this word, and the community will name itself after it ('the … engine', '… jam'). Unity, Godot, LÖVE, bevy — engine names outgrow their languages. Jet's pick decides whether the engine reads as a stdlib feature (core.game) or as a flagship product with its own identity, the way jetpack is to packaging.
decisions.detail: Recommend B (airshow). Flagship product deserves a flagship name in the aviation canon; airshow is the one that means 'flying as play' without explanation, is short enough for a use line typed daily, and searches cleanly. A is the fallback if the owner wants the engine to read as pure stdlib.

options.name: core.game
options.detail: Plain stdlib slot. Zero-brand, maximally discoverable — a beginner browsing the core library finds it alphabetically; no new word to learn. Reads as a language feature, not a product; harder to talk about ('the Jet game module') and 'core.game tutorial' is a weak search term.

options.name: airshow
options.detail: Aerial spectacle — flying as performance and play, which is exactly what a game engine is for. Short, easy to say in any language, clean verb-adjacent energy ('built with Airshow'). Searchable and brandable without whimsy overload.

options.name: barnstorm
options.detail: The barnstormers were the 1920s pilots who flew town to town putting on shows — entertainment flying, the historical heart of the theme. Doubles as a verb with momentum ('barnstorming demo'). Longer word; slightly opaque to non-native speakers.

options.name: afterburner
options.detail: Raw speed and spectacle — the flame out the back of the jet. Instantly evocative, performance-flavored; risks reading as a perf tool rather than a creative one, and it's a long word to type in every use line.

options.name: slipstream
options.detail: The smooth air behind a fast mover — flow, ease, being carried along. Gentle and pretty; less game-flavored than B/C (could name a networking or async library just as well).

comparisons.note: A branded engine name (not lua.game) is what the community organized around — LÖVE jams, LÖVE forums — while staying tiny and beginner-first.
comparisons.code: require('love')  — the name IS the ecosystem

comparisons.note: Same: the engine brand carries the game-dev identity; 'bevy tutorial' is a precise search, 'rust game module' is not.

decisions.title: Beginner-facing core.game loop and scene API
decisions.gist: How a beginner writes the first game loop and scene in core.game.
decisions.story: Maya is making Breakout as her first compiled program. In the first hour she wants a paddle, a ball, input, drawing, sound, and a window. In the second week she wants to open the same project in the planned visual editor from #182, move sprites on a canvas, and keep the hand-written game logic. This choice decides whether `core.game` starts as a draw callback, a stateful app, a scene tree, or an ECS world.

options.name: Single frame callback
options.detail: `Game.window(...).each_frame(...)` is the whole beginner API. It is direct and mirrors the D-GAME1 sketch: open a window, update values, draw shapes. The tradeoff is that world state, assets, collisions, and editor-readable scene data all live in user variables unless later APIs add a second model.

options.name: App object with init/update/draw callbacks
options.detail: A typed app owns state from the start: `init`, `update`, and `draw` are separate callbacks. This teaches durable game state cleanly and keeps drawing separate from simulation. The tradeoff is that the first file has more ceremony before a sprite appears, and a visual editor still needs a separate scene asset format unless the app state becomes that format.

options.name: Scene-first with a frame hook
options.detail: The first-class object is a `Scene`: sprites, shapes, sounds, camera, and input bindings live in durable scene data; `scene.on_frame(...)` is the beginner escape hatch for tiny game logic. This keeps one beginner path while giving #182 a real editable model. The frame hook is not a second engine model; it is script attached to the scene.

options.name: ECS-first world and systems
options.detail: The beginner starts with a `World`, components, queries, and systems. This scales naturally to many entities and advanced tooling, and it lines up with modern data-oriented engines. The tradeoff is learnability: the first sprite requires component vocabulary before the first visible result.

comparisons.note: LOVE is the clearest callback-first model: define update/draw functions and the engine calls them. Excellent for first programs; scene/editor structure is not built in.
comparisons.code:
function love.update(dt) x = x + vx * dt end
function love.draw() love.graphics.circle("fill", x, y, 8) end

comparisons.note: Godot proves scene-first works for beginners and visual editing: scenes are durable data, scripts attach behavior, and the editor sees the same model the runtime runs.
Bevy proves ECS-first can be expressive and high-performance, but the first tutorial starts with systems, components, bundles, and queries.
comparisons.code:
app.add_systems(Update, move_ball);
fn move_ball(mut q: Query<(&mut Transform, &Velocity)>) { ... }

comparisons.note: Pygame teaches the manual loop: poll events, update state, draw, flip. It is explicit, but beginners own every lifecycle rule immediately.
comparisons.code:
while running:
    for event in pygame.event.get(): ...
    ball.x += vx * dt
    screen.blit(ball, pos)
    pygame.display.flip()

decisions.title: HTTPS out of the box
decisions.gist: Whether fetching an https:// URL works in a fresh Jet install, and which TLS engine makes it work.
decisions.explainer: TLS is the encryption layer behind https — essentially every real API requires it. Today core.http's default build is plain-HTTP only; https needs the separate opt-in core.tls package. The engine choices: rustls = the widely-audited memory-safe TLS library the Rust world standardized on; system TLS = whatever the OS ships (OpenSSL on Linux, Security.framework on macOS, Schannel on Windows). Under I6, a vendored library rides the FFI-bridge pattern until end of Epoch 3, after which a native implementation is owed — and TLS is cryptographic code, so 'native' carries a real security obligation, noted per option.
decisions.story: Ana, week one, writes a weather CLI. `http.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/...")` — error: TLS not available, install core.tls. She has never heard of TLS; she copied a URL from API docs like every tutorial on earth. In Python, Go, Deno, and even curl, that line just works. The batteries-included language fails on the second program a beginner ever writes.
decisions.detail: Recommend A. Batteries-included is the ranked priority and https is the battery; rustls is the audited, memory-safe interim consistent with how every other stdlib bridge dep works. The post-E3 native rewrite must be explicitly security-gated — cryptography is the one place 'we rewrote it ourselves' needs outside eyes before it ships as default.

options.name: rustls in the default build (bridge now, native post-E3)
options.detail: Vendor rustls through the established I6 FFI-bridge pattern so https works in every build with zero setup — the Go model. Post-E3 the native-Jet replacement is owed like every other bridge dep; because this one is cryptography, that replacement must carry an explicit security gate (external audit / interop test battery against rustls+OpenSSL) before it may become the default. Approving A approves the rustls bridge dep (I6 owner gate — same governance as the ratified D-DEP-CRYPTO1 seal/sign backend, a separate decision this one does not reopen) and pins certificate verification to system trust roots.
options.code:
$ jet run weather.jet
{"latitude":52.0,"hourly":{...}}   // it just works

// server side too:
svc :: Http.serve(443, handler).tls(cert, key)   // one line, no package

options.name: System TLS via C FFI
options.detail: Bind the OS engine per platform (OpenSSL / Security.framework / Schannel). No vendored crypto, OS owns the patching — but three platform code paths with three behavior sets, error messages that surface OS-specific failure modes (the front end must translate all of them, I2-style), and Linux minimal containers often lack OpenSSL, so 'it just works' gains an asterisk exactly where services deploy.
options.code:
$ jet run weather.jet          # macOS: works (Security.framework)
$ docker run scratch-image jet # error: libssl.so.3 not found
  fix: install openssl in the image   // the asterisk

options.name: Status quo — core.tls stays opt-in
options.detail: No default TLS; the error message gets friendlier. Keeps the compiler distribution crypto-free, keeps Ana's weather app broken until she learns what TLS is.
options.code:
$ jet run weather.jet
error[E4102]: `https` needs the TLS package
  what: this build speaks plain HTTP only
  fix: `jet pkg add core.tls` — then this line works unchanged

comparisons.note: crypto/tls is native in the standard library — the reason `go run` scripts against any API with zero setup. The end-state option A aims at.
Ships rustls inside the runtime — exactly option A's interim shape, permanently.
ssl module wraps system OpenSSL (option B) — historically the source of an entire genre of cross-platform certificate bugs ('pip SSL error' has 100k+ search results).

decisions.title: HTTP server TLS surface
decisions.gist: How a Jet HTTP server turns on TLS.
decisions.explainer: D-TLS1=A says HTTPS should work out of the box and showed a `.tls(cert, key)` server sketch, but the implemented server API is not a builder: `Server.serve(addr, mux)` lowers directly to `jet_http_mux_serve(&addr, mux)`. Adding server TLS therefore needs a public stdlib surface decision before implementation.
decisions.story: Hank ships a webhook receiver for a payments provider. The provider requires HTTPS, and Hank already has a certificate and private key from his deploy platform. The client side now handles https by default, but the server surface in Jet is still the existing plaintext `Server.serve(addr, mux)` function, with no builder object to attach `.tls(...)` to.
decisions.inWild:
use core.http.server as Server

fn run() {
    mux :: Server.mux()
    mux.post("/stripe/webhook", handle_webhook)
    cert :: env.get("TLS_CERT") ?? panic("missing cert")
    key :: env.get("TLS_KEY") ?? panic("missing key")
    Server.serve("0.0.0.0:443", mux, tls: Server.tls(cert, key))?
}

options.name: Named TLS option on `serve`
options.detail: Keep one canonical server entry point. Plain HTTP stays `Server.serve(addr, mux)?`; HTTPS adds a named `tls:` option using a typed `Server.tls(cert, key)` value. Future server options can use the same named-option slot without inventing extra verbs.

options.name: Server builder chain
options.detail: Introduce a configured server value and make TLS a method on it. This matches the `.tls(cert, key)` sketch directly and gives future configuration a natural place, but it changes the server model from a function call to a builder object.
options.code:
use core.http.server as Server

fn run() {
    mux :: Server.mux()
    Server.bind("0.0.0.0:443", mux)
        .tls(cert_pem, key_pem)
        .serve()?
}

options.name: Separate `serve_tls` function
options.detail: Make HTTPS explicit as a separate function while leaving plaintext serving unchanged. The spelling is easy to find, but server setup splits into multiple verbs as more transport options arrive.

comparisons.note: Go keeps plaintext and TLS as sibling functions on the same package.
comparisons.code:
http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler)
http.ListenAndServeTLS(addr, certFile, keyFile, handler)

comparisons.note: Node separates HTTP and HTTPS server constructors, with TLS options passed as data.
Modern Rust servers usually bind a listener plus a TLS config value before serving.

decisions.title: Typed build targets: how are graph targets added and controlled?
decisions.gist: Choose the ergonomic target API for default magic and expert graph control.
decisions.story: Hank is porting a game engine from CMake. He needs one Jet build file to build the editor executable, the reusable engine library, shader assets, tests, docs, and installer output without falling back to CMake target names or shell scripts.
decisions.inWild:
fn build(b: BuildContext) #(Fs) -> BuildPlan ? {
    atlas :: b.add_asset_bundle("sprites",
        inputs: b.find("assets/sprites/*.png")?)

    engine :: b.add_library("engine",
        sources: ["src/engine.jet"],
        assets: [atlas])

    app :: b.add_executable("studio",
        sources: ["src/run.jet"],
        deps: [engine])

    b.add_test("engine-tests",
        sources: ["tests/engine.jet"],
        deps: [engine])

    b.add_doc("api-docs", sources: ["src/engine.jet"], deps: [engine])
    return b.plan(default: app)
}
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: beginner keeps no-build-file magic; expert gets typed handles and full graph control. Recommendation changed from pure constructors to registered add_* methods because one logical target should be declared once, not constructed in one place and restated in the final plan.

options.name: Registered add_* targets returning handles (recommended)
options.detail: One canonical target mechanism: `b.add_executable`, `b.add_library`, `b.add_test`, `b.add_bench`, `b.add_asset_bundle`, `b.add_doc`, `b.add_install`, `b.add_package`, and `b.add_publish` register targets and return typed handles. Beginners omit `fn build`; experts declare each target once, use handles for deps/config, and finish with `b.plan(default: app)` or `b.plan()` for all registered roots.

options.name: Pure constructor values plus explicit plan list
options.detail: Targets are ordinary values from `b.executable`/`b.library`; `b.plan(targets: [...])` is the only registration point. Very explicit, but it splits one logical target across declaration and plan wiring.

options.name: Manifest targets plus build-time selection
options.detail: Targets live in `pkg.jet` or `workspace.jet`; `fn build` selects/configures them. Good for static packages, but loses programmable target generation and dynamic graph composition.

options.name: Source-list BuildPlan only
options.detail: BuildPlan remains `sources/generated/assets`. Beginner-simple, but professional projects still need Make/CMake for tests, assets, docs, install, and package outputs.

comparisons.note: Targets are first-class graph nodes.
Targets own usage requirements and dependencies.
Build steps are programmed in the host language.

decisions.title: Build actions: how does Jet model custom commands without ambient shell soup?
decisions.gist: Choose the custom action API for declared inputs, outputs, argv, env, capabilities, and side-effect commands.
decisions.story: Doris owns a content pipeline. Textures, shaders, translations, and generated bindings all need external tools today. She wants Jet to run them like Ninja/Bazel rules, but her security team needs every input, output, command, and capability visible in the lock and audit output.

options.name: Declared action values (recommended)
options.detail: Cached actions require declared inputs and outputs; argv/env/caps/tool digest are recorded. Side-effect-only commands are a separate explicit target class and are never cached as normal build steps.
options.code:
cook :: b.action("pack-sprites",
    inputs: b.find("assets/*.png")?,
    outputs: ["build/sprites.atlas"],
    run: ["atlas-pack", "assets", "build/sprites.atlas"],
    caps: #(Fs, Exec))

options.name: Raw exec inside #Impure only
options.detail: Users call `b.exec` directly and manually wire results. Powerful, but it trains Make-style hidden dependencies and gives the cache no reliable graph.

options.name: Plugin-only actions
options.detail: Every custom action must be packaged as a sandboxed plugin. Good policy boundary, but too heavy for first-party local generators and simple project tools.
options.code: cook :: b.plugin("atlas-pack").run(inputs: b.find("assets/*.png")?, outputs: ["build/sprites.atlas"])

options.name: No custom actions
options.detail: Jet builds Jet source only. Projects keep Make/Ninja/CMake for everything else, so metaprogramming cannot replace prominent build systems.

comparisons.note: Custom rules declare inputs and outputs.
genrule names srcs, outs, and command.
Rules are powerful but can hide ambient shell state.

decisions.title: Build toolchains: how does Jet model host/target compilers, SDKs, and signing identities?
decisions.gist: Choose the typed model for build and target toolchains.
decisions.story: Earl ships an embedded Linux binary and a macOS app from one repo. He needs Jet to know which compiler runs on the host, which target SDK is used, what linker signs the app, and why a cache hit is valid across machines.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: default host builds stay automatic; expert cross/signing builds use explicit handles. Recommendation is a hybrid: infer the simple case, model every non-default toolchain as a typed, lock-recorded dependency.

options.name: Default inference plus typed toolchain handles (recommended)
options.detail: No toolchain argument means the default host toolchain. Non-default builds use typed handles from jetpack/toolchain deps with host/target roles, SDK identity, linker/signing metadata, lock records, and provenance.
options.code:
b.add_executable("cli", sources: ["src/run.jet"])
arm :: b.toolchain(target: "aarch64-linux-musl", sdk: "core.embedded-sdk#1.4")
b.add_executable("sensor", sources: ["src/sensor.jet"], toolchain: arm)

options.name: Typed handles required for every target
options.detail: Every target names a toolchain handle, including host builds. Fully explicit, but adds ceremony to the beginner/default case.
options.code:
host :: b.toolchain(target: b.host_target())
b.add_executable("cli", sources: ["src/run.jet"], toolchain: host)

options.name: String triples only
options.detail: Targets name strings and Jet picks default tools. Pleasant for simple cross builds, but too little audit data for SDK and signing correctness.
options.code: b.add_executable("sensor", sources: ["src/run.jet"], target: "aarch64-linux-musl")

options.name: Ambient PATH toolchain
options.detail: Use whatever compiler/linker/signing tools are on PATH. Familiar from Make, but cache keys and enterprise audits cannot trust it.

comparisons.note: Toolchains are explicit configured dependencies.
Toolchain files configure cross-build state globally.
Toolchains are derivation inputs, which makes them reproducible.

decisions.title: Configure probes: how does Jet replace find_program, pkg_config, header checks, and compile checks?
decisions.gist: Choose typed probe APIs and how they are classified for reproducibility.
decisions.story: Betty wraps a C database library. On Linux, pkg-config names it one way; on macOS, the SDK supplies a different path. She needs configure-like checks, but CI must know which probes are reproducible and which touched the host.

options.name: Typed probes with reproducibility class (recommended)
options.detail: Probe APIs return typed results and declare whether they are locked/reproducible or ambient/Tier-2. Lock records the result and authority.
options.code:
sqlite :: b.probe.pkg_config("sqlite3", min_version: "3.42")?
cc :: b.probe.compile_check(name: "has_json", includes: ["sqlite3.h"], code: "sqlite3_json_init")?

options.name: Probe through b.exec
options.detail: Users script their own checks. Maximum reach, but no common UX, no stable lock shape, and easy authority leaks.

options.name: No probes; require explicit config
options.detail: Users pass all paths/flags manually. Reproducible, but hostile to native dependency discovery.
options.code: sqlite :: b.c_library(name: "sqlite3", include_dirs: ["/opt/sqlite/include"], libs: ["sqlite3"])

options.name: Import CMake configure results
options.detail: Delegate probing to CMake and import a result file. Good migration ramp, poor Jet-native UX.
options.code:
cfg :: b.legacy.cmake_configure("vendor/sqlite")?
return b.plan(targets: [b.library("sqlite", flags: cfg.flags)])

comparisons.note: CMake has many global probe commands.
Meson probes are typed dependency objects.
Configure scripts are powerful but ambient and hard to audit.

decisions.title: Build cache and remote execution: what is the cache identity contract?
decisions.gist: Choose the action-cache key and when remote cache/execution become valid.
decisions.story: Maria manages CI for a monorepo. She wants Jet builds to reuse generated bindings, shader packs, tests, and cross-compiled objects across machines, but a cache hit must explain exactly why it is safe.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: caching should be automatic and invisible when correct, but fully explainable and overrideable for experts. Recommendation remains full key, now explicit that local action cache is default-on with `jet explain-build` and policy knobs.

options.name: Automatic local cache with full explainable key (recommended)
options.detail: Local action cache is on by default for declared actions. Key includes inputs, declared outputs, argv, env, caps, tool digest, target, policy, compiler version, generated-source hashes, and toolchain identity. Experts can disable or inspect it with `--no-cache` and `jet explain-build`.
options.code:
cache_key = hash(inputs, outputs, argv, env, caps, tool.digest, target, policy, toolchain, jet.version)
$ jet explain-build openapi-client --why-rebuilt
$ jet build --no-cache

options.name: Input files and argv only
options.detail: Fast to understand but misses toolchain, policy, env, and compiler differences that can change outputs.
options.code: cache_key = hash(inputs, argv)

options.name: Manual cache opt-in per action
options.detail: Users mark which actions cache. Precise, but loses magic defaults and lets ordinary projects stay slower than they need to be.
options.code: b.action("codegen", ..., cache: true)

options.name: No action cache; rebuild every time
options.detail: Always correct if actions are correct, but gives up best-in-class build performance and weakens why-rebuilt UX.
options.code: jet build --no-cache

comparisons.note: Action cache keys include declared inputs and command environment.
Derivation hashes include inputs and build recipe.
Compiler cache is fast but narrower than whole build graph caching.

decisions.title: Remote cache and remote execution gate: when may builds leave the local machine?
decisions.gist: Choose the policy gate for remote cache and remote execution.
decisions.story: Sam wants cloud builds for a large workspace. His security team accepts remote cache reads from a trusted service, but remote execution means source files, generated code, and tool inputs leave the machine and need a stronger policy gate.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: beginners never leave the local machine; experts can opt into remote cache and remote execution separately under policy. Remote cache and remote exec are one subsystem with two trust levels, not two unrelated features.

options.name: Local default; remote cache and exec as separate policy grants (recommended)
options.detail: Default builds are local. Remote cache can be enabled by workspace policy with pinned/trusted endpoints. Remote execution is a separate stronger grant after sandbox/provenance proof. Both use the same action-key contract and explain-build surfaces.

options.name: Remote cache and exec together
options.detail: One remote-build grant covers both cache and execution. Convenient, but hides a materially different trust boundary.
options.code: policy: .{ remote_build: allow("https://buildfarm") }

options.name: Remote exec plugin decides
options.detail: Delegate remote execution policy to plugins. Flexible, but weakens the one authority model.
options.code: scheduler: plugin("acme.remote-exec")

options.name: No remote features ever
options.detail: Keep all builds local. Strong default, but large teams lose best-in-class CI performance even when policy would allow it.
options.code: policy: .{ build_remote_cache: deny, build_remote_exec: deny }

comparisons.note: Remote cache and remote execution are core large-repo features.
Binary substituters are remote cache-like; remote builders are separately configured.
Remote compiler cache is narrower than full action execution.

decisions.title: Build scheduler: how does Jet run graph work in parallel without noisy nondeterminism?
decisions.gist: Choose the scheduler and resource-pool model for build graphs.
decisions.story: Walter works on a game with shader compilation, asset packing, codegen, tests, and linking. He wants parallel builds, but logs must stay readable and the linker must not compete with every CPU-heavy tool at once.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: scheduler should be automatic for beginners and tunable for experts. Recommendation is deterministic auto-scheduling with optional named pools/resource hints.

options.name: Automatic deterministic scheduler plus named pools (recommended)
options.detail: Jet runs ready nodes in parallel by default, preserves stable console output, cancels dependents after failures, and supports optional expert pools: cpu, memory, linker, console, gpu, or project-defined pools.
options.code:
b.pool("linker", limit: 1)
b.pool("gpu", limit: 1)
shaders :: b.action("shaders", ..., pool: "gpu")
app :: b.add_executable("app", sources: ["src/run.jet"], pool: "linker")

options.name: Simple job count only
options.detail: `-j N` parallelism without named pools. Familiar, but poor for memory/linker/GPU bottlenecks.
options.code: $ jet build -j 8

options.name: Serial by default, explicit async actions
options.detail: Users manually mark parallel work. Predictable, but pushes graph scheduling burden onto every build author.
options.code: b.parallel([compile_assets, compile_docs])

options.name: External scheduler plugin
options.detail: Delegate scheduling to a plugin. Flexible, but build behavior becomes harder to reason about and audit.
options.code: scheduler: plugin("acme.remote-scheduler")

comparisons.note: Pools limit scarce resources such as console or linker.
Scheduler handles local/remote actions and resource hints.
Jobserver gives parallelism, but resource classes are ad hoc.

decisions.title: Legacy build-system interop: how does Jet call CMake, Make, Gradle, npm, or cargo during migration?
decisions.gist: Choose the migration wrapper model for external build systems.
decisions.story: Norma is moving a service from CMake and npm to Jet. She cannot rewrite every native dependency and frontend asset step on day one, but her CI policy must still see every external tool invocation and file boundary.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: migration should start with declared wrappers and grow toward imported external graphs without changing the authority model. Recommendation folds import into the wrapper path as a stronger mode, not a separate silo.

options.name: Declared Tier-2 wrappers with optional graph import (recommended)
options.detail: External builds start as typed legacy actions with inputs/outputs/caps. When Jet can understand a tool, the same wrapper may import its graph for better deps/provenance. Policy can deny all legacy wrappers in CI.

options.name: Raw exec migration snippets
options.detail: Users write the commands themselves under `#Impure`. Works for anything, but repeats the hidden dependency problem Jet is trying to retire.

options.name: Import external graph only
options.detail: Parse CMake/Gradle/npm/cargo graphs into Jet targets with no wrapper fallback. Good when it works, but brittle for migration edge cases.
options.code:
native_graph :: b.import_graph.cmake("vendor/lib")?
return b.plan(targets: native_graph.targets)

options.name: No legacy interop
options.detail: Force native Jet build descriptions. Clean model, poor migration path for professional codebases.
options.code: // Rewrite vendor build in Jet before using it.

comparisons.note: rules_foreign_cc wraps CMake/Make projects as declared actions.
build.rs can run arbitrary host code, which Jet should not copy invisibly.
Exec tasks are easy but often under-declare inputs/outputs.

decisions.title: Sandboxed build plugins: should reusable build extensions run as WASM components?
decisions.gist: Choose the plugin substrate for shared build extensions.
decisions.story: Olive works at a studio with a proprietary asset compiler. Teams should call it from Jet builds without copying its logic, but org policy must deny third-party plugins by default and review the exact host capabilities exposed.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: teams need easy shared Jet build libraries and stronger isolation for third-party/proprietary tools. Recommendation is one plugin contract with source Jet plugins compiling to WASM components when isolation/distribution is needed.

options.name: One plugin contract: Jet source or WASM component under policy (recommended)
options.detail: First-party teams can use source Jet build libraries. Packaged/third-party plugins compile to WASM components with a versioned host interface and granted capabilities. Both return generated modules/targets/actions through the same BuildPlan APIs; policy can deny plugin packages.
options.code:
use build_plugins.asset_pack
atlas :: asset_pack.pack(b, "assets")

packer :: b.plugin("acme.asset-packer#2.1")
atlas2 :: packer.action("pack", inputs: b.find("assets/*.png")?, outputs: ["build/atlas.bin"], caps: #(Fs))

options.name: WASM component plugins only
options.detail: Every plugin is isolated and versioned. Strong boundary, but too much ceremony for local first-party build helpers.
options.code: packer :: b.plugin("acme.asset-packer#2.1")

options.name: Native executable plugins
options.detail: Plugins are host binaries. Good ecosystem reuse, but weaker sandbox and portability story.
options.code: packer :: b.plugin_exec("atlas-pack", sha256: "...")

options.name: No build plugins
options.detail: Teams share ordinary Jet libraries only. Safe but loses plugin-style distribution for tools that need isolation.
options.code: atlas :: pack_assets(b.find("assets/*.png")?)

comparisons.note: Plugins are powerful but run in-process with broad project access.
Rules extend builds but run inside the build language and action sandbox.
Components give a portable interface and capability boundary.

decisions.title: Public front-end toolkit: how much lexer/parser/semantic power should Jet expose to users?
decisions.gist: Choose the stable public compiler-tooling API for dogfooding and user tools.
decisions.story: Ruth is writing a Jet migration tool and a custom architecture dashboard. She wants the same lexer, parser, diagnostics, and semantic graph Jet uses, but she should not link unstable compiler internals or mutate AST nodes behind sema.
decisions.detail: 2026-07-06 two-facet pass: library APIs and CLI JSON should not be rivals. Recommendation is one stable read-only core.compiler value model, exposed in-process and via CLI JSON for tools that cannot link Jet libraries.

options.name: Stable read-only core.compiler plus CLI JSON mirror (recommended)
options.detail: Expose versioned value APIs for tokens, syntax tree, diagnostics, semindex, and source maps. Internal crates remain private; no AST mutation enters compilation. CLI commands mirror the same model for external tools.
options.code:
tokens :: jc.lex(src)?
unit :: jc.parse(src)?
checked :: jc.check(unit)?
$ jet semindex --json src/run.jet

options.name: Raw compiler crates public
options.detail: Expose internal crates directly. Maximum dogfood reuse, but public stability freezes internals and leaks implementation details.
options.code:
use jet_parser.Parser
use jet_sema.Checker

options.name: CLI JSON only
options.detail: Tools shell out to `jet semindex --json` and `jet fmt/check --json`. Stable and simple, but awkward for in-process tools and compiler-like libraries.
options.code: data :: process.run(["jet", "semindex", "--json"])?

options.name: Mutable AST builder API
