decisions.title: REPL inline docs surface
decisions.gist: How the REPL opens docs for a name.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-REPL1 ratified hybrid REPL depth, but the original ballot explicitly left ?name docs as a follow-up gate. This decides whether docs are a REPL expression-like shortcut, a colon command, or absent from v1 REPL. The goal is one clear docs path, not two rival help systems.
decisions.story: Betty is exploring a library in jet repl. She has a value named `server` and sees a completion for `listen`. She wants the shortest way to ask what `listen` expects without leaving the REPL or searching the website.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet repl
user> server.listen
# completion shows listen(port: Int) -> Result
user> ?server.listen
# docs open inline, then the prompt returns
user> _
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: docs should be discoverable from the place where the question appears. Expert pass: docs need exact symbol identity, signatures, and source/provenance where available. Hybrid pass: the REPL should call the same docs index as jet ? / LSP hover, not maintain separate prose.

options.name: No ?name docs; use jet ? and completion only
options.detail: The REPL keeps completion/signature help but no docs command. Users open jet ? or editor hover for deeper docs. Smallest REPL surface, but breaks the hybrid ballot promise that docs are one keystroke away in the REPL.
options.code:
user> nums.fil<Tab>
filter (f: Fn) -> List

user> :help
# points to jet ? filter

options.name: ?name inline docs over the shared docs index (recommended)
options.detail: ?name is a REPL-only query form, not Jet source syntax. It resolves names exactly like completion/LSP hover, renders signature, short docs, source/module, examples when present, and returns to the same prompt. It preserves one docs index across REPL, jet ?, and editor tooling.
options.code:
user> ?List.filter
List.filter(f: fn(T) -> Bool) -> List<T>
Keeps items where f(item) is true.
Source: core.collections

user> _

options.name: Colon command only: :doc name
options.detail: Docs are explicit commands, not punctuation. This avoids confusion with Jet source, but is slower than the ratified REPL mockup and creates a separate docs spelling from the ?name convention many REPL users know.
options.code:
user> :doc List.filter
List.filter(f: fn(T) -> Bool) -> List<T>

user> _

comparisons.note: Uses ?name and name? to inspect Python objects inline.
Help mode is entered with ?, then a name queries docs.
rustdoc/IDE hover are shared docs surfaces; REPL-like tools should not fork docs text.

decisions.title: REPL rerun semantics
decisions.gist: What rerunning an old REPL turn does to later state.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-REPL1 ratified notebook-style rerun controls, but rerun affects truth: later bindings may depend on the old value, and turns may have effects. This decision chooses the one rerun model so the REPL never shows stale values as current.
decisions.story: Hank defines `rate`, computes `invoice_total`, then notices `rate` was wrong. He hits rerun on turn 1. He needs to know whether `invoice_total` changed, stayed stale, or needs a manual rerun before he trusts the session.
decisions.inWild:
1 user> rate :: 0.07
  0.07 : Float
2 user> invoice_total :: subtotal * (1.0 + rate)
  107.0 : Float
# Hank edits turn 1 to rate :: 0.08 and presses rerun. What happens to turn 2?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: never make stale state look current. Expert pass: side effects and expensive turns need explicit control. Hybrid pass: one replay model can handle both by replaying pure/dependent turns automatically and requiring confirmation for effectful replay.

options.name: Replay from the edited turn forward with effect confirmation (recommended)
options.detail: Rerun rebuilds session state from the selected turn forward, recomputing dependent later turns in order. Pure/binding turns replay automatically. Effectful turns pause with a replay plan and require confirmation or skip/stale-mark. This keeps current state truthful while protecting side effects.
options.code:
rerun turn 1
Replay plan:
  1 rate :: 0.08        auto
  2 invoice_total ...   auto
  3 write_file(...)     confirm effect
Apply? [y/N]

options.name: Rerun one turn only; stale-mark dependents
options.detail: Only the selected turn reruns. Later turns that read changed bindings are marked stale and excluded from current binding truth until manually rerun. Safer for effects, but beginners must understand stale state and manually repair the session.
options.code:
1 rate :: 0.08  ok
2 invoice_total  stale: depends on old rate
current bindings: rate only; invoice_total hidden until rerun

options.name: Scratch rerun; does not change session state
options.detail: Rerun evaluates the old input in a temporary scratch scope and prints the result, leaving every binding untouched. Safe, but the button is not a real notebook rerun and does not help fix a session.
options.code:
rerun turn 1 as scratch
0.08 : Float
# session still has rate = 0.07

comparisons.note: Cells can be rerun out of order, which often leaves hidden stale state. Jet should avoid that footgun.
comparisons.code: Run cell 1, skip cell 2 -> displayed outputs can disagree with kernel state.

comparisons.note: Reactive dependency graph recomputes downstream cells when an input changes.
Command blocks can be rerun, but shell side effects are real; Jet needs stronger state truth because bindings are typed session state.

decisions.title: How a project declares and invokes named tasks
decisions.gist: Pick how a Jet project declares its own named commands (lint, migrate, seed, deploy) and how you run them, without adding a second way to mean "run something."
decisions.explainer: Option A ranks first on the priorities that decide: one-path (I8) — a task is the existing `fn run()`/`fn build()` entry-point mechanism given a user-chosen name, not a second command language, so Jet never has two unrelated ways to 'run something'; safety/beginner — `#Task` is an explicit opt-in (no accidental exposure like D), and a beginner writes one ordinary function and types `jetpack run lint`; expert composability and anti-repetition — typed arguments come free from D-CLIFLAG1, and a cross-task dependency is just a function call, so turbo/just's headline feature (ordered dependencies) needs no DAG DSL and nothing is ever restated (B's failure). C is the strongest runner-up if the owner wants a declarative, greppable graph in `pkg.jet`, and could layer on top of A later (a `tasks:` block whose `run:` references a `#Task fn`) — but on its own it reintroduces untyped shell strings for the common case. Two sub-picks ride on A and need the owner's word: (1) the marker word — `#Task` overloads Jet's concurrency `Task<T>`/task groups (D-TASKRUNTIME1); aviation-family alternatives that avoid the clash: `#Command`, `#Verb`, `#Chore`, `#Recipe`, `#Runbook`, `#Checklist`, `#Preflight`, `#Taxi`, `#Sortie`, `#Waypoint`. (2) the invocation verb — recommend `jetpack run <name>` (reuses the existing `run` verb; `jetpack lint` as unambiguous-name sugar) over a new `jetpack do <name>`.
decisions.story: Priya clones a teammate's Jet web service, `orbit`. She wants to lint it, apply the pending database migrations, seed dev fixtures, and deploy. Today Jet only recognizes the four fixed lifecycle entry points `fn run()`, `fn dev()`, `fn build()`, `fn test()`; anything else the project needs lives in a README as a copy-paste shell incantation. Every rival she has used solves this: `npm run lint`, `cargo xtask`, `pnpm deploy`, `just migrate`, `uv run seed`. Priya wants to type `jetpack <tab>` and see the project's own verbs, run one, and have a wrong name tell her what the real names are — not grep a README. The choice: what does the project author write to declare `lint`/`migrate`/`seed`/`deploy`, and does declaring them fight Jet's existing `fn run()` mechanism or reuse it.
decisions.inWild: The `orbit` package needs four project commands. `lint` shells out to a formatter. `migrate` applies DB migrations and takes a `--to` version. `seed` must run `migrate` first, then load `fixtures/dev.jet`. `deploy` must run `build` and `test` first, then push, with `STAGE=prod` set. A first-class task surface has to cover: a name, an action, typed arguments, environment/working-dir, and one task depending on another — while colliding cleanly when someone names a task `build` (a reserved lifecycle verb) or runs a task that doesn't exist.

options.name: Tasks are functions (`#Task fn`)
options.detail: A task is an ordinary Jet function marked `#Task`, living beside `fn run()` in the package's definition file (same home as `fn build(b)` today). It reuses everything functions already have: types, `?` fallibility, typed-argument CLI parsing (D-CLIFLAG1: `fn migrate(args: MigrateArgs)` derives `--to`), and `@[Doc("...")]` help. A cross-task dependency is just a function call — no separate dependency DSL, nothing restated. `#Task` is an explicit opt-in, so only marked functions become verbs (no accidental exposure). This is the one-path (I8) answer: a task is not a new kind of thing, it is the `fn run()` mechanism generalized to a user-chosen name.
options.code:
// orbit.jet — beside fn run()
#Task
fn lint() -> Void ? {
    shell("ruff check .")?
}

#Task("apply pending migrations")
fn migrate(args: MigrateArgs) -> Void ? {
    db.migrate(to: args.to)?
}

#Task
fn seed() -> Void ? {
    migrate(MigrateArgs.{ to: "latest" })?   // dependency = a plain call
    db.seed("fixtures/dev.jet")?
}

----- run it -----
$ jetpack run seed
migrate: 3 applied
seed: loaded fixtures/dev.jet

$ jetpack run migrate --to 004
migrate: 1 applied (now at 004)

$ jetpack run migrate --help
migrate — apply pending migrations
  --to <version>   target migration (default: latest)

----- undeclared task -----
$ jetpack run deploy
error[E1234]: no task named `deploy`
 --> orbit.jet
  = declared tasks: lint, migrate, seed
  help: mark a function `#Task` to make it runnable

----- collision with a reserved lifecycle verb -----
#Task
fn build() { ... }
error[E1235]: `build` is a built-in lifecycle verb, not a task name
 --> orbit.jet:12
  = reserved: run, dev, build, test
  help: rename it, e.g. `#Task fn build_assets()`

options.name: Shell-string map (`tasks:` in pkg.jet)
options.detail: A `tasks:` field in `pkg.jet` maps a name to a shell-command string, exactly like npm `scripts` or a bare `just` recipe. Zero Jet code, instantly familiar. But: the value is an opaque string (no types, no `--flag` parsing, typos surface only at runtime), it shells out for everything, and it is a SECOND way to "run something" alongside `fn run()` — the project now has two unrelated command surfaces. Dependencies aren't expressible except by re-typing a command inside another, which is exactly the repetition the owner cuts.

options.name: Structured recipe entries with `needs:` (just/turbo style)
options.detail: A `tasks:` field in `pkg.jet` maps a name to a typed struct — the same manifest-data shape as `deps:`/`targets:` — carrying `run:`, a declared `needs:` dependency list, plus optional `env:`/`cwd:`. `run:` is a shell string (or a reference to a `#Task fn`). This gives a real, ordered dependency DAG the runner can print and parallelize, and keeps command config declarative and greppable. Cost: it is still a data-DSL distinct from `fn run()` (a second command surface), and `run:` as a string reintroduces the untyped/no-flag-parsing limits of B for the common case.
options.code:
// pkg.jet
tasks: {
    lint:    { run: "ruff check ." },
    migrate: { run: "orbit-db migrate --to latest" },
    seed:    { run: "orbit-db seed fixtures/dev.jet", needs: [migrate] },
    deploy:  { run: "orbit-db deploy",
               needs: [build, test],
               env:  { STAGE: "prod" } },
}

----- run it (DAG is shown) -----
$ jetpack run seed
» migrate   (needed by seed)
» seed

----- unknown dependency -----
$ jetpack run seed
error[E1236]: task `seed` needs `migrat`, which isn't a task
 --> pkg.jet
  help: did you mean `migrate`?

----- collision with a reserved lifecycle verb -----
tasks: { build: { run: "..." } }
error[E1235]: `build` is a built-in lifecycle verb, not a task name

options.name: Convention dispatch (any `pub fn` is a verb)
options.detail: No marker and no manifest field: any top-level `pub fn` in the package's definition file automatically becomes an invokable verb; private functions stay internal; dependencies are plain calls. Maximum ceremony-free — write a function, make it `pub`, run it. But visibility now does double duty: a helper you export for code reuse silently becomes a CLI command, renaming a `pub fn` is a breaking CLI change, and `pub fn run` collides with the entry point. It makes the footgun the default (I8/kill-criteria) — exposure is implicit, the opposite of a safe opt-in.

comparisons.note: String map in package.json; the familiar baseline (option B). No types, no arg parsing, dependencies via `&&`/`pre`/`post` string chaining.
Dedicated recipe file with first-class dependencies (informs option C's `needs:`). Recipes are shell by default; deps are named, not restated.
The Rust ecosystem's answer to 'tasks should be real typed code, not shell strings' — a normal binary with typed args (informs option A). No bespoke DSL; automation is just the language.
Declares a task dependency graph (`dependsOn`) and runs it in order/parallel — the value option C/A's dependency modeling captures.

decisions.title: On-demand tool execution: ephemeral run + persistent global install surface
decisions.gist: How a user runs a package's binary without adding it as a project dependency — one-off (npx/uvx-style) and installed-globally-on-PATH (pipx/cargo-install/uv-tool-style) — and what verb surface both live under.
decisions.explainer: Option A - a unified jetpack tool run|install|list|uninstall noun. It gives the beginner one discoverable place (jetpack tool <tab> reveals both surfaces, so nobody has to know the npx-vs-pipx-vs-cargo-install split), and it gives the expert a hard isolation guarantee for free by making install an ergonomic entrypoint over the ratified profile engine (D-JPK-PROFILE1): every installed tool is its own atomic generation with rollback and an exact environment, never a host-PATH overlay and never a second store. It is one canonical path (I8) and it disentangles the jetpack run overload instead of deepening it (which is B's and especially D's cost); C leaves the filed beginner hole open. The choice is grounded in discoverability and isolation, not in how much work each surface is.
decisions.story: Priya clones a Jet repo on a fresh machine. She wants to format it with prettier once, without polluting the project's manifest — the npx reflex. She also wants ripgrep and ruff on PATH on every machine she touches, the pipx/cargo-install reflex. Coming from npm/pip she expects one obvious command for each, and she expects jetpack <tab> to show her the way rather than reading docs to learn which of four bespoke tools (npx? pipx? brew? cargo install?) applies. Nothing in jetpack answers her today beyond the nix-only one-shot.
decisions.inWild:
# inside a Jet project that already declares tasks in pkg.jet (#476):
#   tasks: { fmt: "...", serve: "..." }
#
# Priya wants three things, none of which should touch pkg.jet:
#   1. run prettier once over src/
#   2. put ripgrep + ruff on PATH for good
#   3. NOT accidentally clobber the project's own `serve` task with a global tool named serve

options.name: Unified `jetpack tool` noun: run / install / list / uninstall (uv-style)
options.detail: One noun groups both surfaces. jetpack tool run <ref> executes a package's binary ephemerally across ALL providers (generalizing today's nix-only jetpack run); jetpack tool install <ref> adds the package to the user's default profile (D-JPK-PROFILE1) and projects its bins onto PATH as its own generation; jetpack tool list / uninstall manage them. One mental model replaces npx+pipx+cargo-install+brew. It also cleanly separates the two meanings that jetpack run overloads today: jetpack run = run THIS project, jetpack tool run = run an external tool. Fits the grouped-surface direction raised on #468 (D-CLI-SURFACE1). Naming sub-menu for the noun if 'tool' is not preferred (aviation family, all keep the same run/install/list verbs): tool (plain, uv parity) | kit | sortie (a single mission — evocative for the ephemeral half) | taxi | apron. Short ephemeral alias optional: jetpack tool run could also answer to jetpack x as a documented shorthand without adding a second concept.
options.code:
# 1. ephemeral - nothing installed, runs once, then gone
$ jetpack tool run npm:prettier -- --write src/
prettier 3.3.0  (ephemeral; cached in hangar, not on PATH)
src/app.jet  41ms

# 2. persistent global - isolated, on PATH, its own generation
$ jetpack tool install cargo:ripgrep
installed ripgrep 14.1.0  ->  ~/.jet/bin/rg   (profile "tools", generation 7)
$ jetpack tool install pypi:ruff
installed ruff 0.5.0  ->  ~/.jet/bin/ruff     (profile "tools", generation 8)

$ rg --version
ripgrep 14.1.0

$ jetpack tool list
TOOL     VERSION  SOURCE  BIN
ripgrep  14.1.0   cargo   rg
ruff     0.5.0    pypi    ruff

# 3. error - a global tool's bin would shadow this project's task (#476)
$ jetpack tool install npm:serve
error[JPK-TOOL-COLLIDE]: 'serve' is already a task in ./pkg.jet
  the project task wins in this directory, so the global tool would be shadowed here
  fix: install under a different bin name  ->  jetpack tool install npm:serve --as gserve
     or just run it once                  ->  jetpack tool run npm:serve

# rollback is free because install rode the ratified profile engine:
$ jet profile rollback tools
reverted profile "tools" to generation 7  (ruff removed from PATH)

options.name: Two flat verbs: `jetpack x <ref>` (ephemeral) + `jetpack global add/rm/list` (persistent)
options.detail: Two separate top-level verbs, each matching a specific reflex. jetpack x is the short npx/bunx muscle-memory verb for one-off runs; jetpack global is the pipx/cargo-install verb for on-PATH installs. Persistent installs still ride the ratified profile engine underneath (default profile), so rollback/isolation are identical to A - only the surface differs. Wins on the shortest possible ephemeral keystroke (jetpack x prettier). Costs: two unrelated verbs for one concept (on-demand external tools), which pushes AGAINST the #468 grouped-surface direction, and x is opaque to a reader who does not already know npx.
options.code:
# ephemeral - shortest keystroke
$ jetpack x npm:prettier -- --write src/
prettier 3.3.0  (ephemeral)  41ms

# persistent global
$ jetpack global add cargo:ripgrep
installed ripgrep 14.1.0  ->  ~/.jet/bin/rg   (profile "tools", generation 7)
$ jetpack global add pypi:ruff
installed ruff 0.5.0  ->  ~/.jet/bin/ruff

$ jetpack global list
ripgrep  14.1.0  cargo
ruff     0.5.0   pypi

# same collision, but the answer is split across two unrelated verbs
$ jetpack global add npm:serve
error[JPK-TOOL-COLLIDE]: 'serve' is already a task in ./pkg.jet
  fix: jetpack global add npm:serve --as gserve
     or run once: jetpack x npm:serve

$ jetpack global rm ruff
removed ruff  (profile "tools", generation 9)

options.name: Ephemeral now; defer global install to the existing profile engine
options.detail: Ship only the ephemeral half now (jetpack tool run <ref>, all providers), and give NO new install verb - 'install a tool globally' is served by the already-ratified profile engine directly: the user declares a profile.tools and switches to it. A defensible 'ship half now' because global install genuinely already has a home (D-JPK-PROFILE1). Cost: the beginner reflex 'just install this one tool on PATH' has no one-liner - Priya must learn to author a profile block and run jet profile switch, which is real ceremony for a one-tool need and exactly the discoverability hole this card was filed to close. A follow-up ballot could add the install ergonomic later.
options.code:
# ephemeral half ships now, all providers
$ jetpack tool run npm:prettier -- --write src/
prettier 3.3.0  (ephemeral)  41ms

# global install? no verb - use the ratified engine by hand:
$ cat >> env.jet <<'EOF'
profile.tools {
    packages: { ripgrep: cargo:ripgrep, ruff: pypi:ruff }
}
EOF
$ jet profile switch tools
built profile "tools" generation 7  ->  ~/.jet/bin/{rg,ruff}

$ rg --version
ripgrep 14.1.0

# there is no `jetpack tool install one-tool` shortcut in this option

options.name: Fold both into the existing `jetpack run <source>:<pkg>` bridge with a persistence flag
options.detail: No new noun or verb at all. Generalize today's jetpack run nixpkgs:fastfetch to every provider (ephemeral by default) and add a flag - --global (or --keep) - to make a run persist on PATH via the profile engine. Smallest possible surface: one verb, one flag. Cost: a run that silently leaves something installed is a surprising overload of the word 'run', and it collides head-on with the OTHER meaning of jetpack run (run this project / a task from #476). Listing and removing installed tools then have no natural home under a run verb, so --list/--uninstall bolt awkwardly onto a run command.
options.code:
# ephemeral (default), now all providers
$ jetpack run cargo:ripgrep -- --version
ripgrep 14.1.0  (ephemeral)

# persistent via a flag on the same verb
$ jetpack run cargo:ripgrep --global
installed ripgrep 14.1.0  ->  ~/.jet/bin/rg   (profile "tools", generation 7)

# overload problem: which `run` is this in a project dir?
$ jetpack run serve
#   the project's `serve` task, or an external package named serve? ambiguous

# managing installs has no clean verb:
$ jetpack run --list-global
ripgrep  14.1.0  cargo

comparisons.note: One noun, two verbs, one mental model: uv tool run (a.k.a. uvx) for ephemeral, uv tool install for persistent, each installed tool isolated in its own environment. Directly the shape of Option A; its uvx shorthand is the optional jetpack x alias.
comparisons.code:
uv tool run ruff check .
uv tool install ruff
uv tool list

comparisons.note: Ephemeral-only, each a separate bespoke command (npx, pnpm dlx, bunx) with no unified persistent-install sibling - the fragmentation Priya is escaping. There is no 'npm global tool' story that isolates cleanly; global npm installs share one flat prefix and collide.
comparisons.code:
npx prettier --write src/
bunx prettier --write src/

comparisons.note: Persistent-only, each isolated-ish but a different tool per ecosystem, and none has a first-class ephemeral sibling (pipx run is the exception, mirroring uv). Reinforces that the beginner today must know which of four tools applies - the discoverability hole Option A closes with one noun.
comparisons.code:
pipx install ruff
cargo install ripgrep
brew install ripgrep

decisions.title: Concurrency model for Go-scale networking: green-threads/M:N over task+channel, or add @async/await?
decisions.gist: Epoch 3 requires an async runtime capable of 100k+ concurrent connections. The shipped model teaches tasks and channels; the question is whether to keep that model and add an M:N scheduler under it, or introduce @async/await coloring. This is the keystone Epoch 3 decision — coroutines, structured concurrency, and deadline cards all depend on it.
decisions.explainer: The function-color problem (async infects call sites) is the core tradeoff. @async/await requires every function that awaits to be marked, propagating annotation up the call graph — the 'color' spreads. Green-threads / M:N scheduling makes all tasks implicitly concurrent; blocking calls yield automatically; no call-site annotation. Jet already ships `task { }` and channels; green-threads extend that model with a scheduler, not a new surface. @async/await introduces new syntax (D-level decision), a new execution model, and a bifurcated function space — a second way to mean 'this function may yield' next to the task model, which violates I8. A hybrid adds both costs. This decision must be made before coroutines-prim, structured-concurrency, or deadline cards proceed.
decisions.story: I write a server that handles 100,000 simultaneous WebSocket connections. I don't want to mark half my functions `@async` just because they read from a socket. I want to write normal-looking code and have the runtime handle the concurrency.

options.name: Green-threads / M:N scheduler under the task+channel model
options.detail: Add an M:N thread scheduler to the runtime. `task { }` blocks become green-thread yields; socket/IO calls park the task and wake it on readiness. No new surface syntax; no function coloring; the existing task/channel API gains concurrency scale without user changes. Matches Go's goroutine approach. Aligns with the shipped teaching model.

options.name: @async/await + futures
options.detail: Add `@async fn` and `await` expressions. Explicit at every call site that yields; type system tracks async-ness. Functions bifurcate into async/non-async. Introduces function coloring and a second 'this yields' mechanism alongside tasks — I8 tension. Familiar to Rust/JS developers.

options.name: Hybrid: M:N scheduler + @async opt-in for fine-grained control
options.detail: Ship the M:N green-thread scheduler (option A) as the default; allow `@async fn` for callers who need explicit future/poll control (e.g. embedding in C event loops). Two mechanisms for yielding — violates I8 unless the `@async` path is kept to an expert escape hatch with a narrow, documented use case.

comparisons.note: Go's goroutines are the green-thread / M:N model: write normal blocking code, the scheduler handles concurrency. No function coloring; 100k+ goroutines are routine.
Rust uses async/await + a future executor. Every async call site must be marked; function color propagates. High performance, but the bifurcation is a known ergonomics cost.
BEAM spawns millions of lightweight processes (green-threads) with no async annotation. Concurrent IO is the default; no function color. The closest prior art to option A at scale.
comparisons.code:
handle(Socket) ->
    {ok, Data} = gen_tcp:recv(Socket, 0),
    gen_tcp:send(Socket, process(Data)),
    handle(Socket).

decisions.gist: M:N green threads are decided. This card chooses the runtime implementation behind blocking-looking socket/file APIs. It is not user syntax: user code keeps `task { }`, channels, and ordinary reads/writes.
decisions.story: Gary runs a chat server with 50,000 open TCP connections. Most sockets are idle. `socket.read()` should park the Jet task and free the OS thread until the socket is ready, without Gary learning epoll, kqueue, or IOCP.

comparisons.note: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.

options.name: Own platform-native backends (recommended)
options.detail: Implement Linux io_uring/epoll, macOS/BSD kqueue, and Windows IOCP behind one runtime trait. No external event-loop dependency. Highest ceiling and matches Go/BEAM shape: one scheduler, native pollers, task parking, timers, cancellation, and metrics under Jet control.

options.name: Own portable poller first
options.detail: Start with epoll/kqueue/IOCP readiness only; defer `io_uring` batching. Still no external dependency and simpler to test, but leaves Linux peak throughput on the table.

options.name: Use libuv through C FFI
options.detail: Battle-tested portability. Requires explicit owner approval for a runtime external C dependency and a system-library story. Good fallback if owned backends stall, but not the best Jet identity.

decisions.recReason: Owning native backends gives Jet the highest performance ceiling, no foreign event-loop dependency, and full observability/control for the task-scope/task runtime. It keeps the user surface unchanged while letting experts tune the runtime.
decisions.title: Which OS readiness backend parks M:N tasks on I/O?
decisions.explainer: The scheduler needs one park/wake layer per platform. The decision is between owning native backends, owning a lowest-common-denominator poller, or depending on libuv. I6 matters: compiler Source has zero external crates, and runtime-side deps still need owner approval. The E3 goal is better-than-Go networking, so the backend must support task-per-connection scale, O(ready events) wakeups, low allocation pressure, and runtime observability.
decisions.bestCurrent: Go: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.
decisions.recommendation: Build own platform-native backends. Jet needs Go-class scaling as the floor and a higher ceiling through native pollers, structured cancellation, deadlines, and runtime metrics.

decisions.title: M:N tasks, select, channels, and timers
decisions.gist: Choose how Core finishes the task runtime without fragmenting concurrency.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Go-level concurrency capacity with structured ownership and testable typed events.
decisions.story: Lena writes a server with 100k connections. She needs bounded channels, select, timers, cancellation, and task groups that stay structured and testable.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Go-level concurrency capacity with structured ownership and testable typed events.

options.name: Hybrid: structured scopes, select values, and Go-scale runtime (recommended)
options.detail: Task groups remain the lifetime boundary. Channels, timers, deadlines, cancellation, and select all produce typed event values. The runtime can multiplex many tasks, but user code stays structured; expert hooks expose scheduler budgets, tracing, and deterministic test control.

options.name: Async/await future model
options.detail: Familiar in TS/Rust, but v1 explicitly avoids async/await and exposes more ceremony to beginners.
options.code: async fn serve() { await socket.read() }

options.name: Threads plus channels only
options.detail: Simpler mental model but cannot hit Go-scale concurrency efficiently.
options.code: thread.spawn(() => serve(conn))

comparisons.note: Goroutines/channels/select define the ergonomic target.
Structured concurrency/coroutines show the safety model.

decisions.title: Jet shell prompt — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: How the jet env prompt communicates: on demand, always, or only when something changed.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — adaptive's silence as the default, minimal's pull and segments' awareness both available the moment you want them, never before. One status mechanism, three entrypoints (I8).
decisions.story: Sam works four hours inside `jet env` and glances at the prompt hundreds of times. The real choice is a communication policy, not a look: pull (silent until asked), push-always (segments answer every question before he asks), or push-on-event (silence is the all-clear; the prompt speaks once when a build fails or a job runs). All ≤2 lines, one shared theme. Browse: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#prompt (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env
── web-api · dev shell ─────────────────────────
# hours of: edit → jet build → jet test → glance
$ jet build    # fails — how loudly should the prompt say so?
$ jet bench    # runs 90s — how does the prompt show it's alive?
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid prompt, but show the environment name by default and show at least a partial current path for navigation. Keep adaptive status behavior, ^G glance, transient receipts, and opt-in status strip, but the base prompt is not anonymous/bare: it should include env name plus compact path context before the prompt mark.

options.name: Minimal — silent until asked (pull)
options.detail:
Core loop: the prompt stays out of the way until you ask it for status. One line: env marker + chevron; the only persistent signal is the chevron's exit state (green ok / red + code). One keystroke (^G) expands a single dim line with last build/test, then it collapses. For people who want zero prompt noise and are willing to ask. NO_COLOR: chevron color becomes an ok / x N tag.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/prompt/minimal.html
options.code:
web-api ❯ jet test
12 passed
web-api ❯ jet run           (chevron green: last exit 0)
…server exited 1
web-api ❯ 1                 (chevron red + code: last exit 1)
web-api ❯                   (press ^G to glance ↓)
        build ok · 0.4s     test 12/12 · 8ms ago
NO_COLOR:  web-api ok ❯     web-api x 1 ❯

options.name: Segments — everything on, every prompt (push-always)
options.detail:
Core loop: a glance answers every status question before you type. A second info line carries always-on segments — env · jet version · build · test · git — each one truth, color-coded, words not glyphs (so NO_COLOR holds: `build ✗ E0112`, `test stale`, `main •1`). Finished commands collapse to a one-line receipt so history stays skimmable. Costs one extra line every prompt; segments drop right-to-left on narrow terminals.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/prompt/segments.html
options.code:
web-api ❯ jet test                          ✓ 12/12 · 0.3s   (collapsed)
web-api · jet 0.1.0 · build ok · test 12/12 · main ✓
❯ _

after a failed build:
web-api ❯ jet build                         ✗ E0112 · 0.2s
web-api · jet 0.1.0 · build ✗ E0112 · test stale · main •1
❯ _

options.name: Adaptive — speaks only on change (push-on-event)
options.detail:
Core loop: the prompt speaks only when something changed. Clean shell = bare chevron; a running job shows one live spinner line that collapses when done; a failure inserts exactly one line phrased as the next action with a runnable command, gone on your next input. Success adds nothing — silence is the signal. The action line is prompt copy, never a restated diagnostic (I4-safe: it points and hands a command). Needs a build/test event feed; reduced motion freezes the spinner.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/prompt/adaptive.html
options.code:
❯                            (clean: bare chevron)
❯ jet test
⠹ running tests · 6/12 · 0.2s          (live, then collapses)
❯ jet test
12 passed                    (success: prompt adds nothing)
❯

on failure — one inserted action line:
❯ jet test
11 passed · 1 failed
→ 1 test failed. Rerun just it: jet test url_parse
❯
NO_COLOR: spinner ⠹ stays; arrow → degrades to ->

options.name: Hybrid — silent default, pulled and opt-in status
options.detail:
Core loop: the prompt stays silent until something changes — then it shows exactly one line — while ^G pulls a status glance on demand and a per-env flag can pin an always-on strip. Takes: adaptive's foundation (bare chevron, live spinner line, one next-action line on failure) + segments' transient receipts (cmd ✓/✗ · duration) and its always-on strip demoted to opt-in env.jet config + minimal's ^G glance. Left out: the colored-chevron status channel (redundant next to the action line, I8) and always-on segments as default (contradicts silence-is-the-signal). Both status entrypoints render identical words so they can never disagree.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/prompt/hybrid.html
options.code:
❯                                   (clean: bare chevron)
❯ jet test
⠹ running tests · 6/12 · 0.2s       (live, then collapses)
❯ jet test                          ✓ 12/12 · 0.3s   (receipt)
❯

on failure — receipt + one action line:
❯ jet test                          ✗ 11/12 · 0.3s
11 passed · 1 failed
→ 1 test failed. Rerun just it: jet test url_parse
❯

^G glance (pulled, collapses next command):
        build ok · 0.4s     test 12/12 · 8ms ago

opt-in strip (env.jet: prompt.strip = on):
web-api · jet 0.1.0 · build ok · test 12/12 · main ✓
❯ _
NO_COLOR: spinner ⠹ stays; → degrades to ->; receipts are words.

comparisons.note: B builds on its segment model and transient collapse; A and C reuse only the transient collapse and last-exit glyph.
A and C's philosophy: the shell stays minimal and truthful; state you didn't ask about stays out of the way.

decisions.comment: Hybrid prompt, but env name and partial path visible by default for navigation.

decisions.title: jet env prompt status strip config
decisions.gist: How users opt into the always-on prompt status strip.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-PROMPT1 ratified hybrid prompt behavior and kept an optional status strip, but the exact user-facing config key is not ratified. Existing env config already has a simple prompt label. This chooses the one config surface for prompt depth without creating multiple prompt mechanisms.
decisions.story: Doris works in a monorepo where she wants every prompt to show build/test/git state. Walter wants the default quiet prompt with env name and path only. Both should use the same env.jet mechanism, not shell-specific dotfiles.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: default prompt needs no config and already shows env name plus path. Expert pass: teams need a reviewed env.jet switch for always-on status. Hybrid pass: one prompt engine with a mode field is cleaner than shell-specific flags or a second prompt file.

options.name: No config; default prompt only for now
options.detail: Implement env name + path and adaptive receipts, but omit the optional always-on strip. This avoids new config surface, but drops a ratified hybrid depth and forces teams into shell-local customization.

options.name: Structured prompt config in env.jet (recommended)
options.detail: Keep `prompt: "name"` as the beginner shorthand. Add `prompt: Prompt.{ label: "web-api", strip: .On, path: .Short }` for expert control. One env.jet-owned prompt engine handles default, glance, and strip words across shells.

options.name: Shell environment variable opt-in
options.detail: Use JET_PROMPT_STRIP=1 or per-shell rc overrides. Easy to test locally, but not source-reviewed in env.jet and differs by shell/session.
options.code:
JET_PROMPT_STRIP=1 jet env web
# shell-local, not part of project env source

comparisons.note: Prompt behavior is configured in a dedicated file, outside project language semantics.
Project env behavior comes from reviewed project files, but shell prompt customization is usually external.
shellHook can customize PS1, but it is raw shell code and not a typed project setting.

decisions.title: Add generic modules (ML-functor-style module parameterized by a type or value)?
decisions.gist: Jet has generic types and functions. Generic modules — a module parameterized by a type or value at the module level, instantiated to produce a new module — do not exist. This decides whether to add them or keep the surface at generic types and functions only.
decisions.explainer: ML-style functors let you write `module Map(K: Ord)` and instantiate it as `module IntMap = Map(Int)`. The result is a new module with all members specialized to `K = Int`. In Jet, generic types already handle the common case (`Map[K: Ord, V]`); generic modules go further by allowing module-level abstraction (sharing multiple related types, hiding implementation modules, enforcing interface contracts at the module boundary). Under I8, if generic types already cover the use case, a second mechanism is a strike. The complexity is high: module instantiation affects name resolution, the module graph, and comptime. There is no ratified syntax precedent in Jet for module-level generics.
decisions.story: I'm building a pluggable hash-map where the key comparison strategy is a module (not just a function). I want `module HashMap(K: KeyModule)` where `KeyModule` supplies `hash`, `eq`, and an associated `Error` type — none of which are cleanly expressible as a single generic type parameter.

options.name: Add generic modules (ML-functor style)
options.detail: Ratify module-level parameterization. A module can declare type/value parameters; instantiation produces a new named module. Requires new syntax, new name-resolution rules, and comptime integration. Only justified if a concrete use case cannot be served by generic types alone.

options.name: Keep generic types and functions only (status quo)
options.detail: The existing `Type[T: Trait]` and `fn foo[T: Trait]()` cover the overwhelming majority of parameterization needs. Module-level generics add complexity for a narrow use case. Reject until a concrete case proves generic types are insufficient. I8-clean.

options.name: Defer pending concrete use case
options.detail: Don't reject outright — park the card until a real Jet codebase hits the wall with generic types and functions and needs functor-level abstraction. Then revisit with a concrete motivating example.
options.code:
// deferred: no syntax or implementation
// reopen when a concrete stdlib or user case requires it

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are the canonical ML-functor. `module Map.Make(Ord)` produces a map module specialized to `Ord.t`. Widely used but notoriously hard to read for newcomers.
comparisons.code:
module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)
let m = IntMap.add 1 "one" IntMap.empty

comparisons.note: Rust has no module generics — generic types and traits cover the use case. This is the status-quo model Jet already follows; it has proven sufficient for a production systems language.
comparisons.code:
// No generic modules; use generic structs + traits:
struct HashMap<K: [Hash, Eq], V> { ... }

decisions.title: What exact syntax distinguishes generic-module type parameters, value parameters, and instantiation?
decisions.gist: Before choosing a spelling: resolve the conflict with D-GENMOD1's floor example (paren type params) and D-LINALG1's blessed `<N>` value-in-angles. The current option set contains no choice that is consistent with both prior decisions simultaneously. A new option (annotation-kind in `<...>`, no extra keyword) resolves both. The "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling may also close Options A–C entirely; confirm its scope before proceeding.
decisions.explainer: Owner instruction integrated: Jet generics use `<T>`, so generic modules must not invent `[]` for type parameters. Adversarial pass: mixing type and value parameters can become C++-template soup or force users to guess whether an argument is a type or value. Patch: keep type parameters in `<...>`, keep compile-time value parameters in `(...)`, and require instantiation to mirror declaration. If that still feels too large for E3, choose the Epoch 6 defer option and keep ordinary generic structs/functions as the only generic surface for now.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a fixed-size LRU cache package. The key type controls hashing/equality, while the capacity is a compile-time value. She wants one generic module that exports `Cache`, `put`, and `get`, then instantiates `StringCache32` once for the rest of the package.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Address GENMOD2; integrate the instruction that Jet generics use `<T>`, provide better options, and include an option to defer to Epoch 6.
Agent answer: Corrected. The previous `[]` type-parameter option was wrong for Jet because `[]` already reads as list/indexing while `<T>` is the ratified generic form. Updated options now center `<T>` for type parameters, separate compile-time value parameters with `(...)`, and add an Epoch 6 defer option.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIOR DECISION CONFLICTS (must resolve before any option is adopted): D-GENMOD1's ratified code example uses `module Sorted(T: Ord)` — type param in parens; Option A contradicts this. D-LINALG1 blessed Vec<N> (value-in-<...>) as the substrate spelling; Option A puts values in (...), directly contradicting. The comptime section of syntax-decisions.md says "Rejected: const generics in v1" — module value parameters are const generics and this rejection may apply. PARSER HAZARD (Option A): `Lru<String>(32)` is syntactically identical to D-SERDE6 turbofish `fn<T>(arg)`; parser cannot resolve without name-resolution, violating parse-before-sema. VOCABULARY HAZARD (Option B): `const` is a teaching-error-only keyword (S14); using it inside `<...>` is the first real use. MISSING OPTION E: unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` with annotation-kind as distinguisher — consistent with D-LINALG1, avoids all vocabulary collisions.

options.name: Unified `<...>`: annotation kind distinguishes type vs value params (recommended)
options.detail: Both type and value parameters live in `<...>`. A parameter whose annotation is a bound/trait (`K: Hash`) is a type parameter; one whose annotation is a value type (`capacity: Int`) is a value parameter — no extra keyword, no dual-bracket syntax. Instantiation mirrors declaration: `Lru<String, 32>`. Consistent with D-LINALG1's `Vec<N>` substrate (value-in-angles already blessed). Supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example which used parens — that was explicitly a placeholder "until GENMOD2 decides." Parser: distinguishes a type expression (capital-cased, D-CASING1) from a value expression at instantiation sites in `<...>` — mostly mechanical at the lexer level.

options.name: Defer generic modules to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not add module-level type/value parameters now. Ordinary generic structs and functions (`fn sort<T: Ord>`, `struct Vec<T>`) already cover most use cases. Defer if the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling in the comptime section applies to module value parameters, or if the D-LINALG1 `Vec<N>` value-parameter surface needs a unified ruling before any single site commits.

options.name: Ordinary generic types/fns only — no module-level parameters
options.detail: Decline generic modules entirely. Priya's LRU cache is a generic struct with a capacity field; the type-level instantiation story is solved by generic types already. Module-level parameters are a second mechanism for the same parametrization job (I8 risk). Only reconsider if a concrete use case cannot be expressed with generic types.

comparisons.note: Rust uses `<T>` for type parameters and also has const generics in `<...>`. Good precedent for Option B, but Jet should avoid forcing values into type syntax unless needed.
C++ templates mix type and value parameters in angle brackets. Powerful, but visually dense and a known complexity sink.
comparisons.code: template<typename K, int N> struct Lru { ... };

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are module-level generics, but parameters are module-shaped. Powerful, less beginner-direct than Jet’s desired package surface.
Zig uses comptime parameters in function-like declarations; clear for values, but Jet already has `<T>` for type generics.
comparisons.code: fn Lru(comptime K: type, comptime capacity: usize) type { ... }

decisions.recommendation: Unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` — annotation kind distinguishes type vs value parameters in `<...>` (Option A). Consistent with D-LINALG1's Vec<N>; supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example. If the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling applies, choose Option B (defer).

decisions.title: REPL Core effect authorization
decisions.gist: Choose how existing Jet effects are authorized inside the REPL.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has one effect language: D-EFF4's roots, D-EFFTREE1 paths, lexical #Grant regions, and invocation policy through the existing --allow-fs/--allow-env/--allow-exec/--allow-net/--allow-io/--allow-time/--allow-rand flags. This ballot adds no REPL-specific grant names, grant commands, or persistent permission store. All options keep Core's current static bare-root tags; they do not globally retag Core with compiler-minted leaves. Dynamic capability data distinguishes resources and operations beneath a statically proven root. Thus an Env capability may permit reading HOME but not writing HOME; an Exec capability for one pinned Exec.Run target never permits Exec.Exit; an Io capture channel never permits terminal input. The canonical REPL filesystem root is fixed once: `jet repl --project DIR` uses the canonical project root, otherwise the process's starting cwd. The evaluator opens that root as a directory handle before accepting input. A symlink used to reach the starting location is resolved once when opening the root; later path components are descriptor-relative and no-follow. Because `core.os` has no current static effect root and this ballot does not retag Core, every `core.os` operation remains native-only E1802 in the REPL, including host facts and `set_current_dir`; therefore evaluated code cannot mutate cwd, and the fixed root handle never changes. --allow-fs is only the existing Fs invocation ceiling and never broadens reach beyond that fixed root. Every file operation uses verified handles; if the platform cannot enforce race-safe confinement it fails closed. Process execution pins executable identity before authorization, never re-resolves PATH, uses a verified cwd and minimal declared environment, bounds time, forwards interrupt, kills/reaps children, and separately authorizes redirects. Network authority pins scheme, hostname, port, and resolved addresses; redirects or new DNS results require fresh authority. Env.Read and Env.Write are dynamically separate exact-key resources under bare Env; session authorization for one key/direction never covers another. Ambient Time operations (wall clock, local zone, sleep, stopwatch/instant) require Time; a Clock created from an explicit seed/value is injected data and needs no ambient authority. Ambient/OS and secure randomness require Rand; an explicitly seeded Rng is injected data and needs none. `core.crypto.random` remains E1802 while it is native-only; if the interpreter gains it, it follows secure Rand policy. REPL-owned stdout/stderr capture is inherent evaluator plumbing: print/eprint and subprocess Capture write only to the REPL's captured output and require no runtime Io authority. Reading stdin, raw terminal access, inheriting/streaming a subprocess terminal, or redirecting to an external stream requires #Grant(Io) plus Io policy. A subprocess file redirect requires Fs for the verified file handle; Capture alone grants neither Io nor Fs. FFI, tasks, raw memory, display/UI backends, servers, and other native-only facilities remain E1802. Missing lexical authority remains E0712. E1802 remains only for unavailable interpreter features. This decision allocates E1803 to REPL runtime-policy denial, missing invocation policy, or confinement failure after lexical proof. E1803 must be registered in diagnostics with what/why/fix and pinned by a UI snapshot before implementation uses it.
decisions.story: Maya is learning Jet in a cloned service. She wraps a config read in the same #Grant(Fs) construct used by checked programs, then pastes a formatter command. Static checking proves which effect roots the turn can reach, but the REPL must still decide which real project file or executable that erased capability may touch. Maya needs the safe choice explained at the moment it matters. Dev needs the same effect proof with explicit invocation flags in a scripted session, without learning a REPL-only authorization system.

options.name: Prompted invocation policy
options.detail: Require an enclosing #Grant(root) for every effectful turn. In an interactive TTY, when the corresponding existing --allow-root policy was not supplied, pause before each not-yet-authorized external operation and offer once, session, or deny. Once covers exactly the displayed operation/resource tuple and is discarded before execution, so success or failure cannot retain it. Session stores exactly `(root effect, operation kind, resource identity/scope)` in memory: Env.Read HOME does not cover Env.Write HOME, Exec.Run tool A does not cover tool B or Exec.Exit, and a multi-resource turn prompts separately in execution order before performing each newly reached operation. On reuse, the same authorization preflight names the matching session allowance and offers continue or revoke; revoke deletes that tuple before the operation and returns to once/session/deny. This prompt/preflight is the sole inspection and revocation surface, not a second permission mechanism. All session tuples disappear on REPL exit or restart. Existing --allow-root flags skip ordinary root prompts for that invocation but do not relax confinement or lexical #Grant; non-TTY never prompts and requires the corresponding flag. Exec.Exit is never subsumed by Exec.Run, a session tuple, or --allow-exec: every interactive exit gets a separate `[y/N]` consequence prompt, while non-TTY requires #Grant(Exec) plus --allow-exec and exits without prompting. Recommended: beginner authority stays contextual and safe, experts get auditable flags, and both use Jet's one effect model. All shared confinement, pinning, Env, Time, Rand, Io, diagnostic, and native-only invariants above apply. Process Capture is inherent REPL output; Inherit/Stream/file redirects require their separately proven Io/Fs roots and policies.
options.code:
$ jet repl --project /work/api
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Core effect Fs requests runtime authority before this operation.
  operation: read
  target:    config.toml
  confined:  /work/api (descriptor-relative, no symlinks)
  [o] once  [s] exact tuple for this session  [d] deny
s
port = 8080 : Result

user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Using session Fs.Read authority for `config.toml`. [c] continue  [r] revoke
c
port = 8080 : Result

user> use core.env as env
ok
user> #Grant(Env) { caps -> env.get("HOME") }
Core effect Env requests runtime authority: Read key HOME. [o] once  [s] exact tuple for session  [d] deny
s
/work/api : Option
user> #Grant(Env) { caps -> env.set("HOME", "/tmp") }
Core effect Env requests runtime authority: Write key HOME. [o] once  [s] exact tuple for session  [d] deny
d
Error [E1803]: Env.Write for `HOME` was denied
 Why: session authority covers Env.Read for this key, not mutation
 Fix: choose once or session only if this write is intended

user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.run(["jet", "fmt", "build/preview.jet"]) }
Core effect Exec requests runtime authority before this operation.
  executable: /work/api/.jet/toolchain/bin/jet (identity pinned)
  argv:       jet fmt build/preview.jet
  cwd:        /work/api
  env:        minimal declared environment
  timeout:    30s
  redirects:  Capture (inherent REPL output; no Io grant)
  [o] once  [s] exact Exec.Run tuple for session  [d] deny
o
ProcessResult(code: 0, output: , errors: ) : Result

user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(7) }
Core effect Exec requests orderly REPL exit with status 7. [y/N]
y
# terminal restored; children reaped; REPL exits 7

$ printf 'use core.files as files\n#Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }\n' | jet repl --allow-fs
port = 8080 : Result

options.name: Flags only
options.detail: Require #Grant(root) in the turn and the corresponding existing --allow-root flag at REPL startup. Never prompt and never persist policy. The flag opens only that bare-root invocation ceiling; each lexical capability remains dynamically narrowed to the concrete operation/resource. All shared confinement, root fixation, process/network pinning, Env key/direction, Time/Clock, Rand/Rng, Io/Capture, diagnostic, and native-only invariants above apply independently. Thus --allow-env plus #Grant(Env) may perform the exact Env.Read/Env.Write operation reached, seeded Clock/Rng need no flag, Capture needs no --allow-io, Inherit/Stream need #Grant(Io) plus --allow-io, and a file redirect also needs #Grant(Fs) plus --allow-fs. A missing flag reports E1803 after lexical proof. Exec.Exit is a distinct operation never obtained from an Exec.Run resource capability; under this flags-only option it requires #Grant(Exec) plus --allow-exec, performs orderly cleanup, and never prompts. Without both it cannot terminate anything. This is maximally predictable for automation and experts, but beginners must understand invocation policy before their first ambient operation.
options.code:
$ jet repl
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Error [E1803]: this REPL invocation does not allow Fs
 Why: #Grant proves lexical authority, but host policy did not pass --allow-fs
 Fix: restart with `jet repl --allow-fs`; access remains confined to the REPL root

$ jet repl --allow-fs --allow-exec
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
port = 8080 : Result
user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(0) }
# orderly exit: terminal restored, children reaped, status 0

$ printf 'use core.files as files\n#Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }\n' | jet repl --allow-fs
port = 8080 : Result

options.name: Pure REPL only
options.detail: The REPL executes pure Core plus deterministic injected Clock/Rng values only. #Grant remains valid Jet syntax, but external Fs, Env, Exec, Net, Io input, ambient Time, and ambient Rand are intentionally unavailable in this interpreter and therefore report current E1802 with the jet run/build escape. Existing --allow-* flags do not widen the REPL. No dynamic resource capabilities or persistence exist. Exec.Exit is the sole control exception: process.exit(code) does not require host Exec authority and is interpreted as an orderly REPL quit after terminal restoration; process.run/cmd/pipeline remain E1802. This draws the strongest boundary but rejects the accepted goal of exploring side-effect-safe Core in place.
options.code:
$ jet repl
user> use core.encoding.json as json
ok
user> json.parse("{\"port\":8080}")
Data(fields: [port: 8080]) : Result

user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Error [E1802]: the REPL interpreter cannot run `core.files.read()`
 Why: this option keeps external Fs unavailable even inside #Grant
 Fix: put the code in a file and use `jet run`; --allow-fs does not widen the REPL

user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(0) }
# orderly REPL quit; terminal restored

$ jet repl --allow-exec
error: --allow-exec does not widen a pure-only REPL

comparisons.note: Deno separates filesystem, environment, process, and network policy and supports prompts or flags. Jet differs by requiring its existing lexical #Grant proof as well as invocation policy, and by attaching resource limits to capability handles.
comparisons.code:
Deno: --allow-read=./config --allow-net=api.example.com
Jet: #Grant(Fs) { caps -> ... } plus --allow-fs or the option-A prompt

comparisons.note: Capability-oriented filesystems operate relative to an already-open directory handle. This avoids the check-then-open race and symlink swap that realpath-prefix sandboxes miss.
comparisons.code: root_fd -> open child component with no-follow -> operate on returned handle

comparisons.note: Common REPLs inherit ambient host authority. Pasted code can mutate files/environment, launch subprocesses, or connect to the network without a lexical capability proof.
Pure evaluation rejects ambient effects unless impurity is explicitly enabled. This informs option C and the deterministic non-TTY rule in A/B.

decisions.comment: I want to be able to use flags regardless, this way it will be better ux for people who want the language to get out of the way if they know what theyre doing

decisions.title: Place fuzz and LSP in the frequency-ringed CLI
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical homes for the two native commands omitted from D-CLI-SURFACE1's exhaustive rings.
decisions.explainer: Recommend A: fuzzing is part of the test/dev loop and stays flat; LSP is self/tooling infrastructure and moves under `jet self`. The editor integrations change atomically, and bare `jet lsp` becomes the same immediate teaching error required for every moved verb.
decisions.story: Maya fuzzes a parser before release and her editor launches Jet's language server automatically. D-CLI-SURFACE1 precisely names every flat daily verb and every grouped long-tail verb, but today's registry also contains `fuzz` and `lsp`. An implementer cannot remove, group, or retain either spelling without inventing user-facing command law.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp                 # launched by VS Code/Zed, normally not typed

# D-CLI-SURFACE1 currently assigns neither command a destination.
decisions.detail: This ballot only closes D-CLI-SURFACE1=B's two-command omission. It does not reopen its four groups, daily list, or no-alias rule. EngineDispatch front doors (`env`, `push`, `trust`, `bridge`, `services`, `image`, `os`, `config`, `outdated`, `search`, `info`, `logs`, `clean`) remain outside #468's native-verb shrink exactly as the card scoped them; existing product decisions own them. `jet ?`, help, man, completions, shell completion, editor installers, docs, tests and external-command collision checks must all read the same nested registry. A moved spelling is intercepted before external `jet-<name>` discovery, emits E2101 with What/Why/Fix, preserves all following argv verbatim in the printed replacement, exits 2, performs no action, and is never an alias. `--json` emits the existing diagnostic schema with replacement argv. No L2001 deprecation window applies: D-CLI-SURFACE1 explicitly chose teaching errors rather than compatibility aliases. Beginner pass: fuzz remains discoverable beside test; editor setup hides LSP plumbing. Expert pass: `jet self lsp --bench/doctor` retains exact flags and stdio behavior. Hybrid pass: one registry entry owns canonical argv plus migration metadata; generators cannot drift.

options.name: Flat fuzz; self lsp
options.detail: Keep `jet fuzz` in the daily developer ring. Move the machine-facing server to `jet self lsp`; update every first-party editor/installer atomically and teach the old spelling without executing it.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
   PASS  100000 cases
$ jet self lsp             # editor argv

$ jet lsp
Error [E2101]: `lsp` moved under `jet self`
 Why: language-server plumbing belongs with Jet's own tooling
 Fix: run `jet self lsp`

options.name: Self group for both
options.detail: Treat fuzzing and LSP as specialist tooling under `jet self`. This makes the flat ring smaller, but separates fuzz from `test` even though both execute test properties and share fixtures.
options.code:
$ jet self fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet self lsp

$ jet fuzz parser.jet
Error [E2101]: `fuzz` moved under `jet self`
 Fix: run `jet self fuzz parser.jet`

options.name: Keep both flat but hide LSP from human help
options.detail: Preserve current argv for integrations and fuzz users. `lsp` is marked machine-facing and omitted from ordinary help/palette unless searched exactly. This avoids a migration but leaves an undocumented top-level exception to the frequency-ring inventory.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp
# `jet help` omits lsp; `jet ? lsp` still finds it

comparisons.note: Compiler-adjacent protocol servers are commonly launched by editor configuration rather than taught as daily compiler verbs.
Fuzzing stays adjacent to the test/build developer loop even when implemented by specialist machinery.

decisions.title: C-compatible enum layout at the FFI boundary
decisions.gist: Decide whether and how a Jet enum can cross the C boundary. Today every enum at a C signature is rejected (E3203) because no C-safe layout is defined.
decisions.explainer: D-REPRC1 gave structs `#Layout(c)`. Enums have no C layout, so the C ABI stop-line (#436) hard-rejects them. C libraries use enums constantly (status codes, option flags, tagged unions), so the rejection is a real wall. Recommendation A extends the existing `#Layout(c)` mechanism — one layout family, no new sigil — with a beginner-safe default and an expert tag-width override.
decisions.story: Priya binds a C audio library. Its API returns `typedef enum { OK, UNDERRUN, DEVICE_LOST } aud_status;` and takes a configuration union tagged by another enum. In Jet she models both as ordinary enums. The compiler rejects her `#Extern module` signatures with E3203 and offers no path forward — she has to degrade both to raw I32 constants and lose exhaustiveness checking.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: C enum size is formally implementation-defined; payload enums need a tag+union lowering that C callers can actually declare. Patch: fieldless defaults to C `int` width with explicit discriminants required to match the C header's values when nonzero-based; payload enums lower to the well-defined `repr(C)` tag-plus-union form (the layout Rust standardized in RFC 2195); a growable field under `#Layout(c)` stays a compile error exactly like structs (D-REPRC1 family rule).

options.name: #Layout(c) on enums, full — fieldless and payload, expert tag override (recommended)
options.detail: Fieldless enum: C int discriminant, explicit values allowed (`Ok = 0`). Payload enum: repr(C) tag + union lowering, documented byte layout, generated C-side header comment shows the exact struct/union a C caller declares. Expert override `#Layout(c, tag: U8)` pins tag width. One mechanism, same attribute family as structs.

options.name: Fieldless only
options.detail: Fieldless enums get the C int lowering; payload enums stay rejected (E3203) with a fix-it pointing at a hand-written #Layout(c) struct + tag pattern. Covers status codes and flags; tagged unions remain manual.

options.name: Explicit tag always
options.detail: No defaults: every C-boundary enum must state its tag width (`#Layout(c, tag: I32)`). Removes the implementation-defined-int ambiguity entirely, but adds ceremony to the 95% case where C `int` is right.
options.code:
#Layout(c, tag: I32)
enum AudStatus { Ok = 0, Underrun = 1, DeviceLost = 2 }

options.name: Keep rejection
options.detail: Enums never cross the C boundary; users model C enums as Int constants or distinct I32 wrappers. No layout commitment, but every C binding loses exhaustiveness and pattern matching at the seam.
options.code:
// status quo: E3203, bind as
I32 :: aud_poll(dev)

comparisons.note: repr(C) on fieldless enums = C int; repr(C) payload enums have the RFC 2195 defined tag+union layout; repr(u8) etc. pins tag width. Option A mirrors this proven shape.
comparisons.code:
#[repr(C)] enum Status { Ok = 0, Underrun = 1 }
#[repr(C, u8)] enum Packet { Ping(i32), Data(Frame) }

comparisons.note: @objc / C-imported enums carry a fixed raw type; Swift-native enums cannot cross C without one. Same explicit-representation principle.
comparisons.code: enum Status: Int32 { case ok = 0, underrun = 1 }

comparisons.note: enum(u8) pins the tag; extern union + enum tag is the manual tagged-union form. Option C is Zig's always-explicit stance.

decisions.title: REPL persistent history policy
decisions.gist: Choose what the REPL remembers between sessions and how users search or erase it.
decisions.explainer: A gives beginners useful restart continuity while making secret retention explicit and giving experts exact disable, retention, erase, location, permission, and failure controls.
decisions.story: Maya explores a private production incident in Jet, closes her terminal, then returns tomorrow wanting useful commands back without silently retaining secrets forever.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")

options.name: Private persistent default
options.detail: Persist the latest 2,000 successfully parsed submissions per user by default. F3 opens search; `:history search text` is the textual path. `:history clear` erases the whole file. Store at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/repl-history` or the platform state-directory equivalent, owner-only; a corrupt tail is discarded with a warning. All inputs, including effectful or secret-bearing text, are retained because Jet cannot truthfully identify every secret. `JET_REPL_HISTORY=off` disables writes; `JET_REPL_HISTORY_LIMIT=N` changes retention. If storage is unavailable, continue session-only with a visible warning.
options.code:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
$ jet repl
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
› :history clear
History cleared.

options.name: Session only
options.detail: Retain submissions only in memory until exit. F3 and `:history search text` search this session; `:history clear` clears it. No file, environment override, or restart recovery exists.
options.code:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
$ jet repl
› :history search deploy
No history matches.

options.name: Opt-in persistence
options.detail: Default to session-only history. `JET_REPL_HISTORY=on` stores the latest 2,000 successfully parsed submissions at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/repl-history` or the platform state-directory equivalent, owner-only. F3 and `:history search text` search it; `:history clear` erases the whole file; `JET_REPL_HISTORY_LIMIT=N` changes retention. All inputs, including effectful or secret-bearing text, persist. A corrupt tail is discarded with a warning; unavailable storage falls back visibly to session-only.
options.code:
$ JET_REPL_HISTORY=on jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
$ JET_REPL_HISTORY=on jet repl
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")

comparisons.note: Interactive history is commonly persisted through readline configuration and searched interactively.
History persists automatically and exposes explicit search and deletion controls.

decisions.title: REPL multiline editing keys
decisions.gist: Choose how raw-terminal users edit and submit a multiline REPL entry.
decisions.explainer: A preserves instant one-line use, derives the default from Jet syntax instead of modes, and retains explicit expert controls for forced newline and submission.
decisions.story: Iris writes a small function directly at the prompt. She needs ordinary Enter behavior for quick expressions and a predictable way to edit and submit several lines without accidental execution.

options.name: Syntax-aware Enter
options.detail: In raw mode, Enter submits complete input and inserts a newline when the parser says input is incomplete. Alt-Enter, encoded portably as Escape then Enter, always inserts a newline. A blank Enter on an empty continuation line force-submits. One-line Enter remains unchanged; cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.

options.name: Blank line submits blocks
options.detail: One-line Enter still submits. Once Enter encounters incomplete syntax, raw mode enters block editing: later Enter inserts lines even after syntax becomes complete, and an empty line submits the block. Escape then Enter inserts a newline without submitting. Cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.

options.name: Explicit edit mode
options.detail: One-line Enter still submits. F4 opens a multiline editor for the current entry; Enter inserts lines and F4 submits. `:edit` opens it and a `:submit` control line submits without becoming Jet source. Cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.
options.code:
› :edit
· fn total(xs: [Int]) -> Int {
·     return xs.sum()
· }
· :submit
› total([3, 4, 5])
12 : Int

comparisons.note: Syntax completeness starts continuation and a blank line finishes a block.
Enter submits while an alternate Enter chord inserts another line.
comparisons.code:
> const total = (xs) =>
    xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)

decisions.title: REPL Ctrl-C during evaluation
decisions.gist: Choose what Ctrl-C does while submitted Jet code is still running.
decisions.explainer: A matches beginner expectations, preserves truthful prior state, and tells experts exactly which external effects cannot be rolled back while keeping interrupted work addressable.
decisions.story: Noah accidentally starts an endless calculation in the REPL. He presses Ctrl-C expecting immediate recovery without losing useful state created before that turn.
decisions.inWild:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
› saved_result
42

options.name: Interrupt turn, keep session
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore the terminal and prompt within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. Keep prior session state and commit no bindings from the interrupted turn. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Record the turn as interrupted and allow rerun. Outside evaluation, the existing ruling remains: Ctrl-C clears a nonempty line first; Ctrl-C at an empty prompt exits.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
› saved_result
42

options.name: Interrupt and restart session
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore the terminal within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. Then discard every REPL binding and start a fresh session. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Keep the interrupted turn only in history, not as rerunnable live state. Outside evaluation, existing line-clear and empty-prompt exit behavior remains.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back. Session restarted with no bindings.
›

options.name: Exit REPL
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore terminal state and exit within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Outside evaluation, existing line-clear and empty-prompt exit behavior remains.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
$

comparisons.note: Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt and normally returns to the same interactive session.
Ctrl-C interrupts current execution and returns to the prompt; repeated Ctrl-C exits.

decisions.comment: While running interrupt turn but when no turn is running it should exit. If a turn is running in repl, pressing ctrl c twice should exit repl, once to interrupt, the second to exit

decisions.title: Batch semantic codemod object law
decisions.gist: Choose how one replayable codemod object expresses ordered semantic rewrites across examples and UI fixtures.
decisions.explainer: D-CODEMOD1 remains the one engine. `jet codemod dry-run|apply|undo` and existing v1 objects/logs stay valid. A missing `version`, or `version: 1`, with `{entry, operation: "rename", from, to}` lowers internally to one `symbol_rename` rule and keeps today's entry-closure scope and output compatibility. Existing v1 logs remain readable; new logs carry `schema: 2` but undo lowers both schemas to the same verified inverse plan. A v2 object lowers to the same TextEdit plan, journal, log, and undo model; no second executor exists. A v2 object requires `project`, resolved relative to the object file, and `roots`. The canonical project path owns `.jet/codemods/<sanitized-name>.log.json`, `.lock`, and any recovery journal. For card #451, each root names either one regular `.jet` file or a directory, and must canonicalize beneath `<project>/examples` or `<project>/tests/ui`; `..`, absolute escape, and symlink escape fail. Directory discovery recursively sorts regular `.jet` files by project-relative byte path; a file root discovers only that file. Each discovered file is an entry compilation unit; its transitive Jet imports join that unit. The same physical file imported by several entries is indexed and edited once. Imports outside editable roots may be read for parsing, name resolution, and semantic identity but never edited; a rule selecting one fails with its path. Non-Jet files are ignored except the exact paired `tests/ui/<name>.stderr` of a touched UI fixture and declared snapshot inputs. Every rule resolves against the currently staged tree after prior rules. Within each compilation unit, every bare identifier in a match template resolves through semindex at the candidate node; that resolved definition anchor, not spelling, controls the match. Every non-capture identifier introduced by a replacement template must resolve uniquely in that same staged compilation unit before an edit is accepted. A rename destination is checked in every affected definition/reference scope and fails on collision or changed binding. A semantic symbol anchor is `(canonical definition module path, symbol kind, current definition span)`; references bind to that anchor through semindex. Independent same-spelled definitions remain independent anchors; selectors either match all and assert the total or narrow with `defined_in`. If a match source or destination resolves to zero or multiple definitions in any unit, the rule fails with unit path and candidates. Rules run in listed order. Within one rule, overlapping/nested edits fail; overlap across rules is intentional sequencing because rule N sees reindexed output from rule N-1. Duplicate ids, unknown fields, ambiguous anchors, unused captures, invalid replacement nodes, and zero matches unless `allow_zero: true` fail. Validation is transactional data, not a code-only check: a `clean` root must finish with zero lexer/parser/sema diagnostics; every touched `fixture` `.jet` must render a complete stderr snapshot. Without `snapshot_after`, generated stderr must equal the existing paired `.stderr` byte-for-byte. With `snapshot_after`, each value is a project-relative path resolved beneath the canonical project; every component must be non-symlink and the final input must be a regular file. Absolute paths, `..`, project escape, symlink, directory, and aliasing the destination `.stderr` fail. That file contains the complete replacement bytes; generated stderr must equal it byte-for-byte, and the paired `.stderr` becomes a planned edit shown in dry-run and committed/undone with source. Dry-run and apply take the exclusive codemod lock before discovery and hold it through discovery, indexing, every staged rule, validation, diagnostic rendering, final hash verification, and output/commit. The lock coordinates codemod processes only; ordinary editors need not honor it. Therefore the engine fingerprints every discovered source, read-only import, existing `.stderr`, and `snapshot_after` input on first read, rehashes all of them after rendering, and refuses with exact drift paths before printing a ready plan or writing anything if any changed. Apply rechecks every destination immediately before its rename and refuses observed drift. This does not close the check-to-rename race with a noncooperating editor: only codemod peers honor the lock, so an editor can still write after the check and be overwritten by the rename. Apply prints that limitation before confirmation; `--yes` accepts it. It writes same-directory temp files, fsyncs file contents, writes+fsyncs a journal containing transaction id, state, every before/after hash, complete before bytes, temp path, and destination, then fsyncs parent directories.
