decisions.inWild: An importer in examples/features/io/ that opens a File, takes a Lock on shared state, and opens a Db connection, then must release all three on every return path — success, `?` error, and early exit.

options.name: A defer verb and one close word
options.detail: `close(^x)` is the single word that ends any resource — File, Lock, or Connection. `defer close(^x)` schedules that close at scope exit, written next to acquisition. Block release (D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1) still covers the common case. `close` already appears in the FFI and db surface, so this unifies rather than invents.
options.technical:
// using a resource after `^` handed it away:
close(^conn)
rows :: conn.query(sql"...")?

error[E0206]: `conn` was closed and cannot be used
  |
  | close(^conn)
  |       ----- closed here — `^` handed it away
  | rows :: conn.query(sql"...")?
  |         ^^^^ used after close
  = note: a File, Lock, or Connection moves with `^`; it has no copy
options.code:
fn import(path) -> Report {
    file :: File.open(path)?
    defer close(^file)          // runs at scope exit, on every path

    lock :: Lock.acquire(state)?
    defer close(^lock)

    conn :: Db.open("cache.db")?
    defer close(^conn)

    rows :: conn.query(sql"select * from log")?
    Report.from(rows)
}   // close(^conn), close(^lock), close(^file) run here, reverse order

options.name: One close word, no defer
options.detail: Standardize on `close(^x)` for every type and retire `.drop`/`release` spellings for resources. Early release stays block-based (D-SHAPE-RESOURCE1). No `defer`: you write the closes yourself, or let block scope release on `?` returns.
options.technical:
$ jet run import.jet
# works. but if conn.query fails, the three close() lines never run —
# block scope releases them instead, so cleanup lives in two places.

# use-after-close is still caught:
error[E0206]: `file` was closed and cannot be used
options.code:
fn import(path) -> Report {
    file :: File.open(path)?
    lock :: Lock.acquire(state)?
    conn :: Db.open("cache.db")?

    rows :: conn.query(sql"select * from log")?
    report :: Report.from(rows)

    close(^conn)                // one word for every type
    close(^lock)
    close(^file)
    report
}   // any early `?` return still auto-releases via block scope

options.name: defer only, per-type close verbs
options.detail: Add `defer <stmt>` running at scope exit, but keep each type's own close method. A File closes with `close`, a Lock with `release`, a Connection with `disconnect`. No single vocabulary.
options.technical:
// call the wrong verb and you learn each type is different:
defer file.release()

error[E0117]: no method `release` on `File`
  |
  | defer file.release()
  |            ^^^^^^^ did you mean `close`?
  = note: File closes with `close`, Lock with `release`, Connection with `disconnect`
options.code:
fn import(path) -> Report {
    file :: File.open(path)?
    defer file.close()

    lock :: Lock.acquire(state)?
    defer lock.release()        // different word per type

    conn :: Db.open("cache.db")?
    defer conn.disconnect()

    rows :: conn.query(sql"select * from log")?
    Report.from(rows)
}

comparisons.note: `defer f.Close()` runs at function return; Jet's `defer close(^x)` adds the `^` so the handoff is visible.
`with open(p) as f:` scopes cleanup to a block; Jet's block release already does this, and `defer` covers the non-block case.
comparisons.code:
with open(path) as f:
    data = f.read()
# f closed at block exit

recommendation.why: A gives both things the owner asked for: a `defer` verb and one close word. Cleanup sits on the line next to acquisition and runs on every exit path, and `close` is the single vocabulary for File, Lock, and Connection.

whyNot.reason: B has no `defer`, so cleanup drifts to the bottom of the function away from acquisition, and early-return paths lean on implicit block release instead of one visible line.
C keeps a different close word per type — `close`, `release`, `disconnect` — the inconsistent vocabulary the owner asked to remove.

recommendation.tradeoff: A introduces two constructs at once, `defer` and a universal `close`, so there are two new spellings to learn instead of one.

decisions.title: Common scope ladder for eligible markers
decisions.gist: Choose whether eligible markers share block, function, module, and package placement.
decisions.lesson: Placement and meaning are separate. A common ladder can remove repeated declarations, while each marker still needs an applicability rule that rejects scopes where its proof or authority is site-specific.
decisions.story: Alex maintains firmware with a package memory limit, a tighter sensor-module limit, one constrained function, and one smaller calibration block. Alex also needs the compiler to reject a package-wide unsafe authorization and show where each effective setting came from.
decisions.inWild: An embedded package uses arena_bounded at four levels. Memory facts and sound effect restrictions may inherit. Unsafe authorization, lexical grants, taint origins, sanitizer claims, and field wire attributes stay at the exact sites their proofs describe.

options.name: Four-level ladder for eligible markers
options.detail: Eligible markers may attach to a block, function, module, or package. For the same marker key, the nearest declaration wins; unmentioned keys remain inherited, and jet explain shows provenance.
options.technical: A compiler-owned applicability matrix defines legal levels and override rules per marker. Wide #Unsafe authorization, #Grant, #Tainted, #Sanitizer, and field wire attributes remain rejected where their proofs are site-specific.
options.code:
# package.jet — package level
#Policy(arena_bounded(65536))
#Policy(unsafe: .Forbid)               # wide policy may only tighten
name: "meter"

# Source/sensor.jet — module level
#Policy(arena_bounded(8192))
module sensor

# function level
#Policy(arena_bounded(2048))
fn calibrate() -> Reading {
    #Policy(arena_bounded(512)) {       # block level
        return sample_window()
    }
}

$ jet explain marker Source/sensor.jet:9 arena_bounded
effective value: 512 bytes
declared at: Source/sensor.jet:8 (block)
overrides: Source/sensor.jet:6 (function), Source/sensor.jet:2 (module), package.jet:1 (package)

# Unsafe authorization remains site-bound.
#Unsafe("all package code")
name: "meter"

error[E0350]: #Unsafe cannot authorize a package
 What: package scope would authorize raw operations without a written audited region
 Why: each unsafe operation must be inside a user-written #Unsafe block or function
 Fix: use #Policy(unsafe: .Forbid) at package scope, or move
      #Unsafe("reason") to the exact block or function

options.name: Function and package only
options.detail: Eligible markers may set a package default or one function value. Modules and blocks cannot override them, so intermediate and narrow scopes require repeated function declarations.
options.technical: The applicability matrix has two inherited levels. Existing site-specific markers keep their current sites, and wide #Unsafe authorization remains rejected.
options.code:
# package.jet — package level
#Policy(arena_bounded(65536))
name: "meter"

# Source/sensor.jet
#Policy(arena_bounded(8192))
module sensor

error[E0351]: #Policy cannot be placed on a module
 Fix: place it on package.jet or repeat it on each function

# function level
#Policy(arena_bounded(2048))
fn calibrate() -> Reading {
    #Policy(arena_bounded(512)) {
        return sample_window()
    }
}

error[E0352]: #Policy cannot be placed on a block
 Fix: split the block into a marked function

# Every other function needing 8192 repeats the declaration.
#Policy(arena_bounded(8192))
fn read_sensor() -> Reading { ... }

#Policy(arena_bounded(8192))
fn read_backup_sensor() -> Reading { ... }

# Unsafe authorization remains site-bound.
#Unsafe("all package code")
name: "meter"

error[E0350]: #Unsafe cannot authorize a package
 Fix: move #Unsafe("reason") to the exact block or function

options.name: Leave current per-site rules
options.detail: Each marker keeps its current attachment sites. There is no common inheritance rule, so users repeat declarations or reorganize code around each marker's existing grammar.
options.technical: #Policy(no_alloc) remains module-only. #Unsafe remains block/function, effect bounds remain signature or region forms, and field attributes remain field-only.

comparisons.note: Rust lint attributes inherit through the item tree. Crate or module inner attributes set defaults, item attributes refine them, and forbid prevents a child from weakening the rule.
C# pragma warning directives cover a source range until restore or end of file. They support narrow lexical control, but they do not form a package and module inheritance tree.

recommendation.why: A lets one rule cover the needed code at any project size. The applicability matrix preserves site-specific proof boundaries, and provenance makes inherited behavior inspectable.

whyNot.reason: B cannot express a module default or a narrow block override. Users must repeat function declarations or split code only to place a marker.
C keeps different placement rules for each marker and repeats package policy across modules. The effective rule cannot be explained through one inheritance model.

recommendation.tradeoff: A requires one explicit applicability and override entry for every marker. A marker gains only the levels whose semantics remain sound; rejected levels receive normal Jet diagnostics.

decisions.comment: A but at the package level syntax needs to be consistent and coherent within the package syntax

decisions.title: Which side names a conversion
decisions.gist: Choose the one shape for turning a value into another type.
decisions.lesson: A conversion starts with one value and produces a value of another type. Current Jet gives the destination a source-named operation such as `UserId.from_int`; option A keeps that direction. This ballot reopens only which side owns the conversion. It does not reopen S33's ban on general call-site type arguments, record construction, parsing, or constructor recognition.
decisions.story: Maya receives an integer identifier from storage and needs the checked `UserId` wrapper. Text parsing remains a separate operation.
decisions.inWild:
id :: UserId.from_int(raw_id)?
user :: User.{ id: id, role: .Member }

options.name: Destination from source
options.detail: The result type owns conversion. The destination stays visible and the operation names the accepted source kind. Text parsing remains `Type.parse`.
options.technical: Typed conversions use destination-owned source names such as `from_int`; narrowing remains fallible through the normal `?` result type.
options.code: id :: UserId.from_int(raw_id)?

options.name: Source to destination
options.detail: The code reads left to right from source to result. Completion on the source may become crowded with every possible destination.
options.technical: Typed conversions use source-owned destination names such as `to_user_id`; no general call-site type arguments are introduced.
options.code: id :: raw_id.to_user_id()?

options.name: Convert function
options.detail: A neutral function avoids assigning ownership to either type. The expected result type supplies the destination without generic call syntax.
options.technical: `convert(value)` requires one expected destination type; ambiguity is an error and member conversions are rejected.
options.code: id: UserId :: convert(raw_id)?

comparisons.note: `From` and `TryFrom` make destination ownership explicit.
Types expose initializers that accept other values. The destination remains visible.

recommendation.why: The reader sees the promised result first, and completion has one bounded home on the destination type.

whyNot.reason: Source completion grows with unrelated destination types.
A global helper weakens type-owned discovery without improving meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: The text does not begin with the source value. A pipeline can still provide that reading lens after pipe rules are decided.

hybrid.synthesis: Use destination-owned `Target.from_source(value)` conversions. Use ordinary fallibility for checked conversion. Do not add `to`, casts, or aliases.

harvest.use: Keep it directly.
A future pipe may present the same operation as a lens.
Compiler models every `from` member as the same conversion category.

decisions.title: Who should stop me from adding meters to seconds?
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet itself understands physical dimensions or leaves them to libraries.
decisions.lesson:
A quantity is a number with meaning, such as 12 meters or 3 seconds. Adding two lengths makes sense. Adding a length to a time does not.

Division can create a new meaning. Distance divided by time is speed. If every package agrees on that rule, values can move safely across library boundaries.

This vote chooses who owns the rule. Later focused votes choose the exact declaration, type, conversion, and temperature syntax.
decisions.story: Ari writes flight planning code from several packages. One package returns distance, another duration, and a third expects speed. They must agree without sharing a special library.

options.name: Jet understands dimensions
options.detail: The compiler knows that length divided by time is speed and rejects impossible math. Unit information costs nothing at runtime and is shared across packages.
options.technical: Jet owns a small dimension table and scale rules. This does not add general type-level programming. Later ballots choose how users declare and write these types.
options.code:
Length + Length -> Length
Length + Time -> clear Jet error
Length / Time -> Speed
Speed * Time -> Length

$ jet explain-type speed
Speed; stored as Float

options.name: F# directly
options.detail: Host language: F#. Its compiler carries units through math and erases them at runtime. People love getting strong domain checks with very little extra code.
options.technical: Copy F# measure declarations, inferred multiplication and division, and zero-cost erasure.
options.code:
// F#
[<Measure>] type m
[<Measure>] type s
let speed: float<m/s> = 120.0<m> / 2.0<s>

options.name: One shared quantity library
options.detail: Core defines library interfaces and generic wrappers for units. The compiler stays smaller, but packages can still disagree about names, conversions, or math rules.
options.technical: Normal generic types and traits carry every dimension relationship.
options.code:
speed :: Quantity.divide(distance, duration)
fn arrival(v: Ratio<Length, Time>, d: Length) -> Time { ... }

options.name: Separate types in every domain
options.detail: Each project defines unrelated Distance, Duration, and Speed types with named functions. It is safe and explicit, but shared math and cross-package reuse disappear.
options.technical: No language-wide dimension relationship exists.
options.code:
speed :: Speed.from(distance, duration)
arrival :: ArrivalTime.from(speed, distance)

comparisons.note: The best direct compiler implementation. F# is liked because unit safety feels like normal numeric code and disappears at runtime.
Ada also checks physical dimensions for safety-focused software. Its users value explicit contracts and early failure.
comparisons.code: type Speed is new Float with Dimension => ...;

recommendation.why: A gives every Jet package one shared physical truth with no runtime wrapper cost. Beginners write normal-looking values; experts get generic dimensions and clear explanations.

whyNot.reason: F# proves the feature, but Jet should use Jet’s type names and declaration style rather than copy F# syntax.
A library cannot guarantee that every package uses the same dimensions, conversions, and errors.
Separate domain types prevent obvious mistakes but lose useful shared math and cross-package APIs.

recommendation.tradeoff: The compiler gains a small, carefully limited dimension rule. Exact syntax remains separate so this vote does not smuggle in a large type-language change.

decisions.title: Should `_bench` load automatically?
decisions.gist: Choose what automatic discovery does with a module whose name begins with one underscore.
decisions.lesson:
Project discovery lets Jet find pieces without a central import list. Some nearby files are helpers for benchmarks, tests, or tools and should not join the normal project automatically.

Skipping a helper is different from deleting it. An explicit `use` can still ask for that module when normal access rules allow it.

Today, a leading underscore disables a module completely. This vote asks whether “internal and opt-in” is a better meaning.
decisions.story: Mira stores benchmark helpers next to normal project pieces. Production should ignore them, while the benchmark command should still use them on purpose.

options.name: Skip automatically; allow explicit use
options.detail: Discovery ignores `_bench`, but `use project._bench` works when normal access rules allow it. Tools explain that the module was skipped and how to include it.
options.technical: This changes today’s disabled-module rule. The declared module name controls discovery; the filename and scan order do not.

options.name: Go directly: ignored helper file
options.detail: Host language: Go. Files beginning with an underscore are ignored by normal builds. People love the simple directory rule, though an ignored file cannot be used explicitly.
options.technical: Apply the same complete skip to Jet modules. This keeps today’s disabled-module result.

options.name: Treat it like every other module
options.detail: Underscore has no discovery meaning. The root must exclude helpers through project settings, or discovery includes them normally.
options.technical: Module names are ordinary. A separate include or exclude setting owns membership.

comparisons.note: Python commonly uses underscore modules as internal but still allows explicit imports. People like the honest opt-in boundary.
Go ignores files beginning with `_` or `.` during builds. People like the simple directory rule, though explicit use is not available.

recommendation.why: A keeps drop-in discovery clean while preserving a deliberate expert path. It uses the underscore for one understandable idea: internal modules do not load themselves.

whyNot.reason: Go’s complete skip is simple, but it confuses “not loaded by default” with “cannot be used on purpose.”
No meaning moves every helper decision into distant root settings and makes local intent harder to see.

recommendation.tradeoff: Discovery gains a skipped-but-available state that tools must show clearly. That state matches how benchmark and tool helpers are actually used.

decisions.title: Where may inferred effects stay omitted from source?
decisions.gist: Choose whether local and public functions may rely on inferred effects instead of writing an explicit upper bound.
decisions.lesson: Under D-EFF1, Jet infers every function's full effect row. `Fs.Read` means file-read authority; `core.files.read` contributes it transitively. `->` is only the return arrow: omitting `--[...]` does not assert purity. A function is pure when its inferred row is empty, or when explicit `--[]->` bounds it empty. Nonempty bounds such as `--[Fs.Read]->` grant nothing; sema rejects effects outside them. D-EFF3 keeps per-implementation inference for static calls and a declared trait-method upper bound for dynamic dispatch. This ballot decides where ordinary source may omit bounds.
decisions.story: Mina starts with a one-file parser. `read_config` calls `core.files.read`, so Jet infers `Fs.Read` without ceremony. She later exports it from a package. Callers use its effect set for policy and generic bounds. Six months later a helper begins fetching a remote fallback. The package must either reject that new `Net` effect against an explicit bound or report a public API change before release.

options.name: Infer functions; bound dynamic traits
options.detail: Private and public ordinary functions may omit an effect bound. Public API snapshots store the inferred normalized row, and semver rejects row changes. Experts may write a bound anywhere; `--[]->` is an explicit purity proof. D-EFF3 remains intact: static calls use each implementation's inferred row, while a trait method used through dynamic dispatch declares its upper-bound contract.
options.technical: Inference remains D-EFF1 current law. Publishing records normalized closed/open rows and provenance. An explicit row is an upper bound. Trait implementations are checked against the D-EFF3 trait row; direct calls retain their narrower per-implementation inference.

options.name: Infer private; bound public
options.detail: Private functions keep full inference. Every public function writes an explicit upper bound, including `--[]->` for a public purity claim. Promotion from private to public fails until the author states the row. D-EFF3 still infers each implementation for static calls and uses the trait declaration's bound for dynamic dispatch.
options.technical: `pub` functions, public trait methods, and exported callbacks require a closed or open explicit row. Private implementations infer and must remain subsets of public and trait bounds.

options.name: Bound every effectful function
options.detail: Any function whose inferred row is nonempty must write an explicit upper bound, including local helpers and concrete trait implementations. Empty inferred rows are pure without extra syntax; authors may write `--[]->` to make purity contractual. Dynamic trait calls still use the declared D-EFF3 trait-method bound.
options.technical: Sema first infers each body, then requires a source annotation for every nonempty row. Missing annotations fail before codegen. Static calls retain the inferred implementation row; trait declarations remain the dynamic-dispatch contract.

recommendation.why: A preserves D-EFF1's beginner inference, D-EFF3's static/dynamic distinction, and expert compile-time bounds without treating omitted syntax as a purity claim.

whyNot.reason: B turns exporting an otherwise valid helper into required annotation work even though the compiler and API snapshot already know the exact row.
C repeats inferred nonempty rows throughout one-file and private code, making the safe default ceremonial.

recommendation.tradeoff: An ordinary public source signature may omit authority that reviewers want visible without tooling. Stable API snapshots, `jet inspect effects`, LSP expansion, and optional explicit upper bounds keep it auditable.

decisions.title: Package-echelon spelling for scoped policy settings
decisions.gist: Choose the value shape of package.jet's policy: field that carries scoped settings like no_alloc, arena_bounded, gc, and unsafe.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's scoped settings (memory facts, gc, unsafe policy) share one placement ladder: block, function, module, package. At the three source scopes they are written as a `#Policy(...)` marker, for example `#Policy(no_alloc, arena_bounded(65536))`.

The package echelon is different. A package is described by fields in `package.jet`, such as `identity:` and `sources:`, each holding a typed `.{ ... }` value. Two prior rulings already fix where package policy lives: it belongs in the `policy:` field, not a floating marker above the fields. This ballot only decides the shape of the value that `policy:` field holds.

The nearest declaration of a key wins, unmentioned keys inherit, and `jet explain` reports the effective value plus every declaration it overrode. Package policy may only tighten safety: it can forbid unsafe code, but it can never authorize an unsafe operation, which still requires a written `#Unsafe` block or function.
decisions.explainer: This is the package half of the ratified scope ladder. The owner ratified D-MARK-SCOPE1 with the note that package-level syntax must stay consistent within the package syntax; this ballot settles that exact spelling.
decisions.story: Ravi ships firmware for a heap-less controller. He sets a package memory floor once in package.jet, tightens one sensor module to a smaller arena, and forbids unsafe code across the package. He needs the package spelling to read like the rest of package.jet and to trace back through jet explain when a setting surprises him.
decisions.inWild: A firmware package sets no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded(65536), and unsafe: forbid at the package. One sensor module tightens arena_bounded to 2048. A separate service package being ported from TypeScript sets a single gc key. Both use the same policy field.

options.name: Governance keys as typed fields on the policy value
options.detail: The policy: field holds a typed Policy value. Each governance key is an ordinary field, matching how identity: and sources: are written. The source marker #Policy(no_alloc) and the package field no_alloc: true are the same key in two echelon-appropriate spellings.
options.technical: The compiler maps each package policy field to the same key the source #Policy(...) marker uses, so the ladder and jet explain see one key. Package policy may tighten but not authorize unsafe. Reuse is reached through the ratified jet split, which extracts these fields into a Config.

options.name: The #Policy(...) marker reused as the field value
options.detail: The policy: field holds the exact #Policy(...) marker used at the source scopes. The key vocabulary is identical at every echelon, so a user learns one spelling. The trade is that policy: then reads unlike every other Package field, which holds a typed .{ ... } value.
options.technical: The marker call becomes the field value. One key surface spans block, function, module, and package. Package policy still may tighten but not authorize unsafe. The Package record now holds two value shapes: typed .{ ... } for identity/sources and a #-marker for policy.
options.code:
# package.jet — the source marker itself becomes the field value.
identity: .{ name: "meter", version: "1.0.0" }
sources:  .{ roots: ["Source"] }
policy:   #Policy(no_alloc, zero_rc, arena_bounded(65536), unsafe: .Forbid)

# Source/sensor.jet — the identical marker spelling at the narrow scope.
#Policy(arena_bounded(2048))
module sensor

$ jet explain marker Source/sensor.jet arena_bounded
effective value: 2048
declared at: Source/sensor.jet:1 (module)
overrides:   package.jet:4 (package policy:)

# One key vocabulary everywhere, but the record mixes value shapes:
identity: .{ name: "meter", version: "1.0.0" }   # typed value
policy:   #Policy(no_alloc)                        # marker value

# unsafe still cannot widen at the package:
policy: #Policy(unsafe: .Allow)
error[E0350]: package policy cannot authorize unsafe
 Fix: keep unsafe: .Forbid, or write #Unsafe("reason") at the exact site

options.name: Named Config profiles composed into policy
options.detail: The policy: field composes named Config values plus inline keys. A profile such as NoHeap bundles several keys and can be shared across a monorepo's members. Even a one-key package must author or import a Config to use this path.
options.technical: Config is the ratified vocabulary for a typed contribution of package facts. Here policy: takes a use: list of Config references plus inline overrides. jet explain names the contributing Config. A single package still writes a profile list even when one inline key would do.
options.code:
# Policies.jet — a reusable Config value.
NoHeap: Config :: .{
    no_alloc: true
    zero_rc: true
    arena_bounded: 65536
}

# package.jet — compose named Configs plus inline keys.
identity: .{ name: "meter", version: "1.0.0" }
sources:  .{ roots: ["Source"] }
policy:   .{ use: [NoHeap], unsafe: .Forbid }

# Source/sensor.jet
#Policy(arena_bounded(2048))
module sensor

$ jet explain marker Source/sensor.jet arena_bounded
effective value: 2048
declared at: Source/sensor.jet:1 (module)
overrides:   Policies.jet:4 (Config NoHeap, via package.jet:4)

# A package with one key still needs a profile list:
policy: .{ use: [], unsafe: .Forbid }   # empty use: is ceremony for small packages

comparisons.note: Rust source sets lint levels with inner attributes, and Cargo added a manifest [lints] table for the package default. The manifest uses table keys, not a pasted attribute, so the package echelon reads like the rest of the manifest. This matches option A.

C# source suppresses a warning with a #pragma at the site, while the project sets the default severity with a key in .editorconfig. The project echelon uses a plain key, not the pragma spelling. This also matches option A.
comparisons.code:
// source scope
#pragma warning disable CA2000

# .editorconfig — project echelon
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2000.severity = error

recommendation.why: A makes policy: read like every other typed Package field, keeps each governance key identical to its source marker name, and reaches Config reuse through the already-ratified jet split. The owner's coherence note is satisfied without a second manifest spelling.

whyNot.reason: B keeps one key vocabulary but places a #Policy(...) marker where every other Package field holds a typed value. The record then carries two value shapes and policy: reads unlike identity: and sources: beside it.

C forces even a one-key package to author or import a named Config. The ratified jet split already turns an A-shaped policy: field into a Config when reuse is needed, so C's sharing exists without a second inline spelling.

recommendation.tradeoff: A uses field spelling at the package and marker spelling at source, so a memory key has two echelon-appropriate forms. The compiler maps both to one key, and jet explain unifies provenance across the ladder.

decisions.title: One identifier-casing law for the whole language
decisions.gist: Pick the single casing law every Jet name obeys: PascalCase everywhere, snake_case everywhere, or a strict two-tier rule (PascalCase types, snake_case values).
decisions.lesson:
Today Jet has no single enforced law, and the surface shows it. Keywords are mostly lowercase (`fn`, `struct`, `enum`, `mut`, `take`, `loop`, `distinct`), but effect and capability keywords are PascalCase (`Pure`, `Impure`, `Reactive`, `Tainted`, `State`, `Caps`, `Grant`, `Shield`, `Transact`). Types are PascalCase (`Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Point`, `Meters`). Enum variants are PascalCase, and D-SHAPE3b just ratified `Val`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`. Markers are PascalCase behind a sigil per D-CASING1 (`#Unsafe`, `@Pre`, `@Numeric`, `@UnitFamily`).

Fields and methods are snake_case (`data_dir`, `dist_sq`, `from_addr`, `smtp_from_env`); locals are snake_case. Config namespaces are lowercase (`env`, `system`, `image`, `fleet`) while their block types are PascalCase (`Env`, `System`, `Image`, `Fleet`, `Pkg`, `Build`).

Three genuine inconsistencies remain. Modules split by role: code modules are lowercase (`module math`, path segments `core.mem`) but generic module templates are PascalCase (`module Cache<K>`, `IntCache`). Constants split: S54 records PascalCase constants, yet examples use SCREAMING_CASE (`const BASE`, `comptime LOGO`). Unit members are lowercase (`px`, `usd`) but mint PascalCase types (`Px`).

S54 defines a two-tier convention but leaves it unenforced ("No naming lint in v1; jet fmt is layout-only"), so nothing stops the drift. Even the ratified `Ok`/`Err` still appear as lowercase `ok()`/`err()` in error examples. The owner's complaint is exactly this: a rule exists on paper, but the surface is not uniform and not machine-checked.
decisions.story: A newcomer reads two Jet files in one sitting. The first has `module Cache<K>` and `comptime SIZE`; the second has `module math` and a snake_case field. She asks which casing is correct and cannot answer from the code. She wants one law she can predict everywhere, and a compiler that enforces it so no file can drift.
decisions.inWild: The same small program under each law. It has a unit family, a struct with a method, an enum, a match, a module, and a constant, so every naming position is visible. Read the option code blocks below; each one rewrites this exact program.

options.name: PascalCase everywhere
options.detail: Every identifier is PascalCase: types, variants, functions, methods, fields, locals, modules, unit members, constants. Keywords stay lowercase because they are not identifiers. This retains D-CASING1's PascalCase marker names and D-SHAPE3b's PascalCase variants, but explicitly amends S54's value-tier snake_case, lowercase module paths, and D-QUANTITY-DECL1's lowercase unit-member convention. Casing no longer distinguishes a type from a value.

options.name: snake_case everywhere
options.detail: Every identifier is snake_case, including types, variants, and marker names. This explicitly amends D-CASING1's PascalCase marker law (`@UnitFamily` becomes `@unit_family`), D-SHAPE3b's `Val`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`, S54's type tier, and every existing PascalCase type. Leading-dot patterns keep variants distinguishable there, but type and expression positions lose the visual type-versus-value signal.

options.name: Strict two-tier law, machine-enforced
options.detail: One rule per grammatical category, zero exceptions, machine-enforced. Type-like names are PascalCase: types, traits, enum variants, markers, unit-family names and generated unit types, Config blocks. Value-like names are snake_case: functions, methods, fields, locals, module paths, unit members, constants. This preserves D-CASING1, D-SHAPE3b, and D-QUANTITY-DECL1 casing, while explicitly amending S54's no-lint rule and resolving its constant/module-template drift.

comparisons.note: Two-tier convention: PascalCase types/traits/variants, snake_case functions/fields/locals, SCREAMING_SNAKE consts. Enforced by warn-by-default compiler lints (non_snake_case and siblings). Casing decides meaning in match patterns. The #[allow] escape exists mainly for FFI names. The ecosystem is uniform; almost no crate disables the lints.

UpperCamelCase types, lowerCamelCase everything else including enum cases. Not grammar-required or compiler-enforced; convention plus the official swift-format and third-party SwiftLint. Apple's frameworks set the tone and the community follows closely. Enum cases sit on the value tier, unlike Rust.

Casing carries visibility, not category: an exported name is PascalCase, a package-private name is camelCase. This is compiler-semantic, not just style. Universally accepted; Google's and Uber's style guides build on it rather than fight it. Casing cannot also signal type-versus-value.
comparisons.code:
type HttpClient struct { RetryCount int }
const MaxRetries = 3
func SendRequest(c HttpClient) bool { return true } // exported: Pascal
func parseHeader() {}                               // private: camel

comparisons.note: PEP 8 convention: CapWords classes, snake_case functions and variables, UPPER_SNAKE constants. Unenforced by the interpreter; formatters like black touch layout, not names. Linters (flake8, pylint) can warn but are opt-in. Legacy camelCase persists for decades in unittest, logging, and Twisted.

Convention: PascalCase classes, camelCase methods and variables, UPPER_SNAKE constants. Not compiler-enforced; near-universal because the JDK and every IDE follow it. Checkstyle and Google Java Style codify it for teams that want a hard check. Cross-codebase conflicts are rare.

Microsoft guidelines: PascalCase for types, methods, and properties, camelCase for locals and parameters. Unusual in putting methods on the Pascal tier. Enforced optionally by Roslyn analyzers and .editorconfig naming rules. The ecosystem is highly uniform because Microsoft ships and tools the guidance.

Official conventions: PascalCase classes, camelCase functions and properties, UPPER_SNAKE constants. Not grammar-enforced; ktlint and detekt enforce for teams, and IntelliJ warns. JetBrains ships the convention with the toolchain, so adoption is high and drift is low.

No language enforcement of identifier casing at all. Convention is PascalCase types and classes, camelCase values, UPPER_SNAKE constants. Teams enforce per project via ESLint's naming-convention rule. Practice is fragmented; large codebases differ, and cross-project reading suffers.

Partly grammar-semantic: a name starting uppercase is a constant, and class and module names are constants, so they must be capitalized. Methods and locals are snake_case by strong convention (RuboCop enforces). The uppercase-constant rule cannot be violated; the interpreter depends on it.
comparisons.code:
class HttpClient
  MAX_RETRIES = 3        # constant: must start uppercase
  def send_request
    retry_count = 0       # local: must start lowercase
    true
  end
end

comparisons.note: Grammar-enforced. The lexer requires type, constructor, typeclass, and module names to start uppercase, and variables and functions to start lowercase. Violating it is a parse error, so conflict is impossible. No enterprise forks the rule; every codebase looks the same here.
comparisons.code:
data HttpClient = HttpClient { retryCount :: Int }
maxRetries :: Int
maxRetries = 3
sendRequest :: HttpClient -> Bool
sendRequest c = True

comparisons.note: Grammar-enforced like Haskell: types, constructors, and modules must start uppercase, and values must start lowercase. The official elm-format handles layout. Because casing is part of the grammar, no team can adopt a conflicting guide, and none tries.
comparisons.code:
type Status = Success | Failure
type alias HttpClient = { retryCount : Int }
maxRetries : Int
maxRetries = 3
sendRequest : HttpClient -> Bool
sendRequest c = True

comparisons.note: Grammar-enforced and reversed from Haskell: a Capitalized name is a variable, a lowercase name is an atom, including function names. The parser depends on it. Prolog uses the same rule. Teams cannot deviate; the casing question never arises.
comparisons.code:
-define(MAX_RETRIES, 3).
send_request(Client) ->      %% atom fn: lowercase
    RetryCount = 0,          %% variable: Capitalized
    {ok, RetryCount}.        %% ok is an atom

comparisons.note: Style-insensitive: after the first character, identifiers compare equal ignoring case and underscores, so sendRequest and send_request name the same thing. The first letter's case still matters and marks types. Because spellings unify, teams cannot actually disagree on camel-versus-underscore.
comparisons.code:
type HttpClient = object
  retryCount: int
const MaxRetries = 3
proc sendRequest(c: HttpClient): bool = true
# send_request and sendRequest are the same proc

comparisons.note: No language rule and no single authority. The standard library is snake_case, but Google, LLVM, Qt, Unreal, and Boost each prescribe different casing. Every large shop writes its own guide, and reading across codebases is inconsistent. This is the clearest cost of never setting a law.
comparisons.code:
// Google, LLVM, Qt, and Unreal disagree on every line below:
struct HttpClient { int retry_count; };   // Google: member snake
constexpr int kMaxRetries = 3;            // Google k-prefix; LLVM: MaxRetries
bool SendRequest(HttpClient c);           // Google Pascal; stdlib: snake

comparisons.note: Enforced by official lints (package:lints, flutter_lints): UpperCamelCase types, lowerCamelCase members, lowercase_with_underscores files. `dart analyze` warns by default in new projects. FFI and JS interop keep foreign names, suppressed with a lint-ignore comment. Adoption is near-universal because the lints ship with the SDK.

recommendation.why: Adopt C: the strict two-tier law, machine-enforced. It matches what the surface already reaches for, so migration touches the drifting edges rather than every name, and it keeps the just-ratified Val/None/Ok/Err and every #/@ marker. Real consistency is one predictable rule per category plus a compiler check that no file can drift, not making every name look the same.

whyNot.reason: PascalCase on fields, methods, and locals erases the type-versus-value signal and makes every variable read like a type or constant. It also overturns snake_case across the majority of the surface — fields, methods, module paths, unit members — for no readability gain.

The leading-dot pattern keeps matches unambiguous, but type and expression position lose the at-a-glance type-versus-value distinction (fn describe(shape: shape)). It also overturns the just-ratified Val/None/Ok/Err and every type name, the one place casing still carries meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: C keeps two shapes instead of one, so the law is one rule per grammatical category rather than one rule per character. It settles every identifier category named in this ballot: effects and capabilities remain PascalCase keywords, generic module templates follow snake_case module paths, and constants use snake_case.

decisions.comment: Owner question q53x9upn answered: comparisons expanded to 15 languages with code; analysis of enforcement levels and enterprise style-guide conflicts delivered. Evidence: conflicts cluster in languages that never enforced a law; languages born with one see internal guides adopt it. C is the only option keeping the type-versus-value signal while machine-enforced.

decisions.title: FFI escape for the identifier-casing law
decisions.gist: Choose how foreign symbol names in FFI bindings escape the D-SHAPE-CASE1 casing law.
decisions.lesson:
D-SHAPE-CASE1=C makes casing machine-enforced: functions and values are snake_case, types are PascalCase, and drift is a coded diagnostic.

Foreign libraries name symbols by their own rules. C libraries export names like `SDL_Init` and `glGetString`. Jet declares these names in binding modules: the generated `#Bindgen module c.<lib>.__bindgen__`, the user overlay `#Extern module c.<lib>` (S59), and `extern rust` blocks (S50). The ratified ABI law says symbols are used exactly as written (D-CABI-PLATFORM1).

Without an escape, every generated binding fails the casing law the moment it is generated. This ballot decides where the law stops at the foreign boundary. It changes no ABI rule and no binding mechanics.
decisions.story: Rio writes `use c.sdl as sdl`. The header declares `SDL_Init` and `SDL_CreateWindow`. He wants working bindings without hand-renaming hundreds of symbols, and he wants his ordinary Jet code still held to the one casing law.

options.name: Binding modules are exempt zones
options.detail: Casing diagnostics skip declarations inside `#Bindgen` modules, `#Extern` modules, and `extern rust` blocks. Call sites use the foreign spelling verbatim, so a name in Jet code matches the C header, the library manual, and every forum answer. Ordinary Jet modules stay fully enforced. No new syntax; the exemption boundary is a module kind sema already knows.

options.name: Bindgen renames foreign symbols to Jet law
options.detail: `jet inspect bind` maps each foreign symbol to a law-abiding Jet name (`SDL_Init` becomes `sdl_init`) and records the mapping in the binding cache; the overlay may override a mapping. Every Jet source file then obeys one law with zero exemptions. Cost: names stop matching the header and the library's documentation, and bindgen must resolve mapping collisions and keep diagnostics reversible to the original symbol.

options.name: No escape
options.detail: Foreign declarations must satisfy the casing law like any other code. Users hand-write renaming overlays or wrapper functions for every symbol before a binding compiles. Generated bindings fail their own build, and the script tier (`use "raylib.h" as rl`) cannot work without a wrapper file per library.
options.code:
use "raylib.h" as rl
Error[E….]: function names are snake_case
  --> .jet/bindings/c/raylib.jet: `InitWindow`
 Fix: add an `#Extern` overlay renaming each symbol

comparisons.note: The casing lints are suppressed at the foreign boundary: rust-bindgen emits `#[allow(non_snake_case, non_camel_case_types)]` on generated bindings automatically, and hand-written extern blocks do the same. Foreign names stay verbatim.

ffigen emits `// ignore_for_file:` lint suppressions at the top of generated FFI files, and JS interop keeps foreign member names verbatim behind @JS annotations. The official lints stay on for ordinary code.
comparisons.code:
// ignore_for_file: non_constant_identifier_names
external int SDL_Init(int flags);

comparisons.note: cgo places every C name under the `C.` prefix verbatim; Go's own naming rules simply do not apply inside that namespace. The foreign boundary is the package qualifier itself.

recommendation.why: Foreign names stay literally searchable against the header, the library manual, and existing answers, while every ordinary Jet file keeps the enforced law. The exemption boundary is a module kind sema already tracks, so no new syntax is added (I7 untouched) and generated bindings compile as generated.

whyNot.reason: Renaming breaks the one job a foreign name has: matching the foreign documentation. It also adds collision resolution and reversible-diagnostic machinery for no reading gain.
Generated bindings would fail their own build, and every C library would need a hand-written wrapper file, which guts the S59 script tier's no-ceremony default.

recommendation.tradeoff: A file that mixes heavy FFI reads two casings. That is acceptable because the boundary is explicit — `#Bindgen`, `#Extern`, `extern rust` — and ordinary modules never relax.

Owner: 'I have REPEATEDLY instructed only to do appropriately scoped, targeted tests, not the entire suite. The entire suite should be done as part of closeout after a major push.' (2026-07-16). decisions.title: User-defined operators for structs and classes
decisions.gist: How users make `+ - * / == <` work on their own structs, like a `Vec2` or a `Money`.
decisions.lesson:
Operator overloading is powerful and easy to abuse. C++ repurposes `<<`, its bit-shift operator, to mean stream output in `cout << x`, a meaning unrelated to shifting bits. Readers then learn each library's private meaning for a symbol before they can read the code.

The guardrail Jet keeps under every option below: overload only existing symbols, never invent new ones, never let a user change precedence, and keep arithmetic symbols doing arithmetic. `v1 + v2` must read as addition, not a disguised side effect.
decisions.story:
Priya builds a physics demo. She has a `Vec2` struct and writes `pos = pos + velocity`, the obvious spelling. Today Jet rejects it, because `+` is defined only for built-in numbers and lane types.

She falls back to `pos = pos.add(velocity)`, then longer `.add(...).scale(...)` chains that bury the math. She wants the same `+` beginners already use on `Int` to work on her own type.

options.name: Operator hook traits
options.detail: Operators are trait sugar, the same family as `Index`, `Display`, and `Iterable`. You implement one trait per operator family on your type, and the compiler wires the symbol to the method. The beginner front-doors stay: `@Numeric` and `@Comparable` on distinct types, plus auto-derived `Equatable`, generate these same impls. One mechanism, several ergonomic entrypoints.

options.name: Direct operator functions
options.detail: Define the symbol itself as a function, the way C++ and Python spell it. `fn +(a: Vec2, b: Vec2) -> Vec2` reads tersely at the definition site. It adds a second definition plane beside traits: capability lives on `fn <symbol>`, not on a named trait, so generic code has nothing to require.

options.name: Named methods only
options.detail: Follow Go: no operator overloading for user types at all. Users write named methods like `pos.add(vel)` and `a.less_than(b)`. The teaching error for `v1 + v2` points straight at methods and the built-in hooks. Symbols stay reserved for built-in numbers and lane types.

comparisons.note: Operators are traits (`std::ops::Add`, `PartialOrd`), so a generic bound names the capability (`T: Add`). This is the model option A adopts, minus lifetimes.
comparisons.code:
impl Add for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn add(self, o: Vec2) -> Vec2 { /* ... */ } }
fn sum3<T: Add<Output = T>>(a: T, b: T, c: T) -> T { a + b + c }

comparisons.note: Operators are free functions or methods keyed by the symbol, which is option B's plane. No capability name, and `<<` shows how far a symbol's meaning can drift from its arithmetic origin.
comparisons.code:
Vec2 operator+(const Vec2& a, const Vec2& b) { return {a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y}; }
std::cout << v;   // same operator family, now stream output

comparisons.note: No overloading; named methods only, which is option C. Symbols stay honest, but numeric-heavy code turns into verbose method chains.
comparisons.code:
func (a Vec2) Add(b Vec2) Vec2 { return Vec2{a.X + b.X, a.Y + b.Y} }
v := a.Add(b).Scale(2)

comparisons.note: Dunder methods (`__add__`, `__lt__`) are per-class and dynamically dispatched, with no static bound a generic can require. Convenient, but the capability is invisible to a type checker.
comparisons.code:
class Vec2:
    def __add__(self, o): return Vec2(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y)

recommendation.why: Operators are already trait sugar in Jet: `Index` gives `x[i]`, `Display` gives `{x}`, and `Iterable` gives the `loop x in` header. Adding `Add`, `Comparable`, and `Equatable` to that family is the same mechanism, so there stays exactly one way to grant a type new syntax. The beginner bundles `@Numeric` and `@Comparable`, plus auto-derived equality, generate these exact impls, so magic and expert control share one spine (I8).
recommendation.tradeoff: You name the operator's trait (`impl Vec2.Add`) rather than write the bare symbol, so the definition site is a line longer than C++'s `fn +`. In exchange, generic code can bound on the capability (`<T: Add>`), and every operator reaches through the same door as `Index` and `Display`. Adopting this lifts the v1 non-goal on operator overloading and widens D-SIMD1 beyond built-in lane types.

whyNot.reason: A `fn +` plane duplicates the trait mechanism Jet already ships for `Index`, `Display`, and `Iterable`, giving two ways to grant syntax (I8). It also leaves generic bounds nothing to name, so `sum3<T>(a + b + c)` cannot state its requirement.

Named-only regresses beginner readability, priority #2: units and money math decay to `price.mul(qty).add(tax)`. It also contradicts shipped surface, since Jet already overloads operators on lane types and re-exposes them through `@Numeric` bundles, so a flat refusal is inconsistent rather than principled.

hybrid.synthesis:
Ship A as the one mechanism, then fold the other options' virtues into it. Beginner bundles (`@Numeric`, `@Comparable`) and auto-derived `Equatable` become front-doors that generate the same operator trait impls a beginner never has to write by hand.

Option B's brevity survives as short method names (`add`, `compare`) and inline `impl` inside the type body. Option C's restraint survives as the fence: overload only existing symbols, invent no operators, change no precedence, and keep named methods the advised path for mutating or side-effectful work.

harvest.aspect: Operators as trait impls in the existing hook-trait family.
harvest.use: The spine of the decision: one mechanism grants a user type every kind of new syntax, from `x[i]` to `x + y`.
Kept as short method names (`add`, `compare`) and inline `impl` in the type body, without adding a second definition plane.

harvest.aspect: Restraint: no new operators, no precedence changes, named methods for side effects.
harvest.use: Kept as the invariant fence around A and the advised path for mutating or side-effectful operations, where a symbol would mislead.

decisions.title: What is Jet's first-party event system semantic model?
decisions.gist: Choose the core event model Jet should standardize for games, web UI, servers, plugins, hooks, Canvas, and debugging.
decisions.explainer: Events touch too many domains to be a Canvas-only affordance. Jet needs one source-visible, type-safe, lifetime-safe event model that beginners can use with one line and experts can tune for dispatch, ordering, cancellation, async, backpressure, and failure policy.
decisions.story: Doris is building a game HUD and a server dashboard in the same Jet codebase. A button click, a collision, a save hook, and a hot-reload notification should all use the same typed event model, so Canvas, source, debugger, and tests agree on what happened.
decisions.detail: Audit pass: C# gives typed delegates/events but weak lifetime/async policy; DOM gives phases, once/passive, and AbortSignal cleanup but stringly/weak typing; Node EventEmitter is tiny but stringly and has special error/async traps; Godot signals fit games/editor UX but can stay dynamically loose; UnityEvent gives designer-persistent callbacks but ties truth to scene/editor data; Unreal dispatchers feel right visually but live in Blueprint assets. Jet should take typed delegates, signal/editor projection, AbortSignal-style lifetime cleanup, explicit phases/options, and structured-concurrency integration while rejecting stringly names, hidden graph assets, untyped payloads, and unhandled async failures.

options.name: Library-only Event and Hook values
options.detail: Ship Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary Core/runtime types. No special syntax, no compiler-known event diagnostics beyond normal typing. Smallest language surface, but tools/debugger may not get enough semantic facts unless we later make the library magical.

options.name: Language-level event declarations
options.detail: Add first-class user syntax for declaring events and hooks. Excellent readability and toolability, but risks a new mechanism before the semantic model is proven and creates syntax churn across domains.
options.code:
event clicked(Click)
hook before_save(SaveRequest) -> SaveDecision

options.name: Actor/mailbox/channel-first events
options.detail: Treat events as typed messages delivered to actors/tasks. Strong for concurrency and servers, but awkward for UI/game editor workflows where direct owner lifetimes, inspector wiring, and hooks matter.

options.name: Hybrid Event/Hook family: typed values, compiler-known facts, syntax reserved (recommended)
options.detail: Build Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary source-visible values, but make the family compiler/tooling-known for diagnostics, debugger traces, Canvas projection, ownership cleanup, async/failure checks, and docs. Reserve user syntax only after real examples prove library spelling is too noisy. One semantic model serves beginner clicks, game collisions, web lifecycle, server hooks, plugin interception, and expert async/backpressure policies.

comparisons.note: Typed delegates/events, many subscribers, sync invocation by default; lifetime leaks and async policy are not solved by the event type.
EventTarget has phases, once/passive options, and AbortSignal cleanup, but event names are strings and handlers receive generic Event objects.
Signals are editor-friendly and first-class enough for games, but payload/arity checking can remain a runtime/user responsibility.
Event Dispatchers feel right in visual scripting but are tied to Blueprint assets; Jet needs source-owned semantics.
comparisons.code: Bind Event to StartFire; Call StartFire

decisions.title: Complete event dispatch, failure, and hook policy surface
decisions.gist: Choose how Event and Hook expose real queued dispatch, cancellation, typed failures, and intervention outcomes.
decisions.explainer: D-EVENT1=D already fixes one compiler-known family of ordinary source-visible Event and Hook values; this ballot chooses its exact expert API, not a second event model. Every option obeys the same runtime law. An async emission moves atomically Pending -> Queued -> Running -> one terminal state. Pending means a Block producer has not been accepted. Queued means accepted and waiting for a worker. Running means one worker won ownership. Capacity counts Queued only: Running and Pending do not consume a queue slot. queued_count is exactly the number in Queued, running_count is exactly Running, and blocked_count is exactly Pending Block producers; each transition updates these facts atomically before waking observers. Terminal DispatchState is Delivered, HandlerFailed, DroppedNewest, DroppedOldest, Closed, Cancelled, or DeadlineExceeded. DispatchReport<E> contains state, accepted, delivered_handlers, failures, and trace. DropNewest completes the new attempt immediately as DroppedNewest with accepted=false. DropOldest atomically completes the oldest Queued payload's existing task as DroppedOldest with accepted=true, then accepts the new payload; it never evicts Running work. Block returns a task immediately but does not accept its payload until capacity exists; close, cancellation, or deadline wakes that producer exactly once with accepted=false. Capacity must be greater than zero or construction fails with typed EventConfigError.InvalidCapacity. AsyncEvent.close is graceful and idempotent: it rejects new and blocked producers as Closed, lets Running and Queued payloads finish, then closes workers. EventScope.cancel and owner teardown are hard, idempotent cancellation: Queued payloads become Cancelled, blocked producers become Cancelled, and Running handlers receive the same structured task cancellation at their next wait point. An inherited deadline uses DeadlineExceeded instead. The worker-versus-control race is one compare-and-set: Queued -> Running means the worker owns delivery; Queued -> Cancelled/DeadlineExceeded means no handler may observe it. A Running handler that returns before observing cancellation is Delivered or HandlerFailed; if cancellation wins at a wait point it is Cancelled/DeadlineExceeded. Thus every accepted payload reaches exactly one terminal report and is never double-delivered or double-dropped. FailurePolicy.StopFirst stops remaining handlers for that payload after the first E; the queue continues. Collect runs every handler and stores failures in stable priority/subscription order. Log runs every handler, stores no E values in the report, and emits each failure into the event trace. Ignore runs every handler and discards E values and failure trace entries. StopFirst and Collect use HandlerFailed when any E occurs; Log and Ignore use Delivered after all handlers return. A handler panic is never coerced to E: it becomes HandlerFailed with a typed DispatchFailure.Panic task-panic record and stops that payload; the queue continues. Decision hooks use DecisionHook<T,E>; each handler receives the current T and returns HookOutcome<T,E>: Continue keeps it, Transform(value) replaces it for later handlers, Cancel stops with Cancel, and Fail(error) stops with Fail(error). FirstCancelElseTransform processes stable priority/subscription order; zero handlers returns Continue(original). Worked pressure examples never depend on timing: a first handler sends on a started channel and waits on a release channel, the test receives started before enqueueing a payload that must remain Queued, then checks queued_count before the overflow or Block attempt. These laws, queue counts, reports, failures, and lifecycle transitions are debugger and Canvas facts, never reconstructed labels.
decisions.story: Maya builds a multiplayer damage pipeline. Ordinary UI clicks should stay one-line and synchronous. Network damage bursts must use a bounded queue, producers must either wait or drop by an explicit policy, cancellation and deadlines must wake blocked work, and every accepted payload must be delivered or dropped exactly once. A validation plugin must be able to transform or cancel a save, while typed handler failures remain inspectable instead of becoming background errors.
decisions.inWild:
use core.event as event

fn run() {
    owner :: event.scope()
    clicks :: event.new<Click>()
    clicks.on(owner, (click) => { ui.highlight(click.target) })
    clicks.emit(Click.{ target: "save" })

    damage :: event.async_result<Damage, DamageError>(
        event.AsyncPolicy.{ capacity: 2, overflow: event.Overflow.Block },
        event.FailurePolicy.Collect,
    )
    damage.on(owner, (hit) => apply_damage(hit))
    report :: damage.emit_async(Damage.{ amount: 12 }).join()
    print(report.state())
    print(report.failures())

    before_save :: event.decision_hook<SaveRequest, SaveError>(event.HookPolicy.FirstCancelElseTransform)
    before_save.on(owner, (request) => event.HookOutcome.Transform(normalize(request)))
    before_save.on(owner, (request) => validate(request))
    outcome :: before_save.run(SaveRequest.{ path: " notes.txt " })
    print(outcome)
}
decisions.detail: Recommendation: A. It preserves D-EVENT1's ceremony-free synchronous Event<T>/Hook<T,R> while one compiler-known companion family gives experts statically fixed return types, one queue policy per handle, and one inspectable control plane. The recommendation does not depend on implementation effort.

options.name: Typed companion handles
options.detail: Keep beginner Event<T> and Hook<T,R> unchanged and synchronous. Add AsyncEvent<T,E>, constructed by async_result, with one immutable AsyncPolicy and FailurePolicy per handle; emit_async always returns Task<DispatchReport<E>>. Add DecisionHook<T,E>, constructed by decision_hook, whose run always returns HookOutcome<T,E>. One handle therefore has one queue, one ordering domain, one lifecycle, and one statically fixed result type. This is the recommended hybrid: defaults remain tiny, while expert pressure, failure, trace, cancellation, and intervention facts are explicit without changing behavior call by call.

Hook stays one value but run_transform<E> returns HookOutcome<T,E>; run_cancel is removed so cancellation and failure cannot become a second control plane. This makes each call explicit, but one Event can silently split related payloads into three ordering domains.

Bounded mpsc send waits for capacity and wakes with an error when the receiver closes; Jet needs the same exact wake/drop law under scope cancellation and deadlines, integrated with its scheduler rather than exposed as a raw channel.

decisions.title: Make DecisionHook continuation values exact
decisions.gist: Choose how a DecisionHook handler says continue while run still returns the final transformed value.
decisions.lesson:
A decision hook passes one value through ordered handlers. Each handler chooses whether processing continues, transforms the value, cancels, or fails. The next handler must receive the latest value.

Two moments need types. A handler returns a decision about the current value. The completed run returns the final value or the reason processing stopped. Those moments can share one enum only when every variant has one unambiguous payload shape.

D-EVENT2 says a handler returns HookOutcome and that Continue keeps the current value. It also says zero handlers return Continue(original). A unit Continue serves the first sentence but cannot carry the final value. Continue(value) serves the second sentence but lets handlers transform through both Continue and Transform. This decision removes that contradiction.
decisions.story: Maya normalizes a save request, then validates it. The normalizer transforms the request. The validator approves without changing it. Maya must receive the normalized request after the hook finishes, while a plain approval should not repeat or replace the current value.
decisions.inWild:
hook.on(scope, (request) => HookDecision.Transform(normalize(request)))
hook.on(scope, (request) => HookDecision.Continue)
result :: hook.run(original)
// HookOutcome.Continue(normalized)

options.name: One outcome, Continue carries T
options.detail: Keep one HookOutcome<T,E> type. Every handler returns Continue(current) when it makes no change. run returns Continue(final). This preserves one visible enum, but handlers can replace the value through either Continue(other) or Transform(other).
options.technical: HookOutcome variants are Continue(T), Transform(T), Cancel, and Fail(E). A handler returning Continue(T) advances with its payload. Transform(T) also advances with its payload. The runtime cannot distinguish accidental replacement through Continue from an intentional Transform.

options.name: Unit Continue plus separate run record
options.detail: Handlers keep HookOutcome.Continue without a payload. run returns a separate HookRun record containing state, value, and error fields. Approval stays short, but callers must inspect a record with fields that are invalid in some states.
options.technical: Handler HookOutcome variants remain Continue, Transform(T), Cancel, and Fail(E). HookRun<T,E> contains state, value:T?, and error:E?. Validation must reject or prevent impossible combinations such as Continued without value or Cancelled with error.

options.name: Decision input, outcome output
options.detail: Handlers return HookDecision<T,E>: Continue, Transform(T), Cancel, or Fail(E). run returns HookOutcome<T,E>: Continue(T), Cancel, or Fail(E). Each type models one moment, so Continue stays short inside handlers and always carries the final value outside.
options.technical: HookDecision is accepted only from handlers. Continue preserves the current value; Transform replaces it. HookOutcome is returned only by run. Continue(T) contains the final value after every transform. Cancel and Fail(E) stop immediately in both phases. Zero handlers returns HookOutcome.Continue(original).
options.code:
hook.on(scope, (request) => HookDecision.Transform(normalize(request)))
hook.on(scope, (request) => HookDecision.Continue)
result :: hook.run(original)
// HookOutcome.Continue(normalized)

comparisons.note: Rust separates closure control from collected output. The closure returns a local decision, while the operation returns its completed result.
Middleware often returns a local next-or-stop decision, while the completed pipeline returns the final response. The two moments carry different information.

recommendation.why: C gives each semantic moment one valid shape. Handlers cannot transform through Continue, and every successful run contains the final value without nullable fields or hidden context.

whyNot.reason: A creates two spellings for replacement. Continue(other) and Transform(other) perform the same semantic job, weakening review and I8.
B replaces a closed outcome with state plus nullable fields. Callers can observe or construct impossible combinations unless another validation layer repairs them.

recommendation.tradeoff: C adds one small public enum name. The added name exposes a real phase boundary and keeps both handler and caller code total and unambiguous.

hybrid.synthesis: Use C's phase-specific types. Keep A's closed outcome for callers and B's payload-free Continue for handlers. Both feed the same ordered DecisionHook fold.

harvest.aspect: A completed run carries its final value in a closed variant.
harvest.use: HookOutcome.Continue(T) keeps that property only at the run boundary.

harvest.aspect: A handler approves without repeating the current value.
harvest.use: HookDecision.Continue keeps that concise handler spelling without nullable run fields.

harvest.aspect: Input decisions and completed outcomes have distinct valid states.
harvest.use: Keep both closed enums over one canonical fold and one stable ordering law.

decisions.title: How a function is marked as runnable by the tool
decisions.gist: A function the package tool can run is marked two ways: some by a reserved name (fn run, fn dev, fn build), and some by a mark (#Task fn deploy). This decides one way to say 'the tool can run this'.
decisions.lesson: This depends on the marker-plane ballot (D-SHAPE2). It decides whether runnable functions are marked by name, by mark, or stay split between the two.
decisions.story: A developer writes fn run and it becomes runnable because of its name. They add a deploy function and expect the same, but a plain fn deploy is not runnable; it needs #Task in front. Two rules for one idea: this function is a task the tool can run.
decisions.inWild:
Today both are how you make a runnable function:

    fn run() { ... }        // runnable because it is named 'run'
    fn dev() { ... }        // runnable because it is named 'dev'
    #Task fn deploy() { ... } // runnable because of the #Task mark

An error, E0928, exists only to police the line between the two.

options.name: Mark them all with #Task
options.detail: Every function the tool can run carries #Task, including run, dev, and build. One rule: a task is marked, never magic by name. The special-case error E0928 goes away.

options.name: Use reserved names, drop the mark
options.detail: Make runnable functions work by name only, and remove #Task. Fewer marks, but every new task name must be a reserved word the compiler knows, which does not extend to custom tasks.
options.code:
fn run()    { ... }
fn deploy() { ... }   // would need 'deploy' to be a reserved runnable name

options.name: Leave as-is
options.detail: Keep the built-in names magic and custom tasks marked with #Task. No change, but two rules and the E0928 error stay.
options.code: fn run() { ... }   #Task fn deploy() { ... }   // unchanged

recommendation.why: Marking every runnable function with #Task is one rule that works for both built-in and custom tasks. It removes the special-case error that only exists to guard the split.
recommendation.tradeoff: The common built-in tasks (run, dev, build) gain a #Task mark they do not have today. In return there is one rule instead of two, and custom tasks and built-in ones look the same.

whyNot.reason: Names-only cannot cover custom tasks, since every new task name would have to be a reserved word the compiler already knows.
Leaving both keeps two rules for one idea and keeps the error that exists only to police the boundary.

hybrid.synthesis: A takes B's goal of one rule but uses the mark, which is the only form that also covers custom tasks, not just the built-in names.

harvest.use: The chosen rule.
Kept, but achieved by the mark since names cannot cover custom tasks.
Not kept; the built-ins gain a #Task mark so the rule has no exceptions.

decisions.title: How a runnable Output links to code
decisions.gist: Choose the one checked relationship between a runnable Output and ordinary Jet code.
decisions.lesson: A lone `fn run` remains a complete program with no Output declaration. An explicit runnable Output needs a stable link when a Package exposes more than one result. A function reference uses normal name resolution, visibility, rename, navigation, provenance, and role validation. This decision chooses the link; D-ECO-OUTPUT-CALLCONTRACT1 chooses the function signature.
decisions.story: Maya adds an administrator command to a Package and later renames its startup function. Package checking must identify the stale link at the source reference.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's Outputs store `entry: run`, `entry: serve`, and `entry: verify_release`. Each is an ordinary symbol reference, not a file convention or string path.

options.name: Function reference
options.detail: Store an ordinary checked function reference in `entry`.

options.name: Module with run
options.detail: Store a module reference and require its conventional `run` function.
options.code:
admin: Output :: .Executable.{ name: "todo-admin", module: Admin }
module Admin { fn run() {} }

options.name: Text name
options.detail: Store a qualified function name as text and resolve it during Package checking.
options.code:
entry: "Admin.start"
$ jet check
cannot resolve Admin.start; change text to Admin.serve.

recommendation.why: Package linkage reuses Jet's symbol checks and editor model while preserving the unchanged zero-config `fn run` path.

whyNot.reason: A fixed run function makes source module organization part of packaging and requires extra modules for multiple outputs.
A text path loses normal reference safety and can remain stale after a symbol rename.

recommendation.tradeoff: Function and Output references must change together when code is renamed or moved.

decisions.title: C++ binder depth: `cpp.*` — opaque classes, laundered exceptions, on-demand templates
decisions.gist: Decide how deep the C++ binder goes: classes, exceptions, and templates across the boundary.
decisions.lesson:
The C binder (S59) is shipped law, but the world's performance libraries are C++: OpenCV, LLVM, TensorRT, Qt, game physics. C++ has no stable ABI, so every language binds it by generating a C shim layer underneath.

D-FFI-UNIFY1 already fixes the user surface: `cpp.<lib>` with script/project/overlay tiers and a `jet inspect bind cpp` binder. This ballot picks the binder's depth: what happens to classes, exceptions, and templates — the three things C++ has that C doesn't. The swift binder (D-FFI-SWIFT1) set the precedent shape: opaque ref-counted handles, throws mapped to Result.
decisions.story: Grace needs OpenCV's image pipeline. Python users type two lines. Today she would hand-write a C wrapper around every C++ method she touches, recreating the shim layer pybind11 generates automatically for Python.
decisions.inWild:
use cpp.opencv as cv               // project tier: opencv: cpp@"4.10" in pkg.jet

img :: cv.imread("scan.png")?      // cv::Exception -> `? CppError`
blur :: img.gaussian_blur(kernel: 5)?
files.write_bytes("out.png", blur.encode(".png")?)?

options.name: Full depth — opaque classes, `? CppError`, on-demand template instantiation
options.detail:
The binder (clang-based) emits a generated C shim crate per library, cached content-addressed like every bridge. Classes become opaque owned handles with RAII mapped to Jet scope cleanup (S63); methods become ordinary Jet methods on the handle type. Exceptions are caught at the shim and surface as `T ? CppError` — fallibility is visible at every call site.

Templates instantiate on demand: `cpp.vector<Int>` asks the binder to instantiate `std::vector<int64_t>` in the shim on cache miss. Overloads collapse to argument labels (S61); operator overloads become named methods. The overlay tier corrects any wrong guess.
options.code:
use cpp.opencv as cv

img :: cv.imread("scan.png")?        // handle; frees at scope end (S63)
out :: img.gaussian_blur(kernel: 5)?

$ jet check vision.jet   # exception type not convertible
error[E32xx]: `cv.imread` can throw `cv::Exception`
  the call is fallible — write `cv.imread("scan.png")?` and handle `CppError`

options.name: C-surface only — bind `extern "C"` symbols, classes stay out
options.detail:
The cpp binder binds only what the C binder already understands: free functions with C linkage. Libraries exposing C APIs (many do) work day one; anything class-shaped needs a hand-written C wrapper, exactly like today.

Honest and small, but it concedes the actual C++ ecosystem: OpenCV, Qt, and LLVM are class-first. The gap between Jet and Python/Swift interop stays visible in every migration conversation.
options.code:
use cpp.sqlite3 as sq       // works: C API
use cpp.opencv as cv        // fails:
$ jet check vision.jet
error[E32xx]: `opencv` exposes no C-linkage surface
  the cpp binder binds extern "C" symbols only; write a C wrapper for classes

options.name: Full depth minus templates — classes and exceptions, no generic instantiation
options.detail: Everything in A except template instantiation: template types appear only where a library already instantiates them in its own headers. Cuts the binder's hardest surface. Users hit the wall exactly at `std::vector<T>` returns and Eigen-style math libraries — common in the target workloads — and fall back to overlay-tier hand shims.
options.code:
use cpp.opencv as cv
img :: cv.imread("x.png")?          // fine: concrete class
hist :: img.histogram()?             // fails if return is std::vector<float>
error[E32xx]: `histogram` returns `std::vector<float>` — no instantiation support
  add an overlay shim, or vote template support

comparisons.note: pybind11 proved the full-depth model: opaque class handles, exceptions translated, templates instantiated at binding time. It is why C++ libraries feel native from Python.
Swift's C++ interop (5.9+) also chose classes-as-values/handles with throws mapping — the same shape D-FFI-SWIFT1 already ratified for Swift itself.
comparisons.code:
import CxxOpenCV
let img = try cv.imread("scan.png")

recommendation.why: The C++ ecosystem is the single biggest performance-library pool Jet can absorb, and it is class-first. Full depth is what makes `use cpp.opencv` two lines instead of a wrapper project; pybind11 proved the model at scale.

whyNot.reason: It binds the part of C++ that is already C and concedes the actual target — every class-first library stays a manual wrapper project.
Template returns pervade the exact math/vision libraries this binder exists for; stopping there moves the wall two steps back instead of removing it.

recommendation.tradeoff: The binder owns a clang toolchain dependency (jetpack-provisioned, never in Source/ — I6) and template instantiation lengthens first-compile cache misses.

hybrid.synthesis: A ships staged along B→C→A internally — C-linkage binding lands first, classes/exceptions next, templates last — but the ratified surface is A so no intermediate stage becomes accidental law.

harvest.use: ratified as the contract
first internal stage; already proven by the shipped C binder
second internal stage; overlay tier covers gaps until templates land

decisions.title: Inline foreign code: a fourth FFI tier with the Jet signature as the checked contract
decisions.gist: Let a Jet file carry a small foreign function body inline, type-checked against a Jet signature.
decisions.lesson:
D-FFI-UNIFY1 gives every foreign language three tiers. Script tier binds a foreign file (`use "raylib.h" as rl`). Project tier pins a dependency (`use py.h5 as h5`). Overlay tier corrects generated bindings. All three bind code that lives in another file.

Nothing covers ten lines of foreign code that belong inside one Jet file — a checksum kernel, one intrinsic, one tricky syscall wrapper. Today you create a separate header or dependency for it. Other languages solve this with inline blocks: Rust has `asm!`, C++ has `asm`, Zig has inline assembly and C import. None type-check the boundary as a real signature.
decisions.story: Walter ports a hash function whose reference implementation is 12 lines of C. The algorithm is stable; wrapping it as a whole vendored library is absurd. He wants those 12 lines next to the Jet code that calls them, with the call boundary checked like any Jet function.

options.name: `#Foreign(<lang>)` fn — one directive shape for every language
options.detail:
A fourth D-FFI-UNIFY1 tier. The declaration is an ordinary Jet `fn` signature; the body is one multi-line string of foreign source. Sema checks every call site against the Jet signature. The language's existing binder compiles the body on cache miss and generates the same safe marshaling as the script tier.

A body/signature mismatch is a Jet diagnostic naming both sides — no foreign compiler error reaches the user unlaundered (I2). Effects declare like any extern; unsafe-language bodies (c, cpp, asm) additionally require the enclosing `#Unsafe("reason")` gate (S58). One shape, reused by every current and future language.

options.name: No inline tier — script tier is enough
options.detail:
Keep the ratified three tiers. Small foreign snippets live in a sibling file bound by the script tier (`use "./crc32.h" as c`). The surface stays smaller and every foreign line stays in a file its own toolchain can open directly.
