The cost: the ten-line case keeps real friction — a second file, a header/source split for C, and pkg wiring for anything the script tier can't bind. The friction pushes people toward vendoring or toward not using the best tool.

options.name: Typed-text values — foreign code as a checked string type
options.detail: Reuse D-TYPEDTEXT1: a string literal in a `C`/`Py` typed position becomes a checked foreign-code value, compiled and invoked through a Core call. Symmetry with `Sql`/`Html` is elegant. But code-as-value blurs the boundary: the signature lives in a turbofish, call sites read like dynamic strings, and the `#Unsafe` audit gate has no natural declaration to attach to.
options.code:
kernel: C<fn([U8], U32) -> U32> :: """
  uint32_t crc32(const uint8_t* d, size_t n, uint32_t s) { … }
"""
sum :: kernel.call(bytes, 0)?

comparisons.note: Zig's `@cImport` binds headers (Jet's script tier already matches it). Zig still has no inline foreign bodies except asm.
Rust inline is asm-only and the operand contract is spelled in strings, not a function signature. cc/cxx crates need build scripts for anything more.
comparisons.code: unsafe { asm!("rdtsc", out("rax") lo, out("rdx") hi); }

recommendation.why: The signature-as-contract shape is what makes Jet's FFI safer than every host language: sema owns the boundary, binders own the body, and the same spelling scales from asm to Python. It completes D-FFI-UNIFY1 with one rule instead of per-language hacks.

whyNot.reason: It leaves the highest-frequency FFI case (a few lines) with the highest ceremony, which is backwards for a language selling ergonomic interop.
Code-as-value hides the declaration: no natural home for the #Unsafe gate, effects, or docs, and call sites stop looking like ordinary Jet calls.

recommendation.tradeoff: Foreign bodies inside .jet files get editor support only through injected-language regions; the binder cache must rebuild the snippet when the body string changes.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's discipline: bodies compile through the same binder and cache as script-tier files. It also keeps C's checked boundary — the check just lives on a real fn declaration.

harvest.aspect: one directive shape, signature as contract
harvest.use: adopted

harvest.aspect: binder + cache reuse, no second compilation path
harvest.use: A compiles inline bodies through the exact script-tier binder machinery
A keeps the check, attached to the fn signature where audit gates and effects already live

decisions.comment: Instead of foreign, use #FFI(<lang>)

decisions.title: Inline assembly: the `asm` instance of the inline tier, gated by #Unsafe
decisions.gist: Give experts real inline assembly with typed operands, behind the existing #Unsafe gate.
decisions.lesson:
Master-of-ALL bottoms out in assembly: cycle counters, cache-line tricks, crypto with constant-time guarantees, kernel entry stubs, intrinsics the SIMD lane types (D-SIMD1) don't cover. Jet has no asm story today — the expert hits a wall and reaches for C or Rust.

The low-level tier already has the right gates: `use core.mem` for discovery, `#Unsafe("reason")` for audit (S58). Rust lowers inline asm through `asm!`, which rustc verifies per target — Jet's generated-Rust backend can reuse that verification while keeping the user-facing surface and diagnostics Jet-owned (I2).
decisions.story: Dale profiles a hot loop and needs the CPU's cycle counter, not wall-clock time. `core.time` has no such call. In Rust he would write three lines of `asm!`. In Jet today his only path is an FFI round-trip through a C file for one instruction.
decisions.inWild:
use core.mem

#Unsafe("cycle counter — no Core surface exists")
#Foreign(asm) fn rdtsc() -> U64 {
    """
    rdtsc
    shl rdx, 32
    or  rax, rdx        ; -> return
    """
}

start :: rdtsc()
hot_loop()
print("cycles: {rdtsc() - start}")

options.name: `#Foreign(asm)` — asm is a language in the inline tier
options.detail:
Assembly reuses D-FFI-INLINE1's shape exactly: a Jet `fn` signature is the operand contract — parameters map to input registers, the return value to outputs, per a small documented convention with named `; -> return` anchors. Requires `use core.mem` plus an enclosing `#Unsafe("reason")`. Bodies are per-target; the existing `comptime if build.os ==` and `#Target` machinery select variants.

Lowering emits Rust `asm!`, so rustc verifies register/clobber facts per target while every user-facing error stays a Jet diagnostic naming the Jet span (I2). No new sigil, no new block form — the inline tier absorbs asm as just another language.

options.name: Intrinsics library only — no user-visible asm
options.detail:
Instead of asm syntax, `core.mem.intrinsics` grows curated functions (cycle counters, prefetch, CAS variants, crc32 hardware ops), each internally implemented with vetted asm. Beginners never see assembly; every operation is named, documented, and effect-tagged.

The ceiling is real: an expert who needs an instruction Core hasn't wrapped is stuck writing C again. The library also chases every new ISA extension forever, always behind.
options.code:
use core.mem

start :: mem.intrinsics.cycle_count()
hot_loop()
print("cycles: {mem.intrinsics.cycle_count() - start}")

// need CLDEMOTE? not wrapped yet — back to C FFI

comparisons.note: `asm!` is string templates with operand constraints spelled inline; powerful, but the contract is not a function signature and beginners meet it in library code.
Zig treats asm as an expression with typed outputs — closest to option A's spirit; Jet goes further by making the whole fn signature the contract.

recommendation.why: A removes the last wall between an expert and the machine while staying inside gates that already exist. The signature-as-contract convention makes Jet asm more checkable than C's or Rust's, and rustc's verifier rides underneath for free.

whyNot.reason: A curated library is a ceiling, not a floor — the expert one instruction past the catalog falls back to C, which is the outcome this ballot exists to end.

recommendation.tradeoff: Per-target bodies are the user's responsibility; a program using #Foreign(asm) gives up target portability for those functions and must gate variants explicitly.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship A as the floor and let B grow on top. `core.mem.intrinsics` wraps popular cases as ordinary functions implemented with the same #Foreign(asm) mechanism. Beginners meet named functions; the expert path never hits a ceiling.

harvest.use: adopted as the mechanism

harvest.aspect: curated named intrinsics for the common cases
harvest.use: grows in Core on top of A; beginners meet only the named functions

decisions.comment: How about instead of foreign, #FFI(asm)

decisions.title: Raw foreign body spelling for `#FFI(<lang>) fn`
decisions.gist: Pick how a foreign function's body text skips Jet's own string interpolation, so real foreign source code pastes in unchanged.
decisions.lesson:
Every Jet string, `"..."` and `"""..."""` alike, does two things at once. A `{expr}` inside the quotes drops a Jet value into the text (interpolation). A literal brace must be written doubled, `{{` or `}}`, so the lexer doesn't mistake it for the start of a hole. These are S8 and S20, and today they apply to every triple-quoted string with no exception.

D-FFI-INLINE1 lets `#FFI(<lang>) fn` carry a real foreign function as its body, written as one triple-quoted string. That text is not Jet code. It is C, Python, assembly, or another language's actual source, meant to be pasted in verbatim. Most languages use `{` and `}` constantly for function bodies, loops, and blocks — a single opening brace with no doubled partner on the same line.

Because the lexer can't tell 'this string holds foreign code' from 'this string holds Jet text', it treats every one of those braces as an interpolation attempt. This decision picks the spelling that tells the lexer 'don't interpolate this one.'
decisions.story: Walter wants to port a 12-line C reference implementation of crc32 into a `#FFI(c) fn`, exactly as D-FFI-INLINE1's own ratified example shows. He pastes the C function body between the triple quotes and runs `jet check`.

options.name: Implicit raw — `#FFI` bodies never interpolate, zero new syntax
options.detail:
The body of a `#FFI(<lang>) fn` keeps the exact `"""..."""` spelling it already has. Inside that specific position only — the body of an `#FFI` function — `{expr}` interpolation and `{{`/`}}` escaping simply don't run. The text between the quotes reaches the language's binder byte for byte, because it was never Jet text to begin with.

Every other triple-quoted string in Jet is unaffected. This changes meaning only inside a position D-FFI-INLINE1 already defined as 'one string of foreign source'. There's nothing to interpolate against in the first place.
options.technical: Sema, not the lexer, recognizes the `#FFI(<lang>) fn { """...""" }` shape. It reads the string's raw source span directly, ignoring any `StrTokPart::Interp` parts the lexer produced. A body containing `{`/`}` never reaches the lexer's interpolation path, because the parser hands sema the untouched span between the opening and closing `"""`.

options.name: General raw string literal — `raw"""..."""`, usable anywhere
options.detail:
Add a raw string form to Jet's string family, following the same prefix pattern D-TYPEDTEXT2 already ratified for `sql"..."` and `html"..."`: a keyword directly before the opening quote. `raw"""..."""` never interpolates and never needs brace doubling, anywhere it appears — not just inside `#FFI` bodies.

This solves the foreign-body problem and also helps ordinary Jet code that fights `{`/`}` doubling today: JSON templates, regex patterns, Windows paths. The cost is a second string form every Jet user now has to learn and recognize, for a need that — outside `#FFI` bodies — hasn't come up yet.
options.technical: Lexer gains a `raw` prefix keyword recognized immediately before `"` or `"""`. Scanning skips the `{`/`}`/`\` special-case branches entirely and stores the span as a single `StrTokPart::Lit`. This matches how `sql"..."`/`html"..."` already attach a prefix token ahead of ordinary string scanning (D-TYPEDTEXT2).

options.name: Keep interpolating — escape every brace as `{{`/`}}`
options.detail: No new syntax at all. `#FFI` bodies stay ordinary triple-quoted strings: every literal `{` and `}` in the pasted foreign source must be doubled by hand before `jet check` accepts it. This already works today; E0064 stops firing once every brace is doubled. But it means hand-editing every foreign snippet on the way in, then un-doubling it again to test the snippet in its native toolchain.
options.technical: No lexer or sema change; S8/S20 keep applying uniformly to every triple-quoted string, `#FFI` bodies included.

comparisons.note: Rust has no string interpolation at all, so `r"..."` raw strings exist only to skip backslash-escaping, not brace-escaping. Jet's problem is sharper: Jet strings interpolate by default, so foreign brace-heavy code needs an explicit opt-out Rust never had to invent.
comparisons.code: let query = r"SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = \d+";

comparisons.note: Python's f-strings are opt-in (`f"..."`); a plain `"..."` never interpolates, so pasting brace-heavy code into an ordinary string just works. Jet inverts this default for beginner ergonomics (S8), which is what makes this decision necessary.
comparisons.code: body = "uint32_t add(uint32_t a, uint32_t b) { return a + b; }"

recommendation.why: D-FFI-INLINE1 already defines an `#FFI` body as one string of foreign source, not Jet text, so interpolation was never meaningful there in the first place. Option A just makes the lexer's behavior match that ratified meaning, with zero new syntax anyone has to learn.

whyNot.reason: A general raw-string type is a real feature, but it solves a problem beginners haven't hit yet outside `#FFI` bodies. Shipping it now adds a second, rarer string form to learn before the actual gate — the `#FFI` body — is closed.
It forces every pasted foreign function through manual brace-doubling. A beginner's very first `#FFI(c) fn` still won't compile until every brace is found and doubled by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: The same `"""..."""` spelling now means two different things depending on where it appears: plain Jet text everywhere else, raw foreign text inside an `#FFI` body. That's acceptable because the body position is already a distinct, narrowly gated context. It only exists inside `#FFI(<lang>) fn`, already requires `#Unsafe` for unsafe languages, and was never valid as ordinary Jet text to start with.

hybrid.synthesis: A ships as the fix for the actual gate: every `#FFI` body becomes raw automatically. B's real strength, a general-purpose raw string usable anywhere in Jet, stays open as its own future decision. Nothing about A forecloses adding `raw"..."` later if a concrete non-FFI need shows up.

harvest.aspect: zero new syntax, matches D-FFI-INLINE1's existing meaning of an `#FFI` body
harvest.use: adopted as the mechanism

harvest.aspect: a general raw-string form usable outside `#FFI` too
harvest.use: not needed to close this gate; kept as a separate future ballot instead of bundling an unproven general feature into this fix

harvest.aspect: today's actual working escape hatch, `{{`/`}}` doubling
harvest.use: stays available for the rare case a foreign body genuinely needs a literal `"""` sequence the raw form can't represent; not the default path

decisions.title: Inline asm operand and clobber spelling
decisions.gist: Pick how an `#FFI(asm) fn` body says which register holds an input parameter, and which registers it destroys as a side effect.
decisions.lesson:
An assembly instruction reads and writes CPU registers directly, not Jet variables. Two ideas matter here. An 'operand' is a register the instruction reads (an input) or writes (an output) — `add rax, rbx` operates on the registers named `rax` and `rbx`. A 'clobber' is a register the instruction overwrites as a side effect, without that register being a declared input or output. Its old value is gone, and nothing may rely on it afterward.

Rust's `asm!` macro, which Jet's asm bodies compile down to, requires every register the instruction touches to be declared: as an input, an output, or a clobber. Skip one and the compiler may reuse that register for something else at the exact moment the instruction is still using it, corrupting a value silently.

D-FFI-ASM1 already ratified that a Jet function's parameters are inputs and its return value is an output, ending in a `; -> return` comment in the body. What's still open is how the body names the register holding a given input, and how it declares a clobber. Those are the two facts `asm!` needs that today have no spelling at all.
decisions.story:
Priya writes `#FFI(asm) fn add_with_carry(a: U64, b: U64) -> U64`, adding two 64-bit halves of a bignum. She needs to say 'parameter `a` is in this register, parameter `b` is in that one' inside the body — there's no way to write that today.

Her rdtsc-style cycle counter has the same gap from the other side. It writes to `rdx` as scratch space on the way to computing the return value. Nothing today tells the compiler that `rdx`'s final value must be thrown away, not treated as a second output.

options.name: Comment-anchor convention extended — `; in a -> rax`, `; clobbers rdx`
options.detail:
Extends the already-ratified `; -> return` anchor family. An input line names the parameter and the register holding it; a clobber line lists every register the instruction destroys that isn't already an input or the output. Both are ordinary trailing or standalone comments inside the asm text, read by the binder, not by rustc.

No new grammar, and the body stays plain, readable assembly a person could paste into any assembler. The cost: register facts live in free-form comment text — the exact same shape as ordinary human comments everywhere else in Jet, which never carry meaning. A typo in a comment (`; in a-> rax`, missing the space) is easy to miss and has to be caught by string-parsing the comment itself, not by the language's real grammar.
options.technical: Binder scans the raw asm text for lines matching `; in <param> -> <reg>` and `; clobbers <reg>[, <reg>...]`. Each becomes an `in("<reg>") <param>` / `out("<reg>") _` entry passed to Rust's `asm!` macro, alongside the already-ratified `; -> return` anchor's `lateout("<reg>") <return>`.
options.code:
#Unsafe("carry add — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm) fn add_with_carry(a: U64, b: U64) -> U64 {
    """
    ; in a -> rax
    ; in b -> rbx
    add rax, rbx        ; -> return
    """
}

#Unsafe("cycle counter — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm) fn rdtsc() -> U64 {
    """
    rdtsc
    shl rdx, 32
    or  rax, rdx        ; -> return
    ; clobbers rdx
    """
}

options.name: Marker arguments — register and clobber facts on the `#FFI(asm, ...)` line
options.detail:
The operand contract moves out of the body entirely and onto the `#FFI` marker itself: `#FFI(asm, a: "rax", b: "rbx", clobbers: "rdx")`. The body underneath becomes pure, untouched assembly with no Jet-specific comments mixed in. It can be copied straight from an assembler reference and pasted, unchanged.

Every register fact is visible on one line without opening the body, which helps scanning many small asm functions at once. It also duplicates information. For a function with many operands, the marker line grows into a long, body-disconnected list a reader has to match up against the assembly by eye. It's a second place a register name can drift out of sync with the body that actually uses it.
options.technical: The `#FFI(asm, ...)` marker's argument list extends past the language name to accept `<param>: "<reg>"` pairs and a `clobbers: "<reg>", ...` entry. Each lowers to an `in("<reg>") <param>` / `out("<reg>") _` entry passed to `asm!`, the same runtime effect as option A declared in a different place. Today the marker parser closes right after the language name. `#FFI(asm, clobbers("rdx"))` currently fails with `E0003: expected ')' after the foreign language name, found ','`, so this option needs new marker grammar.
options.code:
#Unsafe("carry add — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm, a: "rax", b: "rbx")
fn add_with_carry(a: U64, b: U64) -> U64 {
    """
    add rax, rbx
    """
}

#Unsafe("cycle counter — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm, clobbers: "rdx")
fn rdtsc() -> U64 {
    """
    rdtsc
    shl rdx, 32
    or  rax, rdx
    """
}

options.name: Named template placeholders — `{a}`, `{b}` in the body, plus a clobber line
options.detail:
An input parameter appears in the body as `{name}`, a placeholder the binder fills with whatever register Rust's `asm!` allocator picks. This is the same generic-register model `asm!` itself recommends over hardcoding a register, since the allocator can then avoid an unnecessary spill. Where an instruction mandates one exact register (`rdtsc` always writes `rax`/`rdx`), the body just names that register literally, no placeholder needed. A `; clobbers` line, reused from option A, declares any register touched but never bound to a name.

This mirrors `asm!` most directly: named operands map one-to-one onto `asm!`'s own `in(reg) name` / `out(reg) name` entries. It only works once a `#FFI(asm)` body is non-interpolating (D-FFI-RAWBODY1). Today, `{a}`/`{b}` inside a triple-quoted string is Jet's own interpolation syntax and collides with it.
options.technical: `{name}` maps to `in(reg) name` for a parameter, or `out(reg) name` for the return, alongside the ratified `; -> return` anchor that still marks which line produces it. An unbound but written register on a `; clobbers` line maps to `out("<reg>") _`. This requires D-FFI-RAWBODY1's body text to be raw, not interpolated. Verified today: this exact `add_with_carry` body currently fails with `E0064: an #FFI(asm) function body must be one string of asm source`, because `{a}`/`{b}` triggers ordinary Jet interpolation first.
options.code:
#Unsafe("carry add — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm) fn add_with_carry(a: U64, b: U64) -> U64 {
    """
    add {a}, {b}        ; -> return
    """
}

#Unsafe("cycle counter — no Core surface")
#FFI(asm) fn rdtsc() -> U64 {
    """
    rdtsc
    shl rdx, 32
    or  rax, rdx        ; -> return
    ; clobbers rdx
    """
}

comparisons.note: `asm!` requires every touched register declared as `in`, `out`, `lateout`, or a discarded clobber (`out("reg") _`). The register class can be a specific name (`in("rax")`) or a generic class (`in(reg)`) the allocator assigns, referenced in the template by position or name.

Zig's asm syntax names operands with `[tag] "constraint" (value)`, closer to option C's named-placeholder spirit than to free-form comments, and requires clobbers listed explicitly in a trailing `:::` clause.

recommendation.why: C maps directly onto what `asm!` actually needs: a named placeholder per operand, generic-register by default so the allocator can avoid needless spills. A hardcoded register appears only where the instruction itself mandates one, like `rdtsc`. It reuses the ratified `; -> return` anchor and A's clobber-line spelling unchanged.

whyNot.reason: Register facts live entirely in prose-shaped comments the binder has to string-parse. It is the only place in Jet where a comment carries real semantic weight, so a small typo like a missing space is invisible to the language's actual grammar.

The operand contract exists in two places at once, the marker and the body, for what is usually a one-to-one mapping. A real SIMD function with many operands turns the marker line into a long list disconnected from the assembly that uses each register, and the two can drift out of sync.

recommendation.tradeoff: `{name}` now has three different meanings depending on where it's written. Outside `#FFI` it's ordinary Jet interpolation; inside a raw `#FFI(c)`/`#FFI(py)` body it's nothing at all; inside `#FFI(asm)` specifically it's a register placeholder. That's acceptable because it only appears inside the already-gated, `#Unsafe`-only `asm` body. It's the one place where matching Rust's and Zig's own inline-asm convention matters more than reusing Jet's general string rules.

hybrid.synthesis: C keeps A's clobber-line spelling unchanged — `; clobbers rdx` is still a plain comment, since a clobber has no placeholder to bind and a comment line is enough. It keeps the ratified `; -> return` output anchor untouched. Only the input side moves from prose comments (A) or a marker-level list (B) to `{name}` placeholders resolved directly against the body that uses them.

harvest.use: kept as-is inside C for declaring destroyed registers, since a clobber has no value to name a placeholder after

harvest.aspect: an explicit, auditable register fact separate from ordinary assembly text
harvest.use: C keeps this for instruction-mandated registers (`rdtsc`'s literal `rax`/`rdx`), which stay visible in the body exactly where they're used, instead of duplicated on the marker line

harvest.aspect: named placeholders mapping one-to-one onto `asm!`'s own operand list
harvest.use: adopted as the mechanism for every input and output that isn't instruction-mandated

decisions.title: No-heap backing for mem.Fixed
decisions.gist: Choose how mem.Fixed receives bounded inline storage whose size is known before code generation.
decisions.lesson:
A fixed allocator serves values from one bounded byte region and never requests heap storage. Each allocation aligns its payload within that region. Alignment padding, stored values, and reverse-drop metadata all count against the declared byte bound. The runtime reserves payload bytes from the start and drop records from the end; allocation fails atomically when they would overlap. Reset drops live values in reverse allocation order, clears both cursors, and reuses the same bytes.

A runtime number cannot determine a local variable's storage size. Jet must know the byte count before code generation, or receive an already-sized inline buffer. Jet currently erases [T#N] to Vec and erases Fixed to one size-free runtime type. No option may claim no-heap completion until fixed-size byte storage has a genuine inline representation. Explicit-buffer forms additionally require that representation to preserve the backing address and byte count through sema and codegen.

While Fixed borrows a buffer, that borrow is exclusive: the original buffer cannot be read, written, moved, or borrowed again until Fixed ends. Reset requires no outstanding allocated views. A compiler-synthesized Fixed and every derived view are lexical. They cannot be returned, stored beyond the backing binding, captured by an escaping closure or task, or carried through a longer-lived control-flow join. Sema rejects those escapes before codegen.
decisions.story: Mara writes firmware for a sensor with no heap. One function needs 2048 bytes of temporary packet storage. She wants review tools to prove the backing location, total byte bound, alignment cost, reverse-drop behavior, reset behavior, and deterministic exhaustion path.
decisions.inWild: A packet decoder creates one Fixed allocator, stores temporary records, resets it for the next packet, and must never allocate outside its declared byte region. A DMA path receives a caller-owned fixed buffer whose placement is controlled outside the decoder.

options.name: Short local form, explicit expert buffer
options.detail: Fixed.new keeps the short form for lexical scratch storage. Its size must be compile-time known, and the compiler creates backing beside that direct local binding. Fixed.over uses the same borrowed-buffer runtime when experts supply an inline fixed buffer with externally controlled placement.
options.technical: Fixed.new(size: N) accepts a positive compile-time integer only and is legal only as the initializer of a direct lexical binding. It synthesizes N automatic bytes in that binding's frame and never silently promotes them to heap storage. Fixed.over(&buffer) accepts a genuine inline [Byte#N] only after fixed-size-list lowering stops erasing that type to Vec; card completion requires both forms, not new alone. The shared runtime aligns each payload by advancing within the buffer; every skipped byte counts against N. Payload, alignment gaps, and reverse-drop records share N bytes, with no side allocation. Escapes, captures, longer-lived storage, use of the borrowed buffer, reset with live views, and dynamic new sizes are sema errors.

options.name: Explicit buffer only
options.detail: Every Fixed allocator exclusively borrows caller-provided inline storage. Placement and ownership are always visible, but even ordinary local scratch use requires the caller to create or receive a separate fixed buffer.
options.technical: Retire Fixed.new(size:). Fixed.over(&buffer) accepts only genuine inline [Byte#N], so this option cannot ship while fixed-size lists erase to Vec. The allocator is a non-escaping exclusive view over the buffer. Payload bytes grow upward, reverse-drop records grow downward, alignment padding counts against N, and collision is deterministic exhaustion. The buffer remains inaccessible until Fixed ends, and reset is rejected while allocated views remain live.
options.code:
use core.mem

// The caller controls where this genuine inline buffer lives.
fn decode(backing: &[Byte#2048]) {
    scratch :: mem.Fixed.over(&backing)
    row :: scratch.alloc(PacketRow.{})
    use(row)
    scratch.reset()
}

scratch :: mem.Fixed.new(size: 2048)
error: Fixed requires caller-provided inline backing
Fix: receive or declare genuine [Byte#2048] inline storage and pass it to Fixed.over

options.name: Size in the allocator type
options.detail: Fixed owns its inline storage, and its byte count appears in the type. Placement follows the owning value, but every signature and container carrying Fixed must also carry its size.
options.technical: Add a compile-time value argument Fixed<N>. This option depends on complete value-generic type support and an inline owned backing representation; current monomorphic Fixed and Vec-backed [T#N] cannot satisfy it. The N-byte object contains payload, alignment padding, and reverse-drop records. Moving Fixed is rejected while any view into it is live. Different sizes are different types and require explicit size-generic abstraction.

comparisons.note: Zig's fixed buffer allocator borrows an explicit byte array. Buffer placement and size are visible, matching option B and option A's expert form.
C++ monotonic_buffer_resource accepts caller storage and can use a null upstream resource to forbid fallback allocation. Alignment consumes space inside the supplied region.

recommendation.why: A preserves the short constructor for ordinary lexical scratch space while giving experts exact caller-controlled placement. Both forms lower to one borrowed-buffer runtime, one bounded metadata layout, one alignment rule, one reverse-drop rule, and one exhaustion law. Completion remains honest: the card cannot close until Fixed.over receives genuine inline [Byte#N] storage rather than Vec.

whyNot.reason: B makes placement maximally explicit but requires separate backing ceremony for every small local scratch allocator, even when the compiler can create the identical lexical storage and expose it through inspection.
C spreads the byte count through signatures and containers and depends on incomplete value-generic type support. That cost buys movable ownership where the common use is one lexical scratch scope.

recommendation.tradeoff: A has two constructor spellings and restricts Fixed.new to direct lexical bindings. Fixed.over cannot ship ahead of genuine inline fixed-size storage. Those costs preserve beginner brevity without hiding heap allocation or weakening expert placement control.

decisions.title: What totality law should additive guard syntax use?
decisions.gist: Choose which guard and enum forms must cover every possible path.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's existing `if` spellings remain available. The proposal adds one-line statement guards, braced statement guard tables, and a braced guard expression that produces a value. The owner has separately reopened only the missing-enum-case enforcement policy for research and decision.

A statement may intentionally do nothing. Therefore `if ready -> send()` and a braced statement guard table can safely omit `else`; no matching condition means no action. A value-producing guard expression is different because every path needs a value. Its final `else` is mandatory.

Enum subject dispatch declares another intent: classify one closed value by its variants. Exhaustive checking catches forgotten variants and makes enum growth visible when code recompiles. Partial enum actions remain available through guard syntax. The remaining choice is whether subject-dispatch exhaustiveness stays a fixed compiler guarantee or becomes configurable guidance.
decisions.story: Maya conditionally sends messages, computes a display label from several conditions, and classifies a message state enum. She wants optional actions concise, assignments total, and new enum variants unable to disappear silently.
decisions.detail: Owner constraints: guard syntax is additive. Existing ordinary block `if`, `else if`, `if` expressions, and `if subject == { ... }` remain valid. New `if condition -> statement` stays brace-free. Statement guard tables may omit `else`. New value-producing subjectless guard expressions require final `else`; this decision does not add value-producing subject dispatch. Options differ only on enforcement when existing enum subject dispatch omits known variants.

options.name: Hard totality by intent
options.detail: Statement guards may omit `else`. Value guard tables require it. Existing closed-enum subject dispatch remains a compiler-checked exhaustive classification: list every variant or provide `else`. A configurable style lint guides multi-arm guard tables back to subject dispatch when they repeatedly match one enum.
options.technical:
Statement grammar is `if BoolExpr -> arm-body` and `if { guard-arm+ [else-arm] }`; no match is `Void` with no effect. `arm-body` is one non-`if` statement or a block. Direct nesting requires a block.

Value grammar adds `if { value-guard-arm+ else -> value-body }` wherever an expression is accepted, including bindings, returns, arguments, and nesting. `value-body` is one expression or a value block. Every branch follows existing `if`-expression type unification. `else` is syntactically mandatory because arbitrary Boolean conditions are not solver-proved exhaustive. Inline arrow guards remain statement-only.

Existing `if enum_subject == { ... }` remains statement-only and exhaustive. An unguarded variant pattern covers that variant; an unguarded group or structural `|` pattern covers its union. A pattern combined with `&&` or `||` contributes no exhaustive coverage. Multiple guarded arms never combine into coverage. Every reachable variant needs unguarded coverage, or the table needs final `else`; otherwise compilation fails.

Pattern bindings follow S31. A name is visible to its right through `&&` and in its selected arm body when every successful path establishes it. Parentheses do not widen scope. Bindings under `||` do not reach the body. No binding reaches another arm, `else`, or following code.

Formatter never rewrites existing block `if`. It preserves author-chosen one-arm outer braces. An inline statement guard stays one line when it fits; otherwise formatter widens it once to a one-arm braced guard. Guard expressions always retain outer braces, one arm per line, and final `else`.

Default-on style lint `same_enum_guard_table` requires at least two non-else arms, all led by pattern tests against one closed-enum subject. Existing lint controls may allow it. It never fires for one-line guards, mixed subjects, arbitrary predicates, or value expressions.

options.name: Configurable enum exhaustiveness
options.detail: Guard and value rules match A. Closed-enum subject dispatch is exhaustive by default, but a project compiler option may downgrade missing variants from error to warning. Teams gain policy control, while the same source can become valid or invalid under different project settings.
options.technical: Value-producing guard tables always require `else`; no option changes that semantic requirement. Statement subject dispatch uses an `enum_exhaustiveness = error|warn` project setting. `warn` means no matching variant performs no action. Inline grammar, braced grammar, formatter, bindings, and same-enum style lint equal A.

options.name: Enum exhaustiveness as lint
options.detail: Guard and value rules match A. Missing variants in statement subject dispatch compile and produce a default warning, which normal lint controls may allow or deny. This keeps partial enum switches convenient but makes coverage depend on lint policy rather than syntax intent.
options.technical: Value-producing guard tables always require `else`. Statement subject dispatch with missing closed-enum variants has defined no-action fallthrough and emits `non_exhaustive_enum_dispatch`. Existing lint severity controls decide warning, denial, or allowance. Other grammar, formatter, binding, and style-lint laws equal A.

options.name: Only value contexts are exhaustive
options.detail: Guard and value rules match A. Closed-enum statement subject dispatch may omit variants without warning; an omitted variant performs no action. This follows a strict statement-versus-expression split for the reopened enum question, but enum subject dispatch no longer promises complete classification.
options.technical: Only known-variant coverage changes from A: a closed-enum statement subject dispatch may omit variants, with no error or lint, and an omitted variant performs no action. Value-producing guard tables still require final `else`. All other subject-dispatch fallback laws, grammar, formatter, bindings, and style-lint laws equal A.

comparisons.note: [Kotlin](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/control-flow.html) permits non-exhaustive `when` statements, requires exhaustive value-producing `when`, and requires `else` for subjectless value forms.
comparisons.code:
when { ready -> send() }
val label = when { ready -> "ready"; else -> "waiting" }

comparisons.note: [Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-01-all-the-places-for-patterns.html) requires exhaustive `match` but provides non-exhaustive `if let` for intentional partial actions.
comparisons.code:
match state { Ready => start(), Failed(e) => report(e) }
if let Ready = state { start() }

comparisons.note: [Swift](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/ReferenceManual/Statements.html) requires every switch statement to be exhaustive. `@unknown default` handles future cases while warning about known omitted cases.
comparisons.code: switch state { case .ready: start(); case .failed(let e): report(e) }

comparisons.note: [Zig](https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#Exhaustive-Switching) makes an unhandled enum switch a compile error and permits `else` or `_` for remaining values.

[C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/switch-expression#non-exhaustive-switch-expressions) usually warns for a non-exhaustive switch expression, then throws at runtime if no arm matches.
comparisons.code: var label = state switch { State.Ready => "ready" }; // warning; unmatched throws

comparisons.note: [Go](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Switch_statements) permits statement switches and expressionless condition switches without `default`; no match performs no action.

recommendation.why: A follows the strongest common split. Optional statement guards stay concise; every value assignment is total; enum subject dispatch keeps its classification promise. Partial enum actions remain easy through guard syntax, so no compiler setting must weaken the guarantee.

whyNot.reason: A compiler policy that changes whether source is valid weakens Jet's one-path rule and makes library correctness depend on ambient project configuration.
Lint severity can be disabled, so a subject-dispatch spelling would no longer guarantee that every closed-enum variant has an explicit outcome.
It erases the useful intent difference between subject classification and partial guards, losing the compile-time signal when an enum gains a variant.

recommendation.tradeoff: Intentional partial handling of several enum variants must use guard syntax or add `else -> {}` to subject dispatch. This extra explicitness preserves exhaustive classification without burdening ordinary one-line actions.

decisions.checkInstructions: Compare value-path totality, enum-growth behavior, partial-action ergonomics, configuration-dependent semantics, and whether guard syntax already supplies a clear escape hatch from exhaustive subject classification.

decisions.title: One grammar for every loop header
decisions.gist: Choose whether semicolon clauses replace loop-only `in` and `step` words.
decisions.lesson:
Jet uses one `loop` keyword. Its header explains what repeats and what advances. Today, source iteration uses `in`, range stride uses `step`, and explicit state control uses semicolons.

A clause is one header part with one job. Semicolons can separate those jobs without terminating ordinary Jet statements. Empty headers remain infinite loops, while one Boolean expression remains a condition loop.

An identifier before the first semicolon can select source iteration. A mutable `:=` binding can select explicit state control. This lets the parser identify each mode from written syntax, not inferred types.

An optional third clause can control advancement. Companion ballot D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 chooses whether both controllers use it, only state control uses it, or headers omit it entirely.
decisions.story: Nia writes a parser that walks tokens, scans every fourth byte, waits while input remains open, and occasionally manages a cursor directly. She wants every loop header to read as one family.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: empty, Boolean, and binding/source forms stay short, with one separator for every multi-part header. Expert pass: typed initialization, arbitrary Boolean conditions, explicit afterthoughts, labeled control, source stride, evaluation order, ownership, and generated audit facts remain visible.

options.name: Uniform semicolon clauses
options.detail: Remove loop-header `in` and `step`. Source and state loops use semicolon clauses. Infinite and condition forms remain short. D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 supplies the complete third-clause law.
options.technical: Exact productions are: `loop block`; `loop Bool block`; `loop ident ; source [ ; advance ] block`; `loop ident , ident ; source [ ; advance ] block`; and `loop mutable_binding ; Bool [ ; advance ] block`. Mutable binding is `name [ : Type ] := expr`. Source bindings remain the current one identifier or map two-identifier form; no patterns or typed source bindings are added. Empty clauses, `;;`, missing first or second clauses, and fourth clauses reject. Newlines inside a semicolon header never terminate a statement before its opening brace. Formatter may wrap only after semicolons. D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 defines `advance`. Old `in` and `step` loop spellings retire without aliases or targeted teaching under S14 and D-S14-PAUSE.

options.name: Keep role words
options.detail: Keep current `binding in source`, contextual range `step`, and semicolon counted headers. Each mode names its role clearly, but loop headers continue using two separator systems.
options.technical: This preserves S19, S22/S72, and D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 unchanged. Source iteration uses `in`; numeric range stride uses contextual `step`; explicit state control requires initializer, Boolean condition, and afterthought separated by semicolons.

options.name: Semicolon source, library stride
options.detail: Replace `in` with one semicolon, but keep source advancement inside iterator expressions. Counted loops retain a third afterthought clause. Grammar stays smaller, but advancement moves outside the header family.
options.technical: Source form is exactly `loop binding; source`. Numeric and collection stride use the ratified D-ITER1 `.step_by(n)` adapter. State form remains `loop mutable_binding; condition; afterthought`. No source-loop third clause exists.

comparisons.note: Semicolons separate initializer, condition, and afterthought inside counted headers. Collection traversal uses another construct or range form.
comparisons.code: for i := 0; i < n; i++ { work(i) }

comparisons.note: A role word separates binding from source. Traditional three-clause counted loops are absent, so manual state uses a condition loop.

recommendation.why: A gives every multi-part loop header one separator and preserves Jet's single `loop` keyword. Beginners can read each clause left to right; experts retain explicit state control.

whyNot.reason: B preserves two separator systems and two advancement spellings inside one keyword family, which is the inconsistency this card exists to remove.
C unifies source separation but moves stride outside the header, so equivalent advancement reads differently between source and state loops.

recommendation.tradeoff: A makes semicolon after a source binding look like an ordinary statement boundary. Header grammar and formatting must teach that punctuation as a visible loop-header boundary.

decisions.title: Counted-loop continue semantics
decisions.gist: Choose whether `continue` performs a counted loop's afterthought before retesting.
decisions.lesson:
A counted loop has initialization, a condition, a body, and an afterthought. The afterthought usually advances the variable that makes the condition eventually become false.

`continue` abandons the remaining body and starts another iteration. It must either execute the afterthought first, skip it, or be rejected where an afterthought exists.

Skipping advancement can repeat the same state forever. Labeled `continue outer@` raises the same question when control jumps from a nested loop into an enclosing counted loop.
decisions.story: Omar scans records by index. Invalid records use `continue`. One invalid record must not trap the scanner on the same index forever.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: continue cannot silently repeat the same item forever. Expert pass: unlabeled, labeled, nested, source-controlled, and state-controlled edges have one exact order across every execution tier.

options.name: Advance, then retest
options.detail: A `continue` targeting a counted loop runs that loop's afterthought exactly once, then retests its condition. `break`, `return`, failure propagation, and panic skip it.
options.technical: Unlabeled `continue` targets the innermost loop. `continue name@` targets the named loop. A state target runs its afterthought once, then retests. Abandoned inner loops run no afterthought. A source target advances under D-LOOP-ADVANCE2, then requests its next yielded item. A condition target retests. An infinite target restarts. AOT, JIT, dev, comptime, and debugger stepping must agree.

options.name: Retest without advancing
options.detail: A `continue` jumps directly to the condition. Authors must perform advancement before every continue path. This matches current AOT emission but can accidentally create nonterminating loops.
options.technical: The afterthought runs only when control reaches the body's closing edge. Every early continue bypasses it. Labeled continue also bypasses the target loop's afterthought.

options.name: Reject continue
options.detail: Reject `continue` when its target has an afterthought. Authors use structured conditionals or manual state updates instead. Safe, but removes familiar control from exactly the loops needing it.
options.technical: Sema emits one coded diagnostic for unlabeled and labeled continue targeting state-controlled loops. Source and condition loops keep continue. No backend may receive the rejected form.

comparisons.note: Continue in a three-clause counted loop proceeds through the post or afterthought step before testing again.
comparisons.code: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (skip(i)) continue; }

comparisons.note: Rust has no three-clause loop, so compiler-generated lowerings must place advancement on every continue edge explicitly.
comparisons.code: loop { if !(i < n) { break } body(); i += 1; }

recommendation.why: A preserves the header's advancement guarantee across normal and continue paths. It prevents accidental stalls and matches the established meaning of three-clause counted loops.

whyNot.reason: B makes one keyword silently cancel the header's advancement clause, forcing duplicated updates and making nontermination easy.
C avoids the hazard by deleting useful control flow, even though A gives continue one deterministic and familiar meaning.

recommendation.tradeoff: A `continue` is not a direct jump to the condition because it performs the visible header afterthought first. Readers must understand that one intermediate control edge.

decisions.comment: just note I answered another ballot to rename continue to next

decisions.title: Meaning of the optional third loop clause
decisions.gist: Choose where a third semicolon clause controls loop advancement.
decisions.lesson:
D-LOOP-HEADER2 proposes semicolon-delimited source and state headers. Each begins with setup, then names its controller. A possible third clause says how progression changes between bodies.

A source loop owns an iterator. Its natural advancement is pulling another item. A state loop owns explicit mutable state. Its natural advancement is running an afterthought expression such as `i++`.

One positional slot can serve both controllers with controller-specific types. Another design can reserve that slot for state loops and use the existing `.step_by` iterator adapter for source stride.

If source stride exists, its order must be exact. The source and stride evaluate once. The first item is yielded normally. Later bodies receive every stride-th source item.
decisions.story: Leah samples every fourth sensor reading, then writes a second loop whose cursor advances through a method call. She wants the third clause to have a predictable job in both loops.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: ordinary source loops omit the third clause. Expert pass: stride validation, single evaluation, exhaustion, continue edges, side effects, and explicit state advancement are fully specified.

options.name: Controller-specific advancement
options.detail: Both source and state headers may use the third clause. Source loops receive a positive stride value. State loops receive an afterthought expression executed between bodies.
options.technical: Source stride has type Int and evaluates once after the source. A statically known value at or below zero is E0123. A dynamic value at or below zero raises E0123 before the first iterator pull. Stride one yields every item. For stride N, the first item is yielded; after each normal body or targeted continue, N pulls occur and the final pulled item becomes the next body value. Exhaustion during those pulls exits normally. State afterthought executes once after each normal body or targeted continue, then the Boolean condition retests. Break, return, failure propagation, and panic skip it.

options.name: State-only third clause
options.detail: Only state-controlled loops use a third clause. Source loops express stride through the existing `.step_by` iterator adapter, keeping source advancement inside the source expression.
options.technical: Source headers have exactly two clauses. D-ITER1 `.step_by(n)` owns source stride, validation, and exhaustion. State afterthought follows D-LOOP-CONTINUE2. A third clause after a source is a syntax error.

options.name: No third header clause
options.detail: Every header has at most two clauses. Source stride uses `.step_by`; explicit state updates live in the body. This removes traditional counted-loop afterthought syntax.
options.technical: Source and state headers both reject a third clause. State form initializes once and tests before each body. Authors place every state update on ordinary and continue paths inside the body.

comparisons.note: The third clause is an afterthought expression for explicit state control. Source traversal uses another range or iterator construct.
comparisons.code: for i := 0; i < n; i += stride { use(i) }

comparisons.note: Stride commonly transforms the iterator before looping, so the loop header still has only binding and source roles.

recommendation.why: A follows the requested positional family: first clause establishes the loop value or state, second supplies control, and optional third states advancement. Common loops still omit it.

whyNot.reason: B keeps source stride outside the header while state advancement stays inside, preserving two visible advancement shapes under the same loop family.
C removes the traditional counted afterthought the owner explicitly wants and makes every continue path responsible for manual state progression.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives the same position controller-specific types: positive Int for source stride and effectful expression for state advancement. Readers distinguish them from the written first clause.

decisions.title: Name the loop-continuation control statement
decisions.gist: Choose the word that abandons the rest of a loop body and enters the targeted loop's continuation edge.
decisions.lesson:
Loop control has two separate ideas: what happens immediately, and where execution resumes. This statement immediately abandons the remaining statements in the current body. It then enters the loop's continuation edge, which may begin another iteration or end the loop.

That edge depends on the header and companion rulings. A condition loop retests. A source loop follows the advancement law ratified by D-LOOP-ADVANCE2. A counted loop follows D-LOOP-CONTINUE2: run its afterthought then retest, retest directly, or reject this control form. An infinite loop starts its body again. This ballot chooses only the word; the ratified semantic outcomes apply unchanged.

Most C-family languages call the operation `continue`, meaning continue with the loop rather than continue through the body. That convention is compact for experienced programmers but conflicts with an ordinary-English reading. R, Perl, and Ruby instead use `next`, which more strongly cues progression toward another iteration.

`retest` is exact only for condition loops. Source loops and infinite loops have no user-written condition to retest. Under the conventional counted-loop law, an afterthought also occurs before the test. Using controller-specific words would create several spellings for one semantic operation.
decisions.story: Mina is learning loops. She rejects an invalid record halfway through the body. The statement should say later body statements will not run. Loop continuation—not the rest of this body—comes next. Companion rulings decide whether that produces another iteration or termination.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: the word must not suggest that remaining body statements execute. Expert pass: unlabeled, labeled, fallback, source, condition, counted, infinite, nested, AOT, JIT, dev, comptime, and debugger behavior remains one operation. This ballot changes spelling only; D-LOOP-CONTINUE2 and D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 decide control order.

options.name: Keep `continue`
options.detail: Keep the dominant C-family spelling. Teach it as: skip the rest of this body and continue with the loop. Experienced programmers recognize it immediately, but its plain-English reading can suggest execution continues through later statements.
options.technical: S23 remains `break` and `continue`. Labels remain `continue outer@`. Failure fallback `expr ?? continue` targets the innermost loop; `expr ?? continue outer@` remains rejected. The ratified D-LOOP-CONTINUE2 and D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 outcomes supply target-specific edges.

options.name: Use `next`
options.detail: Cue intended progression toward another iteration, while allowing the continuation edge to terminate when its condition fails or source is exhausted. The word applies across loop modes without pretending every loop has a test. It overlaps existing `next` identifiers; contextual grammar preserves them, except a fallback value named `next` needs parentheses after `??`.
options.technical: S23 becomes `break` and contextual statement control `next`. Bare unparenthesized `next` is control only as a complete control statement or fallback arm; `next outer@` is labeled control, while `next()`, `.next()`, and `fn next` remain call, member use, and declaration. After `??`, bare `next` always means innermost-loop control, so a value fallback named `next` must be parenthesized as `expr ?? (next)`; `expr ?? next outer@` is rejected. The old `continue` source spelling retires under Jet's migration policy, without an alias. Ratified D-LOOP-CONTINUE2 and D-LOOP-ADVANCE2 outcomes apply unchanged.

options.name: Use `skip`
options.detail: Name the immediate action: skip the remainder of this iteration. This is clear at the control site, but can be read as skipping a source item. It overlaps existing `skip` identifiers; contextual grammar preserves them, except a fallback value named `skip` needs parentheses after `??`.
options.technical: S23 becomes `break` and contextual statement control `skip`. Bare unparenthesized `skip` is control only as a complete control statement or fallback arm; `skip outer@` is labeled control, while `skip()`, `.skip(n)`, `.skip_while(...)`, `fn skip`, and bindings named `skip` remain identifiers in their grammatical positions. After `??`, bare `skip` means innermost-loop control, so value fallback uses `expr ?? (skip)`; `expr ?? skip outer@` is rejected. Ratified companion outcomes supply the target-specific edge.

options.name: Use `retest`
options.detail: Make condition-loop behavior explicit. The word becomes metaphorical for source and infinite loops, and cannot itself say whether a counted loop performs its afterthought before testing.
options.technical: S23 becomes `break` and `retest`; labels use `retest outer@`. Failure fallback `expr ?? retest` targets the innermost loop; `expr ?? retest outer@` is rejected. Despite the spelling, source and counted targets follow their separately ratified advancement/continuation outcomes, and infinite targets restart. Restricting `retest` to condition loops would require another control word for other loop modes and is outside Jet's one-mechanism rule.

comparisons.lang: C, Java, Go, Rust, Python, Kotlin, and C#
comparisons.note: Use `continue` to abandon the current body and enter the loop's continuation edge. In a three-clause C/Java/Go loop, that edge includes the post expression before the condition test.
comparisons.code: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (bad(i)) continue; }

comparisons.note: Use `next` for the next iteration. Perl's C-style loop still runs its continue/post block; Perl separately uses `redo` when it means repeat the body without testing or advancing.
Uses `continue`, and a while loop may declare an explicit continue expression. A continue executes that expression before the next condition check, closely matching Jet's counted afterthought.

recommendation.why: B matches Jet's beginner-first priority: in loop context, `next` more strongly cues progression toward another iteration and less readily reads as keep executing this body. It names one continuation intent across every permitted loop mode while leaving exact edges to companion rulings. Contextual parsing preserves existing `next` calls, members, and declarations.

whyNot.reason: A buys immediate familiarity for experienced programmers by keeping the exact ordinary-English ambiguity the owner identified. Jet ranks first-program clarity above convention.

C clearly names the abandoned body, but can mean drop a source element and says less about where control resumes. Its `.skip` method overlap is mechanically manageable just like B's `.next` overlap and is not the deciding cost.
D accurately describes only condition loops. It misnames source and infinite loops and cannot reveal whichever counted-loop continuation outcome is ratified.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet departs from the dominant C-family keyword, so experienced users must learn one small spelling difference. `next` must remain contextual so ratified iterator and reader `.next()` APIs stay source-compatible. This gives bare `expr ?? next` control meaning; authors using an identifier named `next` as the fallback value must write `expr ?? (next)`.

decisions.checkInstructions: Verify every option against all four loop modes, labeled and fallback forms, D-LOOP-CONTINUE2 ordering, existing `Iterator.next()` and reader APIs, S23, and Jet's beginner-first plus one-mechanism priorities.

decisions.title: How does a package declare scaled and affine units?
decisions.gist: Choose one declaration that gives units exact scale, optional offset, and stable cross-package identity.
decisions.lesson: Under D-SHAPE2=A, D-QUAL3 retains its family semantics through the typed applied rule `@UnitFamily(currency) { usd, eur, gbp }`; `12.50usd` has type `Usd`, identified by its canonical family/member declaration. D-SHAPE-QUANTITY1 adds compiler-known dimensions. Scaled and affine units need exact rational metadata. Conversion is `canonical = stored * scale + offset`; inverse is `(canonical - offset) / scale`. API snapshots record dimension, base, scale, offset, and package provenance so conflicts fail and changes are semver-visible. This ballot changes unit metadata, not the D-SHAPE2 marker migration.
decisions.story: A robotics package measures millimeters while a mapping package publishes meters. A climate package uses Celsius points and Kelvin deltas. Their values meet in one application. The compiler must prove compatible dimensions, apply exact conversions, and reject a second package that quietly redefines millimeter as 1/100 meter.
decisions.inWild: Package `core.units.si` owns closed Length and Temperature families through typed `@UnitFamily` rules. Consumers write `use core.units.si as si` and refer to `si.Meter`; the family/member declaration remains the canonical identity. A package may declare its own family, but cannot reopen a foreign one.

options.name: Extend closed @UnitFamily declarations
options.detail: Extend the post-D-SHAPE2 `@UnitFamily` typed rule with one canonical base and exact rational scale/offset metadata. D-QUAL3's family and generated-type semantics remain unchanged. A family is closed in its declaring package; this option invents no downstream reopening syntax. Other packages consume it through ordinary `use ... as ...` qualification or declare a distinct package-owned family.
options.technical: For every member, `canonical = stored * scale + offset`; inverse conversion subtracts offset, then divides by scale. Metadata normalizes as arbitrary-precision rationals at compile time. Identity is the package-qualified family/member declaration. Duplicate bases or members are errors; a same-spelled member in another family is distinct, never silently unified.

options.name: Replace UnitFamily with dimension blocks
options.detail: Introduce a dedicated `dimension` declaration. Choosing B explicitly supersedes D-QUAL3's `@UnitFamily` mechanism after D-SHAPE2. It removes the UnitFamily Rule while retaining D-SHAPE2's one-`@` applied-rule system for every other Rule; `#` remains free. Every existing family, including currency, migrates to a replacement nominal or dimensional block.
options.technical: Syntax.rs removes the UnitFamily Rule and reserves `dimension`, `base`, `unit`, `point`, and the nominal replacement. Formatter/codemod migrate old declarations; retired source follows normal retired-spelling diagnostics. Cross-package identity and the same exact canonical conversion formula match A.

options.name: Closed Core dimensional registry
options.detail: Only Core may declare dimensions and dimensional units. Packages consume named dimensional types but cannot add them. Existing post-D-SHAPE2 D-QUAL3 nominal families remain package-owned `@UnitFamily` rules with their current semantics and identity.
options.technical: The compiler ships a versioned dimensional registry using the same canonical conversion formula. Package dimensional declarations are rejected. Registry changes follow toolchain compatibility; D-QUAL3 nominal family identity remains package-qualified.

recommendation.why: A adds exact dimensional metadata to the post-D-SHAPE2 D-QUAL3 `@UnitFamily` mechanism without changing its family or generated-type semantics. Beginners consume named types; experts define closed package-owned domains with auditable identity.

whyNot.reason: B supersedes the ratified D-QUAL3 UnitFamily mechanism and migrates every existing family without a semantic gain.
C denies expert-defined dimensional domains and makes the toolchain registry a bottleneck for ordinary package types.

recommendation.tradeoff: Families are closed at their declaring package. Adding a unit to a foreign family requires a later owner decision rather than an implicit reopening mechanism.

decisions.title: How does generic public code name a dimension?
decisions.gist: Keep D-QUAL3 concrete unit types and choose whether generic APIs may quantify over a dimension and affine kind.
decisions.lesson: Concrete units remain D-QUAL3 named types. D-QUANTITY-POINT1 separately chooses how affine point/delta kind appears. This ballot does not choose that representation; it asks how generic APIs express dimension and kind across any outcome. Under POINT A, generated names satisfy the generic contract; under B, wrappers do; under C, refined values do. Generic output must still resolve to a concrete unit and kind for zero-cost lowering, Codable, and API snapshots. An undetermined result is rejected.
decisions.story: Kai publishes `mean_distance` for Meter, Foot, or Millimeter inputs without writing one overload per unit. At an HTTP boundary, the returned JSON must still say which unit is encoded. A temperature helper must preserve whichever point/delta representation D-QUANTITY-POINT1 selects.
decisions.inWild: Concrete distance APIs stay `Meter`, `Foot`, and `Millimeter`. A reusable helper names a dimension/kind contract; `jet explain-type` shows the concrete unit and affine representation selected at each call, and the API snapshot records both.

options.name: Compiler-known generic bounds
options.detail: Keep every POINT outcome's concrete value representation. Generic parameters use compiler-known `Quantity<Dimension, Kind>` bounds: generated names satisfy them under POINT A, `Point`/named-delta values under B, and refined values under C. Inputs and outputs must determine one concrete unit and kind.
options.technical: This is a compile-time bound, not a runtime wrapper. Monomorphization retains the selected POINT representation and unit identity. Codable uses the concrete instantiation's wire rule. API snapshots record normalized dimension, kind, and input/output relations.

options.name: Generic value wrappers
options.detail: Generic APIs use `Quantity<Dimension, Kind, Unit>` values. Under POINT A, generated names adapt into wrappers; under POINT B, its point wrapper and named delta map into this common wrapper contract; under POINT C, refined values adapt into wrappers. Concrete APIs keep the chosen POINT representation.
options.technical: The wrapper retains unit and kind as compile-time arguments and erases at runtime. Serialization requires an explicit unit. Public snapshots record wrapper arguments. Generic boundaries introduce a second value form except where POINT B already supplies one side.
options.code:
fn mean<U>(xs: [Quantity<Length, .Linear, U>]) -> Quantity<Length, .Linear, U> { xs.mean() }
fn shift<U>(p: Quantity<Temperature, .Point, U>, d: Quantity<Temperature, .Delta, U>) -> Quantity<Temperature, .Point, U> { p + d }

options.name: Concrete representations only
options.detail: Public and private code uses only the concrete forms selected by D-QUAL3 and D-QUANTITY-POINT1. Under POINT A that means generated names, under B its wrappers/named deltas, and under C refined types. Generic dimension-polymorphic functions do not ship.
options.technical: No new generic bound or common wrapper. API snapshots and Codable remain purely concrete. Cross-unit algorithms normalize explicitly to a chosen type or provide named overloads.
options.code:
fn mean_meters(xs: [Meter]) -> Meter { xs.mean() }
fn mean_feet(xs: [Foot]) -> Foot { xs.mean() }

recommendation.why: A preserves every D-QUANTITY-POINT1 outcome's concrete form while giving experts zero-cost reusable algorithms with exact dimension and kind contracts.

whyNot.reason: B creates a second visible quantity value form around concrete unit and point/delta representations.
C forces duplicate algorithms or arbitrary normalization for every cross-unit generic library.

recommendation.tradeoff: The generic-bound vocabulary adds dimension and kind relations that sema, API snapshots, Codable derivation, LSP, and diagnostics must expose precisely.

decisions.title: How are affine points and differences represented?
decisions.gist: Choose concrete types and constructors for absolute points versus differences in affine dimensions.
decisions.lesson: An affine point has an origin; a difference does not. For temperature, 20°C is a point and a change of 5 Celsius degrees is a difference. Valid algebra is point minus point -> difference, point plus difference -> point, and difference plus difference -> difference. Point plus point and difference minus point are errors. This distinction must survive storage, fields, collections, public signatures, conversion, serialization, generics, and package API snapshots. D-API-CTOR1 requires named constructors; D-SHAPE-CONVERT1 requires destination-owned, source-named conversions. Any option that changes those laws must say so explicitly.
decisions.story: Nora stores an oven target, calibration delta, and readings; she subtracts readings, adds calibration, serializes both, and converts a Fahrenheit point without losing absolute-versus-relative meaning.
decisions.inWild: An oven record stores one Temperature point and one Temperature delta. Its wire schema and API snapshot distinguish them. Point plus delta works; point plus point is rejected with valid alternatives.

options.name: Generated Point and Delta types
options.detail: Each affine unit generates two concrete named types, such as CelsiusPoint and CelsiusDelta. They use existing named constructors/conversions: `CelsiusPoint.from_float`, `CelsiusDelta.from_float`, and destination-owned source-named cross-unit conversions. No constructor-law amendment.
options.technical: Types have distinct nominal/API/Codable identities but share erased numeric representation. Sema owns the closed algebra table. Family declarations define exact scale/offset for Point conversions and scale-only Delta conversions. Generic bounds use D-QUANTITY-TYPE1's point/delta kind if ratified.
options.code:
target :: CelsiusPoint.from_float(200.0)?
tolerance :: CelsiusDelta.from_float(5.0)?
next :: target + tolerance
drift :: next - target

FahrenheitPoint.from_celsius_point(target)?
FahrenheitDelta.from_celsius_delta(tolerance)?

target + target
// error: two Temperature points cannot be added
// fix: subtract them for a delta, or add a CelsiusDelta

options.name: Point wrapper; named unit is delta
options.detail: The existing concrete unit type is the only delta form: `Celsius` means a Celsius-scale difference. Absolute values use `Point<Celsius>`. There is no `Delta<Celsius>` alias or second delta wrapper. Constructors remain destination-owned and source-named.
options.technical: `Point<Celsius>` and `Celsius` have distinct API/Codable identities and erased numeric representation. Sema closes algebra over wrapper points and named-unit deltas. Point conversion applies scale plus offset; Celsius delta conversion applies scale only.
options.code:
target :: Point<Celsius>.from_float(200.0)?
tolerance :: Celsius.from_float(5.0)?
next :: target + tolerance
drift :: next - target

Point<Fahrenheit>.from_celsius(target)?
Fahrenheit.from_celsius(tolerance)?

options.name: One unit name with explicit kind
options.detail: Keep one Celsius family name. Expressions use `Celsius.point(...)` and `Celsius.delta(...)`; stored and public types must spell `Celsius<.Point>` or `Celsius<.Delta>`. This explicitly amends D-API-CTOR1 and makes kind part of public compatibility.
options.technical: Sema tracks kind as a compile-time refinement erased from numeric storage. API snapshots, Codable, reflection, and semver record the explicit kind argument. Bare `Celsius` is invalid in stored/public positions. Destination-owned, source-named cross-unit conversion operates on the kinded type.

recommendation.why: A makes point versus difference visible in every stored and public type, obeys existing named-constructor/conversion laws, and erases to the same runtime number.

whyNot.reason: B splits a paired concept across a generic point wrapper and the existing named unit type for deltas.
C puts a compatibility-critical kind behind one family name and requires explicit amendments to constructor, reflection, Codable, and API laws.

recommendation.tradeoff: Every affine unit generates two public type names, increasing completion results and migration work for existing unit APIs.

decisions.title: How does a value change from one unit to another?
decisions.gist: Choose whether same-dimension units convert only through written calls or also through compiler-proven exact coercions, including the exact result type for mixed arithmetic.
decisions.lesson:
A unit conversion changes scale and chooses a stored numeric representation. Jet already has one conversion mechanism: the destination owns a source-named exact or rounded call. An implicit conversion uses those same normalized scale, offset, provenance, overflow, and diagnostic facts; it is not a second mechanism.

The owner selected pragmatic exact implicit conversion by default. Mixed same-dimension arithmetic chooses the finer operand unit so whole-number measurements remain exact; equal scales keep the left unit. Exact binding and argument conversions may be inserted when sema can prove the concrete expression or complete source domain converts without rounding. If it cannot, E0127 names the checked or rounded destination-owned call. The compiler never silently rounds.

Affine families keep Point and Delta distinct. Point conversion uses scale plus offset; Delta uses scale only. Point plus or minus Delta yields Point, Delta plus Point yields Point, and Point minus Point yields Delta. Point plus Point and Delta minus Point remain errors.

The ratified policy ladder lets a package require written conversions with `policy: .{ explicit_units: true }`; `#Policy(explicit_units)` can strengthen a module, function, or block. Beginners get direct exact arithmetic. Experts and teams can make every boundary explicit without changing the underlying conversion law.
decisions.story: Priya combines a length measured in meters with an inner diameter measured in millimeters. Jet keeps the exact finer-unit result without a dot-method chain. When she asks for whole kilometers and the value would require rounding, the compiler refuses the implicit conversion and names the explicit rounded call. Her CAD package can enable explicit_units once when review policy requires every boundary to be written.

options.name: Written conversion at every unit boundary
options.detail: Every cross-unit boundary uses the destination-owned source-named call. Exact conversion is checked with `?`. Deliberate rounding uses a separate checked call that names its rounding mode. Mixed-unit arithmetic remains E0127 until one operand is converted.
options.technical: `Destination.from_source(v)?` evaluates the exact rational scale and offset, then fails if the destination representation cannot hold the exact result or overflows. `Destination.from_source_rounded(v, mode, digits: n)?` permits only the requested precision loss and still fails on overflow. `n` is a nonnegative count of destination decimal places; integer destinations require zero. Modes are `.TowardZero`, `.Floor`, `.Ceiling`, and `.NearestEven`. Floor moves toward negative infinity; ceiling moves toward positive infinity. Nearest-even sends an exact tie to the even retained digit, so -2.5 becomes -2 and -3.5 becomes -4. Point conversion applies scale plus offset. Delta conversion applies scale only. Same-unit algebra allows Point plus or minus Delta, Delta plus Point, Point minus Point, and Delta plus or minus Delta. Point plus Point and Delta minus Point remain errors.

options.name: Exact implicit conversion by default; explicit-only policy opt-in
options.detail: Same-dimension units convert implicitly wherever the conversion is exact. Mixed arithmetic chooses the finer operand unit so ordinary integral measurements stay exact; equal scales keep the left unit. Exact destination coercions also work for bindings and arguments. The compiler never rounds silently: if exactness cannot be proven, E0127 names the checked or rounded destination-owned conversion to write. Teams may require written conversions with the explicit_units policy at package, module, function, or block scope.
options.technical: Implicit conversion uses the same normalized family scale, offset, provenance, overflow, and diagnostic facts as the destination-owned source-named conversion call. Linear and Delta arithmetic chooses the finer scale; equal scales keep the left unit. Point plus or minus Delta and Delta plus Point use the Point unit, while Point minus Point returns the paired Delta. Point conversion applies scale plus offset; Delta applies scale only. Binding and argument coercion is inserted only when sema proves the concrete value/expression or complete source domain converts exactly; otherwise E0127 requires an explicit checked or rounded call. Point plus Point and Delta minus Point remain errors. `policy: .{ explicit_units: true }` sets the package floor. `#Policy(explicit_units)` may strengthen a module, function, or block; narrower scopes cannot weaken the inherited floor.

options.name: Implicit only when an existing operand type is total
options.detail: The compiler may omit a conversion only when one existing operand type can represent every value of the other type exactly and without overflow. Mixed arithmetic prefers the left unit when both directions are total, uses the sole total direction when only one exists, and otherwise reports E0127. This is more restrictive than B's finer-unit rule and rejects common pragmatic pairs even when the concrete expression has an exact finer-unit result.
options.technical: Sema tests totality over the full numeric source domain, never the current runtime value. Linear and Delta arithmetic considers the left result unit before the right. Point plus or minus Delta uses the Point unit. Delta plus Point uses the Point unit. Point minus Point considers the left Point unit before the right and returns its paired Delta. If no candidate conversion is total, the expression is rejected. Ordinary destination-owned checked and rounded calls use A's overflow and rounding laws. The `explicit_units` policy disables every omitted conversion.

comparisons.note: Measurement converts through a destination unit and returns a typed value; it does not auto-convert when you add two measurements of different units.
Units of measure never auto-convert between scales; the programmer multiplies by an explicit conversion constant, so a scale change is always visible in the code.

recommendation.why: B matches the owner’s pragmatic law: ordinary same-dimension arithmetic, bindings, and arguments stay concise whenever exactness is provable, while the compiler never rounds or hides a fallible boundary. One destination-owned conversion mechanism still owns scale, offset, overflow, diagnostics, and explicit checked/rounded calls. The scoped explicit_units policy gives experts and teams visible boundaries where they want them.

whyNot.reason: A forces a written call at every same-dimension boundary, including exact meter-to-millimeter work, creating the repetitive conversion chains the owner explicitly rejected.
C requires whole-source-domain totality between existing operand types, so it rejects useful exact finer-unit expressions and exact concrete coercions that B accepts safely.

recommendation.tradeoff: Result-unit choice is observable: mixed arithmetic chooses the finer scale, with the left unit breaking equal-scale ties. Code that wants another storage unit writes the existing checked or rounded destination-owned call.

decisions.title: Lua host model — in-process VM vs sidecar worker
decisions.gist: Decide how Lua runs when a Jet program calls `lua.*`. Option A runs Lua inside the Jet binary. Option B runs it as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. A **VM** (virtual machine) is the small engine that executes Lua code. **In-process** means that engine lives inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Lua runs as a separate operating-system process, and Jet talks to it over a typed channel.

An **effect root** is a tag like `#(Lua)` the compiler stamps on any function that touches Lua, so a caller sees the dependency in the type. A **table** is Lua's one data structure, a key/value map; `[K: V]` is Jet's map type.

Lua was built to be embedded. Its whole reason to exist is being a tiny engine you drop inside a host program.
