decisions.story: Marcus Bell ships a tower-defense game written in Jet. The engine core is Jet, but he wants designers to tune enemy waves without a full rebuild, so wave logic lives in small Lua scripts beside `core.game`. On a busy wave the loop spawns hundreds of enemies per frame, and every spawn reads a value the Lua script produced.

options.name: In-process VM — Lua lives inside the Jet binary
options.detail: The Lua VM is embedded in your program. Lua tables become zero-copy `[K: V]` views, so reading `e["pos"]` hundreds of times a frame costs no serialization. Every Lua call carries the `#(Lua)` effect. No extra process, no channel, no copy on the hot path.
options.code:
use lua.waves as w

spawns :: w.tick(0.016)     // [Str: Dyn] view straight over the Lua table
core.game.spawn(spawns[0]["kind"], at: spawns[0]["pos"])
// reads hit the Lua table in place — no copy, no IPC

options.name: Sidecar worker — Lua runs as a separate process
options.detail: Lua runs in its own process behind a typed message boundary, exactly like Python (D-FFI-PY1). Uniform with `py.*`, crash-isolated. But every table crossing the boundary is serialized and copied, and the per-frame call now blocks on IPC. That forfeits the one property Lua was designed for.

comparisons.note: Redis embeds a Lua VM directly in the server so `EVAL` scripts run atomically next to the data, with no cross-process hop. That in-process choice is why Lua scripting in Redis is fast enough to run on the request path.
comparisons.code:
> EVAL "return redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])" 1 counter
// Lua runs inside the redis-server process, no IPC

comparisons.note: OpenResty embeds LuaJIT inside each Nginx worker so request handlers run in-process. Every high-throughput Lua host embeds the VM; none of them shell out to a Lua daemon per call.
comparisons.code:
location /hi { content_by_lua_block { ngx.say("hi") } }
// Lua handler runs inside the nginx worker

recommendation.why: Lua exists to be embedded. In-process is what makes zero-copy table views and per-frame calls viable, which is the reason a beginner reaches for Lua scripting in the first place. The `#(Lua)` effect keeps the dependency honest without a process boundary.
recommendation.tradeoff: You give up crash isolation: a bug in a Lua script can fault the host process. Lua's tiny, well-contained VM makes that risk small, and the expert `@embed`-style escape stays available for the rare script that needs a wall.

whyNot.reason: A sidecar copies and serializes every table across a process wall, so the per-frame call that motivates Lua scripting becomes an IPC round-trip. Uniformity with `py.*` is not worth forfeiting the embedding property Lua is chosen for.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship in-process as the default so the beginner gets fast zero-copy tables with no ceremony. Keep a supervised out-of-process mode as an explicit opt-in for scripts a team wants walled off, reusing the same `lua.*` surface so call sites never move.

harvest.use: The default host: embedded VM, `[K: V]` table views, `#(Lua)` effect on every call.
Offered as an opt-in tier (same `use lua.X` surface) for untrusted or crash-prone scripts that need a wall.

decisions.title: Ruby host model — sidecar worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: Decide how Ruby runs when a Jet program calls `ruby.*`. Option A runs Ruby as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent. Option B embeds libruby inside the Jet binary.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the Ruby interpreter (libruby) runs inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Ruby runs as a separate operating-system process that Jet talks to over a typed channel.

The **GVL** (Global VM Lock) is a lock inside Ruby that lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time. Ruby also keeps large **global interpreter state**, so two Rubies in one process fight over it. A **gem** is a Ruby library; **RubyGems** is its registry.

A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches packages from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1).
decisions.story: Dana Whitfield runs a Jet web service that renders user-authored email templates. A mature Ruby gem, Liquid, already does safe templating well, and rewriting it is not on the roadmap. She wants to call Liquid from a request handler and get a rendered string back, without a Ruby bug taking down the service.
decisions.inWild:
Reusing the Liquid gem from a Jet request handler:

```jet
use ruby.liquid as liquid       // pinned in pkg.jet: liquid: ruby@"5.5"

render :: fn(tpl: Str, ctx: [Str: Str]) -> Str ? RubyError #(Ruby) {
    liquid.Template.parse(tpl)?.render(ctx)?
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker — Ruby runs as a separate process
options.detail: Ruby runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, exactly like Python (D-FFI-PY1). A Ruby crash or segfault cannot take the Jet service down; it restarts the worker. The `#(Ruby)` effect marks every call. RubyGems becomes a jetpack provider for `liquid: ruby@"5.5"`.

options.name: In-process embed — libruby inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libruby directly. Avoids the per-call process hop, but Ruby's GVL serializes all Ruby work onto one thread, and its large global interpreter state makes multiple isolated Rubies in one process hostile. A gem crash faults the whole host.

comparisons.note: Teams that need one gem from another language shell out to a `ruby -e` subprocess and parse stdout. That is an untyped, unsupervised sidecar. The `ruby.*` worker is the same isolation with a typed boundary and laundered errors.
comparisons.code:
$ ruby -e 'require "liquid"; print Liquid::Template.parse($stdin.read).render'
// ad-hoc process + stdout parsing — what the worker replaces

recommendation.why: Ruby's GVL and heavy global state make a clean in-process embed hostile, and the sidecar matches the ratified Python host model (D-FFI-PY1) for a uniform mental model. Crash isolation protects the Jet service from a gem fault.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each call crosses a process boundary, so a value returned from a gem is serialized and copied. For template rendering and typical gem reuse that cost is negligible next to the work done inside Ruby.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libruby inherits the GVL bottleneck and shared global state, so it cannot run isolated Rubies well, and a gem segfault faults the whole host. The saved process hop does not justify losing crash isolation and the py-uniform model.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised sidecar as the sole default, identical in shape to the Python host, so a beginner reuses a gem safely with no ceremony. RubyGems rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a real project proves it needs one.

harvest.use: The default host: typed message boundary, `#(Ruby)` effect, crash isolation, `liquid: ruby@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only if a project needs shared-memory zero-copy and can tolerate the GVL, offered later on the same `use ruby.X` surface.

decisions.title: Perl host model — sidecar worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: Decide how Perl runs when a Jet program calls `perl.*`. Option A runs Perl as a separate supervised process, matching the Python precedent. Option B embeds libperl inside the Jet binary.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the Perl interpreter (libperl) runs inside your Jet binary and shares its memory. A **sidecar worker** means Perl runs as a separate operating-system process Jet talks to over a typed channel.

A Perl interpreter keeps large **global state**; running several isolated interpreters in one process (its multiplicity model) is fragile and rarely used. **CPAN** is Perl's package registry, decades deep in sysadmin and bioinformatics modules.

A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches packages from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1). A **module** here is a Perl library.
decisions.story: Ray Holloway maintains a genomics pipeline. A trusted CPAN module, Bio::SeqIO, already parses the sequence formats his lab uses, and it has been correct for fifteen years. He wants to call it from a new Jet pipeline stage and get typed records back, without porting the parser or wrapping it in a brittle shell script.
decisions.inWild:
Calling a CPAN bioinformatics module from a Jet pipeline stage:

```jet
use perl."Bio::SeqIO" as seqio     // pinned in pkg.jet: "Bio::SeqIO": perl@"1.7"

records :: fn(path: Str) -> [SeqRecord] ? PerlError #(Perl) {
    seqio.read_fasta(path)?           // returns typed records across the boundary
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker — Perl runs as a separate process
options.detail: Perl runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, like Python (D-FFI-PY1). A decades-old CPAN module runs unmodified; a crash in it restarts the worker, not the pipeline. The `#(Perl)` effect marks every call. CPAN becomes a jetpack provider for `"Bio::SeqIO": perl@"1.7"`.

options.name: In-process embed — libperl inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libperl directly. Avoids the per-call hop, but a Perl interpreter's global state makes multiple isolated interpreters in one process fragile, and a module crash faults the whole host. The estate this targets is legacy scripts, which value isolation over shared memory.

comparisons.note: Sysadmin and bioinformatics shops hold enormous, correct Perl estates they cannot afford to rewrite. Today they invoke those scripts through `system()` or a bare subprocess. The `perl.*` worker keeps them callable as-is, with a typed boundary and laundered errors.
comparisons.code:
$ perl -MBio::SeqIO -e '...' < reads.fa   // today: ad-hoc subprocess
// worker: use perl."Bio::SeqIO"; typed records, supervised

recommendation.why: The value here is a huge legacy CPAN estate callable without a rewrite, and the sidecar keeps those scripts running as-is with crash isolation. It matches the ratified Python host (D-FFI-PY1) for one uniform model across scripting languages.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each call crosses a process boundary and copies its result. For pipeline stages that call a module once per file, or per batch, that overhead disappears against the work Perl does inside.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libperl inherits fragile interpreter multiplicity and shared global state, and a legacy module fault would take the host down. Legacy estates value isolation, so the saved hop does not justify losing it or the py-uniform model.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised sidecar as the sole default, shaped like the Python host, so a legacy CPAN module is callable with no rewrite and no ceremony. CPAN rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a concrete project proves the need.

harvest.use: The default host: typed boundary, `#(Perl)` effect, crash isolation, `"Bio::SeqIO": perl@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only if a project needs shared-memory Perl and can accept the multiplicity risk, later on the same `use perl.X` surface.

decisions.title: PHP host model — sidecar worker pool vs embed SAPI
decisions.gist: Decide how PHP runs when a Jet program calls `php.*`. Option A runs a supervised pool of PHP worker processes, in the spirit of PHP-FPM. Option B embeds PHP in-process via its embed SAPI.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **In-process embed** means the PHP engine runs inside your Jet binary through the **embed SAPI** (Server API — PHP's pluggable host interface). A **sidecar worker** means PHP runs as a separate operating-system process Jet talks to over a typed channel.

**PHP-FPM** (FastCGI Process Manager) is PHP's standard production host: a supervised pool of worker processes, one request per worker at a time, recycled after use. A **pool** lets many requests run concurrently across workers.

**Packagist** is PHP's package registry (used via Composer). A **provider** is a jetpack backend that resolves and fetches from a foreign registry (D-JPK-EXTPROV1).
decisions.story: Priya Nair is porting a PHP monolith to a new Jet server one endpoint at a time. The order-pricing logic is thousands of lines of battle-tested PHP she will migrate last. Until then, the new Jet endpoints must call the existing PHP pricing code and get typed results, while serving many requests at once.
decisions.inWild:
New Jet server calling existing PHP domain logic during a piecewise migration:

```jet
use php."app/Pricing" as pricing    // pinned in pkg.jet: "app/Pricing": php@"local"

quote :: fn(cart: Cart) -> Money ? PhpError #(Php) {
    pricing.price_cart(cart)?          // runs in a pooled PHP worker
}
```

options.name: Sidecar worker pool — PHP-FPM-style process pool
options.detail: PHP runs in a supervised pool of worker processes, the model every PHP shop already runs in production. Many Jet requests price carts concurrently across workers; a fatal PHP error recycles one worker, not the server. The `#(Php)` effect marks every call. Packagist becomes a jetpack provider.

options.name: In-process embed — PHP embed SAPI in the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed PHP through its embed SAPI. Avoids the process hop, but PHP's request-scoped global lifecycle assumes one request per interpreter, so concurrency inside one process is awkward, and a fatal PHP error faults the whole server. It fights the FPM model PHP shops already trust.

comparisons.note: Essentially every production PHP deployment uses FPM: a supervised worker pool, one request per worker, recycled on fault. Matching that model makes the `php.*` host behave the way PHP operators already expect and tune.
comparisons.code:
; php-fpm.conf
pm = dynamic
pm.max_children = 32   // the pooled-worker model the sidecar mirrors

recommendation.why: A worker pool is how PHP already runs in production, so concurrency and fault recovery match operator expectations, and a fatal PHP error recycles one worker instead of the Jet server. It fits the ratified sidecar model from Python (D-FFI-PY1).
recommendation.tradeoff: Calls cross a process boundary and results are copied. For request-scoped domain logic during a migration, that cost is trivial next to the pricing work, and the pool absorbs concurrency the way FPM does.

whyNot.reason: PHP's request-scoped global lifecycle assumes one request per interpreter, so an embedded engine handles concurrency poorly and a fatal error faults the whole server. The saved hop is not worth fighting the FPM model PHP shops rely on.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the supervised FPM-style worker pool as the sole default so migrations call existing PHP concurrently with familiar fault behavior. Packagist rides in as a jetpack provider. No embed tier until a concrete project proves it is needed.

harvest.use: The default host: pooled workers, `#(Php)` effect, per-worker fault recovery, `"app/Pricing": php@"…"` resolution.
Deferred; revisit only for a single-threaded embed use case, later on the same `use php.X` surface.

decisions.title: R binder host model — sidecar R worker vs in-process embed
decisions.gist: The `r.*` root is already reserved (D-DATA-BRIDGE1). This ballot decides only how R runs behind it. Option A runs R as a separate supervised process. Option B embeds libR in-process.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. The `r.*` namespace is already reserved by D-DATA-BRIDGE1; this ballot picks its host, not the name. **In-process embed** means the R engine (libR) runs inside your Jet binary. A **sidecar worker** means R runs as a separate process Jet talks to over a typed channel; **Rserve** is R's established protocol for exactly that.

A **data.frame** is R's table type; **`core.data.Table`** is Jet's, so a round-trip maps columns both ways. **CRAN** is R's package registry. A **glm** is a generalized linear model, a common R fitting routine.

R runs as a single global interpreter with heavy shared state (D-DATA-PLOT1 defines Jet's SVG plot values, which R plots can return into).
decisions.story: Ellen Park, a data scientist, keeps her feature engineering in Jet `core.data` but trusts R's `glm` for the actual model fit. She has a Jet `Table` of loan records and wants to fit a logistic regression in R, then read the coefficients back as typed Jet values, plus the diagnostic plot.
decisions.inWild:
Fitting an R glm on a Jet Table and reading typed coefficients back:

```jet
use r.stats as stats            // CRAN-provided, pinned in pkg.jet
use core.data

fit :: fn(t: core.data.Table) -> [Str: Float] ? RError #(R) {
    model :: stats.glm(t, formula: "default ~ income + age", family: "binomial")?
    model.coefficients()          // typed [Str: Float] back across the boundary
}
```

options.name: Sidecar R worker — Rserve-style separate process
options.detail: R runs in its own supervised process behind a typed message boundary, in the spirit of Rserve. A Jet `core.data.Table` round-trips to an R data.frame and back column-typed. A plot returns as an SVG value compatible with D-DATA-PLOT1. CRAN becomes a jetpack provider. The `#(R)` effect marks every call.
options.code:
use r.stats as stats

m :: stats.glm(table, formula: "y ~ x", family: "binomial")?
coefs :: m.coefficients()   // [Str: Float] — typed round-trip from the data.frame
plot :: m.residual_plot()   // returns an SVG value (D-DATA-PLOT1)

options.name: In-process embed — libR inside the Jet binary
options.detail: Embed libR directly. It avoids the process hop for large frames, but R is a single global interpreter with heavy shared state and is not built for concurrent embedding. A fault in R code takes the host down, so it is fragile next to the isolated worker.

comparisons.note: rpy2 embeds R in-process for Python. It is powerful but famously fragile: R's single global interpreter and shared state cause hard-to-debug crashes and threading limits. The sidecar trades that fragility for isolation.
comparisons.code:
import rpy2.robjects as ro
ro.r('glm(y ~ x, family=binomial)')   // in-process embed — fragile under load

comparisons.note: Rserve runs R as a supervised server other languages connect to over a typed protocol, giving isolation and clean marshaling of frames and results. The `r.*` worker follows this proven shape.
comparisons.code:
// client connects to a supervised R server, ships a data.frame, gets typed results
Rconnection c; c.eval("glm(y ~ x, family=binomial)");

recommendation.why: R is a single global interpreter with heavy shared state, so isolating it in a supervised worker gives clean data.frame round-trips, SVG plots into D-DATA-PLOT1, and crash safety. It matches the ratified Python host model (D-FFI-PY1).
recommendation.tradeoff: A large Table is serialized crossing the boundary. For a model fit, the copy is small next to the fit itself, and the isolation prevents an R fault from crashing a data pipeline mid-run.

whyNot.reason: Embedding libR inherits R's single-global-interpreter fragility and no real concurrent embedding, and an R fault crashes the host — exactly rpy2's well-known pain. The saved copy on large frames does not justify losing isolation.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship the Rserve-style supervised worker as the sole default so a data scientist fits an R model on a Jet Table with typed round-trips and safe crashes. CRAN rides in as a jetpack provider, plots return as D-DATA-PLOT1 SVG. No embed tier until proven.

harvest.use: The default host: supervised R, `data.frame ↔ core.data.Table`, SVG plots, `#(R)` effect, CRAN resolution.
Deferred; revisit only for a single-threaded huge-frame case that can accept R's global-state fragility, on the same `use r.X` surface.

decisions.title: Shell as typed text (`Sh`) vs explicit argv-list API
decisions.gist: Decide how a Jet program builds a command line. Option A adds `Sh` as a third typed-text instance beside `Sql` and `Html`, so holes become safe argv items. Option B offers only an explicit argv-list API.
decisions.lesson:
Terms. **Typed text** (D-TYPEDTEXT1) is the ratified mechanism where a string literal in a position expecting `Sql` or `Html` becomes a checked value. Each `{hole}` is a bound parameter (Sql) or an escaped insertion (Html), never raw text. A runtime `String` reaching such a position is error **E0149**.

**argv** is the list of arguments a program receives; a shell splits a command string into argv by whitespace and expands globs like `*`. **Injection** is when attacker data in a string is reparsed as extra commands or arguments.

**Word-splitting** breaks a value on spaces; **glob expansion** turns `*` into filenames. This proposal adds `Sh` as a third typed-text instance: a hole is exactly one argv item, never split or globbed. `Sh.raw` is the sole audited escape; `sh"…"` is the prefix form (D-TYPEDTEXT2).
decisions.story: Tom Ferraro writes a Jet backup tool. It runs `rsync` with a source and destination the user supplies on the command line. A directory called `my backups` or a crafted value like `; rm -rf ~` must never break the command apart or run anything extra. Tom wants to write what looks like a shell line and stay safe.
decisions.inWild:
A user-supplied path with a space, plus the error when a plain `String` reaches the position:

```jet
use core.process

cmd: Sh :: "rsync -a {src} {dest}"   // src = "my backups"; becomes ONE argv item
core.process.run(cmd)?               // exec's rsync directly — no shell parses src
```

```
error[E0149]: a runtime String cannot be used where `Sh` is expected
  |
5 |     core.process.run(user_input)
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^^ this String was never checked as a command
  = help: write it as a typed literal `sh"rsync -a {src} {dest}"`,
          or wrap an audited raw fragment with `Sh.raw(...)`
```

options.name: `Sh` typed text — third D-TYPEDTEXT1 instance
options.detail: A literal in a `Sh` position becomes a checked command; each `{hole}` is exactly one argv item, never word-split or glob-expanded. `core.process.run` exec's the program directly, so no shell ever parses user data — injection is impossible by construction. Same engine as `Sql`/`Html` (I8). `Sh.raw` is the audited escape.

options.name: Explicit argv-list API only — no typed text
options.detail: No `Sh` type. The only safe call passes a program and an argument list: `process.run("rsync", args: ["-a", src, dest])`. Safe, but verbose, and it reads nothing like a shell line. Beginners paste real shell lines into one string, which then needs a shell to run — reopening the injection path this was meant to close.

comparisons.note: `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)` with an f-string is the classic injection footgun; the safe form is a list, `run(["rsync", "-a", src])`. Python makes the safe path the ugly one and the footgun the easy one. `Sh` makes the shell-looking path the safe one.
comparisons.code:
subprocess.run(f"rsync -a {src}", shell=True)   # injection if src is hostile
subprocess.run(["rsync", "-a", src])            # safe list form

comparisons.note: `Sh` is the same ratified typed-text engine as `Sql` and `Html` (D-TYPEDTEXT1), just a third instance. Sql holes become bound parameters, Html holes become escaped insertions, Sh holes become single argv items — one mechanism, three safe surfaces (I8).
comparisons.code:
q: Sql :: "select * from t where id = {id}"   // id -> bound parameter
c: Sh  :: "rsync -a {src} {dest}"             // src -> one argv item

recommendation.why: `Sh` makes the shell-looking line the safe line: holes are single argv items, no shell parses user data, so injection is impossible by construction. It reuses the ratified `Sql`/`Html` engine, so it is one mechanism, not a new one (I8).
recommendation.tradeoff: `Sh` only builds an argv vector, so genuine shell features (pipes, glob, redirection) need explicit APIs or an audited `Sh.raw`. That is the point: the easy path stays safe, and reaching for shell semantics is a visible, audited choice.

whyNot.reason: An argv-list-only API is safe but reads nothing like a command. Beginners fall back to pasting shell lines into a string that needs a shell to run, reopening the exact injection path. It leaves the footgun as the natural default.

hybrid.synthesis: Ship `Sh` typed text as the default safe surface for building commands, and keep the explicit argv-list form as the lower-level primitive `Sh` elaborates into. Beginners write the shell-looking literal; experts can drop to the list or `Sh.raw` when they truly need shell semantics.

harvest.use: The default: `Sh` literal, holes as argv items, E0149 on unchecked String, `Sh.raw` audited escape, `sh"…"` prefix.
Kept as the primitive `Sh` lowers to and the expert entrypoint for programmatic argument building, not the beginner-facing default.

decisions.title: Editor engine architecture
decisions.gist: What machinery answers the editor: today's per-file re-checker, a grown semantic index, or one incremental compiler service shared by everything.
decisions.explainer: Glossary. LSP = the background program editors (VS Code, Zed, Cursor) talk to for errors, completion, rename, go-to-definition. Incremental = after a keystroke, re-analyze only what changed, not the whole file or project. Semantic index = a persistent map of every symbol in the project (where defined, where used), kept up to date as you type. Today jet lsp re-parses and re-checks a whole file on each request and mostly sees one file at a time; jet-semindex exists as a separate batch tool.
decisions.story: Priya has a 30-file Jet web service open in VS Code. Every keystroke re-checks her 2,000-line file from scratch; renaming a function she can only trust for files that are open; the outline pane is empty; project-wide symbol search finds nothing. She never reads the compiler's carefully written error copy — she judges Jet entirely by this laggy hour in her editor. The engine choice decides the ceiling for every editor feature Jet will ever have.
decisions.detail: Recommend C. One semantic brain is the only shape where editor truth and compiler truth cannot drift (I8), it makes jet check/jet dev warm-instant for free, and #182's bidirectional visual editor needs exactly this engine. B is the fallback shape if C is declined — it reaches feature parity sooner but permanently owns a two-brain alignment burden.

options.name: Extend the per-request checker
options.detail: Keep today's shape: each LSP request re-runs parse+check on the current file, plus targeted cross-file lookups. Add features one by one on top. Stays closest to today's shape, but every feature re-derives the world; big files pay full re-check per keystroke, and project-wide answers (rename, find-references, symbols) stay best-effort rather than guaranteed.
options.code:
// What today's shape gives — and its ceiling:
$ edit routes.jet (2,000 lines)
  keystroke -> re-parse + re-check whole file   ~80ms today, grows with file
  F12 on auth.current      ok (single hop)
  rename orders_for        edits OPEN files; closed callers found by re-scan,
                           no guarantee mid-edit state is consistent
  workspace symbol search  full project re-scan per query

options.name: Index-backed engine (grow jet-semindex)
options.detail: Promote jet-semindex (whose versioned query API is already ratified, D-SEMINDEX1) from batch tool to the live heart of the LSP: a persistent project-wide symbol database, updated incrementally on every change. All features (rename, references, symbols, outline, call hierarchy) become index queries. The compiler front end stays as-is; the LSP maintains the index beside it. This is the gopls / clangd shape.
options.code:
$ jet lsp   # first open: index 30 files once (~1s), then:
  keystroke -> re-index one file's symbols       ~few ms
  rename orders_for        index knows all 14 callers, open or closed
  workspace symbol 'ord'   instant — index lookup
  call hierarchy           who-calls-whom already materialized
// Risk to own: two brains — checker semantics vs index semantics
// must be kept in agreement by tests, or they drift.

options.name: One incremental compiler service
options.detail: Rebuild the front end as a demand-driven, incremental query engine (parse-of-file, types-of-item, callers-of-fn — each cached, each invalidated precisely), and make jet check, jet dev, the REPL, and the LSP all clients of that one engine. There is exactly one semantic brain, so editor answers can never disagree with the compiler (I8: one way to mean it). This is the TypeScript model — tsserver IS the compiler — and the road rust-analyzer wishes rustc had taken from the start. Largest rebuild; also the foundation the self-host era and #182 (Blueprint visual editor, which needs live bidirectional semantics) will stand on.
options.code:
$ jet lsp        # same engine as jet check — literally the same queries
  keystroke -> invalidate routes.jet's parse query; types re-derive
               only for items whose inputs changed   ~1-5ms
  rename orders_for        exact: the engine's own resolution data
  editor squiggles         byte-identical to `jet check` output, always
$ jet check      # warm daemon answers from the same cache — instant
// One brain: a fix to type inference fixes the editor the same second.

comparisons.note: tsserver is the compiler — one incremental engine serves tsc, editors, everything. Widely considered the best editor experience in the industry; never drifts.
comparisons.code: tsc --watch and VS Code share one Program instance model

comparisons.note: The cautionary tale: rust-analyzer is a second front end beside rustc. Years of duplicated work, subtle disagreements, and a still-running project (polonius/chalk era) to merge them back.
comparisons.code: rustc says error; rust-analyzer says fine — the bug class Jet can refuse to have

comparisons.note: gopls is index-backed (option B shape) over the go/types checker. Excellent, but gopls and the compiler have disagreed, and keeping them aligned is ongoing work.
comparisons.code: gopls: persistent file cache + per-package invalidation

decisions.title: Editor capability bar
decisions.gist: Which editor features jet lsp must serve — full protocol parity, a curated professional dozen, or beginner-first waves.
decisions.explainer: What exists today: hover, go-to-definition, references, rename, dot-completion, semantic tokens, inlay hints, formatting, code actions. What is missing: outline (the file's structure pane), workspace symbol search, signature help (parameter hints while typing a call), folding, highlight-other-occurrences, incremental sync (today the editor re-sends the whole file every keystroke), snippet/auto-import completion, call hierarchy, prepare-rename validation, semantic token deltas. 'Full parity' means every LSP 3.17 feature that makes sense for Jet.
decisions.story: Ben, week one with Jet, types `svc.request(` and waits for parameter hints that never come — he opens the docs in a browser to remember the four arguments. Ctrl+Shift+O for the file outline: empty. Ctrl+T to find a type project-wide: nothing. Each miss is a moment where the language that promises magic out-of-the-box feels like a prototype. The capability bar decides what 'Jet has great tooling' means, feature by feature.
decisions.detail: Recommend A, delivered in C's order (signature help + outline first). Master-of-all means the tooling bar is parity, not a subset; every advertised capability carries a test, so the surface stays honest (I4 spirit). Effort is the currency we spend.

options.name: Full LSP 3.17 parity
options.detail: Everything applicable to Jet, as one program with exit criteria: incremental sync, outline, workspace symbols, signature help, folding, occurrences, selection ranges, snippets + auto-import completion, prepare-rename, semantic token range+delta, call hierarchy, type hierarchy, document links, code lens (off by default). Each feature lands with an lsp test and a line in the editor README. Delivery ordered by beginner impact (signature help and outline first), but the bar is: all of it.
options.code:
// Exit criteria, testable:
$ cargo test --test lsp
  signature_help_mid_call ........ ok
  document_symbol_outline ........ ok
  workspace_symbol_cross_file .... ok
  incremental_sync_partial_edit .. ok
  folding_regions ................ ok
  occurrences_highlight .......... ok
  completion_auto_import ......... ok
  call_hierarchy_incoming ........ ok
  ... (every capability advertised = every capability tested)

options.name: Curated professional dozen
options.detail: The ~12 features that define how a language feels, then stop: incremental sync, signature help, outline, workspace symbols, folding, occurrences, snippets + auto-import, prepare-rename, semantic deltas, call hierarchy. Skip long-tail protocol surface (type hierarchy, document links, code lens, monikers) until someone asks. Smaller advertised surface, honestly complete.

options.name: Beginner-first waves, re-decide between waves
options.detail: Wave 1: signature help, outline, completion quality (auto-import, snippets). Wave 2: workspace symbols, incremental sync, folding, occurrences. Wave 3: call hierarchy, code lens, the rest. Owner reviews after each wave and re-aims. Most control, three decisions instead of one.

comparisons.note: Ships essentially full parity plus extensions; that completeness is a large part of Rust's professional reputation.
comparisons.code: outline, signature help, 30+ assists, call/type hierarchy, semantic deltas

comparisons.note: Deliberately curated (option B shape) — smaller surface, everything it advertises is polished.
comparisons.code: no code lens by default; core dozen kept excellent

decisions.title: Ship user-authored derives + typed reflection (Epoch 3 exit criterion)?
decisions.gist: Libraries need to author derives (like #[Serialize], #[Codable]) using a typed reflection API. The Epoch 3 exit criterion includes this. The v1 ceiling is already ratified: reflection + derives only, no arbitrary macros. This is the umbrella proceed/kill gate; D-METAREFLECT1 (read API) and D-METADERIVE1 (output) are sub-decisions that open only if this passes.
decisions.explainer: Today only builtin derives exist. User-authored derives require two things: (1) a typed reflection API that lets comptime code inspect a type's fields, types, and markers (D-METAREFLECT1); and (2) a mechanism for derive output to re-enter the compiler and be sema-checked (D-METADERIVE1). D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies the architecture rule (output must re-enter sema, not bypass it). The v1 ceiling (no arbitrary macros) is the I8 guard: derives are a single, scoped metaprogramming job; general macros would be a second surface that can do the same job. Deferring blocks any library that needs Serialize, ORM field mapping, or any type-driven code generation until post-v1.
decisions.story: I'm writing a serialization library. I want to derive Serialize on any user struct automatically — inspect its fields at comptime and emit the encode/decode implementation. I should not need to hardcode this into the compiler.

options.name: Ship user derives + typed reflection within the ratified ceiling
options.detail: Approve opening D-METAREFLECT1 and D-METADERIVE1. Delivers the Epoch 3 exit criterion; enables third-party derive libraries (Serialize, ORM, validation); keeps the ceiling at reflection+derives (no arbitrary macros). D-CTCODEGEN1's architecture constraint (output re-enters sema) applies.

options.name: Builtin derives only; no user-authored derives
options.detail: Keep derives as a closed set in the compiler. No reflection API, no derive output mechanism. Library authors cannot add new derives; every new derive requires a compiler PR. Blocks the serialization, ORM, and validation library ecosystem.

options.name: Defer to post-Epoch 3
options.detail: Treat user derives as post-v1. Epoch 3 ships without a derive authoring API. Third-party serialization/ORM libraries cannot work without manual impl. Re-evaluate after the runtime, async, and other Epoch 3 exits are done.

comparisons.note: Rust derive macros are proc-macros that receive a TokenStream and emit a TokenStream — powerful but operate on syntax trees, not typed reflection. Jet's typed reflection API is safer and simpler.
Swift's Codable is a compiler-synthesized protocol conformance — a builtin derive only. Third-party derives are impossible; every new derive requires a Swift compiler change.

decisions.title: Unicode text completeness
decisions.gist: Choose the Unicode floor for core.text.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: Unicode completeness and beginner discoverability without bloating String with duplicate methods.
decisions.story: Ana builds a terminal UI and search index. Case folding, grapheme clusters, display width, normalization, and segmentation decide whether text works outside ASCII.
decisions.inWild:
use core.text as text

len :: name.length()     // bytes, scalars, clusters, display columns?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: Unicode completeness and beginner discoverability without bloating String with duplicate methods.

options.name: Hybrid: core.text algorithms with String-aware tooling (recommended)
options.detail: core.text owns Unicode algorithms: normalization, case folding, segmentation, width, classification, and UTF-8/scalar helpers. String stays small. LSP/docs expose common text helpers from String contexts but insert core.text calls, preserving one callable surface.

options.name: Methods on String
options.detail: String exposes every Unicode helper directly. Discoverable, but makes the default type feel large and hides the byte/scalar/cluster distinctions.
options.code: cols :: label.display_width()

options.name: ASCII plus UTF-8 validity only
options.detail: Keep text minimal. International users and terminal/editor features keep failing in edge cases.
options.code: if s.bytes_len() > 10 { ... }

comparisons.note: String is grapheme-aware, friendly but sometimes surprising for performance.
Rust keeps algorithms in crates; Jet wants first-party Core breadth.

decisions.title: Terminal display-width policy
decisions.gist: Define how Unicode text maps to terminal columns when standards and terminals disagree.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation B keeps the beginner call deterministic and portable, while one explicit policy value gives terminal authors control over ambiguous-width and control-character handling without creating a second width algorithm.
decisions.story: Mei aligns names and status icons in a Jet terminal dashboard. ASCII works, but CJK punctuation, emoji flags, family ZWJ sequences, variation selectors, and control characters disagree across terminals. A scalar-count heuristic shifts columns and can place later text over earlier cells. Jet must define one predictable default and decide whether terminal authors can match a known terminal profile explicitly.
decisions.inWild:
use core.text as text

name :: "A·界👨‍👩‍👧‍👦"
columns :: text.display_width(name)
print("{(name)}{(" ".repeat(20 - columns))}ready")

options.name: One portable fixed policy
options.detail: display_width measures extended grapheme clusters using Jet's pinned Unicode release. East Asian Wide/Fullwidth and emoji-presentation clusters occupy 2 columns; Ambiguous occupies 1; combining/default-ignorable characters occupy 0 inside a cluster; controls occupy 0. Flags, keycaps, and valid emoji ZWJ sequences count once. The result is deterministic on every host, but applications targeting a CJK terminal cannot request Ambiguous=2.
options.code:
cols :: text.display_width("·界👨‍👩‍👧‍👦")
print(cols) // 5 everywhere: 1 + 2 + 2

options.name: Portable default plus explicit policy
options.detail: The one-argument call uses the same portable policy as A. An optional TextWidth policy changes only disputed terminal choices: Ambiguous narrow/wide and controls zero/reject. Unicode segmentation and property lookup remain the same canonical algorithm. Experts can match a known terminal contract; defaults never inspect locale or environment.

options.name: Follow host locale and terminal
options.detail: The default infers Ambiguous width and emoji behavior from locale, environment variables, and terminal hints. Output may visually match more local terminals without configuration, but the same Jet program returns different widths across CI, redirected output, SSH, and user machines.
options.code:
cols :: text.display_width("·")
// 1 under en_US, 2 under ja_JP; redirected and CI results may differ.

options.name: Unicode East Asian Width only
options.detail: Sum Unicode East_Asian_Width properties per scalar and ignore grapheme/emoji presentation rules. Small specification, but family emoji, flags, keycaps, combining sequences, and variation selectors can be overcounted or split, so it does not meet the terminal-alignment purpose.
options.code:
print(text.display_width("👨‍👩‍👧‍👦"))
// Scalar sum can exceed the 2 columns used by terminals.

comparisons.note: Defines East Asian Width properties but leaves terminal-cell policy, especially Ambiguous characters, to higher-level protocols.
Uses versioned Unicode tables and terminal-oriented width rules, but applications still need policy around ambiguous width and emoji sequences.
Exposes normal and CJK width modes, demonstrating the practical need for a deterministic default plus explicit ambiguous-width control.

decisions.title: Password hashing surface: crypto.password_hash / password_verify
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a misuse-resistant password hashing pair, and what it exposes.
decisions.explainer: A: PHC-string self-description makes upgrades free and misuse hard; matches the ratified misuse-resistant envelope direction (D-CRYPTOENV1) and I1 safe-by-default.
decisions.story: Deb builds her first Jet web app with signup/login. The seal/open envelope (D-CRYPTOENV1) encrypts data but is wrong for passwords; without a blessed surface she will do what beginners do — sha256(password) — which is exactly the breach headline. The stdlib either hands her Argon2id correctly-parameterized, or the footgun is the default.

options.name: Misuse-resistant pair, Argon2id inside
options.detail: crypto.password_hash(pw) -> String encodes algorithm+params+salt in one PHC string (safe defaults, no knobs required); crypto.password_verify(pw, stored) -> Bool re-derives from the stored params — old hashes keep verifying after defaults change. Expert cost overrides via optional args. Backend follows the ratified D-DEP-CRYPTO1 bridge path.

options.name: Expose raw KDF primitives
options.detail: crypto.argon2id(pw, salt, cost…) and friends; users assemble salting/encoding/verification themselves. Full control, but the beginner path is back to holding sharp edges — the opposite of the libsodium lesson.

options.name: Decline — document seal + external services
options.detail: Point auth at hosted identity providers; stdlib ships nothing. Every self-hosted Jet app (the jetos story!) still needs it and will hand-roll worse.
options.code:
// docs: "use an identity provider" — meanwhile:
db.execute("…", [user, crypto.sha256(password)])   // what actually happens

comparisons.note: password_hash/password_verify with self-describing output is the acknowledged best-in-class API shape here — rare praise for PHP.
crypto_pwhash_str/_str_verify — same shape, same reasoning.
both push users to external packages (bcrypt/argon2 crates) — stdlib silence is the common gap, not the standard to copy.

decisions.title: Misuse-resistant crypto suite

decisions.title: Approve the full core.crypto bridge dependency set (I6)
decisions.gist: Whether Jet may temporarily generate eight exact pure-Rust crypto dependencies behind core.crypto while each is replaced natively before Epoch 3 closes.
decisions.story: Mina hashes a password, derives a session key, and opens an X25519 file envelope. Jet generates a tiny Rust bridge manifest for her program, so the repository Cargo.lock does not pin that runtime graph. She needs the generated build to prove—before any network fetch—that every direct and transitive package, checksum, feature, license, advisory revision, platform binding, and native-replacement deadline matches an owner-approved signed record.

decisions.detail:
Scope: approve the exact resolved 55-package temporary bridge superset only. Exact direct specs: argon2 0.5.3 (defaults off; alloc,password-hash), sha2 0.10.9 (defaults off), blake3 1.8.2 (defaults off; std,pure), hkdf 0.12.4 (defaults off), x25519-dalek 2.0.1 (defaults off; precomputed-tables,zeroize), subtle 2.6.1 (defaults off), chacha20poly1305 0.10.1 (defaults off; alloc), and ed25519-dalek 2.2.0 (defaults off; alloc,zeroize). The last two are the exact XChaCha20-Poly1305 and strict Ed25519 implementation gate shared by API1 and KEYWRAP1. blake3/pure disables BLAKE3 SIMD, assembly, and native object compilation, but its Rust build script still uses the approved build-time closure cc 1.2.66, find-msvc-tools 0.1.9, and shlex 2.0.1 and may discover or probe a native compiler. Acceptance requires a trace proving that path compiles and links no C/assembly object and emits no native object on every approved target. No entropy provider or fallback is approved. rand_core 0.6.4 is approved only as a trait/API transitive activated by password-hash without getrandom; it must never source salt, nonce, or key bytes.

Ephemeral session verification evidence and limits. The following /tmp paths identify ephemeral session evidence, not durable source artifacts. Cargo.lock: /tmp/crypto-lock-work/Cargo.lock, SHA-256 42e2879fae279e42e1a99422e94d7a96bc8965a07a4ec7b1f47bbe922c214a2d. Host metadata: /tmp/crypto-lock-work/metadata.json, SHA-256 0447f74ec3e0d21ee3f30092a83b5b09d4201cca8ce51d78ddd4fa77065e6491. Full 55-package SBOM v2: /tmp/crypto-lock-work/sbom-v2.json, SHA-256 dbe299850bf88167eea701a76e6e6f66af493f792c7d48a31ad794f27df8e6fc; it records names, versions, sources, Cargo.lock-derived registry checksums, resolved host features, SPDX expressions, and hashes of discovered license files. Generator: /tmp/crypto-evidence-generator.mjs, SHA-256 ece8aea00431f5ab5332e441644fd2ed9fc836a101ea2a342302baae1108cc39. Linux x86_64 host build trace: /tmp/crypto-lock-work/build-host.trace, SHA-256 c847cb5b539c8daab4eb66c2370509a195c8c0f1882f54beb878a7523586c5e7. It proves one host build, not cross-target process/symbol absence. The approved cc/find-msvc-tools/shlex build closure may perform compiler discovery/probing; acceptance must prove blake3/pure compiles, links, and emits no native object.

RustSec evidence is not a full scan. Provenance: https://github.com/RustSec/advisory-db.git revision e20296422feea6aab5cd36bf993c68d22e4aa24f, tree 0f86dcbe2da77cfc3ade95084200866afc00b5c0, archive /tmp/crypto-lock-work/rustsec-db.tar SHA-256 468b402bffb0ffbc713a2cbaada4b23413c0300b314cb75ad98ba0612ef9320. The current rustsec-audit.json predates this revised 55-package lock and is invalid as evidence for it; it is retained only as historical manual package-name/semver comparison. API1 and KEYWRAP1 remain blocked until a fresh full report covers this exact lock. Release requires cargo-audit 0.21.2 with recorded tool-binary hash and exact command `cargo audit --db VERIFIED_DB --file OPERATION_TARGET_LOCK --json`, stdout JSON, exit 0, DB hashes, and no ignore file, for every minimal lock. Findings, yanks, or unmaintained exceptions require a new owner ballot.

Trust evidence is unsigned. Current hashes prove local identity, not publisher authority. Release requires Ed25519 strict DSSE PAE over payload type application/vnd.jet.crypto-bridge-lock.v1 and RFC8785 fields schema, decision, generator_sha256, lock_sha256, sbom_sha256, rustsec_report_sha256, rustsec_db_sha256, target_matrix_sha256, sequence, valid_from, valid_until. Trust is 2-of-3 toolchain-pinned offline keys. Rotation is sequence+1 signed by 2 old and 2 new keys. Revocation is signed by 2 current keys and names key id plus minimum rejected sequence. Rollback, expiry, duplicate signer, mixed artifact, unknown/revoked key, or stripped signature fails before network. The owner can decide this exact evidence model and graph from the recorded hashes; the unsigned ephemeral /tmp bundle is not durable source or release-ready evidence. Before any generated build or network access, release tooling must deterministically regenerate every artifact, require exact hash matches, and place the matched lock, SBOM, audit, target-matrix, and trace evidence into durable signed release artifacts.

Target matrix: /tmp/crypto-lock-work/target-matrix.json SHA-256 6a73c20ba9ec6a5bc4e4bcf35ab7abf4d5b4abc904c288fde90f254c83125389. Operations: sha2; hkdf+hmac+sha2; blake3 portable; subtle; x25519-dalek+curve25519-dalek+fiat+zeroize; XChaCha20-Poly1305 via chacha20poly1305+chacha20+poly1305+aead+cipher; strict Ed25519 via ed25519-dalek+ed25519+signature+curve25519-dalek+sha2+zeroize; argon2+blake2+password-hash+rand_core. Targets: Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows MSVC x86_64/arm64, WASI preview1. Only Linux x86_64 is currently built. Release is blocked until one minimal lock/SBOM per operation/target exists, full audit runs, clean process/build traces and symbol scans prove no C/assembly/unused direct crate, vectors pass, and all hashes enter the signed bundle.

Conditional getrandom exists only if D-CRYPTO-RNG1=B. Direct: getrandom 0.3.3, defaults off, no features. Lock SHA-256 0eebb0c965f07ee9930db104601ca0e2b6accda166b97f789a3830b9e6202046; metadata 5bcf1433a899596a2c547527e43ba7d4ebac75ee888ae0f61931a2932617554d; seven-package SBOM v2 da37628b1aafecb61e1b39e3513f2043adcd442566fef5bc4978ba05f54c236b with Cargo.lock-derived registry checksums. Superset: cfg-if 1.0.4, getrandom 0.3.3, libc 0.2.186, r-efi 5.3.0, wasi 0.14.7+wasi-0.2.4, wasip2 1.0.4+wasi-0.2.12, wit-bindgen 0.57.1. Removal requires direct-provider parity on all seven targets, failure/cancel/zeroization vectors, independent review, rollback, signed lock/SBOM deletion, and symbol absence.

Before #302/Epoch 3 closes, each direct/transitive security seam has a deletion gate: subtle constant-time implementation plus assembly review; sha2 vectors/differential; hkdf RFC5869 composition; x25519 RFC7748/all-zero/clamping/zeroization/independent review; argon2 RFC9106/PHC/DoS/memory clearing/differential/independent review; blake3 official tree/chunk/boundary vectors and portable review; chacha20poly1305 RFC8439/XChaCha vectors, nonce/AAD/tamper/zeroization and independent review; ed25519-dalek RFC8032 strict-invalid/canonical-key/signature/zeroization and independent review; rand_core removal with password-hash; conditional getrandom gate above. Every row requires all approved targets, differential tests, independent sign-off, rollback, generator/lock/SBOM/cache deletion, and symbol absence.

Beginner: no dependency ceremony. Expert: exact graph and evidence gaps visible. Hybrid: one operation selects one audited minimal closure.

decisions.title: Cryptographic entropy providers and failure contract
decisions.gist: Choose how cryptographic randomness reaches Jet on each platform and how entropy failure reaches the program.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-RANDSPLIT1 separates deterministic core.random from cryptographic core.crypto.random. D-CRYPTO-SUITE1=A requires misuse-resistant envelopes; D-PWHASH1=A requires generated password salts; D-DEP-CRYPTO1=A permits the existing RustCrypto AEAD/signature bridge but does not choose an entropy provider. I1 and I6 remain binding. This ballot owns only cryptographic entropy acquisition, its public failure shape, and migration of callers that internally need randomness. It does not choose Secret/Key types, envelope layout, password cost, or approve a new crate.

Current truth is unsafe. Native core.crypto.random.bytes calls /dev/urandom and falls back to wall-clock SplitMix. The crypto bridge uses /dev/urandom and falls back to a constant-state xorshift for envelope nonces, Ed25519 keygen, and Argon2 salts; Windows therefore takes the predictable fallback. The API is infallible and negative lengths become zero. Comptime contains a deterministic random implementation. All of those fallback paths retire under every option.

Common security law. A cryptographic request either returns exactly the requested number of fresh operating-system bytes or fails before exposing any output. Forbidden forever: core.random, timestamps, process/thread ids, counters, UUID state, hardware identifiers, fixed seeds, reused buffers, all-zero fill, partial success, best effort, user PATH tools, /dev/random, and automatic remote entropy. Provider output is not health-tested or modified by Jet; Jet trusts only the named tier-1 platform facility and reports its failure. No user/workspace/environment setting can replace, seed, downgrade, log, or intercept the provider. There is no deterministic crypto mode, test seed, retry flag, or expert bypass.

Exact public type for A/B is:
```jet
pub enum RandomError {
    NegativeLength
    TooLarge
    Unavailable
}
```
Exact signature is bytes(count: Int) -> [U8] ? RandomError. count < 0 returns NegativeLength without allocation/provider call. count > 1_048_576 returns TooLarge without allocation/provider call. Zero returns ok([]) without provider call. Each positive provider attempt owns exactly one private full-size allocation. That allocation is never shared with another request, never reused concurrently, and never returned until the attempt completes successfully. Linux short-fill/EINTR continuation stays within that attempt and its one allocation. On failure or post-call cancellation the entire allocation is cleared by the std-only non-elidable routine: write every byte with `std::ptr::write_volatile(ptr, 0)`, then execute `std::sync::atomic::compiler_fence(Ordering::SeqCst)` before drop. No ordinary fill/memset is accepted as proof. No partial list escapes. Debug/Display is respectively `cryptographic random length cannot be negative`, `one cryptographic random request is limited to 1048576 bytes`, or `the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness`; no OS status, path, handle, buffer, or backend text appears. Larger protocols make explicit repeated calls and remain responsible for their own framing; the per-call cap is a compatibility promise.

Direct platform contract for A/C. Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64 calls getrandom(buf,len,0), never GRND_INSECURE or GRND_NONBLOCK. It blocks until the kernel pool is initialized, retries EINTR with the unfilled suffix, treats zero or every other errno as Unavailable, and loops over short positive fills. It never opens /dev/urandom. macOS x86_64/arm64 calls Security.framework SecRandomCopyBytes(kSecRandomDefault,...); errSecSuccess with a complete call succeeds and any other OSStatus is Unavailable, with no fallback or retry. Windows MSVC x86_64/arm64 calls BCryptGenRandom(NULL,buf,len,BCRYPT_USE_SYSTEM_PREFERRED_RNG); STATUS_SUCCESS succeeds and any other NTSTATUS is Unavailable, with no CryptoAPI fallback or retry. WASI preview 1 calls random_get over one private zero-initialized full-size buffer. Success returns only that complete buffer. ERRNO_INTR ends that provider attempt and makes its whole buffer tainted: Jet volatile-zeroizes and drops it completely before allocating a distinct fresh full-size buffer for the next attempt, then retries from byte zero, at most 16 consecutive times; at most one WASI attempt buffer exists at a time and no allocation or pointer is reused across retries; the seventeenth returns Unavailable. Every other errno returns Unavailable after the same full-buffer zeroization. No partial WASI buffer or suffix retry is permitted. wasm32-unknown-unknown/browser, Linux musl, iOS/Android, other Unix, and every target not named above are unsupported by this decision and return Unavailable without probing.

Freestanding has no ambient entropy provider. core.crypto.random.bytes and every safe operation needing fresh randomness return Unavailable before cryptographic work. No memory address, cycle counter, device id, unverified RDRAND, or board hook is guessed. This ballot adds no public provider-registration callback: a future hardware entropy API must separately decide device trust, startup/continuous tests, concurrency, failure, and audit. Experts may use deterministic bytes only as explicit inputs to already-ratified expert primitives inside their existing #Unsafe gate; they cannot make safe seal/keygen/password_hash pretend those bytes are fresh entropy.

Blocking, cancellation, and retry. Entropy acquisition is a synchronous native runtime operation and may block only where the named OS call blocks. Jet adds no timeout because abandoning a kernel CSPRNG request cannot make weaker bytes acceptable. Task cancellation is outside RandomError and remains the D-TASKRUNTIME1 control-plane outcome. If already requested before allocation/provider entry, the call performs no provider work and the enclosing task takes its ordinary cancelled outcome. If observed after any provider return, Jet volatile-zeroizes the whole buffer and propagates task cancellation; it returns neither ok(bytes) nor err(RandomError). Linux glibc retries EINTR against the still-unfilled suffix. WASI uses the fresh-full-buffer retry law above. macOS/Windows status failures are final. A retry by user code is a new full request and receives a new buffer. No provider call occurs while holding a Jet scheduler/global lock.

Migration and internal consumers. A/B change random.bytes from [U8] to [U8] ? RandomError, a breaking public signature that ships in a major release plus edition opt-in. Older editions retain the source-level [U8] signature but use the selected provider immediately: invalid length or entropy failure produces existing E3001 at the Jet call with message `core.crypto.random.bytes: <RandomError Display>` and exit 70; no insecure compatibility fallback survives. This is a narrow security correction to runtime behavior, not a claim of compatibility for programs that relied on predictable fallback. This ballot authorizes the provider and random.bytes only. It does not silently change any other public error or artifact contract. Safe seal/file_seal and signing-key generation remain disabled until proposed D-CRYPTO-API1 and D-CRYPTO-ENVELOPE2 ratify their exact signatures and RandomError-cause shape. password_hash remains disabled until proposed D-PWHASH-POLICY1 ratifies its exact entropy-failure shape. CLI/package key generation and any infallible tool consumer remain disabled until proposed D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 ratifies exact Jet diagnostic copy, exit, cleanup, and no-artifact behavior. UUID migration needs its own owning law and is not authorized here. Once each gate ratifies compatibly, that consumer must call this same provider and must never catch Unavailable to substitute bytes.

Comptime/dev/JIT. core.crypto.random is unavailable in comptime, pure evaluation, package/module-field evaluation, deterministic tests, and interpreter execution; reaching it produces the existing native-only/purity boundary and never evaluates a seeded model. Delete the current comptime deterministic crypto-random arm. A native JIT may call the same provider and failure path as AOT only when parity is real; otherwise it declines before execution. core.random remains the sole deterministic/test PRNG and W0410 continues rejecting it in cryptographic contexts. Expert primitives may consume explicit test vectors at comptime only when they are pure operations and their separate law permits it; they never call this provider.

Testing seam. Provider injection exists only behind cfg(test) inside the generated/bridge runtime, is unreachable from Jet source and release artifacts, and can script short fills, EINTR, zero, failure, cancellation, and canary writes. Tests prove exact fill, one active private allocation per attempt, distinct WASI allocations across retries with no overlap/reuse, suffix retry, zeroization on failure, no output on partial failure, cap/negative preflight, and no fallback symbol/string. Released-artifact scans reject SplitMix/xorshift/timestamp fallback and test-hook symbols. Native clean-host CI runs real-provider tests on Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows x86_64/arm64, and a real WASI preview-1 runtime. Unsupported and freestanding targets prove Unavailable. Statistical tests may catch gross wiring errors but never certify security or replace provider/failure tests.

Diagnostics and audit. RandomError is a runtime value for A/B, not a new E-code. Old-edition fail-fast uses existing E3001 exactly as above. CLI/key-generation operations that cannot return RandomError require D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 ratification before shipping; raw OS errors are never printed. Audit output may record provider identity, target, requested length, success/failure, and duration, but never bytes or a reusable provider handle.

Beginner pass: request bytes and handle one typed failure; nonce/salt generation stays internal. Expert pass: provider, target matrix, blocking, retry, cap, cancellation, migration, audit, freestanding behavior, and injection proof are exact. Hybrid pass: safe envelopes, expert primitives needing fresh randomness, CLI keygen, AOT, and native JIT consume one provider implementation; no second debug/test randomness path exists.
decisions.story: Rina deploys the same Jet service on Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64, macOS, and Windows, then builds a WASI worker. It creates session keys, encryption nonces, signing keys, and password salts. An unavailable entropy source must stop that operation clearly; it must never produce a predictable key, silently return fewer bytes, or work on Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64 while becoming deterministic on Windows.

options.name: Direct OS providers, typed failure
options.detail: Recommended. Use the exact Linux glibc getrandom, macOS SecRandomCopyBytes, Windows BCryptGenRandom, and WASI random_get contract above with no new crate. Expose fallible random.bytes and propagate the same failure through every cryptographic consumer. This makes failure recoverable, keeps I6 unchanged, and gives each supported host one auditable provider.

options.name: Audited getrandom bridge, typed failure
options.detail: Use the Rust getrandom crate behind the existing generated runtime bridge, with the same public type, cap, exact-fill, no-fallback, target matrix, migration, and tests. The crate owns platform syscall details; Jet still launders errors into RandomError. This option is conditional on a separate I6 ballot approving the exact crate version, features, transitive graph, audit record, and native-implementation obligation; without that ratification B cannot ship.

options.name: Direct OS providers, fail-fast API
options.detail: Use A's exact direct providers and no-fallback law but retain random.bytes(count) -> [U8]. Invalid length or provider failure always emits E3001 and exits 70 in every edition. This avoids a signature migration, but reusable libraries cannot recover or select a safe alternative, and an expected platform limitation becomes a process-wide panic.

comparisons.note: getrandom centralizes platform CSPRNG selection and returns an error rather than weak bytes. B adopts that backend; A adopts the same fail-closed contract directly to avoid a new dependency.
crypto/rand.Reader is the one security RNG and Read fills or errors. Jet likewise separates it from deterministic core.random and forbids fallback.
getRandomValues uses the host CSPRNG and caps a request. This ballot does not claim browser support until Jet has a separately proven browser runtime provider.

decisions.title: Argon2id password policy and rehash law
decisions.gist: Choose Jet's exact Argon2id writer defaults, hostile-PHC verification limits, and upgrade signal.
decisions.story: Imani launches a login service with no cryptography tuning. Five years later Jet raises its password cost, old accounts still log in, and successful logins upgrade hashes gradually. An attacker submits a PHC string claiming a terabyte of memory and a billion passes; Jet rejects it before allocation instead of exhausting the server.
decisions.detail:
Inherited law. D-PWHASH1=A ratifies one self-describing Argon2id PHC writer, verification from stored parameters, old-hash verification, and expert cost control. D-CRYPTO-SUITE1=A requires safe beginner APIs plus audited expert primitives. Proposed D-CRYPTO-API1 owns Secret and PasswordHash nominal types and final Result spelling; this ballot owns policy values and parser/resource behavior. Proposed D-CRYPTO-RNG1 must ratify a compatible fallible OS provider before password_hash ships. D-DEP-CRYPTO1=A does not by itself approve the final password suite. Proposed D-DEP-CRYPTO-SUITE2 must approve the exact Argon2 implementation version, features, transitive graph, audit record, and native-replacement obligation before any option ships; this ballot approves no crate. Option A exact writer. `password_hash` always writes Argon2id version 0x13 as canonical PHC `$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=1$$`. Memory m is 65,536 KiB total, iterations t=3, lanes p=1, salt is exactly 16 fresh bytes from RNG1, output is exactly 32 bytes. PHC base64 is the PHC alphabet without padding; writer parameter order is exactly m,t,p and decimal integers have no sign/leading zero. Password bytes are used exactly as supplied: no Unicode normalization, trimming, case folding, NUL termination, or text encoding conversion after Secret construction. Empty password is valid; input cap is 1,048,576 bytes. Generated salt, intermediate blocks, derived output before PHC encoding, and password-owned scratch are non-elidably zeroized after last use. Accepted PHC grammar. Safe PasswordHash.parse accepts only `$argon2id$v=19$m=,t=,p=

$$` with exactly six `$` fields, exactly one each m/t/p in any order, ASCII decimal without sign/leading zero, no unknown/duplicate parameter, canonical unpadded PHC base64, and no whitespace/trailing byte. It rejects argon2d, argon2i, missing/other version, padded/noncanonical base64, or decoded mismatch before hashing. Text cap 4096 bytes is checked before scanning. Decoded salt is 8..64 bytes; output 16..64 bytes. m is 8,192..262,144 KiB, t 1..10, p 1..8, m >= 8*p, and checked m*t <= 1,048,576 KiB-rounds. Decimal overflow, product overflow, or any cap violation returns PasswordPolicy before large allocation. Parser stores validated numeric fields and decoded lengths in PasswordHash; verification never reparses unchecked text. Verification and oracle. `password_verify` uses the parsed record's algorithm/version/parameters, constant-time compares the complete derived output, and is operationally fallible: its API1-compatible shape is `Bool ? CryptoError`. Only a completed password mismatch returns `ok(false)`; success returns `ok(true)`. Unsupported resource/platform, admission/allocation failure, or backend failure returns its mapped error, never false. Malformed, unsupported, or over-cap input cannot inhabit PasswordHash. Cancellation is D-TASKRUNTIME1 control flow, not false or CryptoError. No error includes password, salt/hash bytes, PHC text, backend text, or which comparison byte failed. Applications should project unknown user, malformed stored record, mismatch, and operational failure through one externally chosen login response. This ballot does not create a public dummy-hash helper; any such helper and its exact signature belong to D-CRYPTO-API1 and cannot be assumed before that ballot ratifies it. Resource and cancellation law. Argon2 runs on the runtime's blocking CPU pool, never an async/event-loop worker and never while holding a Jet global/scheduler lock. Admission weight is conservative total resident memory, not Argon's block count alone. Before admission compute in checked integers and round up to 1,024 KiB: `m + ceil(m/8) + 2048 + ceil(password_bytes/1024) + 1` KiB. The terms are respectively Argon's exact block allocation, the bridge's maximum auxiliary scratch, fixed allocator/thread/backend overhead, the already-owned password storage charged again conservatively, and salt/output/PHC scratch. The audited bridge must own exactly one m-KiB block arena plus at most `ceil(m/8)+2048` KiB auxiliary memory; it may not hide another arena, spawn per-lane arenas outside m, or borrow caller buffers after return. The default process budget is 311,296 KiB (304 MiB): A at the maximum 1,048,576-byte password weighs 77,824 KiB, so exactly four fit; B weighs 299,008 KiB, so exactly one fits. A job reserves full weight before allocation and releases only after every secret/intermediate buffer is zeroized. FIFO waiters are cancellation-aware. Before admission, cancellation removes the waiter with no allocation. After admission, Jet checks cancellation at each implementation-proved Argon2 pass/slice boundary; if the audited backend cannot stop at such a boundary, it completes the derivation, constant-time discards the result, zeroizes all state, releases budget, then propagates the ordinary task-cancelled outcome. It never returns true, false, PHC, or CryptoError after observed cancellation. The 311,296 KiB budget is fixed in A/B/C; there is no environment, runtime mutation, or expert budget override. No public admission, dummy, budget, or policy helper is created by A/B. C's exact calibration/policy surface is the sole conditional helper set and remains wholly gated on API1. The budget never lowers m/t/p, rewrites a PHC, or turns failure into mismatch. A request whose weight exceeds configured budget returns ResourceUnavailable before allocation. OS allocation/backend resource failure returns ResourceUnavailable for both hash and verify. Unsupported 32-bit/freestanding/comptime/interpreter targets return ResourceUnavailable before secret work; native AOT/JIT share one implementation. Audit may record algorithm/version/m/t/p, conservative weight, wait/duration, success/mismatch/error/cancelled, never password/salt/hash/PHC. Rehash is option-scoped and pure. Under A, `needs_rehash()` is true when salt<16, output<32, m<65536, t<3, or p!=1. Under B it is true when salt<16, output<32, m<262144, t<2, or p!=1. A/B return false for records at or above both selected m/t baselines with salt/output at or above baseline and p=1; Jet never silently downgrades a stronger accepted record. Under C, calibration produces an immutable persisted `PasswordPolicy`; the only honest query is `needs_rehash(current: PasswordPolicy)`, and C cannot borrow A's thresholds or expose zero-argument needs_rehash. C is conditional on API1 ratifying exactly `PasswordPolicy.calibrate() -> PasswordPolicy ? CryptoError`, `PasswordPolicy.parse(text: String) -> PasswordPolicy ? CryptoError`, `.text() -> String`, and `password_hash_with_policy(password: &Secret, policy: PasswordPolicy) -> PasswordHash ? CryptoError`. Canonical policy text is `argon2id-policy/v1;m=;t=;p=1;salt=16;out=32`; applications persist this deployment identity beside configuration. `PasswordPolicy.parse` first rejects text longer than 128 UTF-8 bytes before scanning, then accepts only ASCII bytes in the exact field order and spelling `argon2id-policy/v1;m=;t=;p=1;salt=16;out=32`. There is no whitespace, sign, leading zero, duplicate, unknown, omitted, reordered, empty, or trailing field; m must be exactly 65536, 131072, or 262144 and t exactly decimal 3..10. Non-UTF-8/non-ASCII, malformed decimal, duplicate/reordered/unknown fields, leading zero, whitespace, and trailing bytes map InvalidEncoding; a syntactically exact `argon2id-policy/` prefix maps UnsupportedVersion; canonical syntax with m/t/p/salt/out outside the candidate set maps PasswordPolicy. Parsing never benchmarks, allocates Argon memory, accepts a forged host identity, or widens hard PHC caps. `.text()` emits only this canonical form. Calibration uses fixed public 32-byte password and 16-byte salt, p=1, candidates m in [65536,131072,262144] and t in 3..10. In an otherwise idle single blocking worker it runs two discarded warmups then seven measured hashes per candidate using monotonic time. Eligible median is <=750 ms; choose greatest m, then greatest t, then lower median. If none qualifies, select A's floor m=65536,t=3—never weaker. Missing monotonic clock, any sample failure, or `(max-min) > median/4` for the chosen candidate returns ResourceUnavailable and emits no policy. Calibration is explicit, never automatic at startup or login. Moving hosts keeps the persisted policy and rehash baseline; an operator explicitly recalibrates and atomically replaces deployment policy. needs_rehash compares against the supplied persisted policy; a newly calibrated weaker policy never marks a stronger stored m/t for downgrade. A future algorithm/version replacement must first ballot its acceptance window and ordering. Rehash happens only after `password_verify` returns ok(true), generates a fresh RNG1 salt, returns a new PHC, and never mutates stored data itself. Failure/cancellation leaves the old verified record intact; callers choose transactional persistence. There is no automatic background rewrite. Expert policy. `core.crypto.expert.argon2id` remains inside lexical #Unsafe and may choose m/t/p, 8..64-byte explicit salt, and 16..64-byte output only inside the same hard parser caps and admission budget. A/B expose no `expert.password_hash(policy)` helper. If C and API1 ratify the exact PasswordPolicy surface above, `password_hash_with_policy` generates a fresh salt and returns canonical PHC; deterministic explicit salts are for protocol/import/vector work, never a safe optional argument. #Unsafe does not bypass allocation checks, zeroization, cancellation, PHC canonicality, or the process budget. Safe writer exposes no knobs, environment override, host calibration, benchmark-derived downgrade, pepper, deterministic salt, or algorithm selector. Pepper/keyed hashing needs a separate secret-storage/API decision. Compatibility. Existing arbitrary String password inputs migrate to consumed Secret; `password_hash_with_salt` moves to expert #Unsafe. Existing Argon2id v19 PHCs inside accepted caps continue verifying. Current writer outputs outside the exact default remain readable and `needs_rehash` reports by the law above. Argon2i/d, bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, and unknown PHC ids are not guessed or auto-migrated; applications import them only after a separate algorithm ballot. No alias survives the major-edition migration. Exact errors. Both password_hash and password_verify reject password Secret length above 1,048,576 bytes as PasswordPolicy before admission or backend entry. PasswordHash.parse maps PHC shape, whitespace, decimal syntax, base64 syntax/canonicality, and decoded-length failure to InvalidEncoding; argon2d/argon2i/unknown id to UnsupportedAlgorithm; missing or non-19 version to UnsupportedVersion; syntactically valid numeric values outside m/t/p/product/input/text policy to PasswordPolicy. password_hash maps RNG1 failure to EntropyUnavailable, admission impossibility/unsupported platform/allocation resource failure to ResourceUnavailable, and audited backend invariant failure to Internal. password_verify returns `Bool ? CryptoError`: completed mismatch is ok(false); admission/platform/allocation resource failure is ResourceUnavailable; backend invariant is Internal. Cancellation remains task control flow after finish-discard/checkpoint zeroization, never an error or false. D-CRYPTO-API1 must ratify these categories, fallible verify, PasswordHash/Secret types, and any public policy/calibration/dummy/admission helper before this policy ships. CLI import/rehash tooling additionally waits on D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 exact copy/exits/no-artifact law. Acceptance. Pin Argon2 RFC 9106 and PHC known-answer vectors for exact default and every accepted boundary; deterministic expert vectors prove salt/output. Hostile tests cover 4097-byte text, decimal/product overflow, duplicate/unknown/missing params, every algorithm/version, base64 padding/noncanonical bits, salt/output/m/t/p bounds, m<8p, huge claims before allocation, wrong password, empty/max password, rehash partial order, fresh salts, RNG failure, admission FIFO, cancellation before admission and at every pass/slice/finish-discard boundary, exact weight arithmetic/overflow, 77,824/299,008 KiB weights, four A jobs/one B job under 311,296 KiB, backend arena/scratch ownership ceiling, budget exhaustion, allocation/resource/backend error mapping, zeroization, no secret diagnostics/audit, AOT/JIT parity, and unsupported targets. Parser fuzzing has fixed byte/step/allocation budgets. PasswordPolicy fixtures cover exact 128/129-byte preflight, every field omission/duplication/reorder/unknown, leading zeros/signs/overflow, ASCII and UTF-8 whitespace, trailing bytes, version changes, every allowed m/t pair, forged m/t/p/salt/out values, canonical text round trip, and proof that parse performs no calibration or Argon allocation. Timing tests are regression signals, never constant-time proof. Beginner pass: hash, store one string, verify; no costs or salts. Expert pass: exact version, m/t/p, salt/output, caps, admission, audit, import, and rehash are explicit. Hybrid pass: safe and expert calls share one parser, Argon2 engine, limits, zeroization, scheduler, vectors, and PasswordHash value.

options.name: Balanced fixed default with bounded verification
options.detail: Recommended. Write m=65536 KiB, t=3, p=1, 16-byte salt, 32-byte output; accept only bounded Argon2id v19 PHCs and expose pure needs_rehash. This is predictable across supported hosts, memory-hard, server-safe under weighted admission, and upgradeable without beginner tuning.
options.code:
stored :: crypto.password_hash(&password)?
// $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=1$...$...
parsed :: crypto.PasswordHash.parse(stored.text())?
assert(!parsed.needs_rehash())
assert(crypto.password_verify(&password, parsed)?)

options.name: Memory-first fixed default
options.detail: Write m=262144 KiB, t=2, p=1 with the same grammar, caps, errors, and expert controls. Fresh output establishes B's own rehash baseline: salt 16, output 32, m 262144, t 2, p 1; needs_rehash never borrows A's thresholds. At the maximum password its conservative 299008 KiB weight permits one active B job under the 311296 KiB (304 MiB) default budget.

options.name: Host-calibrated writer
options.detail: Explicitly calibrate the exact bounded candidate matrix and persist canonical PasswordPolicy identity; fresh output plus that policy establishes C's rehash baseline, and callers pass current policy to needs_rehash. Calibration and policy APIs are unavailable unless D-CRYPTO-API1 ratifies the exact signatures in this ballot. This adapts to a deployment but makes policy rollout an operator-controlled configuration migration rather than a Jet-release constant.
options.code:
policy :: crypto.PasswordPolicy.calibrate()?
config.write_atomic("password-policy", policy.text())?
stored :: crypto.password_hash_with_policy(&password, policy)?
// Host moves keep this policy until explicit recalibration.

comparisons.note: OWASP recommends Argon2id with a minimum memory/time tradeoff and periodic upgrades. A exceeds the common floor while pinning a stable fleet policy and explicit rehash signal.
PHP stores algorithm, cost, salt, and hash together and exposes password_needs_rehash. A keeps that upgrade loop but rejects hostile stored costs before allocation.
libsodium offers interactive/moderate/sensitive fixed profiles. A chooses one beginner profile and moves bounded deviations behind Jet's audited expert gate.

decisions.title: Exact safe and expert core.crypto API
decisions.gist: Choose the exact typed value API that makes common cryptography hard to misuse while preserving complete raw-algorithm control under #Unsafe.
