Once import begins secret work, wrong recipient/passphrase, all-zero peer, unwrap failure, payload/tag/header mutation that remains canonically framed, type/public mismatch, or key corruption collapse to one OpenFailed Display/JSON/audit category. No recipient index, match, Argon detail, parser offset after secret work, tag, salt, origin id, backend/OS/dependency prose, or partial key escapes. Operation-count tests cover no-match and wrong-passphrase classes; wall-clock equality is not claimed.

Export, import, and revocation truth. Export accepts Active or Retired references; a Revoked source returns Vault(Revoked). It loads the exact immutable KeyRef, never current(name), and binds every origin field. Export does not rotate, retire, or change current. The wrapped bytes are an independent bearer backup: later source retirement/revocation/deletion cannot recall or invalidate copies. Audit states this before export. Import requires a fresh one-use VaultWrite and never writes before full authentication/type/public validation. A destination repository cannot learn a later revocation made only in the source repository; bearer-copy audit states this. Cross-repository or different-name import creates the destination name's next generation with new opaque id and Imported provenance while preserving immutable origin metadata. It never recreates the origin KeyRef. In the same repository, if the exact origin reference still exists Active/Retired and key/public hashes match, import returns ok(existing_reference), records an idempotent AlreadyPresent audit outcome, and performs no mutation; if it is Revoked, import returns Vault(Revoked) and does not reactivate it. An operator wanting the same bytes after revocation must use explicit #Unsafe raw import to a different name; it creates a new id/generation and audit records reintroduction. No safe import downgrades current or overwrites a generation.

Errors and cancellation. The final KeyWrapError/VaultError closure below is exhaustive and controls earlier shorthand. Cancellation remains task control: export returns no bytes; prepared import before commit zeroizes retained material and mutates nothing; after vault install it follows VAULT1's committed-result/durability law. No error has automatic retry or raw backend text.

Zeroization and platform. Raw key, backup key, passphrase-derived key, ephemeral secret, shared secrets, KEKs, nonces, payload plaintext, caller-owned imported buffers, and bridge scratch are non-elidably zeroized after last use; WrappedVaultKey ciphertext and public header are not secret types. Recipient-only parse/crypto can run on any target supported by compatible API/RNG/dependency law, but vault export/import additionally follows VAULT1: Linux glibc x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows MSVC x86_64/arm64. WASI/browser/mobile/musl/freestanding/comptime/pure/interpreter return UnsupportedProvider through VaultError before key work. AOT/native JIT share one implementation.

Migration and acceptance. No byte sequence from JETW, JETV, JETC, age, PEM, raw 32-byte keys, or historical vault strings is guessed as JVKW. from_bytes requires magic/version. Expert migration explicitly parses the source format under #Unsafe, then exports a fresh JVKW. V1 writer/read fixtures are permanent until a future ballot defines a new version and migration window. Golden vectors pin every byte for both modes, both key types, 1/16 recipients, exact caps and empty/hostile fields. Tests cover KDF/AEAD/HKDF/X25519/Ed25519 vectors, origin/type/generation mutation, wrong unlock, no-match dummy work, source revoke after export, same-repo idempotent-success/Revoked, cross-repo new identity, raw reimport truth, RNG/resource/cancellation, zeroization, backend suppression, AOT/JIT, supported clean hosts, and release artifact scans.

Beginner pass: choose recovery recipients, export one opaque value, import with the matching identity. Expert pass: exact bytes, KDF costs, recipient visibility, origin binding, revocation limits, admission, audit and migration are explicit. Hybrid pass: recipient and passphrase modes share one grammar, payload, AEAD, error collapse, vault mutation and audit path; neither creates a second key type or raw safe escape.

Prepared import integration closure. The only import flow is prepare_import_wrapped<T:VaultKey>(name:String,wrapped:WrappedVaultKey,unlock:KeyUnlock) -> WrappedImportPlan<T> ? KeyWrapError; authorize_wrapped_import<T:VaultKey>(plan:&WrappedImportPlan<T>,reason:String) -> VaultWrite<T> ? KeyWrapError; commit_import_wrapped<T:VaultKey>(write:take VaultWrite<T>,plan:take WrappedImportPlan<T>) -> KeyRef<T> ? KeyWrapError. Preparation authenticates JVKW, recomputes type/public key, retains zeroized key bytes, copies origin fields into the destination plan, and snapshots destination plaintext hash/revision/provider binding. Authorization binds that exact plan hash; commit cannot substitute unlock, wrapped bytes, name, type, origin, or destination. No one-step import_wrapped alias exists.

KeyWrapError and VaultError boundary. KeyWrapError is exactly InvalidEncoding, UnsupportedVersion, UnsupportedMode, UnsupportedKeyType, InvalidLength, WeakPassphrase, OpenFailed, EntropyUnavailable, ResourceUnavailable, Vault(VaultError), and Internal {incident_id}. Direct Revoked, AlreadyPresent, AuthorityDenied, and Conflict variants do not exist. Every VaultError is nested one-for-one without text loss or flattening: InvalidName, NotFound, WrongType, Revoked, Locked, AuthorityDenied, Conflict, UnsupportedProvider, InvalidEncoding, DurabilityUnknown, Crypto(CryptoError), Io {operation,redacted_path}, and Internal {incident_id}. Source revoked and same-repository revoked-origin import therefore return Vault(Revoked); idempotent same-origin import returns ok(existing KeyRef). Destination authority/revision/durability/I/O failures remain their Vault(...) value.

Wrapped-byte/authentication failures never become Vault errors. Passing .Passphrase to mode Recipient or .Recipient to mode Passphrase, wrong recipient identity/passphrase, no stanza match, all-zero peer, unwrap/tag failure, authenticated origin/type/public mismatch, or framed tamper returns the identical direct OpenFailed before any vault plan/mutation. Unknown numeric mode in bytes remains parser-level UnsupportedMode. RNG/KDF failures before vault work are direct EntropyUnavailable/ResourceUnavailable; impossible wrapper invariant is direct Internal. If vault mutation begins only after successful authentication, its later errors use Vault(...). This ordering prevents wrong-unlock oracles while preserving actionable destination lifecycle errors.
decisions.story: Mina keeps release-signing and backup-decryption keys in the repository vault. She must place an offline recovery copy in a second location, restore it on a fresh authorized host, and prove which original key version it came from. A compromised source key is later revoked; the old backup cannot be magically recalled, and importing it must never silently revive the revoked reference.

options.name: Recipient and passphrase recovery
options.detail: Recommended. Ship both exact JVKW/v1 modes above. Recipient mode gives unattended/team recovery without a memorized secret; passphrase mode gives an offline human fallback with fixed Argon2id cost. Both use one payload, origin binding, parser, AEAD, errors and import path.
options.code:
wrapped :: vault.export_to_recipients(&release_ref, [offline.public_key()])?
paper :: vault.export_to_passphrase(&release_ref, &recovery_phrase)?

plan :: vault.prepare_import_wrapped<crypto.SigningKey>(
    "release-restored", wrapped, .Recipient(&offline)
)?
write :: vault.authorize_wrapped_import(&plan, reason: "disaster recovery")?
restored :: vault.commit_import_wrapped(take(write), take(plan))?

options.name: Recipient recovery only
options.detail: Use the exact recipient-mode JVKW/v1 grammar, origin binding, lifecycle, errors, zeroization and import law above; mode 2 is unsupported and no Argon2/passphrase dependency enters this decision. Recovery requires at least one X25519 identity, but automation and team/offline copies avoid password-guessing risk.
options.code:
wrapped :: vault.export_to_recipients(&backup_ref, [ops.public_key(), offline.public_key()])?
// Passphrase request:
Error: this wrapped-key mode is not supported
Fix: choose one or more X25519 recovery recipients

options.name: Passphrase recovery only
options.detail: Use the exact passphrase-mode JVKW/v1 grammar, origin binding, lifecycle, errors, zeroization and import law above; mode 1 is unsupported and no recipient stanza is emitted. One human-held Secret is enough to recover anywhere VAULT1 runs, but every copied blob becomes an offline guessing target and unattended rotation needs an external secret source.
options.code:
wrapped :: vault.export_to_passphrase(&release_ref, &recovery_phrase)?
plan :: vault.prepare_import_wrapped<crypto.SigningKey>(
    "release-restored", wrapped, .Passphrase(&recovery_phrase)
)?
write :: vault.authorize_wrapped_import(&plan, reason: "offline recovery")?
restored :: vault.commit_import_wrapped(take(write), take(plan))?

comparisons.note: age uses X25519 recipient stanzas and a random file key. JVKW recipient mode adopts that recovery shape but pins Jet key type, origin version, caps and vault import semantics.

Encrypted PKCS #8 wraps private-key bytes under password-based encryption but does not know Jet vault generations or revocation. JVKW passphrase mode adds exact origin/type binding and one fixed safe profile.
KMS imported key material keeps external origin and cannot make prior copies disappear after disable/delete. JVKW records the same honest bearer-copy and reimport boundary locally.

decisions.title: Typed crypto errors and misuse diagnostics
decisions.gist: Choose how recoverable cryptographic failures remain typed values and when compile-known misuse becomes E2702 without creating authentication or backend oracles.
decisions.story: Mina opens an encrypted tenant record. A wrong key must look exactly like changed AAD or a corrupt tag, while an unavailable entropy provider and a saturated password-hash worker pool need distinct recovery. During review, her teammate also writes a literal 12-byte nonce for XChaCha in an expert interop call; the compiler can name that mistake before it runs without pretending it can diagnose attacker-controlled ciphertext statically.
decisions.detail:
Inherited gates and current draft status. D-CRYPTO-SUITE1=A and D-PWHASH1=A are live ratified law. D-CRYPTO-API1, D-CRYPTO-ENVELOPE2, D-PWHASH-POLICY1, D-CRYPTO-VAULT1, D-CRYPTO-KEYWRAP1, D-CRYPTO-RNG1, and D-DEP-CRYPTO-SUITE2 are compatibility-required companion decisions proposed in this batch; each grants nothing until independently ratified. API1 owns CryptoError and value JETV/JETW parse/auth boundaries. ENVELOPE2 owns FileCryptoError and file-only JETC behavior. VAULT1 owns VaultError and persistent storage, including internal store atomic backup/recovery only. KEYWRAP1 owns KeyWrapError and portable vault-key export/import. This ballot only selects diagnostic projection; it adds no dependency, algorithm, syntax, envelope field, password cost, runtime JSON schema, or command surface.

Option A closed CryptoError. `CryptoError` is a public closed runtime enum with exactly: `InvalidLength { operation, parameter, expected, actual }`; `InvalidEncoding { operation, value_kind }`; `UnsupportedVersion { operation, version }`; `UnsupportedAlgorithm { operation, algorithm }`; `OpenFailed`; `NonContributoryKey`; `OutputLength { operation, minimum, maximum, actual }`; `PasswordPolicy { reason }`; `EntropyUnavailable`; `ResourceUnavailable { resource }`; and `Internal { incident_id }`. Fields contain only public operation/bounds/version/policy identifiers. No variant contains secret/key/password/plaintext/ciphertext/tag/salt/hash/PHC bytes, parser offset, recipient index/id, OS status/path/handle, dependency type/error, generated-Rust text, or backend prose. Cancellation remains D-TASKRUNTIME1 control flow and is not CryptoError; task cancellation unwinds after zeroization/owned cleanup. Allocation failure before a recoverable reservation is ResourceUnavailable; memory-safety invariant failure is Internal.

Error assignment. Constructor/import length mismatch -> InvalidLength. Canonical public-key/signature/value-envelope framing and PasswordHash PHC shape, whitespace, decimal syntax, base64 syntax/canonicality, or decoded-length failure -> InvalidEncoding. Unknown public value-envelope or PHC version -> UnsupportedVersion; unknown algorithm/PHC id, including argon2d/argon2i -> UnsupportedAlgorithm. HKDF or expert output outside exact bounds -> OutputLength. Direct X25519 agreement that completes with an all-zero result -> NonContributoryKey. Entropy provider unavailable -> EntropyUnavailable, laundering every RandomError.Unavailable; negative/too-large direct random.bytes remains RNG1-owned RandomError. Password Secret above 1,048,576 bytes, or syntactically canonical PHC numeric m/t/p/product/input/text values outside PWHASH hard policy -> PasswordPolicy before admission. Argon2 admission, unsupported platform, or allocation resource failure -> ResourceUnavailable. Audited backend invariant failure -> Internal with a fresh non-secret incident id. password_verify completed mismatch is ok(false); resource/backend/cancellation never becomes false. No backend string is interpolated.

Companion and authentication projection. API1 `Sealed.from_bytes` and `WrappedKey.from_bytes` expose their public framing InvalidLength/InvalidEncoding/UnsupportedVersion/UnsupportedAlgorithm before secret work; after successful construction, value `open`/`unwrap` collapses wrong key/recipient/AAD, all-zero agreement, unwrap, tag, or authenticated tamper to CryptoError.OpenFailed. ENVELOPE2 `file_open` uses FileCryptoError exactly: OpenFailed, SealFailed(CryptoError), SourceIo, DestinationExists, DestinationIo; structurally framed or authenticated file-open failure after source I/O begins collapses to FileCryptoError.OpenFailed. VAULT1 VaultError stays exactly InvalidName, NotFound, WrongType, Revoked, Locked, AuthorityDenied, Conflict, UnsupportedProvider, InvalidEncoding, DurabilityUnknown, Crypto(CryptoError), Io {operation,redacted_path}, Internal {incident_id}. KEYWRAP1 KeyWrapError stays exactly InvalidEncoding, UnsupportedVersion, UnsupportedMode, UnsupportedKeyType, InvalidLength, WeakPassphrase, OpenFailed, EntropyUnavailable, ResourceUnavailable, Vault(VaultError), Internal {incident_id}; wrapped authentication failures are direct OpenFailed and vault failures remain nested. These enums are companion values, never aliases or flattened CryptoError variants. Every projection preserves the owning draft's oracle collapse and redaction.

Stable Display/recovery. InvalidLength: `<operation>: <parameter> must be <expected>; got <actual>` / fix the public input length. InvalidEncoding: `<operation>: <value_kind> is not canonical` / parse or import the documented canonical form. UnsupportedVersion/Algorithm: `<operation>: version/algorithm <n> is not supported` / migrate with the named expert tool or supported writer. OpenFailed: `encrypted data could not be opened` / check the key and expected context, then obtain an intact supported envelope; never say which failed. NonContributoryKey: `X25519 peer key does not contribute to a shared secret` / reject the peer key and obtain a new authenticated public key. OutputLength: `<operation>: output length must be <min>..<max>; got <actual>` / choose a bound value. PasswordPolicy: `password hash is outside Jet's accepted policy` / migrate or regenerate after successful verification. EntropyUnavailable: `the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness` / retry as a new deliberate operation or use a supported host; never substitute bytes. ResourceUnavailable: `<resource> is unavailable for this cryptographic operation` / retry later or adjust the separately ratified process-start budget. Internal: `Jet could not preserve a cryptographic invariant; incident <id>` / stop using the result, restart, and report the id with redacted audit. Secret-bearing values have no Display/Debug, so formatting an error cannot transitively reveal them.

E2702 reachability and precedence. First resolve syntax/effects/types. Expert call outside lexical #Unsafe emits E0510 only. Ordinary nominal-role or generic-bound incompatibility emits the ordinary type diagnostic only. E2702 is considered only after those checks pass, sema resolves a compiler-known `core.crypto`/`core.crypto.expert` callee, and a type or compile-time literal proves crypto misuse at the offending argument/call. Covered facts are only: literal/fixed key/public/signature/nonce length contradicts the selected expert algorithm; literal HKDF output outside 0..8160; literal Argon2 m/t/p/salt/output outside PWHASH hard caps; raw nonce/algorithm argument offered to a safe envelope call; or deterministic/test entropy seam reachable from a release build. `reject_all_zero:false` is not an E2702 case: inside valid #Unsafe it is an allowed expert choice, outside it E0510 wins. Dynamic bytes, attacker input, authentication mismatch, resource/backend/entropy failure, unsupported envelope bytes, password mismatch, and generic key-role mismatch never produce E2702. Dead code remains checked; generics diagnose at definition only when constraints prove a covered fact, otherwise at specialized call site with both spans.

E2702 exact diagnostic. Terminal UTF-8/NO_COLOR frame is `Error [E2702]: crypto API misuse
 --> <file>:<line>:<column>
 ...source span...
 Why: <operation> would use <public fact>, which violates <named requirement>
 Fix: <one exact safe replacement or required bound>
`; no algorithm/backend text beyond the public selected operation. Example Why `XChaCha20-Poly1305 nonce has 12 bytes; this operation requires exactly 24`; Fix `pass a 24-byte nonce, or use core.crypto.seal so Jet generates it`. Literal key length Fix names exact length; safe raw-nonce Fix removes the argument; deterministic seam Fix uses core.random only for non-crypto tests or expert fixed-vector input under #Unsafe. Each reason is a closed enum in compiler data, not formatted free text.

Machine/tool boundary. Compiler-owned E2702 JSON is exactly one `jet.diagnostic/v1` object: `{code:"E2702",class:"user",severity:"error",phase:"sema",what:"crypto API misuse",why,fix,reason,operation,expected?,actual?,primarySpan,relatedSpans:[]}`; field order/schema, workspace-relative paths, spans and redaction are pinned. LSP projects the same compiler diagnostic. DAP has no crypto ErrorResponse mapping. Runtime CryptoError/FileCryptoError/VaultError/KeyWrapError JSON rows are explicitly blocked until a general runtime-diagnostic owner ratifies their schema. First-party `jet crypto`, file, vault, key-wrap, import, rehash, and audit commands are explicitly blocked until their owning ballots plus DIAG1 ratify exact terminal/JSON rows, exits, cleanup and no-artifact law. No draft may claim JSON single-object behavior or CLI availability early.

Handled, unhandled, first-party, and compiler exits. Any handled CryptoError, including Internal, is ordinary program data: no diagnostic and no forced exit. Under A/C, an unhandled non-Internal CryptoError at `fn run` uses existing E3001 class user/tool as owned by runtime and exits 70 after cleanup; unhandled CryptoError.Internal uses E3001 class internal and exits 101 after fail-closed cleanup. A first-party command remains unavailable until it owns a row; once owned, it catches the typed value, emits that command's exact four-line frame, exits 1 for non-Internal operation failure and 101 for Internal, and publishes no artifact on failure. Compiler E2702 is class user, exits 1, and emits no program/artifact. A compiler/rustc/generated-code invariant failure is not CryptoError.Internal: existing compiler-internal ownership emits its compiler diagnostic and exits 101. Cancellation remains task control and follows only the owning runtime/command lifecycle.

Audit/backend suppression. Redacted audit may record operation, public algorithm/version, public sizes/bounds, target/provider identity, wait/duration, result category, cleanup/publication outcome, and incident id. It never records secrets, keys, nonce values, password/PHC/salt/hash, plaintext/ciphertext/tag, recipient identity for failed open, raw OS code, dependency error, parser offset after secret work, or generated source. Backend/dependency errors map through a closed internal table to EntropyUnavailable, ResourceUnavailable, OpenFailed, InvalidEncoding, or Internal; unknown backend errors become Internal. rustc/dependency prose is never shown.

Recovery and cleanup. Invalid input errors have no effect and caller may correct then issue a new operation. OpenFailed returns no partial plaintext and owned temps are removed. EntropyUnavailable exposes no key/nonce/salt/envelope and retry is a new operation. ResourceUnavailable reserves nothing or releases/zeroizes its reservation before return. Internal publishes nothing, performs fail-closed owned cleanup, and forbids reusing ambiguous crypto state. No CryptoError has `retryable`; recovery text distinguishes a new deliberate request from automatic replay.

I4 acceptance. diagnostics.md replaces E2702's reserved text with every covered reason/Why/Fix; `jet explain E2702` matches. UI snapshots cover every E2702 reason in TTY/plain/NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR plus Unicode/path spans, generics, dead code, and precedence proving E0510/type diagnostics suppress duplicate E2702. Compiler JSON schema/goldens, LSP severity/code/actions, exit 1/no artifact, and secret-redaction fixtures are pinned. Runtime value tests cover every CryptoError and companion projection, public framing versus authentication collapse, exact PWHASH parse/policy mapping, password mismatch versus operational failure, cleanup and backend suppression. A/C test E3001 exit70 for unhandled non-Internal and exit101 for unhandled Internal. B snapshots all eleven E2720..E2730 mappings, exact four-line frames/classes, fn-run exits 70/101, and future command exits 1/101, but cannot mark runtime JSON or command rows complete before their owners ratify. Tests assert all affected commands remain blocked and emit no ad-hoc Display/JSON. AOT/JIT parity and bounded operation-class tests apply; timing never claims wall-clock equality proves constant time. Beginner pass: one useful message and safe next action; wrong-key/tamper remains indistinguishable. Expert pass: typed category, public bounds, operation, audit, spans, target/provider, cleanup and incident id remain inspectable at ratified boundaries. Hybrid pass: libraries handle owning enums directly; projections never create a parallel exception taxonomy.

options.name: Typed runtime values plus focused E2702
options.detail: Recommended. Use current API1 CryptoError plus companion FileCryptoError/VaultError/KeyWrapError projections and focused E2702 with explicit precedence. Handled values remain program data; unhandled runtime and future first-party/compiler exits follow the exact boundary law above. Runtime JSON and command rows remain blocked until owned.

options.name: Typed values plus one E-code per runtime category
options.detail: Keep A's typed values and E2702, but allocate exactly eleven runtime projection codes: E2720 InvalidLength, E2721 InvalidEncoding, E2722 UnsupportedVersion, E2723 UnsupportedAlgorithm, E2724 OpenFailed, E2725 NonContributoryKey, E2726 OutputLength, E2727 PasswordPolicy, E2728 EntropyUnavailable, E2729 ResourceUnavailable, E2730 Internal. Terminal frames are exactly `Error [code] [class]`, then one-space-prefixed What/Why/Fix lines from A's pinned Display/recovery text. E2720..27 are class user; E2728..29 class tool; E2730 class internal. Handled values emit nothing. At fn run E2720..29 exit 70 and E2730 exits 101; in an independently ratified first-party command E2720..29 exit 1 and E2730 exits 101. Compiler E2702 remains exit 1. Runtime JSON/CLI emission remains blocked until its owner ratifies exact rows.
options.code:
E2720 InvalidLength       [user]
E2721 InvalidEncoding     [user]
E2722 UnsupportedVersion  [user]
E2723 UnsupportedAlgorithm [user]
E2724 OpenFailed          [user]
E2725 NonContributoryKey  [user]
E2726 OutputLength        [user]
E2727 PasswordPolicy      [user]
E2728 EntropyUnavailable  [tool]
E2729 ResourceUnavailable [tool]
E2730 Internal            [internal]
# fn run: 70 except Internal=101; owned command: 1 except Internal=101

options.name: Typed values with no crypto-specific sema diagnostic
options.detail: Keep A's exact CryptoError/runtime behavior but retire E2702. Literal wrong lengths and raw safe-API arguments receive ordinary type/argument diagnostics or runtime CryptoError; E0510 still gates expert calls. This minimizes diagnostic vocabulary, but a compile-known 12-byte XChaCha nonce gets a generic mismatch instead of the security-specific Why/Fix already reserved for core.crypto.

comparisons.note: Rust libraries return typed errors, while compiler type errors catch role mismatches. Jet adds a narrow security-specific sema diagnostic only where the compiler knows the cryptographic requirement.
Sodium deliberately collapses authentication failure. Jet preserves that collapse in typed values, CLI output, JSON, audit, and debugger projection rather than leaking backend causes.
Tink's safe templates prevent many misuses before execution. Jet makes the remaining compile-known boundary mistakes source-spanned E2702 diagnostics.

decisions.title: WASI entropy retry allocation identity
decisions.gist: Resolve a contradiction in D-CRYPTO-RNG1: a general allocator may reuse an address after a zeroized buffer is dropped, so Jet cannot guarantee both one live attempt buffer and a never-reused pointer.
decisions.lesson:
An allocation has two identities. Its logical identity is the ownership lifetime: a new Vec is a new allocation request even when the allocator later returns the same numeric address. Its physical identity is that address. Once an old buffer is zeroized and freed, a normal allocator may legally reuse its address.

Preventing address reuse requires retaining old storage, padding buffers, or owning a custom arena. Those choices contradict D-CRYPTO-RNG1's other requirements that each WASI attempt use exactly one full-size buffer and that at most one attempt buffer exist at a time. Address reuse after complete volatile zeroization does not reuse entropy state; it only reuses memory.
decisions.explainer: D-CRYPTO-RNG1 requires each WASI EINTR retry to allocate a distinct fresh full-size buffer, forbids allocation or pointer reuse, and also permits at most one attempt buffer at a time. Those statements cannot all hold under Rust's allocator: after zeroization and drop, the next exact-size Vec may receive the same address. The current attempted workaround allocates count plus padding and passes a shifted slice, which makes pointer values differ but violates the exact full-size allocation rule and proves no security property. Every option preserves the security law: exactly count zero-initialized bytes reach random_get; any non-success volatile-zeroizes the whole attempt; only success returns bytes; at most seventeen calls; no fallback.
decisions.story: A WASI host interrupts random_get twice before succeeding. Jet must throw away every tainted attempt and begin again without exposing partial bytes. The implementation must also be mechanically testable without pretending that a shifted slice pointer is a fresh allocation.
decisions.detail: This decision amends only WASI allocation identity language in D-CRYPTO-RNG1. It does not change providers, retry count, error type, cap, cancellation, supported targets, or zeroization. Tests use an injected provider and allocation-generation counters owned by the test seam; they never treat numeric address inequality as evidence of fresh entropy.

options.name: Fresh lifetime, address reuse allowed
options.detail: Recommended. Each retry constructs a new exact-count zeroed Vec after the prior Vec has been fully volatile-zeroized and dropped. Numeric address reuse is allowed because allocators own addresses; no bytes, capacity object, provider state, or reference crosses lifetimes. Tests prove generation count, one live attempt, exact length, full taint zeroization, seventeen-call cap, and no output on failure.

options.name: Reserve old allocations
options.detail: Keep each zeroized failed Vec allocated until the request ends, forcing the allocator to choose a different live address for the next Vec. This preserves physical pointer inequality but amends the one-live-buffer rule and can retain up to seventeen MiB for a maximum-size request.

options.name: One monotonic retry arena
options.detail: Allocate one bounded arena and give each retry a distinct exact-count slice. This preserves distinct provider pointers and one provider-visible attempt at a time, but amends the rule that every retry owns a separate allocation and reserves up to seventeen times the requested memory.

comparisons.note: Dropping a Vec ends its ownership lifetime but does not reserve its address. A later Vec may legally reuse that address, so address inequality cannot define freshness.
comparisons.code: drop(old); let next = vec![0u8; count]; // next.as_ptr() may equal old_ptr

comparisons.note: The host fills the caller's slice or returns an errno. Security comes from discarding and zeroizing failed attempts, not from comparing allocator addresses.

recommendation.why: A preserves every security property with exact-size bounded memory and states the allocator contract honestly. Freshness means a new cleared ownership lifetime and a new provider call, not a numeric address promise the allocator cannot make.
recommendation.tradeoff: Tests cannot assert pointer inequality. They instead assert exact length, generation count, one live attempt, complete zeroization, retry bounds, and absence of escaped bytes.

whyNot.reason: B makes address inequality true by retaining up to seventeen failed allocations, contradicting the one-live-buffer bound without improving entropy safety.
C replaces distinct allocations with slices of one large arena and multiplies reserved memory, again changing a useful bound for no security gain.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's exact-size fresh ownership lifetime. Borrow B's explicit proof that prior bytes remain zeroized until release, and C's generation-indexed tests, without retaining their extra storage.

harvest.use: Adopt as the runtime contract and primary proof.
Keep its zeroization evidence, but drop storage immediately instead of retaining it.
Use generation counters in the test-only provider seam, not a production arena.

decisions.title: Package key generation entropy failure
decisions.gist: Choose the exact fail-closed behavior when package-signing key generation cannot obtain operating-system entropy.
decisions.lesson:
Package key generation crosses two ratified laws. D-PKGSIGN1 requires `jet registry keygen` and automatic key creation on first publish. D-CRYPTO-RNG1 forbids key generation until its entropy failure has an exact command diagnostic, cleanup, exit, and no-artifact rule. D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 deliberately did not invent that command row.

Without a row, the helper exits silently and the caller currently misreports a generic helper-build error with cargo-install advice. That is neither safe product behavior nor an honest explanation. The command must either own a precise Jet diagnostic or remain unavailable.
decisions.explainer: This ballot owns only entropy failure for package-signing key creation through `jet registry keygen` and automatic first-publish keygen. It does not change Ed25519, key paths, overwrite protection E1248, signing policy, RandomError, runtime CryptoError, or other crypto commands. All options forbid fallback bytes and partial key files. A new diagnostic code is required for a command-specific row because E3001 is the unhandled Jet runtime-value boundary, while E0704 is a helper-build failure with unrelated recovery.
decisions.story: Mina publishes her first package on a supported host, but the operating system refuses the entropy request. Jet must not create a predictable signing key, leave half a keypair, modify the registry, or tell her that Cargo is missing. She needs one accurate recovery action.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet registry keygen
Error [E1275]: signing key generation needs cryptographic randomness
 What: Jet could not create the package-signing key
 Why: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
 Fix: retry as a new operation on a supported host; no key files were created
decisions.detail: Under A, E1275 is class tool and exits 1. Terminal output is the exact four-line frame shown above, with normal color policy and no raw OS status, path, helper stderr, dependency name, generated Rust, or key bytes. Stdout is empty. `jet registry keygen` creates neither secret nor public file. Automatic keygen aborts publish before package upload, index mutation, signature publication, or key-file rename. Temporary files are absent or removed; secret buffers are volatile-zeroized before return. An existing valid key bypasses entropy and is never changed. JSON remains unavailable until a separate command-JSON owner ratifies its schema.

options.name: Add exact E1275 command row
options.detail: Recommended. Preserve explicit keygen and beginner auto-keygen. Launder provider failure into one command-owned E1275 frame, exit 1, publish nothing, remove temporary files, zeroize secret buffers, and allow only a new deliberate retry. The helper returns a closed internal status; only the Jet command renders copy.

options.name: Disable package key generation
options.detail: Keep `jet registry keygen` and first-publish auto-keygen unavailable until another future command-diagnostic design. Publishing with an existing valid key still works. This follows the strict block in D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 but suspends D-PKGSIGN1's beginner auto-keygen promise.

options.name: Project through E3001
options.detail: Treat helper entropy failure like an unhandled Jet runtime RandomError: emit E3001 and exit 70. This reuses an existing code but gives a first-party command the wrong error class and lifecycle, contrary to D-CRYPTO-DIAG1's command boundary.
options.code:
Error [E3001]: panic: package keygen: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
// exit 70

comparisons.note: Key generation stops when secure randomness fails and does not substitute a deterministic key. Jet adds its own stable diagnostic and artifact cleanup contract.
E3001 owns an unhandled program error. A first-party package command instead needs a command-specific class, exit, cleanup, and recovery row.
comparisons.code: fn run() -> T ? CryptoError // unhandled value boundary, not CLI keygen

recommendation.why: A reconciles both ratified promises: beginners keep automatic signing-key setup, while entropy failure remains fail-closed, accurate, recoverable, and artifact-free.
recommendation.tradeoff: It allocates one new stable diagnostic code and requires terminal snapshots plus command cleanup tests. Runtime JSON remains intentionally unavailable.

whyNot.reason: B avoids a diagnostic row by removing the already-ratified beginner path and leaves first publish needlessly blocked.
C misclassifies a tool operation as a program panic and gives it the wrong exit and recovery contract.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's exact E1275 projection. Keep B's rule that no command ships before its terminal lifecycle is tested, and C's reuse of the provider's redacted Display sentence only as the Why line, not as E3001.

harvest.use: Adopt the diagnostic, cleanup, exit, and retry contract.
Require snapshots and artifact tests before enabling the entropy-failure path.
Reuse only the redacted provider sentence inside E1275 Why.

decisions.title: Resolve the package-keygen diagnostic code collision
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTO-KEYGEN-DIAG1 selected E1275, but E1275 already belongs to the ratified Jetpack sandbox diagnostic. Choose a unique code without changing the keygen failure behavior just approved.
decisions.lesson:
A diagnostic code is a stable identity, not decoration. Tools, snapshots, documentation, and `jet explain` use it to mean exactly one failure. Two unrelated errors cannot share E1275.

E1275 already means that required build sandboxing is unavailable under D-JPK-NODAEMON1. The new keygen ballot accidentally reused it for entropy failure. Every word of the newly approved keygen lifecycle can remain unchanged if only its code moves to the next unassigned Jetpack slot.
decisions.explainer: The live diagnostics ledger assigns E1275 through E1291. E1292 is the next unassigned Jetpack code. This ballot changes only the code selected by D-CRYPTO-KEYGEN-DIAG1; its class tool, four-line copy, exit 1, redaction, zeroization, retry, and no-artifact rules remain exact.
decisions.story: Mina's editor receives E1275 after signing-key generation fails. Today E1275 tells tooling to explain sandbox policy, while the terminal says cryptographic randomness failed. A unique code keeps humans and machines on the same explanation.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet registry keygen
Error [E1292]: signing key generation needs cryptographic randomness
 What: Jet could not create the package-signing key
 Why: the operating system could not provide cryptographic randomness
 Fix: retry as a new operation on a supported host; no key files were created
decisions.detail: E1275 remains unchanged for sandbox-required/unavailable. Under A, every E1275 reference and test stays intact; the keygen implementation, diagnostics ledger, `jet explain`, snapshots, explicit keygen tests, and automatic-publish tests use E1292. No syntax, provider, error class, JSON schema, or cleanup behavior changes.

options.name: Move keygen to E1292
options.detail: Recommended. Keep E1275 stable for sandbox policy and assign the exact approved keygen entropy row to the next free Jetpack code, E1292.
options.code:
E1275 = sandbox required but unavailable
E1292 = package-signing key generation lacks OS entropy

options.name: Move sandbox off E1275
options.detail: Keep keygen on E1275 and renumber the older sandbox diagnostic. This changes an already-shipped code, its JSON output, snapshots, documentation, and automation solely to preserve the newer accidental assignment.
options.code:
E1275 = package keygen entropy failure
E1292 = sandbox required but unavailable

options.name: Share E1275
options.detail: Let both errors use E1275 and distinguish them by message text. `jet explain E1275`, machine consumers, and stable-code guarantees become ambiguous.
options.code: E1275 = sandbox failure OR keygen entropy failure // ambiguous

comparisons.note: Stable machine identities must not name unrelated failures. Reusing one identifier forces consumers to parse prose, defeating the identifier.

recommendation.why: A preserves the existing stable code and changes only the new, not-yet-implemented assignment. It is the smallest truthful reconciliation.
recommendation.tradeoff: The newly ratified ballot's example changes from E1275 to E1292; all other approved behavior remains identical.

whyNot.reason: B breaks existing sandbox diagnostics and consumers to protect a newer accidental collision.
C destroys one-code-one-meaning and makes `jet explain` and JSON consumers ambiguous.

hybrid.synthesis: Use A's unique E1292 assignment. Preserve B's concern for complete propagation by updating every new keygen fixture and durable document together; reject C's ambiguity entirely.

harvest.aspect: Preserve old code and allocate next free code
harvest.use: Adopt as the diagnostic identity law.
Apply only to the new keygen references, not the existing sandbox row.
Keep the implementation small, but retain unique identities.

decisions.title: Should Jet commit to a layered reactive UI stack as a strategic pillar?
decisions.gist: The proposed stack is: reactivity → view model → typed styles → headless+styled component kit → motion/app kit — each layer building on the previous. This is the TypeScript/Swift UI replacement play. Gated on D-REACTCORE1 (how reactivity works) and D-RENDERTGT1 (backend seam). No layer of this stack should be built until those two gate decisions are made.
decisions.explainer: Committing to this stack means Jet's stdlib eventually includes a full UI framework, not just a signal library. That is a large scope addition — UI frameworks are notoriously hard to get right and to maintain. The payoff is that Jet becomes a genuine TS/Swift alternative for app developers. The risk is years of stdlib work that distracts from language correctness and performance. This decision is about strategic direction, not immediate implementation — no code ships before D-REACTCORE1 and D-RENDERTGT1 are resolved. I8: the stack must have one canonical mechanism at each layer, not multiple competing approaches.
decisions.story: I want to build a web or native app entirely in Jet — not reach for React or SwiftUI. That means Jet needs a first-party UI layer that is reactive, composable, and ships real components.

options.name: Adopt layered stack, sequenced after gate decisions
options.detail: Commit to the strategic direction. Build each layer in order, gated on D-REACTCORE1 + D-RENDERTGT1. No code before those are decided. Long roadmap but gives Jet a genuine app-dev story.

options.name: UI is third-party only
options.detail: Jet ships no UI framework. The signal library (D-REACT1) is the ceiling of stdlib UI support. Third parties build frameworks on top. Keeps stdlib small; risks ecosystem fragmentation (multiple incompatible UI libs).

options.name: Defer — decide at v1
options.detail: No commitment now. Revisit after the language core is stable. Safe for the near term but defers the TS/Swift replacement play indefinitely.
options.code: // No decision — UI story TBD post-v1

comparisons.note: Apple committed to a layered reactive UI stack (Combine → SwiftUI) early. The two-layer seam (reactive model + declarative views) has held up well across platforms.
Elm built the reactive model into the language (The Elm Architecture) and owns the full UI stack. Extremely coherent but brittle to extend beyond its core use-case.
comparisons.code: update Increment model = { model | count = model.count + 1 }

decisions.title: UI tree node shape: typed enum vs dynamic record
decisions.gist: Should UI view-model nodes be a typed enum (Text, Box, Button) or a dynamic tagged record?
decisions.story: Dorothy is building a to-do app. She needs text labels, containers, buttons, and input fields. She wants the compiler to catch a typo in a node kind at build time, not at runtime.

options.name: Typed constructors: ui.text(), ui.box(), ui.button() (recommended)
options.detail: Each node kind is a distinct constructor. The compiler knows statically that ui.button() produces a button node and ui.text() produces a text node. No stringly-typed fields, no runtime kind-check. Consistent with closed-type direction.

options.name: Dynamic tagged record: ui.node({ kind: "text", content: "..." })
options.detail: A single ui.node() function accepts a record with a "kind" string field. Flexible for dynamic node creation but kind typos are runtime errors. Inconsistent with Jet's static-safety direction.

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:      Text("hello") / VStack { ... } / Button("ok") {}  — typed constructors, each is a distinct type
Flutter:      Text("hello") / Column(children:[...]) / ElevatedButton(...)  — same pattern
React JSX:    <Text>hello</Text> / <View> / <Pressable>  — tagged strings compiled to typed calls
HTML:         <div> / <span> / <button>  — string tags, no compile-time kind checking
Android XML:  android:layout_width="match_parent"  — string attributes

decisions.title: Style API shape: flat record vs builder chain
decisions.gist: Should ui.Style be a flat value record or a builder-method chain?
decisions.story: Walter is styling a submit button: red background, white text, 12px padding, 80px wide. He wants to define the style as a reusable constant and pass it to multiple buttons.

options.name: Flat value record: Style { color: rgb(255,0,0), width: px(80) } (recommended)
options.detail: Style is a pure value — comparable, hashable, passable as a constant. Consistent with Jet's value semantics: no mutable builder state, no object identity, no method chain side effects. A partial style (only some fields set) uses default values for the rest.

options.name: Builder chain: Style.new().color(rgb(255,0,0)).width(px(80))
options.detail: Familiar from many UI frameworks but introduces mutable builder state. A Style mid-chain is not a value — you cannot store it, compare it, or pass it without calling a terminating method. Inconsistent with Jet's value-oriented surface.
options.code:
// Not easily reusable as a constant:
SUBMIT_STYLE :: Style.new()
    .background(rgb(220, 38, 38))
    .color(rgb(255, 255, 255))
    .padding(px(12))
    .width(px(80))
    .build()   // or is this the value? when is it a value?

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:     Text("hi").foregroundColor(.red).frame(width: 80)  — builder chain on the node, not style
Flutter:     TextStyle(color: Colors.red, fontSize: 16)              — flat struct
CSS:         { background: red; width: 80px; padding: 12px }        — flat key-value
Tailwind:    "bg-red-500 text-white p-3 w-20"                       — string class list
React:       {{ backgroundColor: 'red', width: 80, padding: 12 }}   — plain object
SwiftUI (StyleSheet): not idiomatic — styles via modifiers on views

decisions.title: Motion timing: injectable Clock vs global time signal
decisions.gist: Does core.motion.spring() take a Clock capability parameter, or does it read a global time signal?
decisions.story: Doris is building a loading spinner that animates with a spring. She needs to write a unit test that asserts the spinner reaches its target position after 300ms — without waiting 300 real milliseconds.

options.name: Injectable Clock: spring(target, clock, stiffness, damping) (recommended)
options.detail: Clock is passed in explicitly. Tests inject FakeClock.new() and call clock.advance(ms) for deterministic results. Production code passes the real system clock. Consistent with D-DET1 (all time/randomness is injectable). Flutter uses the same pattern (TickerProvider).

options.name: Global time signal: core.motion.time_signal() read internally
options.detail: Motion reads a module-level time signal automatically. Simpler call site but tests must stub the global, which requires framework-level mocking support (jest.useFakeTimers equivalent). Less consistent with D-DET1.

decisions.comparisons:
React Spring:   useSpring({ from: {x:0}, to: {x:1} })          — global RAF/time; not testable without mocking
Framer Motion:  useAnimate(), animate(el, {x:1}, {duration:0.3}) — global time; testing needs jest fake timers
SwiftUI:        withAnimation(.spring()) { state = 1 }           — global CADisplayLink; XCTest uses waitFor
GSAP:           gsap.to(el, {x:1, ease:"elastic.out"})          — global ticker; test with gsap.ticker.tick()
Flutter:        AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: ...)  — vsync injected via TickerProvider (close to option A)

decisions.title: A11y diagnostic gating mechanism
decisions.gist: How are accessibility diagnostics triggered — automatic on --release, explicit jet lint --a11y, or per-file #A11yStrict?
decisions.story: Hank's team ships a web app. He wants his CI to catch missing ARIA roles and unlabeled buttons before they reach users. But he doesn't want beginners running jet build to see a wall of a11y warnings on their first hello-world.

options.name: --release build flag enables a11y lints automatically
options.detail: Hank runs jet build --release for production and a11y lints fire automatically. But a beginner who runs jet build --release for their first deployed app also sees a wall of a11y errors on components they didn't write. Surprise on first real build.
options.code:
jet build --release
# output includes:
# W2930: button "X" has no accessible label (E2930)
# W2931: ui.text used as interactive element without role (E2931)
# 2 accessibility warnings — use --no-a11y to suppress

jet build              # no a11y lints (dev builds)
jet build --release    # a11y lints fire automatically

options.name: jet lint --a11y explicit separate step (recommended)
options.detail: A11y linting is an explicit step Hank adds to CI. It never surprises beginners. Consistent with existing lint profile pattern — same as running jet lint --unused or jet lint --style.
options.code:
# CI pipeline (Hank adds this step):
jet lint --a11y

# output:
# src/nav.jet:3: W2930: button "X" has no accessible label
# src/nav.jet:4: W2931: interactive text missing role
# 2 accessibility issues

# Beginner dev loop:
jet build     # no a11y lints — not surprised
jet run       # no a11y lints
jet lint      # base lints only
jet lint --a11y  # only when explicitly requested

options.name: #A11yStrict file-level opt-in marker
options.detail: Files with #A11yStrict at the top get a11y lints; others don't. Hank can enforce it on specific modules. Very granular but obscure — beginners don't know to add it, and it requires discipline across a large team.

decisions.comparisons:
ESLint a11y:    eslint --rule jsx-a11y/...  explicit plugin; CI adds --rule flags
axe-core:       separate npm run a11y  — entirely separate tool run
Lighthouse:     CI step: lighthouse --only-categories=accessibility
SwiftUI:        XCUIAccessibilityAudit  — explicit test call in test suite
Android:        AccessibilityScanner    — separate IDE plugin, not build-time

decisions.title: Native OS platform gating for #Extern backends (Phase 8 blocker)
decisions.gist: How does Jet source say "this function/module only compiles on Linux (or macOS, or Windows)" so a native GTK/AppKit/Win32 FFI backend doesn't break builds on the other two platforms?
decisions.story: Walter is shipping a desktop app. His `LinuxWindowBackend` calls into GTK via #Extern C FFI. He needs the compiler to leave that code out entirely when building on macOS (no GTK there) and swap in an AppKit-backed implementation of the same JetBackend trait instead — without a runtime crash or a linker error on the wrong platform.

options.name: Extend the existing #Target marker with OS variants (recommended)
options.detail: D-WASM1 already established #Target as "module-level target marker" with Browser/Wasm/Js as the first instances. Add Os.Linux / Os.Macos / Os.Windows as more instances of the SAME marker family, so there is exactly one marker for "what environment does this code run under" (web bucket or native OS) — I8 one-way-to-mean-it. Sema rejects mixing a web variant and an OS variant on the same item (two different axes, one marker, mutually exclusive values).

options.name: New dedicated #Os marker, separate from #Target
options.detail: #Target's existing job (web WASM/JS partitioning) is a genuinely different compilation axis from "which native OS." A distinct #Os(Linux) marker keeps the two concerns from ever being conflated in sema, at the cost of one more marker family to learn.

options.name: Manifest-level gating (pkg.jet / env.jet), no in-source marker
options.detail: No per-function marker at all — the whole file/package is included only when the target platform in pkg.jet's payload matches. Coarser granularity (whole file, not per-impl), and inconsistent with how every other conditional-compilation-flavored feature in Jet (#Reactive, #Extern, #Unsafe, D-WASM1's #Target) is an in-source marker, not a manifest switch.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust: #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] — attribute-based, same shape as option A/B.
Swift: #if os(macOS) ... #endif — source-level directive, same shape.
React Native: Button.ios.js / Button.android.js — filename convention, same shape as option C.
Zig: builtin.target.os.tag comptime check — comptime-if, closer to option A/B than C.

decisions.title: File-level + manifest-level default build target (web without --target=web every time)
decisions.gist: A .jet file (or its pkg.jet once it's a managed package) can declare "I'm a web app" so jet run/dev/build default to the web backend without --target=web typed every time.
decisions.story: Nate is iterating on a loose example file and is tired of typing --target=web on every jet dev invocation. Once he promotes the file into a real package, he wants that same intent to live in pkg.jet instead of the source file, since a packages target is project config, not a per-file concern.

options.name: #Target(Web) file-level marker + pkg.jet target: "web" field, CLI flag always wins
options.detail: Extends the EXISTING #Target(...) marker (today only #Target(Wasm)/#Target(Js), both already file/module-scope-only ceilings, never per-function) with a third value, Web -- distinct in meaning (default backend selection, not a partition ceiling) but same lexical form, no new marker family (I8). pkg.jet's payload gains a parallel target: "web" key. Precedence: --target=<x> CLI flag overrides pkg.jet target which overrides file-level #Target(Web) which overrides the native default. No automatic file-to-manifest migration tool for now -- a manual edit, or a later jetpack convenience, not blocking this decision.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev counter.jet                 // infers web from the marker
$ jet dev counter.jet --target=native  // flag still overrides

decisions.title: Explicit companion-HTML marker for jet build/dev --target=web
decisions.gist: Replace the silent <stem>.html filename convention with an explicit #Html("path.html") marker at the top of the .jet file, so the pairing is visible in the source and errors loudly if the file is missing.
decisions.story: Nate renamed a file mid-project and jet dev silently started serving the generic fallback page instead of his real one -- no error, just a confusingly plain-looking dashboard. He wants the source itself to say which HTML file it pairs with.
decisions.inWild:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev app.jet   // uses dashboard.html, or a clear error if it's missing
decisions.detail: AMENDED 2026-07-01: option B added — manifest-level pairing for managed packages composes with the file marker; single-option ballots decide nothing.

options.name: #Html("path.html") file-level marker, same family as #Target(Web)
options.detail: Precedence when building for web: explicit #Html(...) wins; else the existing sibling <stem>.html convention (kept for backward-compat with 190-197's existing examples, none of which will be forced to add the marker); else the generic auto-generated page. A referenced #Html(...) path that doesn't exist on disk is a build-time error naming the missing file, not a silent fallback.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

options.name: pack.jet target field for managed packages, #Html(...) for single files — composed
options.detail: Once a project has a manifest, pairing belongs with the target declaration: executable { entry: "src/run.jet", html: "dashboard.html" }. Single-file apps keep the #Html marker (option A). Precedence: CLI flag > manifest field > file marker > sibling <stem>.html > generated page. Missing referenced file is a build error either way.

decisions.title: Style length spelling: unit literals vs Length wrappers vs bare numbers
decisions.gist: How a user writes a length like 320 pixels in a UI style.
decisions.story: Betty is laying out the settings page of her recipe app: a card 320 wide, 180 tall, 12 of padding. She wants to type those three numbers once, have the compiler catch a unit typo, and not wonder later whether 320 meant pixels or something else.

options.name: Unit-family literal: width: 320px (recommended)
options.detail: core.ui.style declares a #UnitFamily(length) { px } (D-QUAL3), so the ratified unit-literal syntax (D-UNITLIT1) applies: 320px is a compile-checked Px value. One canonical unit mechanism in the whole language (I8) — style lengths use the same machinery as 500ms and 12.50usd. Unit typos are compile errors (E0134); if a second unit ever ships, cross-unit math is a compile error too (E0127). Reads like the CSS every beginner has already seen.

options.name: Enum with per-unit variants: width: .Px.{value: 320.0}
options.detail: Length is an enum whose variants carry the value: Length { Px(value: Float) }. Fully typed and pattern-matchable, and the field type stays a single Length even if more units are added. But it duplicates what unit families already do with a second, style-only mechanism (I8), and every length costs a variant-construction spelling.

options.name: Flat pair record: width: Length.{value: 320.0, unit: .Px}
options.detail: Length is a two-field struct (value + LengthUnit enum) — the shape Phase 3's example shipped. Plain user-space types, nothing new to learn beyond structs. But it's the most ceremony per length, the unit and value can be read independently without matching (a backend can use .value and forget .unit), and it's a second unit mechanism next to unit families (I8).

options.name: Bare Float logical pixels: width: 320.0
options.detail: No Length type at all — style dimensions are Float, pixels by convention, like SwiftUI/Flutter. Least typing and no unit concept for beginners to learn. But the unit lives in documentation instead of the type: 320.0 could be anything, a duration mixed into a width compiles fine, and adding real units later changes every Style field's type.

options.name: CSS string: width: "320px"
options.detail: Lengths are strings parsed at render time, exactly like inline CSS. Familiar to web developers and trivially copy-pasteable from CSS. But every typo becomes a runtime failure in the user's running app, the compiler can't help with math on lengths, and stringly-typed values are the opposite of the typed-styles goal this phase exists for.

decisions.comparisons:
CSS:            width: 320px;              — unit-suffix literal, the shape every web tutorial teaches
Jetpack Compose: Modifier.width(320.dp)     — typed Dp via extension property; 320 alone is a type error
SwiftUI:        .frame(width: 320)         — unitless CGFloat points, unit is implicit convention
Flutter:        SizedBox(width: 320)       — unitless logical pixels, same implicit convention
React inline:   {{ width: 320 }}           — bare number silently means px; {{ width: '320px' }} string also accepted
Typst:          width: 320pt               — unit-suffix literal, checked at compile time
decisions.rec: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).

decisions.title: Phase 8 native UI backends: how do GTK/AppKit/Win32 toolchain deps enter the dev environment?
decisions.gist: Building a real native UI backend needs OS toolkit headers/libs the dev shell does not have; decide how they get there.
decisions.story: Hank wants the reactive UI showcase to open a real Linux window instead of the web renderer. The compiler side (OS gating, renderer seam) is ready, but the flake devShell has no GTK headers or pkg-config, so nothing can link. Nothing an agent does can proceed until the dependency route is chosen.

options.name: nixpkgs devShell deps now (recommended)
options.detail: Add gtk4 + pkg-config (Linux) to the flake devShell per the existing owner guidance for native deps (nixpkgs stopgap, jetpack core provider owns it long-term). macOS/Windows backends wait for contributors on those hosts. Non-Nix users get a clear "install gtk4" message.
options.code:
# flake.nix devShell
buildInputs = [ gtk4 pkg-config ];

# then Phase 8 builds:
nix develop -c jet run ui_showcase.jet   # real window

options.name: Defer Phase 8 to Epoch 4
options.detail: Ship Epoch 3 UI as web-renderer only; native backends land with the jetpack core provider that owns native deps properly.
options.code:
// e3: web target stays the only real renderer
jet build --target=web ui_showcase.jet

options.name: Headless native backend first
options.detail: Build the native backend against a stub/offscreen renderer (no toolkit linkage) so the seam is exercised end-to-end; real toolkits follow later behind A or B.
options.code:
#Target(Os.Linux)
impl HeadlessBackend: JetBackend { /* draws to a buffer, asserts in tests */ }

comparisons.note: system gtk4 via pkg-config; user installs it (apt/brew/nix).
bundles its own engine — zero system deps, huge binary.
comparisons.code: flutter build linux   # no gtk headers needed

decisions.rec: A — matches the ratified native-deps guidance (nixpkgs stopgap while jetpack matures); unblocks Phase 8 for the primary dev host without new invariant pressure.
decisions.recommendation: A — matches the ratified native-deps guidance (nixpkgs stopgap while jetpack matures); unblocks Phase 8 for the primary dev host without new invariant pressure.

decisions.title: How does ungated code get "the impl for this OS"?
decisions.gist: #Target(Os.*) now gates impls, but plain main has no ratified way to construct/dispatch to whichever gated impl survived the build.
decisions.story: Doris writes a desktop app. She gates LinuxBackend and MacosBackend impls per D-OSTARGET1. Now her ungated main needs a backend value. Constructing LinuxBackend directly in main is (correctly) E-OSTARGET-UNMATCHED-CALL — main is not Linux-only. There is no blessed way to say "give me the one that matched this build."

options.name: fn-level #Target(Os.*) + one-survivor rule (recommended)
options.detail: Extend gating to fns: several fns share one name/signature, each gated to a different OS, exactly one survives per build; ungated code calls it like any fn. Missing an OS the build targets = compile error listing covered OSes. Mirrors Rust cfg/Go build tags; no new expression syntax.

options.name: Comptime OS switch expression
options.detail: A compiler-known comptime value (e.g. build.os) usable in a match whose non-matching arms are discarded before OS-gating checks run. More general (any per-OS choice), but new comptime surface + a second way to express what A does (I8 pressure).

options.name: Status quo — gated modules own the choice
options.detail: Ungated code never touches gated types; each app ships a per-OS gated module exporting a common fn. Works today only if fn-level gating exists somewhere, which it does not — effectively forces apps to gate their whole main, hollowing the check.
options.code: // every call chain from main must itself be OS-gated — main per OS.

comparisons.note: #[cfg(target_os)] fns — one survives per build.
build tags: one file per OS defines the same fn.
comparisons.code:
//go:build linux
func newBackend() Backend { return gtk{} }

comparisons.note: comptime switch on builtin.os.
comparisons.code: const b = switch (builtin.os.tag) { .linux => Gtk{}, .macos => AppKit{}, else => unreachable };

decisions.rec: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).

decisions.title: What is Jet’s compile-time build entrypoint?
decisions.gist: Give Jet a build-time main: one explicit `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`, selected by the build surface.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s `#run` is powerful because build code is just language code. Jet should import that power through a single auditable entrypoint instead of hidden module-level execution. Local `comptime {}` remains for value computation; the build entrypoint owns graph construction: targets, generated source, assets, toolchains, profiles, and package/workspace integration. Generated source still re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema (R11).
decisions.story: Marcus is building a game. He wants to pack textures, generate an enum from asset names, compile shaders, and then build the game binary with one command. His studio security team wants the same build to explain exactly what ran and what files/network endpoints it touched.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a build-time main can become Cargo build.rs with better syntax: dependency code executes before users inspect it. Patch: one selected root entrypoint, BuildContext authority only, D-CTEFFECT1 tiers, dependency Tier 2 denied by default, generated-source re-check, lock/provenance, and jet explain-build. Do not let every imported module have hidden build hooks. STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-01: an earlier edit claimed the lifecycle-verbs law (jet <verb> -> fn <verb>(); syntax-comparison-proposal.md §36A) was ratified — it is NOT; it is an open proposal, related open ballot D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1 (jet dev). Option B stands on its own merits and the owner direction recorded 2026-07-01 (a fn-main-equivalent build entry that maps cleanly to jet build); if the verb law later ratifies, B becomes one instance of it. D-BUILDPOLICY1 governs authority either way. Scope ladder (single file / package / workspace) is D-BUILDSCOPE1; generated-source home is D-BUILDGEN1.

options.name: `Build.entry` selects `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`
options.detail: One explicit build-time main. The marker makes the authority boundary visible; `Build.entry` makes selection explicit for tools and CI. Local `comptime {}` remains separate.

options.name: fn build(b: BuildContext) via the lifecycle verb map (recommended)
options.detail: Not name magic and not dependent on any unratified law: jet build runs fn build(BuildContext) when the root defines one, else the batteries default pipeline runs. The typed BuildContext parameter is the visible authority boundary. Aligns with the OPEN lifecycle-verbs proposal (jet run -> fn run(), jet dev -> fn dev()) without depending on it.

options.name: `comptime main` in any module
options.detail: Maximal #run feel. Rejected unless owner accepts hidden import-time execution risk.
options.code: comptime fn main(ctx: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ? { ... }

options.name: No build entrypoint; only declarative `Build.{}` plus local `comptime {}`
options.detail: Safest and easiest to audit, but cannot replace Jai/Zig/Make-class orchestration.
options.code: build: Build.{ sources: ["src/main.jet"] }

comparisons.note: `#run` can execute arbitrary compile-time code and participate in build orchestration. It is fun and direct, but authority is broad by default.
`build.zig` is a programmatic build file with explicit steps. Strong model, but separate from ordinary source entrypoints.
`build.rs` runs before compilation and communicates through files/env instructions. Powerful but stringly and historically easy to abuse.

decisions.title: What authority does build-time code get by default?
decisions.gist: Build code gets pure and locked reproducible inputs by default; ambient effects require source audit plus policy.
decisions.explainer: Build metaprogramming is supply-chain code execution. Jet needs a policy model that is fun locally but enforceable in CI and enterprises. D-CTEFFECT1 gives the effect tiers; this decision fixes the build-system default: root builds may request authority, dependencies are denied ambient authority unless project/org policy grants it, and every granted capability is recorded in lock/provenance.
decisions.story: Alicia maintains a fintech service. She is fine with a root build script reading `schema/*.sql`, but she cannot allow a transitive dependency to read CI secrets or hit the network during build.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: too much policy can make game-dev builds feel bureaucratic. Too little policy loses enterprise adoption. The compromise is profile-sensitive: developer default allows pure + locked Tier 1 and prompts for Tier 2; CI strict/offline deny drift; enterprise can allowlist roots/domains/tools. The model must not rely on wrapper scripts.

options.name: Tiered policy with `BuildContext` authority only (recommended)
options.detail: Pure + locked Tier 1 by default. Tier 2 needs `#Impure("reason")`, CLI/project/org permission, and provenance. Dependencies get no Tier 2 unless explicitly granted.
options.code:
jet build --profile=ci --locked --deny-impure
jet audit-effects

options.name: Warn-only policy for impure build effects
options.detail: Fast and friendly, but CI can accidentally ship non-reproducible builds.
options.code: Warning [L3102]: build reads `$HOME/.token`

options.name: Pure-only build code
options.detail: Maximum reproducibility, but blocks shader compilation, bindgen, asset packing, and real-world package builds.
options.code: // ctx.exec, env, unpinned network: always errors

options.name: Jai-style unrestricted build execution
options.detail: Most fun and powerful locally; unacceptable supply-chain default for Jet.
options.code: #run { run_process("curl https://...") }

comparisons.note: Builds are sandboxed and inputs are explicit; reproducibility is excellent but general programming ergonomics are specialized.
Actions declare inputs/outputs and remote cache keys. Strong enterprise model; BUILD language is separate from app language.
Build scripts are easy but broad; policy/audit is mostly convention and sandboxing is external.

decisions.title: Where does fn build live at each scale, and how do workspace builds compose?
decisions.gist: One build-entry model from a single file to a monorepo: where the entry lives at each rung, and who grants its authority.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDENTRY1 picks the entry spelling; this decision fixes its home per scale and the grant chain. Owner direction (2026-07-01): effect/capability declaration must travel with the code so a lone .jet file works with no manifest; pkg.jet is where a project grants standing permission; the workspace is where an org caps everything. Composition: a workspace build runs member builds in dependency order; whether it may only observe/cap members or also contribute targets is part of this choice. Declaration stays one mechanism (code-site #Impure/effect tags, D-CTEFFECT1); permission and policy are the two layers above it — nothing is declared twice (I8).
decisions.story: Earl writes a one-file jam game that bakes a sprite atlas at build time. It grows into a package, then his studio pulls it into their 40-package monorepo. Earl's build fn should survive each move unchanged, and the studio's security lead needs one file that caps what every member build may touch in CI.
decisions.detail: Grant chain at a glance: single file = per-invocation grant (flag or interactive prompt); package = standing grant recorded in pkg.jet; workspace = ceiling that member grants cannot exceed. Each rung caps the rung below; jet audit reads all three without executing anything.

options.name: Entry lives in the unit's existing definition file at every rung
options.detail: Single file: fn build beside fn main. Package: fn build inside pkg.jet. Workspace: fn build inside workspace.jet. Zero new filenames; the grant chain (flag -> pkg.jet build: block -> workspace policy block) mirrors containment. Workspace fn build may add workspace-level targets and cap members, never mutate a member's plan.

options.name: Dedicated build.jet beside the manifest
options.detail: Package and workspace each get a build.jet next to pkg.jet / workspace.jet; single file keeps fn build in-file. Manifests stay purely declarative; build logic gets its own home. Cost: a fourth special filename (env.jet, pkg.jet, workspace.jet, build.jet) and a two-file story for small packages.

options.name: Any source file, selected by an explicit pointer
options.detail: pkg.jet points at the entry: build: .{ entry: tools.release_build }. Most flexible layout; auditors must follow the pointer instead of grepping one location, and two packages can spell the same thing two ways.

options.name: Package scope only (no single-file, no workspace entry)
options.detail: The Cargo build.rs shape: only packages get a build entry. A lone script cannot use build-time generation without first creating a package, and an org has no first-class ceiling — policy lives in external CI scripts.
options.code:
// jam.jet
fn build(b: BuildContext) ... // error: build entry requires a package manifest

comparisons.note: build.rs is package-only, ambient-authority, and has no workspace-level build or policy file; orgs bolt policy on with external tooling.
comparisons.code: // build.rs — full process authority, no grant chain

comparisons.note: build.zig is a dedicated per-package build program (option B shape); no capability layer, no workspace ceiling.
BUILD per package + WORKSPACE/MODULE at root — the two-rung shape of option A/B, but in a separate dialect from the app language.
One flake.nix serves every scale and evaluation is pure by default — the closest existing grant-chain model, in a specialized language.

decisions.title: Where does build-generated Jet source live, and how is it addressed?
decisions.gist: Build code emits real Jet modules (D-CTCODEGEN1). Decide the on-disk home, lock hashing, staging, and the additive-only rule.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratified the pipeline law: generated code re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema like hand-written source. This decision fixes the user-visible surface on top of it: where generated files land, whether they are committed, how b.generate() addresses them, whether a later generation round may observe an earlier round's output (bounded staging vs single round), and the additive-only law — generation may ADD modules but never mutate or shadow user-written source, so reading a file always tells the truth. That last rule is the deliberate break from Jai's #insert, whose output never exists anywhere a person or an LSP can open.
decisions.story: Doris generates a typed API client from openapi.json. She wants to open the generated file, set a breakpoint in it, and point a teammate at line 214 in review; her CI must prove the artifact byte-matches the spec hash recorded in the lock.
decisions.detail: All options share the ratified floor: re-entry through the front end, hash recorded in .jet/lock, diagnostics pinned to the trigger site with the generated fragment as optional context. Staging recommendation carried in each option: generation runs in bounded, deterministically ordered rounds; a cycle is a compile error naming the chain — no Jai-style loop-until-quiescent.

options.name: Derived state under .jet/generated/, never committed
options.detail: Generated modules are build products, addressed by module name and materialized under .jet/generated/<package>/. Real files: LSP go-to-def lands in them, debugger steps through them, jet explain-build diffs them. Lock records source-input and output hashes, so CI verifies without committing. Source tree stays clean; no drift class of bugs.

options.name: In-tree build/generated/, committing optional
options.detail: Files land inside the project at build/generated/; each project decides whether to commit them. Visible without any flag, but the committed/uncommitted split means two ecosystems and --locked must handle both.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> build/generated/api_client.jet   (gitignore or commit — project choice)

options.name: Checked-in generated/ required
options.detail: Go-generate model: generated source is always committed, reviewed in every diff. Maximum review visibility; the cost is a standing drift hazard (artifact vs input) that CI must re-verify anyway, plus generated noise in every review.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> generated/api_client.jet   committed; CI fails if regeneration differs

options.name: Virtual only — no files, dump on demand
options.detail: Generated modules exist only inside the compilation; a flag dumps them for forensics. This is the Jai/#insert and Rust-proc-macro feel: nothing to open, breakpoint, or review. Listed to reject.
options.code: // nothing on disk; jet build --emit-generated is the only window

comparisons.note: OUT_DIR + include! hides generated code; cargo-expand exists because nobody can otherwise read what a proc-macro produced.
go generate commits artifacts (option C): perfectly visible, drifts unless CI regenerates and compares.
Generated files are derived outputs under bazel-out/, addressable as labels — the option A shape with strong caching.

decisions.title: May build code read the whole checked program and enforce custom rules (ladder rung B)?
decisions.gist: Rung B of the D-METADEPTH1 ladder: read-only whole-program reflection plus first-class custom diagnostics, from the build entry only. No mutation, no macros — rung C stays frozen (c154).
decisions.explainer: D-METADEPTH1=A ratified that rung B (a read-only lint-style rejection pass) rises 'only by a future vote'. This ballot is that vote, scoped to the fn build arc. Grant if ratified: the build entry receives a post-sema, read-only snapshot of the whole program through the existing D-METAREFLECT1 TypeInfo surface scaled up (program -> packages -> types/functions), and a diagnostic-emission API whose signature structurally requires code + what/why/fix, so I4 quality holds by construction. Runs only at the selected build entry (D-BUILDENTRY1) — never at module import time, so no hidden execution and no action at a distance. Rung C (mutation, message loop, user macros) is untouched and stays frozen on c154 (e7).
decisions.story: Walter runs the platform team at a 40-team company on one Jet monorepo. Org rules — 'no panic reachable from a net handler', 'every Entity type has archive()' for GDPR export — live on a wiki and die in code review. He wants the build itself to enforce them with compiler-grade errors no team can miss, without granting anyone the power to rewrite code invisibly.
decisions.detail: Why this is the safe rung: reading the checked program cannot change what any file means — local reasoning survives, the LSP model survives, and generated diagnostics are the only output. The enterprise value is policy-as-code with the compiler's own error quality, in the language the team already writes. The adversarial cost to weigh: a build entry that fails builds on custom rules is a new way for a dependency to be annoying — mitigated because only the ROOT's build entry runs rules (dependencies' rules do not run for you) and D-BUILDPOLICY1 authority applies.

options.name: Stay at D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection + derives only)
options.detail: Status quo. Org rules remain external linters with their own parsers that drift from the language; the wiki stays the enforcement mechanism.
options.code:
// jet has no answer; Walter writes a tree-sitter script that re-parses Jet
// and breaks on every syntax release

options.name: Read-only program snapshot + structured diagnostics from the build entry
options.detail: The Roslyn-analyzer shape: typed read-only API, structured diagnostics, zero mutation. Scoped to the root build entry; dependency build code gets no rule execution in your build.

options.name: Full message loop / mutation (Jai rung)
