decisions.title: Canonical JSON semantics
decisions.gist: Choose the exact JSON bytes produced for hashing and signing.
decisions.explainer:
Live `json.canonical(Data) -> String` is a shipped prototype: it sorts Rust strings, formats Float with Rust debug syntax, renders Bytes as a JSON number array, and cannot fail. Those bytes are deterministic only accidentally and are not RFC 8785. Ratified D-ENCSTREAM1=A requires whole-value and stream modes to share one codec; queued D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1 additionally requires canonical and ordinary JSON writers to share rejection/lifecycle law. This ballot chooses the one canonical JSON meaning used by both. `json.to_string` and `json.to_string_pretty` remain ordinary JSON renderers and are not hashing contracts.

Common law for every replacement option: canonicalization is recursive, emits UTF-8 without BOM or trailing LF, emits no insignificant whitespace, preserves array order, rejects duplicate object keys, never normalizes Unicode, never coerces Bytes/numbers/Text, and never emits NaN or infinity. A failure is `encoding.EncodingError` with format JSON, cause None, byte_offset 0, line/column None, the exact Data path, and the option's kind/reason. `json.canonical` therefore becomes `canonical(data: encoding.Data, limits: encoding.EncodingLimits = encoding.EncodingLimits.safe()) -> String ? encoding.EncodingError`. Whole-value canonicalization validates EncodingLimits in queued field order before traversal. buffer_bytes and expansion fields are retained for one shared type but unused; max_depth bounds Data container nesting with root container depth 1; max_total_bytes, when Val(n), bounds final UTF-8 output bytes; max_item_bytes bounds aggregate live canonical-object workspace. It renders arrays directly into one final output allocation and buffers object members for sorting. Excluding caller-owned Data and the returned String after transfer, codec-owned live heap is at most current_output_bytes + max_item_bytes + (256 * max_depth) + 65536 bytes; a prospective output/workspace crossing returns Limit before retaining the crossing bytes. Under D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1=A, `json.writer(..., canonical:true)` uses the identical primitive serializer, key comparator, domain checks, errors, and output bytes. For both entrypoints, aggregate live canonical-object workspace is the sum of encoded keys, UTF-16 comparison keys, separators, and not-yet-emitted canonical child bytes across every simultaneously open nested object; that aggregate, not each object independently, must remain <= max_item_bytes. The stream writer buffers through ObjectEnd, rejects a duplicate key or invalid value before accepting/emitting that buffered object, and otherwise obeys queued finish/terminal/allocator law. Whole-value and stream output for the same event tree are byte-identical.

Option A exact RFC 8785/JCS law: input must be I-JSON. Bool/Null spell normally. Text is preserved scalar-for-scalar; U+0008/U+0009/U+000A/U+000C/U+000D use `\b/\t/\n/\f/\r`, other U+0000..U+001F use lowercase `\u00xx`, quote and reverse-solidus escape, every other scalar emits unchanged, and slash never escapes. Invalid Unicode rejects, though ordinary Jet String cannot construct a lone surrogate. Object keys sort recursively by unsigned UTF-16 code units of the raw unescaped key; prefix-shorter sorts first.

JCS numbers use the RFC 8785 frozen ECMAScript `Number::toString`/ECMA-262 7.1.12.1 Note-2 shortest-round-tripping binary64 algorithm, verified against RFC 8785 Appendix B. Float -0.0 emits `0`; finite Float uses that algorithm; NaN and either infinity reject Unsupported with reason `JCS cannot encode a non-finite Float`. Data Int is admitted exactly when IEEE-754 roundTiesToEven conversion to binary64 represents the same mathematical integer; 9007199254740992 is admitted, while 9007199254740993 is not. An admitted Int is serialized by the same ECMAScript algorithm. A non-representable Int rejects Unsupported with reason `JCS requires Int exactly representable as IEEE 754 binary64; encode this integer as Text`. Bytes rejects Unsupported with the already-queued reason `JSON cannot encode Bytes; encode bytes as Text explicitly`. Duplicate keys reject Syntax with reason `JCS requires unique object keys`. No locale, host formatter, Unicode normalization, decimal pre-rounding, or external crate participates.

Compatibility and migration: choosing A/B/C is a breaking correction to the return type and, for some existing values, bytes. Per ratified release policy, it first ships in Jet 2.0.0 behind new edition `"2027"`; Jet 1.x and edition `"2026"` retain the exact old infallible signature and prototype bytes. Before changing `edition: "2026"` to `edition: "2027"`, the owner runs existing `jet fix`; its D-JSONCANON1 migration rewrites each `json.canonical(x)` to `json.canonical(x)?` when the enclosing function is fallible, otherwise to `json.canonical(x) ?? panic("value is not canonical JSON")`, inserts an explicit limits argument only when prior code already carried a project encoding limit, and reports every hashing/signing fixture for review. Then the owner explicitly bumps pkg.jet to `edition: "2027"`. Single-file programs use the toolchain's newest stable edition, so Jet 2.0.0 applies the new fallible law immediately; such code can be placed temporarily in a package and fixed before upgrade. Within edition 2027 there is one engine: no legacy alias, overload, flag, or hidden branch. Edition 2026 compatibility is the release-policy boundary, not a second 2027 mechanism; its implementation is frozen and receives no new canonical features. L2001/E2002 behavior follows the already-ratified deprecation registry and existing copy/snapshots; no new diagnostic code is invented here. Canonical byte fixtures must be re-pinned explicitly. D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1 must be ratified/reconciled before the public stream half ships.

Beginner pass: ordinary JSON Data within the familiar interoperable number range needs one `json.canonical(data)?` call. Expert pass: exact input domain, UTF-16 ordering, number algorithm, errors, buffering bound, byte output, and edition transition are auditable. Hybrid pass: beginner whole-value and expert stream entrypoints invoke the same semantic writer; there is no separate signing serializer.

Acceptance: vendor RFC 8785 sample/key-order/Appendix-B vectors with source+license+hash manifest; test every Float Appendix-B bit pattern, -0, exponent cutovers, exactly representable and adjacent non-representable Int values, controls, slash, BMP/astral key ordering, duplicate keys, Bytes/nonfinite, nested objects, every stream chunk boundary, aggregate nested-object max_item_bytes boundary, whole max_total/output/workspace boundary, whole/stream/AOT/comptime byte parity, terminal error stability, and migration rewrites. Compiler/runtime code remains std-only; no external dependency is approved here. Exact new compiler diagnostic codes/copy, if any, remain I4-gated; runtime EncodingError text above is decided here.
decisions.story: Leila signs a deployment policy in Jet and verifies it in a browser and a Java service. The same Data value must produce the same UTF-8 bytes everywhere, including awkward floats and non-ASCII keys; unsupported values must fail loudly instead of changing type or producing plausible but incompatible signatures.

options.name: Strict RFC 8785 JCS
options.detail: Use the interoperable JSON Canonicalization Scheme exactly. Safe-range Int and finite Float share the specified ECMAScript binary64 serializer; unsupported Jet-only values fail rather than changing meaning. Recommended: hashing/signing bytes match browsers, Java, and other JCS implementations while one explicit fallible boundary protects Jet's richer Data.

options.name: Jet A-canonical JSON subset
options.detail: Use Jet's A-canonical rules: arbitrary Int shortest decimal, no Float at all, keys sorted by unsigned UTF-8 bytes, direct Unicode scalars, lowercase control escapes, and the same Bytes/duplicate rejection. This preserves every integer and gives simple audit bytes, but output is not JCS and cross-language verifiers must implement Jet's scheme.

options.name: Extended JCS with exact Jet Int
options.detail: Use JCS string escaping, UTF-16 key ordering, and Float serialization, but emit every Data.Int as its exact shortest decimal even outside binary64's safe range. Jet integers stay lossless and ordinary cases match JCS, yet one large integer silently moves the document outside RFC 8785 and can produce a different signature in an otherwise JCS-compatible verifier.

options.name: Keep best-effort prototype
options.detail: Keep infallible String output, Rust Float formatting, scalar-order keys, and Bytes-as-array coercion; document it as stable display text rather than cryptographic canonical JSON. Existing calls stay unchanged, but #296's hashing/signing requirement remains unmet and the name `canonical` continues to promise more than the bytes guarantee.

comparisons.note: Defines I-JSON input, ECMAScript binary64 number bytes, UTF-16 key ordering, exact escaping, recursive sorting, and UTF-8 output for hashing/signing interoperability.
JSON.stringify supplies JCS primitive spelling, including -0 to 0 and shortest binary64 numbers; JCS adds recursive UTF-16 property sorting and I-JSON validation.
Compact output is deterministic for many values but is not itself a JCS contract; interoperable signatures need an explicit canonicalization profile.
comparisons.code: json.Marshal(v) // ordinary JSON, not an RFC 8785 API

comparisons.note: Ratified D-ENCBIN1 gives binary Data a separate RFC 8949 deterministic path. JSON canonicalization should likewise name one exact standard rather than borrow CBOR's richer numeric domain.

decisions.title: Exact public CBOR verbs and deterministic encoding
decisions.gist: Choose the one public CBOR API for ordinary values, typed values, and stable bytes.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-ENCBIN1=A selects CBOR (RFC 8949), native binary strings, the worked `to_bytes`/`decode<T>`/`to_bytes_canonical` spelling, and deterministic bytes for hashing. Ratified D-ENCSTREAM1=A requires the same core.encoding.cbor adapter identity for whole and stream modes. Ratified D-ENC-DYN1 keeps Data closed to Object, Array, Int, Float, Text, Bool, and Null; there is no public Data.Bytes variant. This ballot fixes the exact whole-value surface without reopening those decisions.

Option A exact namespace and verbs. Only core.encoding.cbor exports CBOROptions, CBORError, CBORErrorKind, parse, decode, to_bytes, and to_bytes_canonical; shared Data remains core.encoding.Data. `parse(bytes:[U8], options:cbor.CBOROptions=cbor.CBOROptions.safe())->encoding.Data ? cbor.CBORError` decodes one complete item to Data. `decode<T:Codable>(bytes:[U8], options:cbor.CBOROptions=cbor.CBOROptions.safe())->T ? cbor.CBORError` decodes through the same checked CBOR event/value engine directly into T. `to_bytes<T:Codable>(value:T)->[U8] ? cbor.CBORError` emits preferred interoperable CBOR. `to_bytes_canonical<T:Codable>(value:T)->[U8] ? cbor.CBORError` selects RFC 8949 Section 4.2.1 Core Deterministic Encoding in that same encoder. No public canonical-mode enum/flag exists; one hash/signature spelling has one byte law (I8). Data satisfies Codable, so both byte verbs accept Data without a second overload or encoder. There is no CBOR `to_string`: binary `parse`/`to_bytes` are the exact analogues of text `parse`/`to_string`.

Codable and Data law. Codable [U8] encodes as CBOR major type 2 and decode<[U8]> accepts major type 2; it never degrades to an integer array. Other Codable lists use major type 4, structs/maps use major type 5 with text keys, strings use major type 3, and scalar mappings follow their Jet types. parse into Data rejects a major-type-2 byte string as Unsupported because D-ENC-DYN1 has no lossless public Data case; callers that expect bytes use decode<[U8]> or a Codable field. parse also rejects tags, bignums outside Int, non-text map keys, duplicate text keys, undefined/unsupported simple values, and values outside Data, never coercing. decode<T> may accept only CBOR shapes that T's single Codable schema admits. Thus native binary strings and one closed Data algebra both remain honest.

CBOROptions is exactly {max_depth:Int,max_items:Int,max_bytes:Int,require_canonical:Bool}. safe() is {max_depth:256,max_items:1000000,max_bytes:1073741824,require_canonical:false}. Legal inclusive ranges are max_depth 1..4096, max_items 1..1000000000, max_bytes 0..1073741824. Validation follows field order before reading input. require_canonical false accepts every otherwise-supported RFC 8949 encoding, including valid Section 4.2.3 length-first map order as ordinary noncanonical input; true requires the one Section 4.2.1 Core deterministic form.

Counter law: a root scalar has depth 0; a root array/map/indefinite string has depth 1; entering each nested array/map/indefinite string adds one. max_items counts each encoded data item exactly once: each scalar, array/map container, map key under the same scalar/container rule, map value under that rule, and each definite chunk inside an indefinite text/byte string; a map key has no additional key surcharge and break bytes add zero. A tag counts before rejection. max_bytes first bounds input length, then independently bounds peak live requested allocation. Requested allocation is counted by actual requested capacities before allocator calls: byte/text payload capacity in bytes, array capacity times size_of(Data), map capacity times size_of((String,Data)) plus key capacities, decode stack capacity times frame size, and error/path String capacities. Reallocation prospectively replaces old capacity charge with new; freeing subtracts it. Input slice storage and allocator metadata are excluded. Every counter and capacity product uses arbitrary-precision arithmetic; crossing returns Limit before allocation/retention, so overflow cannot wrap. Tests pin both logical accounting and a counting-allocator ceiling of max_bytes plus allocator metadata for the exact allocation sequence.

CBORError is exactly {kind:cbor.CBORErrorKind,byte_offset:Int,path:String,reason:String}. CBORErrorKind is the closed enum Syntax, Truncated, Unsupported, Limit, TypeMismatch, TrailingData, NonCanonical. byte_offset is the zero-based input byte that begins the failing item, or input length for missing required bytes; encoder/type errors use 0. path grammar is unambiguous: root is `$`; an array index appends `[<unsigned-decimal>]` with no leading zero except 0; a text map key appends `[<JSON-string>]`, where JSON-string includes quotes and uses JSON escapes with lowercase `\u00xx`; examples are `$[0]`, `$["payload"]`, `$["a.b"]`, and `$["x\"y"]`. No bare `.key` form exists. Before a key decodes, the map path is its container prefix; otherwise path is the deepest known prefix. reason names the rejected major/additional value, target Codable expectation, limit, or canonical rule. parse/decode reject trailing bytes with TrailingData. No partial Data/T escapes; runtime failures are Core values, not compiler diagnostics. Wrong static argument/target types reuse existing Core type diagnostics; any new compiler diagnostic still requires diagnostics.md and tests/ui under I4.

Default to_bytes is deterministic for one Jet value within one toolchain but promises only valid preferred CBOR interoperability, not cross-version hash identity: structs follow Codable field order and Data.Objects preserve their semantic order. It emits definite lengths, shortest integer/length arguments, UTF-8 text, direct byte strings, and preferred Float representation, and never emits tags or indefinite containers. to_bytes_canonical is the one hash/signature mechanism. It uses definite lengths, shortest integer/length arguments, preferred shortest Float width preserving the Jet Float value, canonical NaN 0xf97e00, preserved signed zero, and duplicate encoded-key rejection. RFC 8949 Section 4.2.1 Core ordering sorts map keys by pure unsigned bytewise lexicographic order of each complete deterministic encoded key; no length pre-pass exists. Section 4.2.3 length-first bytes remain valid ordinary input but are never emitted or advertised as Jet canonical bytes. Same semantic Codable value and canonical version yields byte-identical output in AOT, JIT, comptime, and every target. Changing Core bytes is breaking and requires a major+edition migration decision.

Decoder canonical law. require_canonical checks original bytes, not a re-encoded approximation: true validates pure encoded-byte lexicographic Core ordering and rejects length-first-only ordering, indefinite lengths, non-shortest arguments, non-preferred floats/NaNs, duplicate keys, and every other Core-profile violation with NonCanonical at the first offending item. Normal parse/decode accept noncanonical but valid supported encodings and return the same semantic value. Neither mode accepts a semantic value outside the Data/Codable laws above.

Compatibility and migration. Live drift currently exports `encode(Data)->[U8]` and `decode([U8])->Data ? String`; tests/examples use those names, but ratified D-ENCBIN1 specifies `to_bytes`/typed `decode`/`to_bytes_canonical`. The breaking correction first ships in Jet 2.0.0 behind edition `"2027"`. Edition `"2026"` retains the exact live encode/Data-decode signatures, bytes, and String errors unchanged on every supporting Jet 2.x/3.x toolchain. Edition 2027 is the one exact migration window: throughout Jet 2.x it exposes deprecated `encode` and Data-return `decode` forwarding entrypoints, with L2001 naming `to_bytes` and `parse`. Jet 3.0.0 introduces edition `"2028"`; in edition 2028 those two forwarding entries are removed and E2002 names the replacement. Supporting edition 2026 remains unaffected by their 2028 removal. No later edition restores them.

`jet fix` plus explicit edition upgrade are the sole migration authority. Before upgrading 2026 to 2027, `jet fix` rewrites `cbor.encode(x)` to `cbor.to_bytes(x)` and Data-result `cbor.decode(bytes)` to `cbor.parse(bytes)`; an explicitly typed `decode<T>` remains decode. It also migrates String-error handling to CBORError handling and lists every changed golden/wire fixture. L2001/E2002 use their ratified diagnostics.md copy and snapshots; any CBOR-specific new diagnostic still requires I4 docs/tests before emission. There is no permanent alias, return-type-only overload, or second canonical encoder in editions 2027/2028.

Stream dependency. If D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1 ratifies codec-native pull handles, CBORReader/Writer use the same DataEvent/Codable engine, CBORError semantic kinds projected field-by-field to the queued shared EncodingError, and the same deterministic writer mode. If another stream option wins, its handle/callback/event spelling is reconciled before shipping. This ballot does not invent stream names or let stream mode bypass the Data, limits, error, or canonical laws.

Beginner pass: `to_bytes(value)?` and typed `decode(bytes)?` are the complete ordinary story; no mode object or CBOR vocabulary is required. Expert pass: parse to Data, exact typed errors/offsets/paths, bounded decoding, canonical validation, native bytes, and RFC deterministic output are explicit. Hybrid pass: parse, decode, default bytes, canonical bytes, comptime, and future streams share one codec engine and one Codable mapping. No facade or proof-only path exists.

Exact queued stream error projection under D-ENCSTREAM-SURFACE1=A: CBORError Syntax maps to EncodingErrorKind.Syntax; Truncated to Truncated; Unsupported to Unsupported; Limit to Limit; TypeMismatch, TrailingData, and NonCanonical to Syntax. format is CBOR, byte_offset/path/reason copy exactly, line and column are None, and cause is None. Underlying FileReader/FileWriter IO bypasses CBORError and maps directly to EncodingErrorKind.IO with its handle-free EncodingCause. No CBORErrorKind maps to State; State is reserved for writer lifecycle/order misuse. Terminal clone/equality follows the shared stream law.
decisions.story: Marco records signed multiplayer replays. New teammates need to turn a Codable Tick into bytes and back without learning CBOR terms. His integrity pipeline also needs RFC-defined deterministic bytes, while an ingestion service must inspect untyped partner payloads with exact offsets and safely reject CBOR values Jet Data cannot represent.

options.name: Format-native parse, decode, and byte verbs
options.detail: Export parse for Data, decode<T> for Codable, to_bytes for ordinary interchange, and to_bytes_canonical for RFC-stable bytes under the exact common law. Recommended: it honors the ratified examples, mirrors text codecs by medium rather than inventing strings for binary data, and gives beginners one obvious pair while keeping expert determinism explicit.

options.name: One encode/decode pair with a mode
options.detail: Keep live encode/decode and add mode:.Data or .Typed plus canonical:true. Fewer top-level verbs, but decode behavior depends on expected type/mode and every beginner call sees a policy parameter; canonical hashing becomes a flag that wrappers can silently omit.

options.name: Explicit Encoder and Decoder values
options.detail: Expose configured CBOR Encoder/Decoder objects for both whole values and future streams. Configuration is reusable and expert-visible, but one-shot beginner work requires constructors, the object names overlap stream state, and canonical correctness depends on which configured object reaches the call.

options.name: Canonical bytes only
options.detail: Make every encoding RFC-deterministic and expose only to_bytes/decode/parse. One byte form is attractive, but ordinary interoperability and hash-contract stability become inseparable: any canonical-profile evolution breaks every network/cache caller, and the ratified explicit to_bytes_canonical spelling disappears.

comparisons.note: CBOR defines preferred serialization and deterministic encoding separately; A exposes that difference directly without a second codec.
comparisons.code:
Core §4.2.1: unsigned bytewise lexicographic order of each complete encoded key
§4.2.3 legacy profile: length-first, then bytewise

comparisons.note: Rust separates typed serde decode from dynamic Value. A keeps the same distinction through Jet Codable and Data, while preserving one adapter.
Python makes canonical encoding an explicit option. A gives the hash-grade operation a name, preventing an omitted flag at security boundaries.

decisions.title: Canonical RFC 4648 decoder policy
decisions.gist: Choose which base64, base64url, and base32 text Jet accepts, and how existing programs migrate.
decisions.explainer:
Current implementation has no settled decoder law. AOT standard base64 removes every ASCII whitespace byte and requires filtered length divisible by four; comptime removes any trailing '=' and accepts unpadded lengths except remainder one. base64url trims outer whitespace, accepts padded or unpadded text, then delegates to those different decoders. Base32 in both paths ignores ASCII whitespace and every '=' byte anywhere, accepts lowercase, and never checks legal length, padding position/count, or unused bits. Encoders are already deterministic: standard base64 emits RFC 4648 padding, base64url emits no padding, and base32 emits uppercase RFC 4648 padding. This ballot settles public behavior; it adds no language syntax.

Common strict law for A, B, and C's `decode_canonical` / `decode_url_canonical` functions. `base64.encode` remains padded standard alphabet; strict `base64.decode` accepts exactly that canonical spelling. `base64.encode_url` remains unpadded URL alphabet; strict `base64.decode_url` accepts exactly that canonical spelling, including empty input, and rejects every '='. `base32.encode` remains uppercase and padded to eight characters; strict `base32.decode` accepts exactly that canonical spelling. All strict decoders reject ASCII whitespace, non-ASCII, the other alphabet, lowercase base32, missing/excess/interior padding, impossible encoded lengths, and non-zero unused bits. Thus `decode(encode(bytes))` succeeds and `encode(decode(text)?) == text` for every accepted strict input. Encoders never wrap lines and never gain policy flags.

Exact strict matrix: standard base64 accepts `Zg==`, `Zm8=`, `Zm9v`, and empty text; rejects `Zg`, `Zg===`, `Z=g=`, `Zg==\n`, URL `-`/`_`, and `Zh==`. Base64url accepts `Zg`, `Zm8`, `Zm9v`, and empty text; rejects `Zg=`, `Zg==`, whitespace, standard `+`/`/`, a length congruent to one modulo four, and `Zh`. Base32 accepts `MY======`, `MZXQ====`, `MZXW6===`, `MZXW6YQ=`, `MZXW6YTB`, and empty text; rejects `MY`, `my======`, `MY=======`, `M=Y=====`, `MY======\n`, `0`/`1` aliases, and `MZ======`. Strict padding counts follow RFC 4648 final quanta: base64 only zero, one, or two trailing '=' as required; base32 only zero, one, three, four, or six as required.

Exact strict error contract for A, B, and C's canonical functions; exact allowance API for A. `core.encoding.base64` declares `pub fn encode(bytes: [U8]) -> String`, `pub fn decode(text: String, allow_whitespace: Bool = false, allow_missing_padding: Bool = false) -> [U8] ? String`, `pub fn encode_url(bytes: [U8]) -> String`, and `pub fn decode_url(text: String, allow_whitespace: Bool = false, allow_padding: Bool = false) -> [U8] ? String`. `core.encoding.base32` declares `pub fn encode(bytes: [U8]) -> String` and `pub fn decode(text: String, allow_whitespace: Bool = false, allow_missing_padding: Bool = false, allow_lowercase: Bool = false) -> [U8] ? String`. First failure returns `invalid <base64|base64url|base32> at byte <N>: <reason>`. N is zero-based byte offset in original UTF-8 input; EOF failures use original input byte length. Hex digits are uppercase. Reasons are exactly `ASCII whitespace is not allowed`, `byte 0xNN is not in the <standard base64|URL-safe base64|base32> alphabet`, `padding is not allowed`, `padding may appear only at the end`, `expected <N> padding characters`, `unexpected padding`, `encoded length cannot represent whole bytes`, or `non-zero unused bits`. Examples: `base64.decode("Zg")` -> `invalid base64 at byte 2: expected 2 padding characters`; `base64.decode("Zg==\n")` -> `invalid base64 at byte 4: ASCII whitespace is not allowed`; `base64.decode("Zh==")` -> `invalid base64 at byte 1: non-zero unused bits`; `base64.decode_url("Zg==")` -> `invalid base64url at byte 2: padding is not allowed`; `base32.decode("my======")` -> `invalid base32 at byte 0: byte 0x6D is not in the base32 alphabet`; `base32.decode("MZ======")` -> `invalid base32 at byte 1: non-zero unused bits`.

Allowance automaton for A. `allow_whitespace` recognizes only ASCII bytes 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0D, and 0x20, at any position including before, between, or after padding; it removes them while retaining an origin-offset map. Other Unicode whitespace remains a forbidden UTF-8 byte. `allow_lowercase` maps base32 a..z to A..Z after whitespace removal and accepts mixed case; it never maps 0/1 aliases. `allow_missing_padding` for standard base64 accepts either exact RFC padding or no '=' with cleaned data length modulo four 0, 2, or 3; modulo one fails at original EOF, partial/interior/excess padding still fails, and unused bits remain zero. Base32 `allow_missing_padding` analogously accepts exact RFC padding or no '=' with cleaned data length modulo eight 0, 2, 4, 5, or 7; remainders 1, 3, or 6 fail at EOF. Base64url is canonically unpadded; `allow_padding` additionally accepts exactly the RFC-required zero, one, or two trailing '=' for its data length, never partial/interior/excess padding. Combined options execute in this fixed order: scan original bytes left-to-right classifying selected-alphabet bytes, recognized '=' padding tokens, and allowed whitespace; return the first disallowed whitespace or byte that is neither in the selected alphabet nor '='; remove allowed whitespace while preserving origins; fold allowed base32 lowercase; validate every recognized '=' in the alphabet-specific padding phase and report the first offending original '=' offset; validate cleaned length/padding count at original EOF; validate unused bits at the original final data-symbol offset; decode. '=' is never reported as a non-alphabet byte: padding phase exclusively owns padding-not-allowed, interior, partial, and excess-padding errors. Thus options relax only named forms and never change error precedence or offsets. A shared std-only parser and table-driven RFC 4648 vectors must produce identical bytes/errors in AOT, `comptime`, `jet eval`, REPL, and `jet dev`; parity tests compare every option combination and malformed corpus case byte-for-byte.

Compatibility law. Any stricter omitted-argument default is a breaking behavior change: it ships only with a major release plus edition 2027. Edition 2026 first receives one shared compatibility parser across AOT, `comptime`, `jet eval`, REPL, and `jet dev`; it accepts the union of every input successfully decoded by either historical AOT or historical comptime implementation and returns the same bytes everywhere, never preserving backend drift. For standard base64 that union includes AOT's ASCII-whitespace-filtered padded path and comptime's no-whitespace trailing-padding-stripped/unpadded path, including their accepted non-zero unused bits and legacy padding placements. Base64url applies the historical outer trim/alphabet substitution/autopadding before that union. Base32 preserves its historical ASCII-whitespace removal, removal of every '=' position, and case-insensitive alphabet. Exhaustive short-input and corpus tests prove union membership and byte parity; any input for which historical successful paths produced different bytes becomes an implementation-blocking compatibility case, not an arbitrary winner. For rejected edition-2026 input, every execution mode in one toolchain returns Err with byte-identical String bytes; wording is explicitly not a release-stable API and may change in a patch, so programs must branch on Err and must not parse it. Golden parity tests pin each toolchain build, while edition-2027 strict errors remain the exact stable offset/reason contract above. Edition 2027 projects and manifest-free single files use the selected new default. `jet fix --edition 2027` is the only automatic source migration. Under A it rewrites calls to explicit allowances for whitespace, omitted standard/base32 padding, padded base64url, and lowercase base32. It emits an irreconcilable-data audit for each call whose runtime input may rely on interior/excess padding, stripped arbitrary base32 '=', non-zero unused bits, or another 2026-union quirk because no A allowance admits those ambiguous forms and source rewriting cannot prove data cleanliness. User must clean data or remain on edition 2026. No API item is removed or renamed, so L2001/E2002 deprecation does not apply and the deprecation registry stays unchanged. Old-edition accepted input never silently stops decoding.

Beginner pass: encoder output always decodes; default rejects ambiguous/corrupt text at the exact byte. Expert pass: A offers named, narrow interoperability controls without accepting unrelated damage; whole-program and comptime paths share identical policy. Hybrid pass: A keeps one decoder per alphabet, with strict defaults and explicit allowances on the same mechanical path rather than a second permissive codec family.
decisions.story: Asha verifies signed webhook payloads. Two spellings decode to the same bytes today: one contains whitespace, another changes unused pad bits. Her signature cache keys the original text while the verifier checks decoded bytes, so permissive decoding creates ambiguous identities. She needs safe canonical defaults, but her mail importer must still read MIME-wrapped base64 when she explicitly asks for that transport behavior.

options.name: Strict default with narrow named allowances
options.detail: Recommended. Edition 2027 uses common strict law. Same decoder accepts only specifically requested transport deviations through full signatures defined above: whitespace, omitted standard/base32 padding, padded base64url, and lowercase base32. Every argument defaults false. Options combine under the fixed allowance automaton; none permits wrong alphabets, partial/interior/excess padding, impossible lengths, 0/1 base32 aliases, or non-zero unused bits. `jet fix` enables relevant allowances, then reports irreconcilable 2026-union data cases. One parser and error contract serve beginner and expert use.

options.name: Strict-only new edition
options.detail: Edition 2027 uses common strict law and adds no allowance arguments. Signatures are base64/base32 `encode(bytes: [U8]) -> String`, `decode(text: String) -> [U8] ? String`, plus base64 `encode_url(bytes: [U8]) -> String` and `decode_url(text: String) -> [U8] ? String`. Cleanest identity rule: every accepted string is encoder-canonical. Edition 2026 retains shared compatibility-union behavior, but projects consuming MIME wrapping, padded base64url, lowercase base32, or omitted padding must normalize data themselves before upgrading. `jet fix` cannot safely invent that normalization, so it produces an audit list for every decode call.

options.name: Compatible default plus explicit canonical decoder
options.detail: Keep shared compatibility-union `decode(text: String) -> [U8] ? String` behavior in every edition and add `decode_canonical(text: String) -> [U8] ? String` to base64/base32 plus `decode_url_canonical(text: String) -> [U8] ? String` to base64. Canonical `encode(bytes: [U8]) -> String` / `encode_url(bytes: [U8]) -> String` remain unchanged; security-sensitive callers opt in. This avoids an edition behavior break, but unsafe ambiguity remains beginner default and each alphabet gains two ways to perform one decode job.

comparisons.note: Requires padding unless a referring specification says otherwise, requires rejection of non-alphabet bytes unless explicitly relaxed, defines uppercase base32, and requires encoder pad bits to be zero. It permits decoders to reject non-zero pad bits; Jet A/B do so to guarantee one textual identity per byte sequence.
comparisons.code:
base64: Zg==
base64url: Zg
base32: MY======

comparisons.note: Separates standard and URL alphabets and exposes strict decoding as explicit configuration. Jet A keeps alphabet-specific entrypoints already shipped, but makes canonical validation default and exposes deviations as readable named arguments.
Common default discards non-alphabet characters unless validation is requested. C resembles that compatibility posture; A reverses it so beginners cannot accidentally accept covert-channel bytes.

decisions.title: Canonical full-stack Jet application model
decisions.gist: Choose how Jet composes its already-ratified HTTP, router, reactive UI, event, style, accessibility, and web-target mechanisms into one full-stack application.
decisions.explainer:
This decision does not reopen Router, JetDom, signals, typed views, styles, accessibility, or the JS/WASM backend. It chooses where application-wide client/server/render/data metadata lives. Every option keeps executable bodies in TIR, generated source re-enters the front end, and single-file rootless applications remain complete.

Fable hybrid review: Option A never states when or how the builder is evaluated, so dynamic registration (routes added in a loop over runtime config) would silently break every whole-app guarantee it promises — the exact failure mode of Next.js static analysis; B forfeits the first-class graph that explain, adapters, and security proofs need; C forfeits static checking entirely and turns route conflicts into runtime failures. The hybrid pins the evaluation law, keeps the sema-owned graph, adds a sound declared escape for dynamic composition, and states the hydration-mismatch and effect-boundary law the ballot detail demands but no option delivers.
decisions.story: Maya starts with one file and later splits the same product into routes, server actions, streaming pages, client islands, and deployment adapters. She needs one inspectable model from the first prototype through production, without learning a second framework language.
decisions.detail: The application graph may contain typed route, data, action, asset, render-boundary, and adapter facts, but never a second executable IR. Sema owns graph validation; function bodies remain executable TIR for AOT, dev, and web. The chosen model must show nested routing, SSR streaming, hydration mismatch behavior, client/server effect boundaries, asset splitting, adapter selection, generated-plan inspection, security defaults, and exact Jet diagnostics.

options.name: Sema-owned typed application graph
options.detail: Ordinary Jet builders compose existing Core mechanisms. Sema records and validates one typed application graph, enabling whole-app route/effect/security checks, SSR and client splits, code splitting, and exact explanations. Executable code stays in TIR; any generated source re-enters parser and sema.

options.name: Compile-time Core application plan
options.detail: A Core library evaluates the same builders at compile time and emits ordinary checked Jet source. The compiler knows only the resulting declarations and TIR, not a first-class application graph. This preserves a smaller compiler surface but weakens cross-route and adapter analysis.

options.name: Runtime-only typed composition
options.detail: Router, data loaders, rendering, and actions are ordinary runtime values. The compiler type-checks each call but has no application topology. This is simple and dynamic, but forfeits whole-app effect checks, static route conflicts, optimal splitting, and build-time deployment proof.

options.name: Static-eval builder graph in sema with declared dynamic mounts (hybrid)
options.detail: Sema evaluates the `fn app()` builder chain as statically evaluable composition over TIR and records the one typed application graph (A); a route, action, or adapter constructed from a runtime value outside a declared mount is a compile diagnostic with fixes, never a silently unanalyzed edge. `.mount(prefix, handler)` declares a typed dynamic subtree whose prefix, effects, and security policy remain static facts, so conflict, splitting, and effect checks stay sound. Client/server boundaries reuse the ratified Browser-effect partition and #Target ceilings; a server-only effect reachable from an island is a whole-graph diagnostic naming the path. Hydration mismatch is law: dev shows an overlay diagnostic with both server and client spans; release keeps server HTML and emits one structured core.log event. The graph is exposed via `jet expand --facts web` and `jet explain --web-graph` with stable `--json`; bodies remain executable TIR and generated source re-enters the front end (B's re-entry law).

comparisons.note: React Compiler and Server Components provide build-wide knowledge; Next integrates routing, server functions, streaming, and splitting. Jet should gain those benefits without a separate JSX or framework language.
comparisons.code: export default async function Page({ params }) { ... }

comparisons.note: Svelte compiles fine-grained reactivity while SvelteKit unifies routes, loading, actions, SSR, and adapters. Jet already has the component primitives; this ballot chooses the application-level owner.

decisions.title: Full-stack application authoring: explicit graph and optional conventions
decisions.gist: Choose how single-file and multi-file web applications author the application model selected by D-WEBAPP1.
decisions.explainer:
R9 requires a complete rootless single-file path. Conventions may remove repetition in larger projects only when they expand visibly into the exact explicit builder model. A builder/convention collision is always a compile diagnostic; there is no precedence rule or hidden winner.

Fable hybrid review: Option A's 'a package may opt into' never says where the opt-in lives, so directory presence becomes the activator — the Next.js footgun where any stray file in routes/ silently ships as a live endpoint; C's regeneration codemod is proven drift in every framework that tried it; B pays full wiring ceremony forever. The hybrid moves the opt-in into the builder itself — visible in the one inspectable place, single-file law intact — makes expansion exhaustive with a diagnosed disposition for every file, and keeps A's both-spans conflict law.
decisions.story: Noah wants `jet dev shop.jet` to work immediately. Six months later, his team wants predictable route files and layouts, while reviewers still need one command that shows exactly what the conventions generated.
decisions.detail: All options use ordinary Jet source and the application model selected by D-WEBAPP1. Generated or convention-expanded source and graph facts are inspectable. Every option must support explicit route/data/action/effect boundaries, single-file operation, deterministic conflicts, rename-safe tooling, and stable build output.

options.name: Explicit builder plus optional visible conventions
options.detail: A single file uses the builder directly. A package may opt into route/layout/data/action file conventions; those expand into the same graph and are shown by explain/LSP. If an explicit entry and a convention claim the same semantic slot, Jet rejects both with a conflict diagnostic and fixes; neither silently wins.

options.name: Explicit builder only
options.detail: Every route, layout, loader, action, island, and adapter is registered in ordinary Jet code. This is maximally explicit and rootless but repeats wiring in large applications and gives the IDE less conventional navigation structure.

options.name: One-shot scaffold emits an explicit builder
options.detail: No live conventions exist. `jet new web shop --emit-builder` creates ordinary route modules plus one explicit app builder. Users edit generated Jet afterward; regeneration is a reviewed codemod, never a hidden build input.
options.code:
$ jet new web shop --emit-builder
created shop/app.jet
created shop/routes/home.jet
// app.jet contains the complete editable web.app() builder

options.name: Conventions opted into inside the builder, exhaustively diagnosed (hybrid)
options.detail: The explicit builder is always the canonical model and a single file is complete (B); conventions exist only when the builder itself declares them with `.routes(from: "routes")`, so no directory presence, manifest field, or scaffold state ever activates routing invisibly. Expansion is deterministic and exhaustive: every `.jet` file under the declared root either maps to exactly one graph entry, is explicitly non-routed by a leading underscore, or is a compile diagnostic — a stray file can never become a deployed endpoint. Builder/convention collisions reject both registrations with both spans (A); `jet expand --facts web` and the LSP show every expanded entry with its source file, making renames graph-checked. `jet new web` scaffolds the builder with the `.routes(from:)` line already written (C's nothing-hidden-at-birth), never a regeneration codemod.

comparisons.note: File routing is highly productive but can hide precedence and generated topology. Option A keeps the productivity while making the expansion and conflicts explicit.
Explicit registration is easy to audit and works in one file. Option A preserves that complete path rather than requiring framework layout.

decisions.title: Notebook client and Jupyter interoperability surface
decisions.gist: Choose the user-facing notebook clients over the already-ratified REPL session, addressable-turn, and effect-confirmed rerun semantics.
decisions.explainer:
Every option uses the same REPL engine, typed state, rollback, interrupt, DAP, and D-FE-REPL-RERUN1 dependency replay. No option permits stale Jupyter-only state. This decision depends on D-NOTEBOOK-DOC1 and D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1 for persistence and rich-output safety.

Fable hybrid review: A builds a third first-party UI stack when ratified law (D-FE-CANVAS1=E, D-STUDIO-CANVASBRIDGE1=C) already mandates shared renderer/trust/proof components — duplicated sanitizer and sandbox code is duplicated attack surface. B demotes stale-turn and effect-confirmation truth to 'may be less discoverable' protocol extensions, an enforcement hole in exactly the clients most people use; C amputates live Jupyter interop entirely. The hybrid keeps A's surface and token law, reuses the Canvas component stack, folds in C's view as a lens of the same session, and converts B's weakness into a stated enforcement floor (stdin_request confirmation, no stale display in any client).
decisions.story: Nia opens an analysis with one command, edits an upstream cell, sees exactly which downstream turns are stale, confirms effectful reruns, then sends the same document to a teammate who uses JupyterLab.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet notebook analysis.jetnb
serving http://127.0.0.1:43127/#token=...
session: typed; stale turns: none; environment: workspace lock 8c2f...
decisions.detail: Option A's exact surface is `jet notebook PATH`, which launches a loopback-only first-party browser client and one REPL session. A random bearer token is placed in the URL fragment, not logs. Non-loopback bind requires explicit `--bind` plus `--auth-file` authority. The Jupyter kernelspec command is `jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}` and uses the same session engine. All options define rich MIME, completion, inspect, stdin, interrupt rollback, debug, profile, package/workspace environment, side-effect receipts, disconnect/reconnect, and headless protocol tests.

options.name: First-party notebook client plus Jupyter adapter
options.detail: Jet owns an ergonomic, source-truthful client and also installs a Jupyter kernelspec. Both are projections of one session. The first-party client can surface typed values, stale dependency edges, effect receipts, diagnostics, debugger, profiler, and trusted output state without protocol compromise.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb
jet notebook install-jupyter
# kernelspec argv: jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}
jet notebook analysis.jetnb --bind 0.0.0.0 --auth-file ./token  # explicit remote authority

options.name: Jupyter clients only
options.detail: Jet ships the kernelspec and protocol server over the same REPL engine but no first-party notebook UI. JupyterLab and compatible clients own rendering; Jet-specific stale/effect/debug facts use protocol extensions and may be less discoverable.
options.code:
jet notebook install-jupyter
jupyter lab analysis.ipynb
# kernel still enforces typed addressable-turn replay and effect confirmation

options.name: Canvas notebook view only
options.detail: Canvas becomes the only first-party client over the same REPL engine; Jet may export/import Jupyter documents but does not install a live Jupyter kernel. This unifies Jet UI but weakens existing notebook ecosystem reach.
options.code:
jet canvas analysis.jetnb --view=notebook
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb

options.name: One shared first-party client plus enforcing Jupyter adapter (hybrid)
options.detail: `jet notebook PATH` keeps Option A's exact surface — loopback-only serve, bearer token in the URL fragment, non-loopback only via explicit `--bind` plus `--auth-file` — but the first-party client is assembled from the shared Canvas/Studio protocol components (rich renderer, D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1 sandbox, receipt and proof widgets) under D-STUDIO-CANVASBRIDGE1's strict boundary, so Jet ships one renderer and one trust engine, and `jet canvas PATH --view=notebook` opens the same live session as a lens, never a second truth. The kernelspec `jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}` is an enforcing projection, not best-effort: in foreign clients stale turns are recomputed per D-FE-REPL-RERUN1 before display, effectful replays confirm through `stdin_request`, and an output that would be stale renders as an explicit staleness notice, never a cached value. Headless protocol tests cover both projections; a Jupyter client can never observe session state the first-party client would refuse to show.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb                 # loopback + fragment token
jet canvas analysis.jetnb --view=notebook   # same session, Canvas lens
jet notebook install-jupyter
# foreign client: effect confirm via stdin_request; stale output never displays

comparisons.note: The kernel protocol and ecosystem are essential interoperability targets, but traditional notebooks allow hidden stale state. Jet's adapter must preserve addressable-turn truth.
Reactive dependency execution prevents stale cells. Jet can combine that truth with explicit side-effect confirmation and its typed REPL state.
comparisons.code: editing an upstream cell recomputes dependent cells

decisions.title: Canonical notebook document, output cache, merge, and ipynb round-trip
decisions.gist: Choose the source of truth for ordered Jet and Markdown cells and define exactly where outputs and foreign notebook facts live.
decisions.explainer:
Notebook code cells always contain ordinary Jet source; the container is data, not a second language. Stable cell identity drives dependency replay, merge, output cache, diagnostics, and Jupyter interop. Ambient packages or interpreter state are never embedded as invisible environment truth.

Fable hybrid review: A's per-cell `source+environment` cache key omits the upstream dependency closure, so editing cell 1 leaves cell 9's cached output presentable — directly contradicting its own 'no stale output displays' law and D-FE-REPL-RERUN1; its import 'generates stable IDs' non-deterministically, churning identity on every re-import, and says nothing about duplicated-cell ID collisions. B inherits ipynb's JSON merge pain and embedded-output staleness; C splits review truth across two files and cannot interleave Markdown freely. The hybrid keeps A's architecture and fixes all three holes with concrete key, ID, and round-trip law.
decisions.story: Leah reviews a notebook diff, reorders two cells without losing identity, resolves a branch conflict, opens it offline against the pinned workspace, and exports an ipynb whose losses are explicit rather than silent.
decisions.inWild:
format: 1
notebook_id: "sales-q3"
environment: { kind: "workspace", root: ".", lock: "sha256-8c2f..." }

cell: {
  id: "01J4Q7M6B8Y9P0K2D3F4G5H6J7"
  kind: "markdown"
  source: """
# Q3 sales
This report is source-reviewed.
"""
}

cell: {
  id: "01J4Q7P1M2N3R4S5T6V7W8X9Y0"
  kind: "jet"
  source: """
use core.data
use core.files
csv_text :: files.read("sales.csv") ?? panic("can't read sales.csv")
sales :: data.csv<Sale>(csv_text) ?? panic("bad csv")
sales.group_by(.region).sum(.revenue)
"""
}
decisions.detail: Option A defines `.jetnb` v1 as the bytes shown above: a versioned Jet-data envelope, not executable Jet. Strings use Jet triple-string escaping; a literal triple delimiter is written `\"\"\"` and backslash is escaped. New cells receive a 128-bit OS-CSPRNG ID stored in the file; reorder preserves it. A same-ID divergent edit is a merge conflict; `jet notebook merge` aligns by ID, emits both source spans, and refuses execution until resolved. The environment references a relative workspace/package root plus semantic lock digest; a standalone notebook receives an explicit notebook lock. Outputs never enter canonical source: `.jet/notebooks/<notebook-id>/<cell-id>/<source+environment-hash>.jnbout`, ignored by default. Cache miss says `not run for this source and environment`; no stale output displays. `jet notebook export PATH --ipynb [--with-outputs]` embeds only matching cache entries. Import preserves safe opaque metadata, quarantines outputs under D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1, maps Markdown/code cells, generates stable IDs, and writes an exact loss report for unsupported widgets, attachments, magics, metadata, or MIME. Re-export reports any fact that cannot round-trip.

options.name: Mergeable `.jetnb` source plus detachable output cache
options.detail: The readable container above is canonical. It stores ordered ordinary-Jet/Markdown source, stable IDs, and exact environment identity. Outputs are reproducible ignored cache; committed publication is an explicit export artifact. Cell-aware merge and ipynb import/export always report losses.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb
jet notebook merge base.jetnb ours.jetnb theirs.jetnb
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb --with-outputs
# output cache: .jet/notebooks/analysis/<cell>/<hash>.jnbout

options.name: `.ipynb` is canonical
options.detail: Standard Jupyter JSON stores source, IDs, metadata, and outputs. Jet adds environment and dependency metadata under a namespaced key. Interoperability is maximal, but diffs/merges and active-output trust inherit ipynb complexity; first-party tooling must still reject stale outputs.

options.name: Ordinary `.jet` source plus notebook layout sidecar
options.detail: A `.jet` module is canonical executable code. Top-level semantic items/expressions become code cells; doc comments become attached Markdown. A `.jetnb.layout` sidecar stores stable cell IDs, order, free-standing Markdown, environment identity, and output-cache links. This preserves ordinary source but splits review truth and cannot represent arbitrary interleaving in one file.

options.name: Mergeable `.jetnb` with closure-keyed cache and ID-faithful ipynb (hybrid)
options.detail: The canonical `.jetnb` v1 container, environment identity, CSPRNG cell IDs, and merge-by-ID law are Option A's, with the output-cache key hardened to source + environment + transitive dependency-closure hash: an upstream cell edit invalidates every downstream entry, so no stale output can ever display or export and the cache is exactly D-FE-REPL-RERUN1's replay truth materialized. Paste or duplicate always mints a fresh ID; ipynb import derives cell IDs deterministically from nbformat 4.5+ cell ids and export writes Jet IDs back, so round-trips preserve identity instead of churning it, with exact loss reports in both directions. `jet notebook merge` registers as an opt-in Git merge/textconv driver per D-MERGE-VCS1, and `jet notebook export --jet` projects cells to an ordinary reviewable `.jet` module as a stated-loss export (C's virtue), never a second truth.
options.code:
jet notebook merge base.jetnb ours.jetnb theirs.jetnb
# cache: .jet/notebooks/analysis/<cell>/<source+env+deps-hash>.jnbout
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb --with-outputs  # only closure-fresh entries embed
jet notebook import report.ipynb   # deterministic IDs from nbformat ids + loss report

comparisons.note: Universal support and rich outputs are valuable, but embedded outputs and JSON diffs invite stale state and merge pain. Option A treats ipynb as a loss-reported interchange format.
comparisons.code: nbformat 4 JSON with cells and outputs

comparisons.note: Text-first notebooks improve review and reactive identity. Jet adds an exact environment reference and separates reproducible output cache from source truth.
comparisons.code: text source paired with notebook metadata

decisions.title: Notebook rich-output trust and active-content authority
decisions.gist: Choose how HTML, SVG, Markdown, CSS, widgets, and JavaScript outputs render without turning an imported notebook into ambient code execution.
decisions.explainer:
Plain text is always available. Sanitized passive MIME is the default. Active content never inherits parent page, kernel, filesystem, storage, cookie, credential, or network authority. Trust is local authority, not source metadata, and cannot travel with a notebook.

Fable hybrid review: A's per-payload prompts are the right key with the wrong ergonomics: Jupyter's core lesson is trust fatigue, and A even blocks zero-capability widgets the user just executed locally — beginner-hostile for `display(widget)` — while its `jet notebook trust` forks a second grant surface against the ratified one-authority-graph law (D-JPK-GRANTCMD1=A, D-WD1=B). C institutionalizes fatigue into notebook-wide grants (Jupyter's `trust` mistake with better hashes); B amputates interactive notebooks. The hybrid makes empty-sandbox active content promptless, collapses remaining prompts by intent with a full-audit drawer, and homes grants in the ratified trust graph.
decisions.story: Chen opens a notebook from a pull request containing a plot, SVG, links, and a custom widget. The report should render safely; the widget should remain inert until Chen reviews and grants its exact capabilities.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet notebook report.jetnb
active output blocked: cell 01J... requests JavaScript and network
plain-text fallback shown
$ jet notebook trust report.jetnb --cell 01J... --allow-widget sales.chart --allow-origin https://data.example
decisions.detail: Recommended passive sanitization covers HTML, SVG, Markdown links, CSS, data/blob URLs, dimensions, recursion, decompression, and total output size. Active output runs only in an opaque-origin sandbox iframe with strict CSP; forms, navigation, workers, objects, parent access, kernel access, storage, cookies, credentials, and external URLs are blocked by default. The trust key is notebook source hash + active payload/renderer hash + locked environment identity + policy version. Trust state lives only in per-user local state and is never imported, exported, committed, or synced. Any source/payload/renderer/environment/policy edit or import revokes it. Expert widgets require an origin/capability allowlist and a typed message bridge; network defaults to none. When any renderer fails policy, Jet shows safe `text/plain`.

options.name: Sanitized passive output plus hash-bound capability trust
options.detail: Passive MIME renders after strict sanitization and size limits. Active widgets/JavaScript require a local grant bound to exact source, payload, renderer, environment, and policy hashes. They run in an opaque sandbox with only explicitly granted typed messages and origins. Changes revoke trust automatically.
options.code:
jet notebook trust report.jetnb --cell 01J... \
  --allow-widget sales.chart \
  --allow-message SelectionChanged \
  --allow-origin https://data.example
# no parent/kernel/storage/cookie authority; source or lock edit revokes

options.name: Passive rich output only
options.detail: HTML, SVG, Markdown, images, tables, and plots render through the sanitizer, but JavaScript, active widgets, forms, and network are never executed. This is simplest and safest but excludes interactive notebook applications.
options.code:
display(plot)       // sanitized SVG/PNG works
display(widget)     // blocked; text/plain fallback and export hint

options.name: Trust the whole local notebook environment
options.detail: A user may mark a notebook and locked environment trusted; all its active outputs run until source or lock changes. Sandboxing and CSP remain, but capability review is notebook-wide rather than payload-specific. This is more convenient and grants substantially broader authority.
options.code:
jet notebook trust report.jetnb --all-active
# local only; source/renderer/lock/policy change revokes the notebook-wide grant

options.name: Passive-equivalent sandbox default plus unified intent-card trust (hybrid)
options.detail: Passive sanitization, the opaque-origin empty-capability sandbox, hash-bound grant keys, local-only non-traveling trust, and revoke-on-any-change are Option A's, with one beginner fix: active content that requests no capability beyond the empty sandbox — first-party plots, tables, zero-capability widgets — renders without any prompt, because a sandbox with no messages, origins, storage, kernel, or parent reach is passive-equivalent by construction. Capability-requesting widgets keep the full key (source + payload + renderer + locked environment + policy version), but grants live in the unified `jet trust` authority graph (D-WD1, D-JPK-GRANTCMD1) and prompt as one per-notebook intent card with an expert drawer expanding exact per-cell hashes, origins, and typed messages (D-CANVAS-ACTIONAUTH1) — C's one-review convenience without notebook-wide authority. Imported ipynb outputs always quarantine; any source, payload, renderer, lock, or policy change revokes to safe `text/plain` fallback.
options.code:
display(sales.chart)   # zero-capability widget: sandboxed, renders, no prompt
jet trust notebook report.jetnb --cell 01J... \
  --allow-widget sales.chart --allow-origin https://data.example
# intent card: "sales.chart wants network: data.example" — drawer shows hashes/messages
# grants live locally in the jet trust graph; any edit or import revokes

comparisons.note: Notebook trust historically signs cells to permit active output. Jet tightens the key, isolates origin, strips ambient authority, and grants explicit capabilities.
Opaque-origin iframes plus CSP and typed postMessage-style bridges provide a strong containment base when default capabilities are empty.

decisions.title: Which values may ExpiringSecret own?
decisions.gist: Choose the value contract that makes expiry erase every secret without letting a copy escape.
decisions.lesson:
An expiring secret owns sensitive data until a deadline. After that deadline, access fails and the stored bytes must be erased. Erasing a generic value is not automatic. A string owns heap bytes, a signing key has its own drop law, and a user struct may contain several secret fields.

A callback loan prevents the wrapper from returning an owned copy by accident. It does not prevent callback code from explicitly copying an ordinary string. Jet therefore needs two guarantees: every admitted value knows how to erase itself, and the borrowed value cannot become an owned result or escaping capture.

The existing Secret and private-key types already reject display, comparison, serialization, and cloning. Ordinary String and [U8] do not. The choice is whether ExpiringSecret accepts only that closed safe family, opens a public zeroization contract for user types, or narrows to one Secret byte container.
decisions.story: Maya keeps a database signing credential for fifteen minutes. The expiry callback may sign a request, but it must not return or store another owned credential. When time expires or the wrapper drops, every byte must follow a defined erase path.
decisions.inWild:
use core.crypto as crypto
use core.vault as vault

clock := Clock.system()
ttl := Duration.minutes(15)?
key := crypto.Secret.from_bytes(load_key())
leased := vault.ExpiringSecret.new(key, ttl, clock)
signature := leased.with((borrowed) => sign_request(borrowed, request))?
// returning or copying `borrowed` is rejected; expiry erases the stored Secret

options.name: Closed secret-value family
options.detail: ExpiringSecret accepts Secret and the existing non-cloneable private-key types. Text or bytes must first enter Secret. Callback loans cannot be returned, copied, or captured. The public surface stays small and every admitted type has an audited erase path.
options.technical: Add one compiler-owned SecretValue classification for Secret, SigningKey, and X25519SecretKey. ExpiringSecret<T> requires that classification. Sema marks the callback parameter as a non-escaping loan and rejects clone, return, storage, and escaping capture. Drop and expiry dispatch to each type's existing zeroization law.
options.code:
raw := crypto.Secret.from_text(env.api_key)
secret := vault.ExpiringSecret.new(raw, ttl, clock)
secret.with((key) => call_service(key))?

// rejected
copy := secret.with((key) => $key)?
Error: an ExpiringSecret loan cannot escape its callback

options.name: Public Zeroize protocol
options.detail: Any type may opt in after proving how every field erases. ExpiringSecret stays broadly generic. Users gain typed application secrets, but Jet adds a permanent security protocol and must audit derived implementations across nested containers.
options.technical: Ratify a sealed-by-default Zeroize protocol plus an explicit derive for structs. ExpiringSecret<T: Zeroize> calls zeroize on expiry and Drop. The same non-escaping callback-loan checks from A remain mandatory. Unsafe custom implementations require an audited region.

options.name: Secret bytes only
options.detail: ExpiringSecret owns only Secret, with no type parameter. This is easiest to teach and erase, but typed signing and key-agreement secrets need conversion or a second lifecycle path.
options.technical: Amend D-TTLVAL1 so ExpiringSecret is monomorphic. Reuse Secret's existing non-clone and zeroizing Drop behavior. Keep the non-escaping callback-loan check. Do not add a Zeroize protocol or a second wrapper.
options.code:
key := crypto.Secret.from_bytes(load_key())
secret := vault.ExpiringSecret.new(key, ttl, clock)
secret.with((bytes) => sign_bytes(bytes, request))?

comparisons.note: SecretBox restricts exposure through a borrow and requires zeroizing ownership for protected values. Ordinary clone and formatting are intentionally unavailable.
comparisons.code: secret.expose_secret() // borrowed view; protected owner zeroizes on drop

comparisons.note: User structs can derive Zeroize, but every field must support the contract and compiler optimizations require audited volatile handling.

recommendation.why: A completes the ratified safety feature through types that already forbid copying and own audited erase paths. It keeps one vault lifecycle wrapper and avoids a broad protocol before real user-defined demand exists.

whyNot.reason: A public security protocol permanently widens the language contract and lets incorrect field coverage become a secret-retention bug. Current protected types already cover the shipped crypto and vault use cases.
It discards useful type identity for signing and key-agreement secrets, forcing conversions or a second lifecycle mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: Application-specific secret structs must use Secret fields separately until concrete demand justifies reopening the public protocol choice.

decisions.title: Sigil planes: # attributes, @ locations
decisions.outcome: Owner 2026-07-23: 'I want to go back to using exclusively # for markers/attributes/etc. We transitioned to @ but I want all of them to be transitioned to #. This should likely be highest priority so no additional rework is required for any parallel in flight tasks. Conceptually I want # to mark attributes, instructions, properties, etc. Then I want @ to mark locations, addresses, sources, etc.' Amends D-SHAPE2/D-MARKERMOVE1; restores the D-ATTR1 # plane. Loop labels (D-LOOPLABEL2), provider@target (U6), path@host (D-JPK-OSHOST1) stay @ as locations.

This should likely be highest priority so no additional rework is required for any parallel in flight tasks. Conceptually I want # to mark attributes, instructions, properties, etc. Then I want @ to mark locations, addresses, sources, etc.' Amends D-SHAPE2/D-MARKERMOVE1; restores the D-ATTR1 # plane. Loop labels (D-LOOPLABEL2), provider@target (U6), path@host (D-JPK-OSHOST1) stay @ as locations.

decisions.title: Interpolation debug spelling under the # plane
decisions.gist: How a debug-print request inside a string is spelled after the sigil flip.
decisions.lesson:
Jet strings can embed live values: writing {user} inside a string prints the user value using its normal, human-facing rendering. Sometimes a developer wants the raw, warts-and-all rendering instead, with every field visible. That developer view is called the Debug rendering.

Today the developer view is requested by adding a marker after the value name: {user@Debug}. The @ sign here is not part of the value; it is an instruction meaning 'render this the developer way'.

You just ratified a split of the two sigils: # marks attributes, instructions, and properties, while @ marks locations, addresses, and sources, such as github@owner/repo or a loop label. The interpolation marker sits on the boundary. It is an instruction about rendering, which points to #. But it lives inside string braces, a spot no other marker uses, so it could also keep its own spelling. This ballot picks its spelling so the flip leaves no stragglers.
decisions.story: Priya is debugging a failed import job. Her log line prints {record}, which shows the tidy summary, hiding the field that is actually wrong. She reaches for the developer rendering and needs to remember one thing: is it spelled with #, with @, or with a colon?

options.name: Flip to {value#Debug}
options.detail: The debug request is an instruction, so it moves to # with every other instruction. One rule to learn: instructions are always #, and @ never appears inside a string. Existing code using @Debug gets a teaching error naming the fix.

options.name: Keep {value@Debug} as-is
options.detail: Interpolation keeps its current spelling; only declaration-site markers flip. Nothing to migrate in strings. The cost: one instruction stays spelled with the location sigil, so the clean rule 'instructions are #' gains an exception beginners must memorize.
options.code:
log("parse failed: {record@Debug}")   // unchanged

#MustUse
fn parse(s: Str) -> Record { … }      // declarations still flip to #

options.name: Colon format spec: {value:Debug}
options.detail: Inside braces, a colon introduces a rendering request, matching what Python and Rust users already know. Reads naturally, and leaves room for later requests like width or precision. The cost: a third spelling convention exists only inside strings, alongside # and @ outside them.

comparisons.note: Uses a colon plus ? inside braces for the developer rendering.
Uses !r for raw rendering and a colon for format specs.

recommendation.why: The ratified concept says instructions are #. A debug-rendering request is an instruction applied to a value, so # keeps the whole surface to one rule with zero exceptions, in strings and out.

whyNot.reason: Keeps one instruction on the location sigil, so the rule you just ratified ships with a built-in exception.
Adds a third convention that exists only inside strings, when the marker plane already covers this with one spelling.

recommendation.tradeoff: Colon format specs, if ever wanted for width or precision, would need their own future decision instead of arriving free with option C. That is acceptable because no such feature is ratified or planned today.

decisions.title: Named-loop label spelling
decisions.gist: How a loop gets a name, and how break and next use that name.
decisions.lesson:
When loops nest, break normally exits only the innermost one. A loop label gives an outer loop a name so break or next can target it directly from deep inside. The label is purely a name; it changes nothing about how the loop runs.

Today the name is written with a trailing @: outer@ loop { ... }, and control statements repeat it as break outer@ or next outer@.

History matters here. The original design used a leading @ (@outer loop), but at that time @ also introduced attributes like @Unsafe, so a leading @outer looked like an attribute and was moved to the suffix. You have now ratified that attributes use # and @ marks locations. That frees the leading position, so every spelling is back on the table. A label is a place in the code that break jumps to, which is why it sits on the @ side of the split at all.

Two more facts shape the options. Jet already names things with ::, as in total :: nums.reduce(...), so a loop can be named the same way. And Jet separates picking from doing: .Track picks a choice with no parens, while nums.sort() does an action with parens. Break and next are actions, so if they are spelled with a dot they take parens. A loop name would exist only at compile time: it is not a value you can store or pass, and misusing it as one is a teaching error.
decisions.story: Marisol is scanning a grid for the first defective cell. She has a row loop with a column loop inside, and wants break to leave both at once. She writes a label on the outer loop and needs the spelling to feel obvious six months later.

options.name: Binding name + dot exits: outer :: loop, outer.break()
options.detail: The loop is named like any other binding, and exits are actions on that name, found by typing outer. in the editor. Parens always, because actions take parens. Plain break and next still work for the innermost loop. The costs: empty parens when no value is carried, and outer := loop must be rejected since a name cannot be reassigned to a loop.
options.technical: Sema binds the name with a compile-time label kind in the ordinary namespace; normal shadowing diagnostics apply. Label-in-value-position is a dedicated teaching error. break/next remain keywords for the innermost-loop case; named exits are only outer.break()/outer.next(). D-ORRETURN-CANON1 composes as expr ?? outer.break().

options.name: Binding name + keyword exits: outer :: loop, break outer
options.detail: Same naming, but exits stay keywords with the name after them. No parens anywhere and only one exit spelling. The cost: typing outer. in the editor teaches nothing, so you must already know the keyword shape.

options.name: Location name + dot exits: @outer loop, outer.break()
options.detail: The name is declared with the location sigil, reading as the place named outer, and exits are the same dot actions as option A. The cost: a second way to introduce a name when :: already does that, and one more sigil on screen.

options.name: Keep today: outer@ loop, break outer@
options.detail: No change and no migration. The trailing @ marks the name at both ends. The costs: the suffix position was chosen to dodge the old @-attribute plane, which no longer exists, and the editor cannot suggest anything from the name.

comparisons.note: Tick-prefix labels, referenced bare after break.
Colon label, bare reference.
comparisons.code:
outer:
for _, row := range grid { break outer }

comparisons.note: Colon label, bare reference.
comparisons.code: outer: for (const row of grid) { break outer }

recommendation.why: It reuses the one naming mechanism Jet already has, and exits become discoverable: typing outer. shows break and next in the editor. Parens follow the existing rule that actions take parens, with no exceptions to memorize.

whyNot.reason: Gives up editor discovery, the main gain of naming loops like values, and keeps a keyword shape you must already know.
Mints a second way to introduce a name when :: already names things.
Keeps a position chosen to dodge a collision that no longer exists, and teaches nothing in the editor.

recommendation.tradeoff: Named no-value exits carry empty parens, outer.break(). That is accepted deliberately: it keeps the picking-versus-doing parens rule exception-free.

decisions.title: Package and host ref shape: what@where
decisions.gist: The order and separators used when a ref names a package, its version, and where it comes from.
decisions.lesson:
A ref is a short string that tells jetpack what to fetch and from where. Refs appear in three spots. A pkg.jet manifest lists dependencies and can define named sources. A named source is an upstream, like a GitHub repo. The command line takes refs too, as in jetpack run fastfetch from the nixpkgs source. And jet os takes a host selector picking a machine config, today spelled path@host.

Today a source ref is provider-first: github@owner/repo, path@../local, nixpkgs@... . So the @ currently reads 'provider at target', with the place on the left.

Two pieces are already settled and stay fixed. Versions pin with #, as in textkit#1.2.0, because # marks a pinned number. And you ratified that @ marks locations and sources. The open question is only the shape. Which side of @ names the thing, and which side names the place? And the version could ride along in the same string, like an email address putting the name before the place.
decisions.story: Tom adds a teammate's library to his project. He knows three facts: the package is called textkit, he wants version 1.2.0, and it lives on GitHub. He wants to type those three facts in an order he can say out loud: textkit, 1.2.0, from GitHub.

options.name: Email order everywhere: name#version@source
options.detail: One atom reads like an address: the thing, its pinned number, then where it lives. The same shape works in deps, on the CLI, and for hosts, so you learn it once. Local paths stay bare, with no provider word. Caution: npm users read pkg@18 as a version; here @ is always a place and # is always the version.
options.technical: Grammar: name['#'version-or-channel]['@'source]. source = named source | provider ref. Provider refs in sources: are target'@'provider (acme/helpers@github). Bare ./ ../ / values are path refs, no provider word; the path provider name retires. D-JPK-OSHOST1 host selector becomes host['@'root]. VERSION-# and D-JPK-CHANNEL1 semantics unchanged.

options.name: Scheme first everywhere: source:name#version
options.detail: Every ref starts with where it comes from, like a URL scheme: github:acme/helpers, nixpkgs:fastfetch. The CLI already works this way today, so nothing changes there. The cost: it reads place-first rather than the way you say it, and the @ sigil disappears from refs even though sources are exactly what @ now stands for.

options.name: Keep provider@target as-is
options.detail: No change, no migration. Sources stay github@owner/repo and hosts stay path@host. The cost: the @ reads backwards under your new rule, because the place sits on the left and the thing on the right, and manifest refs and CLI refs keep two different shapes.

comparisons.note: Uses @ for the version, the opposite of Jet's #; a known confusion source worth owning deliberately.
Name first, place second — the mental model option A borrows.
Scheme-first refs, the model option B borrows.
Host-first module paths, closest to option C's place-on-the-left.

recommendation.why: It matches how the fact is spoken: textkit, pinned 1.2.0, from vendor. One shape serves manifests, the CLI, and host selectors, and it is the only option where @ consistently means 'at this source', the exact rule you just ratified.

whyNot.reason: Reads place-first instead of thing-first, and abandons @ in the one grammar that is literally about sources.
Keeps @ reading backwards, place on the left, and keeps two different ref shapes between manifest and CLI.

recommendation.tradeoff: npm veterans must relearn that @ is the place and # is the version, one deliberate difference. That is acceptable because # as the pin is already ratified and the split is taught once by teaching errors.

decisions.title: Which verbs may create a fresh value?
decisions.gist: New surface ships fresh values four ways: ExpiringSecret.new, expiring.new, SigningKey.generate, and time.clock. The ratified constructor law requires a ballot for any new construction shape. This closes the fresh-value verb set.
decisions.lesson: The ratified law gives .new to fresh stateful values as a type-owned call. Shipped code also mints values through lowercase module functions and a generate verb. An expert who learned one spelling cannot predict the next type's spelling. The surface already uses underscore compounds: add_new for storage, from_* for conversions. A new_ prefix family would group every constructor under one completion stem: type Type.new and the tools list every way to make one. One law interaction matters: rand and gen are not on the blessed-abbreviation list (len/fmt/args/env/mem), so a short suffix must also bless its abbreviation. This ballot picks the fresh-value rule only; conversions and views stay untouched.
