decisions.story: A developer learns Deque.new() and vault.ExpiringSecret.new(). They need an expiring cache and write ExpiringValue.new("fresh", ttl, clk). The language wants expiring.new(...), a module function. Their guess fails.
decisions.inWild:
One example file, examples/features/memory/expiring_secret.jet, uses all four shapes today:

    clk := time.clock(1000)                                  // module factory
    cache :: expiring.new("fresh", ttl, clk)                 // module fn named new
    key := crypto.SigningKey.generate() ?? panic("key")      // fifth verb
    secret := vault.ExpiringSecret.new(^key, ttl2, clk2)     // the ratified shape

options.name: One verb, type-owned
options.detail: Every fresh value is Type.new(...), with inferred .new where context proves the type. Module factories and side verbs retire with teaching errors. Key generation becomes SigningKey.new() and stays fallible.
options.code:
clk :: Clock.new(1000)
cache :: ExpiringValue.new("fresh", ttl, clk)
key :: SigningKey.new() ?? panic("key")

options.name: Two separate verbs: new, and generate for randomness
options.detail: Deterministic fresh state is Type.new(...). An entropy-drawing constructor is Type.generate(...). The call site shows randomness, but the two words share no stem, so completion on Type.new never surfaces generate.
options.code:
clk :: Clock.new(1000)
cache :: ExpiringValue.new("fresh", ttl, clk)
key :: SigningKey.generate() ?? panic("key")

options.name: Prefix family, plain word: new and new_random
options.detail: Every constructor starts with new. Typing Type.new lists new() and new_random() in completion, so discovery needs no docs. Entropy stays visible at the call site. Plain English, so the blessed-abbreviation list is untouched.
options.code:
clk :: Clock.new(1000)
cache :: ExpiringValue.new("fresh", ttl, clk)
key :: SigningKey.new_random() ?? panic("key")

options.name: Prefix family, short suffix: new and new_rand (or new_gen)
options.detail: Same family shape as C with a terser suffix. Neither rand nor gen is on the blessed-abbreviation list, so this option also blesses the chosen suffix as a D-API-LEN1 extension. The exact suffix is picked at ratification.
options.code:
clk :: Clock.new(1000)
cache :: ExpiringValue.new("fresh", ttl, clk)
key :: SigningKey.new_rand() ?? panic("key")   // or SigningKey.new_gen()

options.name: Leave as-is
options.detail: Keep module factories and per-type verbs. Each module documents its own spelling. No churn, but a new type's constructor stays a documentation lookup.
options.code:
clk := time.clock(1000)
cache :: expiring.new("fresh", ttl, clk)
key := crypto.SigningKey.generate() ?? panic("key")

recommendation.why: Every fresh value starts with new, so one completion stem discovers the whole family. The plain suffix keeps the entropy draw readable at the call site and leaves the closed abbreviation list untouched.
recommendation.tradeoff: new_random is longer than generate, and crypto convention usually says generate for keys.

whyNot.reason: Folding key generation into new hides the entropy draw at the call site, weakening the visible-footgun rule for the code that most needs it.
generate shares no stem with new, so completion on Type.new never surfaces it; the discoverability goal is lost and beginners are back to a docs lookup.
Same family win as C, but it opens the closed abbreviation list for one case; the plain word costs three letters and keeps that law intact.
Four spellings remain for one job, every new module invents its own factory, and the expert's guess keeps failing.

decisions.title: Positional arguments in the @Cli derive
decisions.gist: Whether `todo add "buy milk"` works out of the box with the @Cli derive, and how an expert opts a field out.
decisions.lesson:
A command-line tool takes two kinds of input. A flag is named, like `--text "buy milk"`. A positional argument is bare: its meaning comes from where it sits, like the file name in `git add file.txt`.

Jet has two ways to build a command-line tool. The builder spells everything out and already supports positionals through `.positional(...)` (D-ARGS1). The `@Cli` derive is the magic path: you write an enum of commands and Jet generates the parsing and the help text.

The derive currently turns every field into a flag. There is no way to say a field is positional. So a todo app made with the derive rejects `todo add "buy milk"` and demands `todo add --text "buy milk"`.

Nearly every real tool leads with positionals. `git add file.txt`, `cp a b`, `npm install express`. People type the bare form first and reach for flags second. Whatever the default is here, it is the first thing every new Jet CLI author's users experience.

This ballot decides the default and the escape hatch. A new field marker is user-typeable surface, so the spelling needs a ratified decision (I7).
decisions.story: Devon, a TypeScript backend developer, built a todo CLI with the @Cli derive in his first Jet session. His first real command was `todo add "buy milk"`. It failed and asked for `--text`. The builder could have done it, but he had picked the derive because that is the advertised magic path.

options.name: Positional by default, @[Flag] to opt out
options.detail: The common case is the magic case. In each command, required fields fill from bare arguments in declaration order, with no annotation. Every field also always accepts its named `--field` spelling, so the flag form never stops working. Fields with defaults stay flag-only. An expert marks `@[Flag]` on a field to remove it from positional filling. The cost: declaration order of required fields becomes part of the command's interface.
options.technical: Per variant: required fields fill positionally in declaration order. Optional fields (with defaults) are flags only. The named `--field` spelling is always accepted for every field and wins over position when both appear. `@[Flag]` excludes a field from positional filling. Help lists positionals first, then flags.

options.name: Explicit @[Positional] opt-in
options.detail: Nothing is positional until you mark it. The command's shape is fully spelled in the source. The cost: the common case needs ceremony, and every derive author must discover the attribute before their users' first bare command works. Beginners get the failure Devon got until they learn it.
options.technical: Marked fields fill positionally in declaration order. An optional positional after a required one is allowed, the reverse is a compile error.

options.name: Flags only, with a smarter error
options.detail: The derive stays flags-only. When a bare argument matches exactly one missing required flag, the error suggests the flag form. The command still fails. The cost: the first thing a new user types keeps failing forever, and the builder stays the only path to normal CLI shapes.
options.technical: No parsing change. The unknown-argument diagnostic gains a did-you-mean when exactly one required flag is unfilled.

comparisons.note: Derive fields with no flag attribute are positional by default. This is the expectation Jet's derive users arrive with.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Parser)]
struct Add { text: String }  // positional by default

comparisons.note: The name shape decides: bare names positional, dashed names flags. Zero-annotation positionals here too.
No positional support at all. Everyone hand-rolls os.Args slicing — the gap Jet's derive should not repeat.
comparisons.code:
flag.Parse()
args := flag.Args() // manual from here

recommendation.why: This is the dual-facet shape. The beginner pass: the command virtually everyone types first works with zero annotations, and the generated help teaches the rest. The expert pass: `@[Flag]` opts any field out, the named spelling always exists for scripts that must survive reorders, and the builder remains below for full control.

whyNot.reason: It puts ceremony on the common case. The magic path should not require discovering an attribute before the obvious command works.
The new user's first command still fails, permanently. The derive's pitch is beating commander and yargs, not apologizing better.

recommendation.tradeoff: Declaration order of required fields becomes interface, so reordering them is a breaking change. Accepted because the always-available named spelling gives scripts a stable form, and the publish-time API diff on card #6 reports command-shape changes.

decisions.title: Telemetry: what the toolchain may ever send home
decisions.gist: Whether jet and jetpack ever send usage data anywhere, and under what consent rule.
decisions.lesson:
Telemetry is a tool reporting facts about its own use back to its makers: which commands run, what crashes, how long builds take. Makers want it because it shows what to fix. Users fear it because it runs silently on their machines.

The consent rule is the whole decision. Opt-in means nothing is sent until the user explicitly turns it on. Opt-out means sending is on by default and the user must find the switch.

History is one-sided here. Go proposed opt-out telemetry in 2023, the community revolted, and it shipped opt-in with data kept in local files until the user chooses to upload. Audacity added telemetry in 2021 and the trust damage outlived the revert. Homebrew's opt-out analytics remain a recurring complaint years later.

Jet has no telemetry today and no written policy. That means the real policy is whatever code ships next. A policy chosen now is cheap. A policy walked back later costs trust that does not come back.

One boundary matters for Jet specifically: jetpack talks to a package registry as its normal job. A registry query necessarily reveals a package name and a version to the server. The policy must say what those requests may carry beyond the minimum.
decisions.story: Amara runs infrastructure for a hospital. She is evaluating Jet for internal tools and reads the network policy before anything else. If she cannot state in one sentence what the toolchain sends and when, Jet is out, whatever the language is like.
decisions.inWild:
# what Amara audits before adopting a toolchain:
$ strace -f -e trace=network jet build 2>&1 | grep connect
# expectation: nothing, unless she asked for a package

$ jetpack add core-http@1.2
# acceptable: one request naming core-http 1.2 to the registry
# unacceptable: machine id, os fingerprint, command history riding along

options.name: Zero telemetry, forever
options.detail: The toolchain never sends usage data. Network traffic happens only for operations the user asked for, and carries only what that operation needs. Crash reporting exists but is user-initiated: a command builds a report bundle the user can read before choosing to send it. The promise is written in the docs as permanent policy. The cost: the project never gets passive usage data.
options.technical: Policy: no background or piggybacked transmission of usage, environment, or crash data. Registry requests carry the package name, version constraint, and protocol necessities only. `jet report` writes a local bundle and prints its path, sending is a separate explicit step.
options.code:
$ jet build
# no network traffic, ever

$ jet report
# wrote /tmp/jet-report-8f3.tar (you can inspect it)
# to share: jet report --send /tmp/jet-report-8f3.tar

options.name: Opt-in, local-first (Go's model)
options.detail: Telemetry is off until a user runs an explicit enable command. Counters collect in readable local files either way, uploads happen weekly only after opt-in, and published data is aggregate. Real usage data arrives from the fraction who opt in. The cost: a standing uploader lives in the toolchain, and every prompt nudging users to enable it spends trust.
options.technical: Local counter files under the user's config dir, human-readable. `jet telemetry on|off|status`. Upload only while opted in, aggregates public.
options.code:
$ jet telemetry status
# telemetry: off (local counters only, nothing is sent)
$ jet telemetry on
# weekly aggregate upload enabled — thank you

options.name: Opt-out anonymized
options.detail: Anonymized counters send by default, with a documented disable flag. Maximum data for prioritizing work. This is the shape that burned Go's proposal, Audacity, and Homebrew: the default does the sending, so trust is spent for every user who never found the flag.
options.technical: On by default, `JET_NO_TELEMETRY=1` or config to disable, anonymization documented.
options.code:
$ jet build
# (sent: command=build, duration, os, toolchain version)
$ export JET_NO_TELEMETRY=1   # the flag Amara has to discover

comparisons.note: Proposed opt-out in 2023, community revolted, shipped opt-in local-first. The consent rule was the entire fight.
Added telemetry in 2021, reverted under pressure, forks and distrust persisted anyway.
Opt-out analytics since 2016, still a recurring complaint and a standard hardening-guide entry.
Opt-out at scale, tolerated mostly because users already accepted the vendor relationship. A young language asking for trust has no such credit.

recommendation.why: Jet asks users to trust it as their language, their package manager, and eventually their operating system. A flat never is the only promise that is verifiable at a glance, survives every future audit, and compounds trust for decades.

whyNot.reason: Even Go's careful design keeps a standing uploader in the toolchain, and every nudge to enable it spends trust the project does not need to spend.
The opt-out shape has burned every tool that tried it, and for a project that wants to run your OS the blast radius of that mistake is total.

recommendation.tradeoff: The project gives up passive usage data for prioritization. Accepted because the audit-driven board already sets priorities from direct evidence, and user reports remain available on request.

decisions.title: Byte constant-time equality name
decisions.gist: How byte lists name their constant-time equality check.
decisions.lesson:
A normal equality check can stop at the first different byte. That timing can reveal where two secret values differ. A constant-time check examines the complete input before it returns.

Jet has two such checks in `core.crypto`. One accepts `Secret` values and is named `constant_time_equal`. One accepts byte lists and is named `constant_time_eq`. The closed naming law forbids `eq`, so the byte name must change.

Expanding `eq` to `equal` would give both functions the same module name. Jet does not overload one module function name with different parameter types. This choice must keep the byte operation distinct, remove it, or move comparison ownership to the values.
decisions.story: Priya verifies a protocol tag stored as bytes. The same service also compares move-only secrets. She needs both checks without guessing which data shape one shared name accepts.
decisions.inWild:
tag_ok :: crypto.constant_time_eq(received_tag, expected_tag)
secret_ok :: crypto.constant_time_equal(stored_secret, supplied_secret)

options.name: Name the byte input
options.detail: Keep both module functions. Rename only the byte check to `constant_time_equal_bytes`. Existing Secret code stays unchanged. The longer name states why this second function exists.
options.technical: Registry keys remain unique: `constant_time_equal_bytes([U8], [U8]) -> Bool` and `constant_time_equal(Secret, Secret) -> Bool`. The old byte name emits an E1004 teaching error.
options.code:
tag_ok :: crypto.constant_time_equal_bytes(received_tag, expected_tag)
secret_ok :: crypto.constant_time_equal(stored_secret, supplied_secret)

options.name: Retire the byte helper
options.detail: Keep only `constant_time_equal` for `Secret`. Code with byte lists must convert them to `Secret` first. This leaves one operation name but adds secret wrapping and ownership ceremony.
options.technical: Remove the `[U8]` fixed signature and codegen route. `Secret.from_bytes` becomes the only safe entry for byte-backed constant-time comparison.
options.code:
received :: crypto.Secret.from_bytes(received_tag)
expected :: crypto.Secret.from_bytes(expected_tag)
tag_ok :: crypto.constant_time_equal(received, expected)

options.name: Move equality onto values
options.detail: Make constant-time equality a type-owned method. Secret values and byte lists use the same method spelling because the receiver selects the implementation. This changes the existing Secret API.
options.technical: Retire both module functions. Add type-directed methods for `Secret` and `[U8]`; each lowers to its existing constant-time helper.
options.code:
tag_ok :: received_tag.constant_time_equal(expected_tag)
secret_ok :: stored_secret.constant_time_equal(supplied_secret)

comparisons.note: Node uses one byte-buffer function. Its parameter types identify the data kind.
Go puts the byte comparison in a specialist package and names the operation directly.
Rust uses a type-owned trait method, similar to option C.

recommendation.why: It obeys the plain-word law, keeps both real jobs, and preserves the shipped Secret API. The byte qualifier makes the distinct fixed signature visible.

whyNot.reason: Public protocol bytes are not always secrets. Wrapping them adds ownership and zeroization ceremony only to reach an operation Jet already has.
It reopens the shipped Secret API and adds a cryptographic method to ordinary byte lists. The naming fix does not need that wider surface change.

recommendation.tradeoff: The byte function name is longer and repeats a type fact visible in its arguments. That cost keeps the two safe operations distinct and discoverable.

decisions.title: Markers declare signatures; arguments use the ordinary call grammar
decisions.gist: Every # marker declares a typed parameter list, and marker arguments are written exactly like a normal Jet function call.
decisions.lesson:
A marker is a word you attach to code with the # prefix, like #Test("name") or #Unsafe("reason"). It tells the compiler to apply a rule to the next declaration, expression, or brace scope. Jet has about sixty of them.

Many markers take arguments in parentheses, and today each one invents its own argument style. #Pre takes two positional values. #Meta takes only named fields, like #Meta(category: X). #Unsafe takes a positional reason plus one hard-coded named field. #Layout(c, tag: U8) mixes both through a special case. Each style has its own hand-written parser and its own error wording.

A signature is the parameter list a function declares: which arguments exist, their names, their types, and which are optional. This decision asks whether markers should declare signatures too. Then one shared reader handles every marker, arguments follow the same rules as ordinary calls, and a wrong argument always produces the same style of error naming the expected parameters. Nothing about what any marker does changes; only how its arguments are read and checked becomes uniform.
decisions.story: Priya has written #Pre(x > 0, "positive") a dozen times, so she writes #Meta("tuning note") the same way. It fails: #Meta secretly accepts only named fields. The error text explains nothing about why these two parenthesized lists follow different laws.
decisions.inWild:
#Pre(cents > 0, "cents must be positive")   // positional
#Meta(category: Pricing, tunable)            // named only — its own parser
#Unsafe("bounds checked", obligations: .Track) { … }  // positional + one blessed name
#Layout(c, tag: U8)                          // label special-cased in the parser
#Every("03:00")                              // bespoke string-or-unit reader
decisions.detail: Owner direction in chat 2026-07-23: adopt signatures. This ballot records the pick. Parser survey found roughly twelve bespoke marker-argument parsers across crates/jet-parser.

options.name: Signatures + one call grammar
options.detail: Every marker declares parameters like a function: positional values, named fields, defaults, and optional parts. One shared reader parses all marker arguments. Wrong arguments give one consistent error family that names the marker's real signature. Existing spellings stay valid because current forms become signatures rather than special cases.
options.technical: Registry entry per marker: name, params (name, type, positional or named, default), legal sites, form (prefix, block, expression), status. Parser, sema, formatter, LSP, and explain read the same table. E0355/E0927 keep their codes; argument-shape errors consolidate into one family.

options.name: Keep bespoke grammars
options.detail: Each marker keeps its own argument reader and its own error wording. No user-visible change now. The cost stays: every new marker hand-rolls parsing, and users cannot transfer what they learned from one marker to the next.

options.name: Named-only arguments everywhere
options.detail: All marker arguments must be name: value pairs, like #Pre(cond: cents > 0, msg: "…"). Maximum explicitness, but common one-argument markers get heavier, and every existing example and test changes spelling.

comparisons.note: Attribute contents are raw token trees; each macro parses its own, so argument errors differ per attribute — the failure mode option B keeps.
Attributes are constructor calls with real signatures — positional then named — which is option A's model.

recommendation.why: One learned rule covers sixty markers, argument errors become teachable product copy, and adding a marker means declaring a signature instead of writing a parser.

whyNot.reason: Keeps twelve private grammars and per-marker error wording that users cannot predict from experience.
Forces name: ceremony onto one-argument markers like #Test and #Every, taxing the beginner surface for no added clarity.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few current shapes bend to fit one law, and their snapshots re-bless. That is acceptable because the spellings users already write remain valid.

decisions.title: Stacking markers: bare when single, one bracket list when multiple
decisions.gist: One marker is written bare (#Skip); two or more must share one bracket list (#[PublishedSchema, Codable]).
decisions.lesson:
Several markers can apply to the same declaration: a struct can be both Codable and PublishedSchema, and a field can be both Renamed and given a Default.

Today three stacking styles coexist. You can repeat bare markers on one line: #Numeric #Printable #Comparable. You can write one bracket list: #[PublishedSchema, Codable]. And by habit, field markers always use brackets even when there is only one: #[Skip]. All three are legal, so the same program can be spelled many ways, and readers learn nothing from seeing brackets or not.

This decision picks one law for when brackets appear. The candidate rule is simple: brackets mean list. A single marker never needs them; two or more markers must share one bracket list. Under that rule, seeing #[ tells you more than one rule applies, and seeing #Name tells you exactly one does. The formatter can rewrite old spellings automatically, so no one has to fix files by hand.
decisions.story: Ana reviews a teammate's diff. One struct says #Codable, the next says #[Codable], a third stacks #Numeric #Printable #Comparable across the line. She asks in review which form is house style; today the honest answer is all of them.
decisions.detail: Owner direction in chat 2026-07-23: single markers do not require brackets; more than one requires them. Ballot records the rule and its edges: single-item brackets and bare stacking become formatter-fixable errors.

options.name: Bare single, brackets required for two or more
options.detail: #Skip alone; #[Rename("x"), Default(3)] together. Single-item brackets and bare stacking are errors with an automatic formatter fix. Reading rule: #[ always means several rules, #Name always means one. Field markers drop their habitual brackets when alone.
options.technical: Grammar: decl-attached markers are either one bare application or one bracket group with two or more comma-separated applications. jet fmt rewrites legacy forms; diagnostics carry the rewrite as a fix-it. Block markers (#Unsafe { }) are unaffected — they never stack in one group.
options.code:
#Codable
struct Invoice {
    #Skip cached_total: Int
    #[Rename("customer"), Default("anon")] who: String
}

#[Numeric, Printable, Comparable] Usd :: distinct Int

#[Codable]      // error[E0931]: one marker needs no brackets — write #Codable
#A #B fn f() {} // error[E0932]: several markers share one list — write #[A, B]

options.name: Brackets always
options.detail: Every marker application is bracketed, even alone: #[Codable], #[Skip]. Fully uniform and list-ready, but the most common case — one marker — pays two characters of ceremony forever, and prose-like markers read worse: #[Test("name")].

options.name: Both forms free; formatter canonicalizes
options.detail: Keep today's freedom; jet fmt silently rewrites to option A's shape. No errors, but unformatted code still varies, and the language spec has two spellings for one thing.
options.code:
#Codable struct A { … }
#[Codable] struct B { … }   // both legal; fmt rewrites B to A

recommendation.why: Brackets become information: they appear exactly when more than one rule applies. The common single-marker case stays the lightest possible spelling, and the formatter migrates old code automatically.

whyNot.reason: Charges bracket ceremony on every single-marker use, which is the overwhelmingly common case in real files.
Keeps two legal spellings of one thing, against the one-mechanism ratchet; variance survives anywhere fmt has not run.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing files with #[Skip] or bare stacks need one formatter pass, and snapshots re-bless. That is acceptable because the rewrite is fully automatic.

decisions.title: Merge #InlineAlways into #Inline(Always)
decisions.gist: The two inlining markers become one marker with an argument: #Inline is the hint, #Inline(Always) is the checked promise.
decisions.lesson:
Inlining copies a function's body into its caller so the call itself disappears, trading code size for speed. Jet exposes two strengths. #Inline is a soft hint the compiler may ignore. #InlineAlways is a checked promise: if the compiler can prove the call genuinely cannot be inlined, it rejects the program with an error naming why.

Today those strengths are two separate marker names, plus a third error (E0920) just to forbid writing both on one function. That error exists only because the strength choice was split across two names.

With marker signatures ratified, strength can be an argument instead: #Inline for the hint, #Inline(Always) for the promise. One name, one concept, and the mutual-exclusion error becomes structurally impossible — a single marker cannot conflict with itself.
decisions.story: Tomas profiles a hot loop and reaches for inlining. Autocomplete offers #Inline and #InlineAlways; he writes both to be safe and hits E0920, an error that exists only to police the split between two names for one dial.
decisions.detail: Owner accepted this condensation in chat 2026-07-23; ballot records it. Checked-rejection diagnostics E0917/E0918/E0919 keep their behavior under the merged spelling.

options.name: One marker: #Inline / #Inline(Always)
options.detail: Strength is an argument with a default. Bare #Inline stays the hint everyone already writes. #Inline(Always) is the checked promise with the same rejection errors as today. E0920 retires because the conflict cannot be typed anymore.
options.technical: Signature: #Inline(strength: InlineStrength = .Hint), argument spelled Always. E0917/E0918/E0919 unchanged. #InlineAlways becomes a retired spelling with a fix-it to #Inline(Always).

options.name: Keep two names
options.detail: #Inline and #InlineAlways stay separate, E0920 stays to forbid combining them. No migration, but the marker list carries two names and one policing error for a single dial.

recommendation.why: One name for one concept, the strength dial reads at the call site, and a whole error code disappears because the invalid combination can no longer be written.

whyNot.reason: Preserves a second marker name and a dedicated error whose only job is guarding the seam between the two names.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing #InlineAlways uses migrate via fix-it and snapshots re-bless. That is acceptable because the rewrite is mechanical and the old spelling teaches its replacement.

decisions.title: Reduce operations become enum values: v.reduce(.Max)
decisions.gist: SIMD reduce operation selectors leave the marker plane and become ordinary enum values — v.reduce(.Max) instead of v.reduce(#Max).
decisions.lesson:
A reduce operation folds all lanes of a vector into one number: add them, multiply them, take the smallest or largest. The operation you choose is data — a value you pass to the reduce method — not a rule applied to your code.

Jet currently spells that choice with markers: v.reduce(#Add), v.reduce(#Max). These four names sit in the marker registry as bare strings with no decision ID, and examples already use v.reduce(#Avg), which was never registered at all. They are also the only markers that appear in argument position, which makes the marker plane harder to describe: markers apply rules to declarations, expressions, and scopes — except these four.

Jet already has the right tool. Enum values are written with a leading dot, like .Input or .Track, and the parameter's type tells the compiler which enum is meant. Making reduce take a ReduceOp enum turns the selector into ordinary typed data, gives autocomplete the full list of operations, and shrinks the marker plane by its four least lawful members.
decisions.story: Lena reads the marker chapter and learns markers apply rules to code. Then she meets v.reduce(#Max), where the marker is an argument, and v.reduce(#Avg), which the registry has never heard of. The exception costs more teaching than the feature.
decisions.detail: Owner accepted this condensation in chat 2026-07-23; ballot records it. Also closes the unregistered #Avg hole found in the examples sweep.

options.name: ReduceOp enum values
options.detail: reduce takes a ReduceOp enum: .Add, .Mul, .Min, .Max, .Avg. The selector becomes ordinary data with autocomplete and exhaustive definition in Core. The four string-literal registry rows retire, and marker teaching loses its one exception.
options.technical: Core: enum ReduceOp { Add, Mul, Min, Max, Avg }; reduce(op: ReduceOp). #Add/#Mul/#Min/#Max become retired spellings with fix-its to the dot form. Codegen keys on the enum value; SIMD lowering unchanged.

options.name: Register the marker family properly
options.detail: Keep #Add/#Mul/#Min/#Max, add #Avg, give the family a decision ID and expression-position law. The hole closes but the marker plane keeps its only argument-position members, and every new operation is a registry change instead of an enum variant.
options.code:
let total := prices.reduce(#Add)
let mean  := samples.reduce(#Avg)   // now registered

recommendation.why: Selecting an operation is choosing a value, and Jet already has one spelling for typed value choice — the dot enum. The marker plane becomes fully uniform: every marker applies a rule.

whyNot.reason: Ratifies the marker plane's only exception and turns future operations into syntax-registry work instead of a Core enum variant.

recommendation.tradeoff: Existing reduce call sites migrate via fix-it. That is acceptable because the sites are few and the rewrite is one token.

decisions.title: One capability plane: #Comparable and #Printable mean one thing everywhere
decisions.gist: Merge the derive markers and the distinct-type capability bundles so #Comparable and #Printable carry one meaning on any type.
decisions.lesson:
Jet has two features that answer the same user wish: my type should support comparison, or printing, or encoding.

On a struct or enum, #Comparable is a derive — the compiler generates the comparison code from the fields. On a distinct type, like Usd :: distinct Int, #Comparable is a capability bundle — it re-exposes the base integer's comparisons while keeping Usd a separate type. Same spelling, same intent, but two mechanisms in the registry, disambiguated only by what declaration follows. The registry itself carries a comment explaining the collision.

Merging them makes #Comparable one concept: this type exposes comparison, derived from fields on a struct, re-exposed from the base on a distinct type. The compiler already knows which kind of declaration it is looking at, so it picks the right implementation with no new syntax. #Printable merges the same way. #CodableAsBase stays distinct-only, because coding as the base type has no meaning without a base.
decisions.story: Sofia marks her struct #Comparable and it works. She then mints Usd :: distinct Int, marks it #Comparable, and asks whether that is the same feature. Today the honest answer is no — two registry rows, one spelling — for no reason she can use.
decisions.detail: Owner accepted this merge in chat 2026-07-23; ballot records it. CodableAsBase is out of scope: it stays a distinct-type capability because its meaning requires a base type.

options.name: One capability concept per name
options.detail: #Comparable and #Printable each become one registry entry legal on structs, enums, and distinct types. The compiler derives from fields or re-exposes from the base according to the declaration. Users learn one word for one wish; the positional disambiguation comment disappears.
options.technical: Registry: one row per name with sites Type and DistinctType; implementation dispatches on declaration kind. D-CAPBUNDLE1 wording amended; no user-visible spelling changes.
options.code:
#[Codable, Comparable]
struct Invoice { total: Int, issued: Date }   // derived from fields

#[Numeric, Printable, Comparable] Usd :: distinct Int   // re-exposed from Int
// one #Comparable, one meaning: this type supports comparison

options.name: Keep two planes
options.detail: Derives and bundles remain separate mechanisms sharing spellings. Nothing changes for users today, but the registry keeps duplicate rows, and any future capability must be added twice or explained twice.
options.code: // unchanged surface; the split lives in the registry and the docs

recommendation.why: One word carries one meaning on every type, which is exactly the one-mechanism ratchet, and future capabilities are defined once instead of twice.

whyNot.reason: Preserves duplicate registry rows and a docs split for a distinction users cannot observe or exploit.

recommendation.tradeoff: The spec section for capability bundles is rewritten and its snapshots re-bless. That is acceptable because no user-visible spelling changes at all.

decisions.title: Lawful spellings for the lowercase const markers #static and #inline
decisions.gist: The two lowercase const markers get PascalCase spellings: #Static, and const inlining folds into the existing #Inline.
decisions.lesson:
Constants can be compiled two ways. An inlined constant is copied into each place it is used and has no address of its own. A static constant lives at one fixed memory location you can point to. Jet spells this choice with markers on the const declaration: today #inline and #static, both lowercase.

Casing law D-CASING1 says every marker is PascalCase, with lowercase #[allow(...)] as the single exception — it names a lint code, not a feature. The const markers are a second, unratified exception, parsed by their own private code path that the registry's PascalCase gate cannot even see.

Two repairs are possible. Recase both, and fold const inlining into the existing #Inline marker, which already means make this inline for functions. The registry records it as legal on functions and constants; the declaration kind disambiguates. Or bless the lowercase pair as a ratified exception and amend the casing law. There is also a naming wrinkle either way: #Inline on a const and #Inline on a fn would be the same word for closely related, but not identical, ideas.
decisions.story: Rae learns that markers are PascalCase, then reads Core and finds #static const beside #Static-nothing. She recases it to #Static and gets an unknown-marker error, because the lowercase pair lives outside the registry the error consults.
decisions.inWild:
#static const LOOKUP: [Int#256] = build_table()
#inline const MASK: Int = 0xFF

#Inline fn hot(x: Int) -> Int { x & MASK }   // PascalCase two lines later
decisions.detail: Owner accepted the recase in chat 2026-07-23; the open sub-choice is whether const inlining folds into #Inline or keeps its own name. The fold option assumes D-MARKSIG1 registry sites.

options.name: #Static, and fold const inlining into #Inline
options.detail: One inlining word everywhere: #Inline on a fn hints call inlining, #Inline on a const means copy the value into each use. #Static is the recased address form. The lowercase pair and its private parser retire with fix-its. The casing law keeps exactly one exception.
options.technical: Registry: Inline sites Function and Constant; Static sites Constant. #static/#inline become retired spellings with fix-its. The hand-rolled const_def match retires in favor of registry dispatch.

options.name: Recase to distinct names: #Static and #Copied
options.detail: Both recase, but const inlining gets its own word so #Inline stays purely about functions. No word does double duty; the cost is a brand-new marker name to learn for a niche dial.
options.technical: Registry: Copied sites Constant. Same retirements and fix-its as option A otherwise.

options.name: Bless the lowercase pair
options.detail: Amend the casing law: #[allow(...)], #static, and #inline are the lowercase exceptions. No migration, but the one-exception law becomes a three-exception list and the private parser path stays.
options.code: #static const LOOKUP: [Int#256] = build_table()   // now lawful by decree

recommendation.why: Inlining stays one word across the language, the casing law keeps its single exception, and the last private marker parser retires into the registry.

whyNot.reason: Invents a new name for a niche dial when the existing inlining word already says exactly what happens to the value.
Grows the casing law's exception list and keeps a parser path the registry cannot see, for zero user gain.

recommendation.tradeoff: #Inline means value-copied on consts and call-inlined on functions — one word, two close readings. That is acceptable because both readings are this is duplicated into its use sites.

decisions.title: Secure shared-store architecture
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jetpack supports cross-user store sharing and how privilege separation works.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A abandons the epoch parity claim and gives CI hosts nothing; option C forces a resident privileged daemon on every machine, gutting D-JPK-NODAEMON1 far beyond need. Option B is right in shape but vague where implementers will bleed: no admission law, no builder-identity isolation rule, no fallback semantics, and 'broker' quietly re-introduces a resident daemon. The hybrid states the admission proof, makes the broker transient/socket-activated to preserve NODAEMON1's spirit, defines transparent fallback, and wires status/audit surfaces.
decisions.story: Hank runs a CI host used by thirty developers. They should share identical gigabyte toolchains without letting one user inject bytes another user trusts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker
root: /var/lib/jet/hangar
builders: isolated identities
user writes: private namespace
decisions.detail: Rootless beginner path stays intact; shared machines gain secure dedup and isolated trust.

options.name: Per-user stores only
options.detail: Preserve D-JPK-NODAEMON1 without exception. Users never share local objects; teams rely on remote caches. Selecting this explicitly drops secure cross-user local-store parity from the epoch claim.
options.code:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: per-user
parity exception: multi-user local store

options.name: Per-user default plus optional broker
options.detail: Default remains rootless. Admins may install a narrowly-scoped broker that owns the shared store, verifies immutable objects, isolates builders, and never evaluates user package source. Explicit amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only for shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker

options.name: Always-installed system daemon
options.detail: All Jetpack operations use one privileged service and shared store, matching classic multi-user Nix architecture. Explicitly amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1.
options.code:
$ jetpack daemon start
all users share /var/lib/jet/hangar

options.name: Per-user default; verifying transient broker opt-in, scoped amendment (hybrid)
options.detail: Default stays rootless per-user per D-JPK-NODAEMON1; every command works identically with no broker present. Admins opt in via `jetpack shared-store install`, which installs a socket-activated transient broker (no resident daemon) owning the shared store; the broker admits objects only after re-verifying canonical output digest, signatures, and provenance inside its own privilege domain — user-supplied bytes are never trusted on assertion — and it never evaluates user package source. Builds it performs run as ephemeral isolated builder identities inside the strong sandbox; user writes land in private namespaces, and promotion to shared follows D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 writer law. Clients fall back to per-user mode transparently when the broker is absent, and `jetpack hangar status` plus `jet audit` report mode, broker version, and admission policy. This is an explicit audited amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 scoped solely to shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install   # admin, once
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker (socket-activated, non-resident)
admission: digest+signature+provenance verified
user writes: private namespace
$ jet audit broker
builders: ephemeral isolated identities

comparisons.note: Multi-user mode uses a privileged daemon and isolated build users.
A system daemon owns the store and performs builds.

decisions.title: What should manual Hangar-root actions be called?
decisions.gist: Choose one naming family for creating, removing, and listing manual roots under `jet hangar`.
decisions.lesson:
Garbage collection, or GC, is cleanup that deletes stored software Jet can prove nobody still needs.
Output: one immutable result already stored in Hangar.
Realized: already built or downloaded.
Closure: an output plus every stored dependency it needs.
Root: a durable record telling GC to keep one output and its closure.
Lease: temporary protection tied to running work, such as a build or process.
Manual root: durable protection created for software outside Jet.
Etag: a version stamp that blocks stale updates.

Jet creates roots automatically for projects, profiles, toolchains, and JetOS generations. It creates leases automatically while programs and builds run. An external backup appliance falls outside those lifecycles.

Creating a manual root never builds or downloads anything. It accepts only an output already in Hangar. Removing the root, or reaching its expiry, ends protection only when no other root or lease reaches that closure.

Ratified decisions already put physical lifecycle actions under `jet hangar` and require one noun-then-verb grouped grammar. This ballot still needs owner confirmation for the three new user-facing action names.
decisions.story: Asha's nightly backup service loads an SDK from Hangar. Its project disappears Friday. Saturday's `jet clean` must not delete the SDK before Sunday's backup, so Asha creates a named root.
decisions.inWild: Nix exposes GC roots as filesystem links. Indirect roots add another link under Nix's automatic-root directory, and operators inspect roots separately. Rust, Go, and npm caches do not durably declare that an outside service needs one complete immutable dependency closure. Jet uses one typed record with expiry and stale-update protection. This expert escape hatch exists because no project, profile, process, or build owns the appliance's SDK.

options.name: Add, remove, list external roots
options.detail: Use `add-external-root`, `remove-external-root`, and `list-external-roots`. Help and audit logs always state the stored object and operation. The names are long but immediately literal.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  add-external-root
  remove-external-root
  list-external-roots

$ jet hangar add-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar add-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Register, unregister, list external roots
options.detail: Use `register-external-root`, `unregister-external-root`, and `list-external-roots`. Register says Jet records an existing output without building or downloading it. Unregister clearly removes only that record.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  register-external-root
  unregister-external-root
  list-external-roots

$ jet hangar register-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar register-external-root backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Keep, release, list kept
options.detail: Use `keep`, `release`, and `list-kept`. These names are quick to type and read naturally as lifecycle actions. Help and audit logs need surrounding Hangar context to reveal root semantics.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  keep
  release
  list-kept

$ jet hangar keep backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar keep backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

options.name: Pin, unpin, list external pins
options.detail: Use `pin-external`, `unpin-external`, and `list-external-pins`. Pin is familiar cache language and makes retention intent obvious. It can be confused with package-version pinning elsewhere in Jet.
options.technical: This confirms only three action spellings. Existing root lifecycle, plan/apply, etag, ownership, expiry, audit, and JSON laws remain separate contract material.
options.code:
$ jet hangar help
Actions:
  pin-external
  unpin-external
  list-external-pins

$ jet hangar pin-external backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --expires-in 12w --yes
Plan external root
+ backup-sdk
  closure objects: 3
  etag: 1.1
  expires: 2026-10-07T18:00:00Z
created external root 1.1

$ jet hangar pin-external backup-sdk nixpkgs:ripgrep#2.0.17 --if-etag 1.0 --yes
Error [E1320]: External root `principal:mzxw6ytboi2dknjvgy3tqojqge/backup-sdk` changed; expected etag `1.0`, current etag is `1.1`.
 Why: Compare-and-swap and never-reused incarnations prevent lost updates and delete-and-recreate identity reuse.
 Fix: Inspect the current root and audit, then retry with `--if-etag 1.1` only if that state is intended.
No requested root mutation was applied.

comparisons.note: Nix manual roots use filesystem links. Jet uses named typed records, so moving a working directory cannot silently change root identity.

recommendation.why: Register precisely describes creating durable metadata for an existing output. It scans clearly in help, distinguishes registration from realization, and makes removal scope explicit in audit logs.

whyNot.reason: Add and remove are familiar, but add can suggest importing or realizing an output instead of recording retention metadata.
Short verbs are pleasant interactively, but `keep` and `list-kept` hide root kind in help, scripts, and detached audit records.
Pin and unpin clearly imply retention, but Jet users may confuse them with package-version pins.

recommendation.tradeoff: Register and unregister are long, formal words. Manual roots are rare expert actions, and precision matters more than saving keystrokes.

decisions.checkInstructions: Ratify exactly one three-action family with no aliases. Do not infer or reopen lifecycle semantics from this naming ballot.

decisions.title: Safe authority for dev-service trees
decisions.gist: Choose whether safe background dev services activate per platform or wait until every supported platform has complete-tree authority.
decisions.lesson:
A process identifier, usually called a PID, is a reusable number. A start time detects common reuse, but it cannot bind a later signal to the process that was checked.

A service is a changing process tree. A child can create a new session with `setsid`, leave its parent's process group, and keep running after a parent-only shutdown.

Safe shutdown needs an operating system authority that owns the complete tree. Linux systemd user units can own a delegated control group. Windows Job Objects can contain a suspended child before user code runs.

macOS launchd can identify its registered job, but ordinary launchd control cannot contain a hostile descendant after `setsid`. A random label avoids PID reuse for the main job, not escaped-tree survival.

Startup must also survive crashes without guessing. `Pending` means user code is blocked. `Ready` means containment is proved and release is authorized. `Stopping` forbids replacement until the exact authority is empty.

Every state replacement and containing directory is synced before the next step. An old generation cannot be replaced until its authority is empty and its state removal is durable.

This decision adds no Jet syntax, manifest field, command, or flag. Existing service commands work automatically where policy permits. Unsupported authority returns E1332 before user code starts.

The narrow no-daemon amendment permits only per-service lifetime authority. It allows an existing user system manager and a Windows guardian while that declared service runs. Root, package background work, and a global Jetpack daemon remain forbidden.
decisions.story: Mira starts a database, then stops it after the original shell PID has been reused. A plugin creates a new session. Jetpack must stop only the original tree. If startup crashes halfway, the next command must resume one durable transition instead of trusting a PID file.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet services up
web: starting
web: healthy

$ jet services health --json
{"service":"web","state":"healthy","authority":{"version":2,"generation":"7cb8…","phase":"Ready","backend":"systemd-user-cgroup","containment":"complete-tree"}}

$ jet services down
web: stopped

When policy cannot activate safe background authority:

$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

options.name: Activate each proved platform
options.detail: Enable background services where complete-tree authority is proved. Linux uses a transient systemd user unit with a delegated control group. Windows uses a project-local guardian and Job Object. macOS fails before spawn. Existing commands remain ceremony-free. Structured output exposes backend, generation, phase, containment, and recovery facts.
options.technical: This narrowly amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1. A declared service may use an existing user system manager or one per-service Windows guardian only during that service's lifetime. Root, a global Jetpack daemon, package background work, new syntax, new manifest fields, and new CLI remain forbidden. D-JPK-PLATFORM1 is narrowed only for macOS background service containment. E1332 has one exact copy. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` Linux creates a random transient user unit whose wrapper blocks on a generation gate. Jetpack proves manager authority, unit identity, delegated control group, and complete-tree containment before Ready. Missing authority returns E1332 before release. Stop targets the unit and control group, never a PID. systemd remains owner after Jetpack exits; Jetpack never claims its own loss kills that tree. Windows creates the child suspended. A guardian creates the sole non-inheritable Job handle, denies breakaway, enables KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, assigns the child, and acknowledges containment. Jetpack publishes durable Ready before requesting resume. Guardian loss closes the last Job handle and kills the contained tree. Down authenticates the random-generation endpoint and terminates the Job. macOS returns E1332 before spawn. Start writes and syncs Pending with generation and backend, spawns blocked, proves containment, atomically publishes and syncs Ready, then sends an idempotent release. Pending recovery stops provisional authority, proves it empty, removes state, and syncs the directory. Ready recovery retries release when acknowledgement is absent. Explicit release rejection first publishes durable Stopping. Down publishes and syncs Stopping before termination. Stopping recovery repeats exact-authority shutdown until empty, then removes state and syncs the directory. Old generation replacement cannot start before old authority emptiness and durable state removal. Spawn or containment failure removes Pending only after proving no child ran or provisional authority is empty. Ready publication failure stops containment and retains Pending when cleanup is uncertain. Ambiguous release retains Ready for idempotent recovery. No path signals from PID, start time, process name, or legacy record.
options.code:
$ jet services up
cache: starting
cache: healthy

# Crash after Ready sync, before release acknowledgement:
$ jet services up
cache: recovering Ready generation 7cb8…
cache: healthy

$ jet services down
cache: stopped

# macOS, or missing proved authority:
$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

options.name: Wait for universal authority
options.detail: Disable background services on every supported platform until all platforms provide atomic complete-tree authority. Every host returns E1332 before spawn. Linux and Windows backends remain inactive despite their proofs. This preserves one universal availability boundary and the same safety contract. Existing service declarations remain captured but cannot run in background mode.
options.technical: No backend activates until Linux, Windows, and macOS all pass the same native authority contract. D-JPK-NODAEMON1 remains unchanged while background mode is disabled. When the universal gate opens, it receives only the same per-service lifetime amendment described by Option A. E1332 uses the same exact copy on every host. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` No unsafe override or cooperative exception exists. `jet dev` stops before user code when a declared service cannot start. Activation still requires the complete transaction. Start writes and syncs Pending with generation and backend, spawns blocked, proves containment, atomically publishes and syncs Ready, then sends an idempotent release. Pending recovery stops provisional authority, proves it empty, removes state, and syncs the directory. Ready recovery retries release when acknowledgement is absent. Explicit release rejection first publishes durable Stopping. Down publishes and syncs Stopping before termination. Stopping recovery repeats exact-authority shutdown until empty, then removes state and syncs the directory. Old generation replacement cannot start before old authority emptiness and durable state removal. Spawn or containment failure removes Pending only after proving no child ran or provisional authority is empty. Ready publication failure stops containment and retains Pending when cleanup is uncertain. Ambiguous release retains Ready for idempotent recovery. No path signals from PID, start time, process name, or legacy record.
options.code:
$ jet services up
Error [E1332]: Safe service authority is unavailable for `web`.
 Why: Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.
 Fix: Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.
No service command was started. No process was signaled.

comparisons.note: A transient user unit owns a control group. Control-group shutdown reaches descendants after new sessions, while unit authority survives the Jetpack command that created it.
A suspended child cannot escape before Job assignment. Denied breakaway contains descendants. A sole guardian handle makes guardian loss terminate the Job tree.
A launchd label avoids PID reuse for the registered job. It does not prove containment of a descendant after that descendant creates a new session.
comparisons.code: launchd label authority != hostile descendant containment

recommendation.why: It spends availability only where complete-tree authority is absent. Linux and Windows keep ceremony-free safe services. macOS refuses before user code starts. Experts receive exact lifecycle and containment evidence without a hidden fallback.

whyNot.reason: It is safe, but disables already-proved Linux and Windows authority. Waiting for macOS adds no stronger containment to those hosts and removes a useful safe default.

recommendation.tradeoff: Background dev services remain unavailable on macOS until complete-tree authority exists. A loud pre-start refusal is accepted because false shutdown success would violate the service safety contract.

decisions.checkInstructions: Reserve genuinely free E1332 with exactly this diagnostic. What: `Safe service authority is unavailable for {name}.` Why: `Jetpack cannot prove atomic ownership and complete-tree containment on this host. PID, start-time, and process-name checks can race or miss escaped descendants.` Fix: `Run the service directly. Background mode stays disabled wherever Jetpack cannot prove complete-tree authority.` Add this exact what, why, and fix to `docs/spec/diagnostics.md`. Add UI and CLI snapshots before shipment; I4 forbids claiming the diagnostic exists without both registry and snapshot coverage. Add no Jet syntax, manifest field, CLI command, or flag. If A wins, amend D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only for declared-service lifetime authority. Permit an existing user system manager and one per-service Windows guardian while that service runs. Continue forbidding root, global daemons, and package background work. Narrow D-JPK-PLATFORM1 only for macOS background containment. Prove every Pending write, directory sync, blocked spawn, containment proof, Ready replacement, Ready sync, release, Stopping replacement, Stopping sync, termination, emptiness proof, state removal, and final directory sync failpoint. Prove old-generation replacement cannot begin before old authority is empty and old state removal is durable. Force PID reuse between every probe and stop; unrelated processes must survive. Spawn descendants that call `setsid` during graceful and forced shutdown. Linux passes only when the transient user unit and delegated control group remain authoritative and empty after stop. Never claim Jetpack loss kills a Linux control group. Windows passes only with create-suspended ordering, sole non-inheritable Job authority, no breakaway, KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, guardian-loss tree kill, and resume after durable Ready. Under A, macOS must return E1332 before spawning user code. Under B, every host must return the identical E1332 copy before spawning user code. Prove legacy PID-only and PID/start records are quarantined without signaling. Native Linux, Windows, and macOS CI must execute real platform paths; source-token tests cannot substitute.

decisions.title: Storage location for connected receipts
decisions.gist: Choose where action and activation evidence lives without creating a second merge authority.
decisions.lesson: `.jet/lock` is the reviewable Package graph index and sole merge-history authority. A receipt connects locked input, action, output digest, parent generation, readiness, activation observation, and rollback evidence. Receipt storage must preserve immutable identity, retention, export, and signatures without copying graph merge history.
decisions.story: Rin builds `todo.cli` and activates Halcyon generation 42 several times while the Package source stays unchanged. The lock must remain reviewable while each realization keeps durable evidence.
decisions.inWild: The proposal stores immutable receipt objects in Hangar and records their digests in the lock or generation. `jet os proof` loads the receipt and follows its locked-input reference.

options.name: Hangar objects referenced by lock or generation
options.detail: Store receipts as immutable Hangar objects and keep only digest references in graph and generation records.
options.code:
.jet/lock contains `receipt sha256:91b8…`
$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
receipt: sha256:91b8…
locked inputs: sha256:20f1…
Export copies the receipt closure.

options.name: Inline every receipt in .jet/lock
options.detail: Append action, log, output, readiness, and activation evidence directly to the Package lock.
options.code:
.jet/lock
  build todo.cli action: ...
  build todo.cli logs: ...
  system gen-42 readiness: ...
  system gen-42 activation: ...

options.name: Package-local receipt directory
options.detail: Store mutable-path JSON receipt files beside generated Package state.
options.code:
.jet/receipts/gen-42.json
$ jet os proof halcyon --name gen-42
loaded .jet/receipts/gen-42.json

recommendation.why: Hangar already owns content identity, deduplication, signatures, retention, export, and generation roots while the lock remains the one graph index.

whyNot.reason: Local realization logs and observations would grow source resolution state and obscure reviewable merge changes.
Mutable paths require another identity and tamper model for evidence already suited to content-addressed storage.

recommendation.tradeoff: Human review uses `jet proof`, `jet inspect`, or an exported receipt rather than opening one source-adjacent receipt file.

decisions.title: Default Hangar ownership and path
decisions.gist: Choose the default physical Hangar ownership model across Linux, macOS, and Windows.
decisions.lesson: Hangar stores verified immutable objects, closures, and receipts. The default path determines whether first use needs administrator setup and whether objects can be shared across a user's Packages. Shared organization storage remains a separate optional broker decision.
decisions.story: Asha installs Jet without administrator rights and runs her first Package on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The same workflow must work without a setup prompt.
decisions.inWild: The proposal uses each platform's native per-user data location and exposes the resolved value through `jet hangar path`. `/etc/jet/hangar` stops being the default.

options.name: Native per-user data path
options.detail: Use platform user-data directories and allow an optional shared broker.
options.code:
Linux:  $XDG_DATA_HOME/jet/hangar, fallback ~/.local/share/jet/hangar
macOS:  ~/Library/Application Support/Jet/Hangar
Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Jet\Hangar

$ jet hangar path
/home/asha/.local/share/jet/hangar

options.name: /etc/jet/hangar where possible
options.detail: Keep a root-owned shared path as the default on systems that provide it.
options.code:
$ jet run
permission denied: /etc/jet/hangar
rerun installer as root or configure a store

options.name: Package-local .jet/hangar
options.detail: Store objects inside each Package's generated state directory.
options.code:
weather/.jet/hangar/sha256-...
todo/.jet/hangar/sha256-...
# identical object stored once per Package

recommendation.why: Per-user storage gives rootless first use, native cross-platform behavior, and sharing across one user's Packages.

whyNot.reason: A root-owned default breaks first use without administrator setup and has no native Windows equivalent.
Package-local stores duplicate verified bytes and prevent user-wide cleanup and reuse.

recommendation.tradeoff: Each user initially owns a separate physical cache unless an administrator installs the optional shared broker.

decisions.title: Optional shared Hangar broker boundary
decisions.gist: State the privilege and lifetime boundary that keeps a shared Hangar optional and non-resident.
decisions.lesson: Jet's no-daemon rule prohibits a required resident privileged build service. An optional shared Hangar still needs a narrow authority that can verify and promote objects across users. A socket-activated process can start per request, exit when idle, refuse source evaluation, rebuild under ephemeral sandbox identities, and re-check bytes, signatures, provenance, and writer authority.
decisions.story: An administrator wants deduplicated verified objects across a build lab. Developers must still build with their own Hangars when the shared socket is absent, and the privileged component must never execute repository source.
decisions.inWild: The proposal's installer creates an optional socket. A build reports verified promotions, then the broker exits idle. Missing socket falls back to the per-user Hangar without changing Package behavior.

options.name: Socket-activated transient verifier
options.detail: Install an administrator-controlled request-bounded verifier that never evaluates source.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
Installed socket-activated shared-store verifier.

$ jet build
shared broker verified 3 objects; broker idle exit.

# missing socket
using user Hangar

options.name: Resident build daemon
options.detail: Run a root service continuously and submit source evaluation and builds to it.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
Enabled root build daemon.
$ jet build
submitted Package source to resident daemon

options.name: No privileged process ever
options.detail: Forbid all shared-store promotion and keep every Hangar per user.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
unsupported

recommendation.why: Request-bounded lifetime, independent verification, ephemeral builders, and no source evaluation preserve the no-daemon promise while enabling explicit shared storage.

whyNot.reason: A resident privileged build service overturns the no-daemon and source-evaluation boundary.
A complete ban removes the already-ratified narrow path for secure cross-user promotion and canonical Nix projection.

recommendation.tradeoff: Administrators who opt in must maintain the broker socket and promotion policy.

decisions.title: Anonymous union types
decisions.gist: Whether messy one-of-several data works with zero declarations (`Int | String` inline), while named enums stay the expert's stable form.
decisions.lesson:
A union type holds a value that is one of several types. Jet already has this power through enums. `enum Id { Num(Int)  Name(String) }` declares it, and pattern matching takes it apart safely.

An anonymous union skips the declaration. In TypeScript you write `number | string` directly in a signature, with no named type anywhere. It shines when data is messy — a web API that returns a number one day and a string the next.

Jet has already decided part of this space. D-ANY-JAI1 rejected a general Any type: there is no type that means anything at all. That is ratified law and this ballot does not touch it.

The open question is the middle ground. When a JSON field can be a number or a string, today you must stop and declare an enum for someone else's inconsistency. The mess is not yours, but the ceremony is.

The timing matters more than the feature. The encoding, dataframe, and web wave is baking stdlib APIs right now. Go waited ten years for generics, and the casts that filled the gap calcified into every API. Whatever Jet's answer is, the stdlib should be built on it, not around it.
decisions.story: Priya, a data analyst, pulls a vendor's JSON where order_id is sometimes 1042 and sometimes "1042-B". In Python she never notices the mess. In Jet she must stop her report and invent a type for someone else's inconsistency.

options.name: Anonymous unions as enum sugar
options.detail: The messy case needs zero declarations. `Int | String` works in type position, a `#[Codable]` field can be a union directly, and a plain `Int` passes where `Int | String` is expected with no wrapping. Underneath it is still just an enum, taken apart by the same pattern matching. Experts keep named enums as the stable, documenting form for public APIs, with explicit conversion both ways. The cost: a second spelling for sum types, and the generated cases need clean names in matches and errors.
options.technical: `A | B` denotes a closed structural sum, order-insensitive and duplicate-free, desugared to a compiler-generated enum whose arms are named by the member types. A member value widens implicitly into the union at binding, argument, and return positions. Matching uses type names as arm heads and exhaustiveness applies as usual. Codable derives decode multi-shape wire fields into union fields directly. Union-to-named-enum conversion is explicit. Composes with `T ? E` so `T ? ParseError | IoError` needs no wrapper.

options.name: Named enums stay the only union, bless the decode idioms
options.detail: No new type grammar. The stdlib commits to typed decoding instead: the value tree for fully-dynamic JSON, and derive support that decodes an either-shaped wire field into your named enum. Declaring OrderId stays the answer, and the name documents the vendor's mess. The cost: the ceremony lands on the person with the least context — the beginner holding someone else's messy data — and layered error types keep needing wrapper enums.
options.technical: Encoding derives map a multi-shape wire field onto a user enum through existing derive machinery. No type-system change.

options.name: Unions in error position only
options.detail: `T ? ParseError | IoError` unions error types without a wrapper enum, the way Zig error sets do. Value-position unions stay out. Experts get the composition win where layering hurts most. The cost: the beginner's messy-data case is exactly the one left unserved, and the where-allowed rule is itself something to teach.
options.technical: The grammar admits `|` only on the error side of `T ? E`. Error unions flatten and deduplicate. Value positions reject `|` with a fix pointing at enums.

comparisons.note: Unions plus implicit widening are why TS absorbs messy web data so well. Its separate `any` escape is the part Jet already rejected.
Ten years without generics filled the stdlib with interface{} casts that never left. The lesson is timing, not the feature itself.
comparisons.code: func ParseId(raw interface{}) string // cast inside

comparisons.note: Error sets are exactly option C: unions on the error channel only, and they compose across layers well.
Enums only. The wrapper-enum boilerplate on the error side spawned the thiserror crate ecosystem.

recommendation.why: This is the dual-facet shape. The beginner pass: messy data costs zero declarations — the union sits inline, decode fills it, a plain value passes without wrapping, and the match still teaches safety. The expert pass: named enums remain the stable documenting form, conversions are explicit, and error signatures compose without wrapper boilerplate. One mechanism underneath, which is exactly the flexible spelling the one-mechanism law permits.

whyNot.reason: It puts the ceremony on the person with the least context, and the stdlib bakes decode idioms around a gap the language could close for good.
It serves only the expert half. The beginner's messy-data case is the one that drives people back to Python and TypeScript, and it stays unserved.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two spellings for a sum type exist, and implicit member widening is one more inference rule the checker must explain well. Accepted because the generated arms carry the member type names, so every error and match reads in the user's own vocabulary.

decisions.title: How can a local Jet report be shared?
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet sends report bundles, and under which privacy contract.
decisions.lesson:
A report bundle is a small local directory that helps diagnose the toolchain. Jet now creates it only when a person runs `jet report`. The person can open both text files before sharing anything. The bundle excludes source, paths, arguments, environment values, hostnames, user names, machine identifiers, network addresses, crash data, and package names.

Sharing adds a separate trust decision. A destination is where the bundle goes. A transport is how bytes reach it, usually an encrypted Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure connection. Authentication proves which person or service is allowed to send. Retention says how long the receiver keeps the report. These rules must be fixed before a command may send anything.

Even a minimal upload reveals facts outside the bundle. A server normally sees the sender's Internet Protocol address and request time. An authenticated service also learns the account identity. A public issue may keep the report indefinitely. Jet cannot promise zero telemetry while leaving those facts implicit.

The safe mental model is two doors. `jet report` opens the local door and never reaches the network. A later sharing step opens the network door only after the person inspects the bundle and names or accepts its destination. This ballot chooses whether Jet owns that second door.
decisions.story: Amara maintains a hospital service on a restricted workstation. A Jet compiler problem appears, so she creates and reads a local report. Before sharing it, she must know the receiver, the account used, the server facts exposed, and when the copy will be deleted.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet report
wrote local report bundle to .jet/reports/8c9d…
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/README.txt
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/report.txt

# What, if anything, should the next explicit step do?
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d…

options.name: Keep sharing outside Jet
options.detail: Jet creates and explains the local bundle, then stops. The person attaches it through a support channel they already trust. Jet never handles a destination, account credential, or network request.
options.technical: Do not ship `jet report --send`. Amend the illustrative D-TELEMETRY1 example so its separate explicit sharing step is manual. Jet's privacy boundary ends at the local content-hash directory.
options.code:
$ jet report
wrote local report bundle to .jet/reports/8c9d…
$ less .jet/reports/8c9d…/report.txt
# Attach the directory to the chosen private issue or support case.

options.name: Send to a fixed Jet report inbox
options.detail: Jet sends only to one project-owned service. No account is required. The service sees the source address and request time, keeps the bundle for 30 days, then deletes it.
options.technical: `jet report --send <bundle>` performs one HTTPS POST to `https://reports.jet-lang.org/v1/bundles` using system certificate roots. It sends the two bundle files and their content hash. No cookies or stable client identifier are sent. The server returns an opaque receipt. Server access logs and bundle data have a 30-day maximum retention.
options.code:
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d…
destination: https://reports.jet-lang.org/v1/bundles
includes: README.txt, report.txt
server observes: source address and request time
retention: at most 30 days
sent; receipt: R-4M7K2

options.name: Attach to a named GitHub issue
options.detail: The person names a Jet issue. Jet uses an existing GitHub login, so GitHub and the issue readers learn the account identity. Retention and visibility follow that issue.
options.technical: `jet report --send <bundle> --issue <Jet GitHub issue URL>` invokes the installed `gh` client. `gh` owns HTTPS transport and OAuth credentials; Jet never reads the token. Only issues in the configured Jet organization are accepted. Public issues make the bundle public and retain it with issue history; private issue access follows repository policy.
options.code:
$ jet report --send .jet/reports/8c9d… \
    --issue https://github.com/jet-lang/jet/issues/412
destination: public GitHub issue #412
identity: existing gh login
retention: issue history
attach these two files? [y/N]

options.name: Send to a destination named each time
options.detail: Experts can name any secure web endpoint. This gives organizations full control, but Jet cannot promise who receives the data or how long that receiver keeps it.
