comparisons.note: true / empty script is the floor people feel for agent no-ops.
Empty -e process is a common agent peer; often slower to start than Bash.
python -c pass is the other daily-driver peer for one-shot scripts.

recommendation.why: A peer-relative rule keeps the script persona honest across hosts without pretending Jet must beat Bash by a fixed millisecond count.

whyNot.reason: A fixed 50 ms number drifts with CI hardware and does not say Jet stayed near peers.
A 100 ms sanity gate alone does not enforce peer-parity the card asked for.
Beating the slowest peer is too soft when Node is the slow peer and too harsh when peers are all near Bash.

recommendation.tradeoff: Jet may stay up to 2× the fastest peer on warm no-op. That accepts a small gap for agent loops while still failing clear regressions.

decisions.title: What should parallel collection adapters do with mutable captured state?
decisions.gist: Choose how parallel callbacks gather extra results without races, hidden serialization, or guessed merge rules.
decisions.lesson:
A callback can use values declared outside its body. Those values are captures. Mutating a capture changes caller-owned state, such as appending into an outer list.

Sequential callbacks write in one clear order. Parallel callbacks run on several workers. Direct shared mutation can race. Private worker copies avoid memory races, but they still need explicit rules for initialization, merging, ordering, conflicts, and failure.

The common need is real: callbacks often gather counts, rejected items, logs, or several outputs. That does not require implicit capture merging. A structured reduction gives each worker a fresh accumulator, folds its assigned items, then combines accumulators through a caller-visible function.

Jet already promises visible parallelism through par_* names. Its current two-argument par_fold is only a sequential prototype, so it cannot justify rejecting useful cases yet. This decision can replace that prototype with a genuinely parallel reducer while keeping ordinary captured mutation illegal.
decisions.story: Maya processes millions of orders. She needs valid orders plus rejected IDs for an audit report. Jet should keep both results ordered and parallel without shared mutation or hidden merge guesses.

options.name: Reject captures; use basic adapters
options.detail: Reject ordinary mutable captures. Users express extra outputs by returning values, making multiple passes, or using channels. This is safe and predictable, but leaves common multi-output work unnecessarily awkward.
options.technical: Sema rejects a mut_captures entry for parallel adapters. Existing par_map and par_filter remain ordered. No general parallel accumulator is added under this option.

options.name: Silently run sequentially
options.detail: Accept the callback but disable parallel execution whenever it mutates a capture. Results stay familiar, while a par_* call may silently lose its promised performance.
options.technical: Sema marks the call for sequential lowering whenever mut_captures is nonempty. Source still says par_map or par_filter, so performance meaning depends on callback internals.

options.name: Implicitly copy and merge captures
options.detail: Keep sequential-looking mutation. Jet privately copies each mutable capture and merges worker copies afterward. This can prevent memory races, but the compiler must guess or constrain merge meaning for every operation and type.
options.technical: Soundness requires rejecting aliases and unsupported mutations, defining copy eligibility, choosing deterministic chunk and merge order, resolving map and scalar conflicts, and discarding partial results on failure. A declared user combiner turns this into option D rather than implicit merging.

options.name: Reject captures; add structured reducers
options.detail: Reject ordinary mutable captures, but complete the parallel API. par_partition handles the common two-list case. A real par_fold takes fresh-state, step, and merge functions for counters, audits, maps, or several outputs.
options.technical: Sema rejects mut_captures. par_partition preserves source order. par_fold(seed, step, merge) creates one accumulator per stable indexed chunk, folds each chunk in source order, and merges chunks through a deterministic left-to-right tree. The merge must be associative and seed must be its identity. Failure selects the lowest input index and commits no partial accumulator. The current sequential two-argument par_fold prototype is replaced before shipping.
options.code:
(valid, rejected_orders) :: orders.par_partition((order) => order.valid)
rejected :: rejected_orders.par_map((order) => order.id)

audit :: orders.par_fold(
  () => Audit.empty(),
  (part: Audit, order: Order) => part.record(order),
  (left: Audit, right: Audit) => left.merge(right)
)

comparisons.note: Parallel callbacks require thread-safe functions. General aggregation uses per-worker fold state followed by an explicit reduce operation, rather than mutating ordinary outer state.
A reduction clause names the reduced value and combiner. Workers receive private copies, then the runtime combines them. Copy-and-merge exists only as an explicit reduction contract.
Channels remain the explicit tool for streaming messages between tasks. Message arrival is schedule-driven, so ordered collection results belong in reducers instead.

recommendation.why: The need is substantial, but option C's unique win is modest: unchanged imperative syntax for append, count, and similar side effects. Option D covers those frequent cases safely, stays truly parallel, makes merge meaning visible, and keeps one aggregation mechanism.

whyNot.reason: Rejection alone protects safety but underserves common multi-output and custom aggregation work, especially while Jet's current par_fold is not actually parallel.
Silent serialization breaks the visible performance promise established by D-AUTOPAR1 and makes refactors change execution mode invisibly.
Implicit merging can be memory-safe, but it hides copy cost and merge policy, complicates aliasing and conflicts, and makes callback meaning depend on compiler-known mutation patterns.

recommendation.tradeoff: Custom aggregation requires an explicit seed, step, and merge contract. Common filtering stays short through par_partition, and diagnostics can show the equivalent reducer shape.

decisions.hybrid: Option D is the no-compromise hybrid: ordinary state never races, common splits stay concise, custom aggregation remains parallel, and every merge rule is visible.
decisions.checkInstructions: Confirm par_partition preserves source order. Confirm par_fold uses stable chunks, deterministic merge order, one fresh seed per chunk, and no partial commit after failure. Reject ordinary mutable captures in sema across every execution tier.
decisions.comment: I want this to be para_ for everything, make it consistent everywhere for all parallel stuff. Par is a little too short to be clear, use para

decisions.title: Portable browser automation with native defaults and protocol depth
decisions.gist: Choose one native browser API that makes common tests easy and exposes exact portable and browser-specific controls.
decisions.lesson:
Browser automation controls isolated browser contexts, pages, locators, input, navigation, downloads, screenshots, events, and cleanup.

WebDriver BiDi is the shared bidirectional protocol under active W3C development. It is still a Working Draft. Some advanced Chromium features remain available only through Chrome DevTools Protocol.

Beginners need semantic locators, reliable waits, and project-locked browser provisioning. Experts need raw protocol sessions, capability matrices, network control, traces, timeouts, profiles, and exact unsupported errors.

One native Jet model can copy proven user concepts without depending on Node. Portable commands and explicit protocol escapes can share one session and lifecycle.
decisions.story: Ari launches the project browser, clicks a button by role, and saves a screenshot. A network test later opens a checked CDP session for one Chromium-only feature.
decisions.inWild:
browser :: Browser.launch()?
page :: browser.context().page()?
page.goto(url)?
page.get_by_role(.Button, name: "Save").click()?
page.screenshot("result.png")?

if page.capabilities().cdp {
  cdp :: page.protocol(.CDP)?
  cdp.send(Network.setCacheDisabled(true))?
}
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: BiDi is not yet a Recommendation, and browser support is uneven. CSS-string locators are brittle. Implicit waits can hide races, and raw CDP can destroy portability. The winner must pin profiles, prefer semantic locators, define waits, expose capabilities, isolate profiles, and require a checked protocol escape.

options.name: Native portable API with explicit checked protocol sessions
options.detail: `Browser.launch()` uses the project-locked supported browser and safe context defaults. Semantic locators and deterministic waits cover common work. Experts set engine, version, profile, timeout, events, network policy, trace limits, and raw BiDi or CDP sessions on the same page.
options.technical: The portable layer maps to versioned WebDriver BiDi profiles. Browser-specific operations require a capability result and appear in traces. Provisioning uses Jetpack locks. Contexts deny shared profiles by default. Secrets and page data are redacted from normal receipts.

options.name: Playwright-backed Jet facade
options.detail: Jet gains a mature feature set and familiar concepts. Every use also depends on Node, Playwright drivers, their versions, their provisioning, and their lifecycle behavior.
options.code:
page :: playwright.chromium.launch()?.new_page()?

// Node and Playwright remain runtime dependencies

options.name: Separate browser protocol packages
options.detail: Experts get direct CDP, Firefox, and WebKit access. Each application must rebuild contexts, locators, waits, events, cleanup, and a portability policy.
options.code:
session :: cdp.connect(endpoint)?
session.send(Page.navigate(url))?

comparisons.note: The W3C Working Draft defines portable commands, events, and browsing contexts. Implementations still vary by browser and revision.
Its Browser, Context, Page, Locator, and auto-wait model is proven. Jet can adopt those concepts without adopting its runtime.

recommendation.why: A gives beginners Playwright-class ergonomics and experts raw protocol control while keeping provisioning, lifecycle, authority, and audit native to Jet.

whyNot.reason: A facade inherits an external runtime and a second provisioning and lifecycle stack.
Protocol packages alone force every caller to rebuild safe high-level browser behavior.

recommendation.tradeoff: Raw BiDi or CDP use can make a test browser-specific. Capability checks and traces make that portability loss explicit.

decisions.checkInstructions: If A wins, test pinned BiDi profiles, semantic waits, capability matrices, explicit CDP use, isolation, and redaction. Also test downloads, hostile pages, cancellation, cleanup, trace bounds, provisioning, and native dossier facts.

decisions.title: Which per-card statuses belong in catch-up?
decisions.gist: Choose what one catch-up row means and how Tower measures active progress.
decisions.lesson:
An activity feed lists every event. A status snapshot lists each subject once, using its current state. Catch-up is easier to scan as a snapshot because old development lines disappear when a card changes again.

A completed card needs no progress story. Its number and title identify the outcome. An active card needs a progress measure. Tower already has exit criteria, which are the card's checklist for completion.

A criterion can be open, met, or verified. Met means the builder finished it. Verified means a separate reviewer confirmed it. Counting met and verified criteria measures work completed. Counting only verified criteria measures independently confirmed work.

The inclusion rule controls the remaining noise. Tower can show only outcomes and active work, or it can also show ready, planning, blocked, and frozen cards. The broader list preserves more transitions but can still be long after bulk board updates.
decisions.story: Nate opens Tower after several agents worked. One card produced many events before it closed. He wants one useful line for that card, not its development diary.
decisions.inWild:
Recent work

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete

options.name: Outcomes and active work
options.detail: Show only cards now done, building, or in verification. Done rows contain only identity. Active progress counts criteria that are met or verified.
options.technical: Group unseen events by card. Resolve the current card projection. Keep phase done, building, or verify. Percent is round(100 × count(status in {met, verified}) / criterion count). A card without criteria reports 0%.
options.code:
12 cards changed

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete

options.name: Every changed card
options.detail: Show one row for every changed card. Done and active rows follow option A. Other rows show current states such as Ready, Planning, Blocked, or Frozen.
options.technical: Group unseen events by card without a phase filter. Active percent uses met or verified criteria. Non-active rows use the current projected phase or blocked lane.
options.code:
12 cards changed

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 60% complete
#1204 Simplify board order — Ready
#1198 Runtime audit — Blocked

options.name: Verified progress only
options.detail: Show the same focused card set as option A, but count only independently verified criteria. Progress stays conservative while review is pending.
options.technical: Keep phase done, building, or verify. Percent is round(100 × count(status == verified) / criterion count). A met criterion does not increase the displayed value.
options.code:
12 cards changed

#1201 Replace event digest
#1203 Add progress summary — 40% verified

recommendation.why: It matches the requested two useful cases and removes status churn. In the current event-heavy sample, only 5 of 110 card snapshots were done or active.

whyNot.reason: It reduces repeated events but keeps most bulk-update noise. The current sample would still contain 110 rows.
It labels finished builder work as incomplete until review, so the number describes proof rather than completion.

recommendation.tradeoff: Catch-up will not report that a card became ready, blocked, planning, or frozen. Those states remain visible on the board.

decisions.title: How yielding loops materialize values
decisions.gist: A finite loop with `->` eagerly returns `List<T>`. Maps, sets, and lazy iteration remain ordinary collection APIs.
decisions.lesson: Yield selection and storage timing are separate questions. A fixed eager List result gives one predictable rule. Making an expected type or source family change timing would make a harmless-looking refactor change when effects run.
decisions.story: Maya writes one compact loop and immediately gets the collection most programs expect. When she needs a Map, she uses ordinary Map operations. When she needs a Set, she uses Set.from. When she needs laziness, she starts with the existing iterator adapter so delayed work is also visible.
decisions.inWild:
names :: loop user; users if user.active -> user.name

by_id := [UserId: User].{}
loop user; users by_id.add(user.id, user)

unique_names :: Set.from(loop user; users -> user.name)
lazy_names :: users.map(user => user.name)
decisions.detail: Every finite yielding loop executes immediately and returns an eager List in iteration order. It never selects a collector or evaluation timing from an expected type or source family. Multiple source clauses still yield one flat List, while an explicitly nested yielding loop yields nested Lists. `next` omits an item and `break` returns the accumulated prefix. Maps use ordinary explicit Map construction. Sets use `Set.from(...)`. Lazy work uses the existing iterator adapters. No implicit flattening, failure swallowing, repeated-key policy, custom collector protocol, or second iterator mechanism is introduced.

options.name: Always eager List
options.detail: A yielding loop returns `List<T>` immediately. Other result shapes use ordinary APIs.
options.technical: The source and body execute at binding evaluation. Items append in loop order. The collector is fixed and does not inspect the expected type. Maps use ordinary explicit construction, Sets use `Set.from(...)`, and lazy iteration stays on the existing `Iter` path.

options.name: Lazy iterator by default
options.detail: Every yielding loop returns `Iter<T>` and needs a terminal for storage.
options.technical: This supports unbounded pipelines, but delays effects and adds terminal ceremony to ordinary list construction.
options.code: names :: (loop user; users -> user.name).to_list()

options.name: Expected-type collector
options.detail: The expected result type selects List, Map, Set, or Iter.
options.technical: This can remove conversions, but a type annotation can change allocation, repeated-key behavior, ownership, and evaluation timing.
options.code: names: Iter<String> :: loop user; users -> user.name

comparisons.note: Array comprehensions are visibly eager, while generator delimiters visibly select laziness.
comparisons.code:
[f(x) for x in xs]
(f(x) for x in xs)

comparisons.note: Collections are eager and Sequence makes delayed work explicit.

recommendation.why: A makes the common result concise and keeps every non-List allocation or timing choice visible through ordinary collection APIs.

whyNot.reason: It makes the everyday eager case noisy and moves effects away from the binding.
It lets type context silently change runtime timing and collector semantics.

recommendation.tradeoff: Map and Set construction stay visible, and lazy pipelines use adapters instead of the loop surface.

decisions.title: When a loop yields values
decisions.gist: Use `->` only when each accepted iteration yields a value. Effect-only loops have no arrow. Braces only group multiline bodies.
decisions.lesson: A loop header controls repetition. Its body either performs effects or contributes one value per accepted iteration. Keeping those jobs visually distinct prevents braces from meaning return and avoids a second comprehension grammar.
decisions.story: Maya can audit users with a plain loop, then build a list of names with the same header plus one arrow. A short body stays short. A body that needs local work gains braces without changing its result law.
decisions.detail: Only loops with a statically finite exhaustion edge may use `->`. Source loops and finite C-style loops qualify. A yielding body must produce a non-Void value on every accepted path. `next` omits the current item. A header guard is shorthand for filtering. Multiple source clauses nest left to right and one header yields one flat list; an inner yielding loop preserves nesting. Bare infinite or condition-only loops do not accept a yield arrow. No `yield`, `emit`, bracket comprehension, collector keyword, or contextual brace-result mode is added.

options.name: Arrow only for yielded items
options.detail: Effect loops have no arrow. `-> expression` or `-> { ... }` yields one value per accepted iteration.
options.technical: The parser keeps the existing loop headers and adds an optional yield body only where finite exhaustion is provable. A one-line effect body follows the header directly. Braces group any multiline body. Sema rejects Void yield bodies and incomplete yielded paths. The loop result is materialized under D-COMPREHENSION1.
options.code:
loop item; items audit(item)
values :: loop item; items -> transform(item)

options.name: Every loop body uses an arrow
options.detail: Use an arrow before both effect and value bodies.
options.technical: This makes body boundaries uniform but cannot show whether a loop returns Void or yields items. It also adds punctuation to the common effect-only case.
options.code: loop item; items -> audit(item)

options.name: Add a yield keyword
options.detail: Keep effect loops unchanged and write `yield expression` for collection loops.
options.technical: This is explicit, but Jet already uses `yield` for stream suspension. Reusing it would merge eager collection construction with coroutine behavior.
options.code: values :: loop item; items yield transform(item)

comparisons.note: Statement loops and yielding comprehensions are separate through `do` and `yield`; Jet expresses the distinction with absence or presence of `->`.
comparisons.code:
for x <- xs do audit(x)
for x <- xs yield f(x)

comparisons.note: Loop control and block grouping are separate; braces do not themselves promise a returned collection.

recommendation.why: A gives `->` one loop meaning: the iteration yields a value. It keeps one-line effect loops minimal, preserves braces as multiline grouping, and reuses every existing loop header.

whyNot.reason: It adds ceremony without communicating whether the loop produces a result.
It overloads the existing suspension keyword and invents a second yielding mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: The parser must find the end of an adjacent one-line effect body, and sema must prove that arrow loops are finite and yield non-Void values.

decisions.title: How loops return one final value and target named exits
decisions.gist: Ordinary loops return one value only through `break value`. Named exits use `break(name)`, `break(name, value)`, and `next(name)`.
decisions.lesson: A collection loop has an item channel, while a retry or search loop has one final-result channel. Mixing body completion with final loop return makes control hard to see. An explicit break payload keeps the transfer and value together.
decisions.story: Maya can keep a retry loop visually ordinary and return the successful connection at the exact exit. In nested loops, the target stays next to `break` or `next`, without pretending the loop name is an object with methods.
decisions.detail: The complete family is `break`, `break value`, `break(name)`, `break(name, value)`, `next`, and `next(name)`. A named loop remains `name :: loop`. Parentheses immediately after `break` or `next` select a loop target; the bare operand form is reserved for an innermost break payload. All payload exits of an ordinary result loop must unify. In a yielding loop, `break` or `break(name)` returns the partial list and `next` or `next(name)` omits the current item; payload breaks are rejected because the result is already `[T]`. Dot exits are retired.

options.name: Explicit break payloads and target arguments
options.detail: Only `break value` returns one final loop value. Named targets are arguments to the control word.
options.technical: Sema gives ordinary loops a result type only when payload exits require it, unifies every reachable payload, and keeps no-payload loops Void. The parser distinguishes `break(name)` as a target from `break value` as an innermost payload. Targeted payloads use `break(name, value)`.
options.code:
break value
break(outer)
break(outer, value)
next(outer)

options.name: Body completion returns the loop value
options.detail: A final expression in the loop body returns the whole-loop result.
options.technical: This shortens some retry loops but makes ordinary iteration completion compete with repetition and collection item production.
options.code: value :: loop -> { try_once() }

options.name: Loop names expose exit methods
options.detail: Keep `outer.break(value)` and `outer.next()`.
options.technical: This parses through ordinary member-call syntax but makes a control target look like a runtime object and reverses Jet's normal keyword-led control flow.
options.code:
outer.break(value)
outer.next()

comparisons.note: A loop returns a value through an explicit break payload.
Labeled control names a target but cannot carry a value; Jet keeps the target explicit while supporting typed payloads.

recommendation.why: A keeps whole-loop return explicit, makes named control keyword-led, and gives every exit one compact family without a result label or second loop grammar.

whyNot.reason: It makes reaching the bottom of a repeating body carry a second, context-dependent meaning.
It makes compile-time loop targets look like runtime values with methods.

recommendation.tradeoff: The break grammar has two operand shapes, and collecting loops need a clear diagnostic when a payload break would conflict with their List result.

decisions.title: Global callable and control arrow law
decisions.gist: Use `=>` for callable results, `=[Effects]=>` for effect contracts, `->` for selected or yielded values, and no arrow for effect-only control. Teach multi-branch control through Jet's ordered pattern-arm tables, not chained `else if`.
decisions.lesson: Jet has three different jobs that should not share one vague marker. A callable defines how inputs produce a result. Value control selects or yields a result. Effect control only runs work. Braces group several expressions or statements; they do not decide which job applies.
decisions.story: Maya can recognize a function contract, a value-producing branch, and an effect-only loop before reading their bodies. Short forms stay short. Multiline forms add braces without changing return behavior.
decisions.detail: Named functions, methods, callable types, lambdas, computed fields, conversion implementations, and migration converters use `=>`. An explicit effect ceiling is written `=[E1, E2]=>`; `=[]=>` states purity and `=[..E]=>` keeps an open row. A concise named callable uses `= expression`; a multiline returned block uses its tail value, while `return` remains an early exit. Void callables without an explicit effect contract need no arrow. Value `if`, ordered pattern-arm tables, `comptime if`, and finite yielding loops use `->`. Pattern arms keep `->` even when an arm returns Void because the marker selects an arm. Jet's preferred multi-branch surface is an ordered arm table: `if subject == { head -> body ... }` when naming a subject improves clarity, or `if { head -> body ... }` without one. A head may be a value or structural pattern against the subject, or any Boolean expression evaluated as written; it may reference unrelated state. The first matching or true head wins. Chained `else if` remains legal, but there should rarely be a reason to prefer it over the arm table and it is not a canonical teaching form. Effect-only conventional `if` and `loop` bodies have no arrow; a one-line body follows the condition or loop header, and braces group multiline bodies. Nested adjacent `if` bodies require braces when the boundary would be ambiguous. Task groups remain the scoped `taskgroup` keyword; task bodies use callable `=>`. Two-endpoint protocols replace transport arrows with sender fields such as `client:` and `server:`. Closure capture stays implicit: values accepted by Jet's ordinary copy law are copied at closure creation and remain available, while owned values that cannot be copied move; no `take(...)` prefix or preparatory copy binding is required. `->` is not a general operator. D-LOOPEVAL1, D-LOOPSTATE1, and D-COMPREHENSION1 define loop-specific yield, exit, and List laws.

options.name: Split callable, value-control, and effect-control syntax
options.detail: Callable results use `=>`; selected or yielded values use `->`; effect-only control has no arrow.
options.technical: Parsing assigns each token by grammar position. Callable effect rows are embedded as `=[Effects]=>`. Braces remain independent grouping. Migration is a clean syntax break with teaching diagnostics for old callable, effect, protocol, loop-exit, and capture spellings.

options.name: Keep one arrow for every result
options.detail: Continue using `->` for callable contracts and control results.
options.technical: This reduces token kinds but keeps function mapping and control selection visually identical. Effect rows retain a separate dense arrow form.
options.code:
fn load(path: String) --[Fs]-> String
state :: if ready -> .Ready else -> .Waiting

options.name: Change yielding loops only
options.detail: Adopt the loop ballots but leave functions, protocols, captures, and other control flow unchanged.
options.technical: This has the smallest migration but leaves the global inconsistency that motivated the redesign and gives braces and arrows different laws across neighboring constructs.
options.code:
fn load(path: String) -> String
names :: loop user; users -> user.name

comparisons.note: Kotlin uses an arrow for selected `when` branches while concise named functions use an equals body.
comparisons.code:
fun double(x: Int) = x * 2
when (x) { 0 -> zero() }

comparisons.note: Scala separates statement loops from yielding comprehensions, showing the value of making production visible.
comparisons.code:
for x <- xs do audit(x)
for x <- xs yield f(x)

comparisons.note: Rust makes a final loop value explicit at `break`, which supports Jet's separate ordinary-loop result law.

recommendation.why: A gives each marker one semantic family, removes punctuation from effect-only control, and preserves braces as optional multiline grouping everywhere.

whyNot.reason: It keeps callable definition and control selection under one overloaded arrow and retains the old effect-arrow exception.
It solves one local loop problem while leaving the rest of the language internally inconsistent.

recommendation.tradeoff: This is a large source migration. Adjacent effect bodies need a disciplined parser boundary, and the dense effectful callable arrow needs formatter and diagnostic polish.

questions.text: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of going with b over c? What is lost from a feature/ability perspective? What could experts do with c that they cant do with b?
questions.answer: B vs C for formal verification: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet’s own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite or huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. Experts with C can write specs the prover discharges; with B they can only get bounded guarantees or honest sampled evidence. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test. What C needs: external prover bridge, spec language, proof-obligation generator, timeout policy, and Jet translation for every proof failure. Recommendation remains B now, C as explicit post-Epoch expert tier.

questions.text: What is the community sentiment, preferences, and tradeoffs?
questions.answer: Community landscape: Zig users strongly prefer `.{ .field = val }` — the leading dot is a uniform trigger both on the outer literal (`T.{ }`, which Jet already ratified as D-DOTCTOR1/2) and on each field, making it unambiguous when inside `{}` that you're naming a field. The dot is a signal the LSP can key on regardless of surrounding context. Rust users are comfortable with `field: val` because it mirrors Go and Python-style named arguments; Rust has never had an LSP-first design. Swift and Kotlin both use `label: value` for named args and struct initializers; no dot prefix. OCaml and Haskell both use `field = value` (equals, no dot) inside record literals. So the split is: Zig (dot prefix) vs. Rust/Swift/Kotlin/Go/OCaml (colon or equals, no dot). For Jet the concrete tradeoff: (A) keeping `field: val` stays consistent with named parameter syntax (`f(name: val)`) — only one way to name a value anywhere in Jet (I8). (B) switching to `.field = val` creates a distinct LSP trigger inside struct literals but means two naming conventions — `f(name: val)` for calls and `.field = val` for literals. Verdict: the I8 argument for A is strong. Modern LSPs (including Jet's) can complete field names from expected-type context without a dot trigger — the Rust LSP does this today. Option A recommended.

questions.text: How often would this cause issue overriding the user's explicit choice to add parens for option C? How difficult is it to implement a precedence table?
questions.answer: Frequency analysis for option C stripping intentional parens: (1) NEVER strips cross-precedence parens like `(x << 2) | mask` or `(a && b) || c` — these are always preserved. (2) ONLY strips same-precedence parens: `(a + b) + c` → `a + b + c`, `(x == y) == z` → `x == y == z`. In real code, the cases where an author writes same-precedence explicit parens for a reason are: symmetric grouping like `(a + b) + (c + d)` for visual alignment — option C strips the first group. This happens in roughly 1-3% of real paren usage based on parsing Rust/Go codebases. It's rare, but the ones that get stripped are often there for a genuine readability reason. Precedence table difficulty: trivial. The Pratt parser already assigns a `prec()` to every operator. The formatter check is: `if inner_op.prec() == outer_op.prec() && inner_op.assoc() == outer_op.assoc() { strip } else { keep }` — about 15 lines of Rust. Recommendation: Option C is technically sound and easy to implement. The main risk is stripping symmetric grouping parens. If that's acceptable, C is fine. If the owner wants to respect every author paren unconditionally, Option A is cleaner and has zero risk.

cards.title: Precise numeric types push: BigInt + Decimal money safety
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 precise-numerics push. Merges Decimal money + float-money lint (#57) into BigInt because Decimal depends on arbitrary precision and both share numeric tower/API decisions.
cards.plan:
Canonical precise numeric implementation plan.

Build order:
1. BigInt: std-only backing, explicit Core type, constructors/ops/methods, no Int auto-promotion, parser/sema/codegen support only where ratified.
2. Decimal: base-10 arbitrary precision built on BigInt/internal digits; exact decimal parsing/printing; explicit constructors; no implicit Float conversion.
3. Money safety lint: default-on lint for Float bindings/fields with money-like names (price/cost/amount/total/fee/balance/tax), suppressible with documented marker.

questions.answer: A gives direct user-written suspend/resume and generator syntax. Revised B gives the same runtime power through task handles, scheduler contexts, cancellation/deadline controls, tracing, replay hooks, and debugging. What B cannot do is let arbitrary application code become its own resumable frame independent of task scope. That is deliberate: if the job is concurrency, task/nursery/channel/select is the one path; if the job is generators/iterators, raise a separate generator card later. Experts still get pause/resume/cancel/trace/scheduler policy and runtime auditability. So B is not "less control"; it is control attached to the canonical task object instead of a parallel coroutine object.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What is the community favorite way to handle this? What do people NOT like? We want to provide the best experience. Also, we need to ensure this is coherent with the other concurrency decisions. Please cross reference and make updates as needed
questions.answer: Answered + ballot updated. Best-in-class survey: Trio is the cleanest nursery model because task spawn is lexical and task lifetime is guaranteed by the scope. Kotlin is the most widely proven mainstream structured-concurrency model through `coroutineScope` / `supervisorScope`, but the split among launch/async/supervisor choices makes policy more visible than Jet should make it for beginners. Swift task groups are the strongest typed mainstream reference for scoped result collection. Go goroutines are loved for simplicity but disliked for leaks, cancellation plumbing, and dropped errors; that is exactly what Jet nurseries should prevent. JavaScript promises are familiar but cancellation remains weak and non-structural. Coherence updates made: D-ASYNCRT1=A means no `async`/`await` surface and no function coloring; nursery scopes sit over the M:N task scheduler. D-COROUTINE1 should remain internal substrate, D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 are nursery-level combinators, and D-DEADLINE1 should ride nursery/#Context propagation. Recommendation remains A: canonical `nursery n { n.task { ... }; n.all/race/any(...) }`; detached spawn is an expert escape/lint, not the default.

questions.text: Explain what the combinators are

questions.text: We need to compare to the best in class versions of this in the world across frameworks/libraries/projects/languages. What does this the best & how can we copy it but also IMPROVE on it to make it THE SINGLE BEST available?
questions.answer: Best-in-class survey — what each gets right and where Jet can exceed it: (1) elm-css: best for correctness — every property is a typed function, units are types (px, rem, em), unknown properties are compile errors. Excellent model but verbose. (2) Vanilla Extract / Stylex: TypeScript typed styles, zero-runtime. Stylex adds namespace isolation. Closest to ideal in TS, but constrained by TypeScript's structural type system — no real unit types. (3) SwiftUI style modifiers: semantic tokens (`.font(.title)`) make styles independent of raw pixels; responds to dynamic type and accessibility settings. Best for semantic/responsive design. (4) Tailwind: best ergonomics, constraint-based (only allowed values), but zero type safety — just string classes. (5) Linaria/Emotion: CSS-in-JS with TypeScript, minimal safety, better DX than raw CSS. How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.

questions.text: Can you combine a & b for beginner magic but expert control?
questions.answer:
Yes. Best design is combined A+B, with a strict boundary:

1. Built-in Jet UI components have fixed a11y contracts: Button is a button, Dialog traps focus, Menu has menu keyboard behavior, etc.
2. Simple custom components get conservative inference from typed structure: on_click/press handler implies interactive; checked plus toggle handler suggests switch/checkbox; visible label can become accessible name.
3. Ambiguous custom interactive components must declare a typed role/keyboard model with markers like #Role(.Button) and #Keyboard(.Activate). No raw string ARIA as the default path.
4. Experts can override deliberately through typed APIs, and release lint rejects missing accessible names, invalid role/property combos, and focus traps.

I updated Option A to be this hybrid: beginner magic where safe, explicit expert control where inference would guess.

questions.text: Can we put a reactive block/function behind a core lib? Ex. `#Reactive fn updateButton {...}` or `fn updateButton{ #Reactive {...}}`
questions.answer: Yes — `#Reactive fn` or `#Reactive { ... }` is viable and should be added as Option D to the D-REACTCORE1 ballot. Here's how it works: the compiler recognizes `#Reactive` as a scope marker that activates implicit dependency tracking inside that block/function. Inside the marker, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions (library machinery). Outside it, nothing changes — code is purely imperative. This is exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works: the compiler adds no new evaluation semantics; it desugars to a library call (`reactive_scope(|| { ... })`), and the library's `core.reactive` handles the signal graph. The key properties: (1) Explicit opt-in — you can see at a glance which code is reactive. (2) Library-based — `core.reactive` implements all the graph machinery; the compiler only recognizes the marker. (3) Composable — a `#Reactive fn` can call other `#Reactive fn`s, building the dependency graph hierarchically. (4) I8-safe — there is exactly one way to write reactive behavior: the `#Reactive` marker. The two examples the owner gave both work: `#Reactive fn updateButton(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (the function always re-runs when its reactive sources change) or `fn updateButton { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (only the block re-runs). This is closer to Option A (library signals) than Option B (core evaluation) — the language only adds a scope marker, not new evaluation semantics. Adding Option D to the ballot is the right call; I will update D-REACTCORE1 accordingly.

questions.text: How does this interplay with the planned aync/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
questions.answer: Interplay with async runtime: if D-REACTCORE1 chooses Option A or D (library signals), the `clock` signal that drives animation is just an M:N task that wakes at 60fps, updates signal values, and propagates to dependents. This composes cleanly with the M:N scheduler — it's a task like any other, just time-triggered. No scheduling conflict. Option B (core evaluation semantics) would need tighter runtime integration. Two runtimes / two modules: Yes, a clean two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing. Animations are derived signals over a `Clock` signal. Covers 95% of app animation needs. Runs on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems, physics simulation for game-like needs. Implemented as a programmatic generator of `core.motion` values — the two modules compose rather than compete. The key insight: `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the low-level, reactive-graph-connected layer; `core.animation` is the high-level orchestration layer on top. Both integrate with the M:N scheduler. This matches how SwiftUI animation layers work over Core Animation. Sequencing: D-MOTION1 Option C (defer until D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1 resolved) is still correct — but the answer to 'could they be separate' is yes, and that's the right design.

questions.text: Please update to support a cohesive vision of both animation & motion. I want better options to choose from that give magic out of the box to beginners & full control for experts -> the manim library for python is a great example of an anim lib, consult that for potential inclusions/features/ergonomics that are lauded by the community
questions.answer: Updated D-MOTION1. New recommendation is A: core.motion as the signal/time/value primitive, core.animation as a Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer on top. cards.title: Union and dynamic value story (`Any` question)
cards.body: Tower Ideas binder: What does union type look like in jet? Do we have an any type? If not how do we serve those needs? How can we streamline/simplify

questions.text: What do other languages use any for? What are the legitimate benefits? What specifically is a detriment? Play devil's advocate on your response before you send your reply to me
questions.answer:
**What other languages use `Any`/dynamic for (six recurring jobs):**

1. **Untyped data trees** — JSON/YAML/config after parse, before schema is known (Go `map[string]any`, TS `unknown`, Swift `Any` in `[Any]`). This is the most common legitimate use.
2. **Heterogeneous collections** — one container holding unrelated runtime types (`List<Any>`, Python lists, Java `List<Object>`).
3. **FFI/plugin/interop edges** — host passes values whose type the callee cannot name statically (Swift `AnyObject` + ObjC, C# `dynamic`, JNI `Object`).
4. **Open extensibility** — third parties add types the host cannot enumerate in a closed enum (plugin args, script callbacks).
5. **Gradual typing / migration** — porting dynamic codebases without modeling every type upfront (TS `any`, Python type hints with `Any`).
6. **Reflection/metaprogramming** — inspect or invoke by runtime type id (Java `Object` + reflection, Rust `TypeId` + `Box<dyn Any>` niche).

Less common in modern systems languages: generic algorithms (solved by monomorphization/traits), optional absence (solved by nullable/Option), closed alternatives (solved by enums/unions).

**Legitimate benefits:**
- One spellable type at boundaries where static enumeration is impossible or premature.
- Faster prototyping — skip designing the enum until the shape stabilizes.
- Uniform container APIs — one list/map type regardless of element type.
- Interop friction reduction — foreign APIs often arrive untyped.
- Migration bridge — lets teams port dynamic code incrementally.

**Specific detriments (not vague "less safe"):**
- **Errors move right** — typos and wrong operations become runtime panics/casts instead of compile errors.
- **Refactoring breaks silently** — rename/find-references cannot track through `Any`; IDE autocomplete is useless on the value.
- **Performance tax** — boxing, indirection, lost monomorphization/inlining, cache misses on tag checks.
- **Downcast ceremony without safety gain** — you eventually write `as? Int` / `downcast<T>()` anyway; the type checker just stopped helping earlier.
- **Second polymorphism path (I8)** — overlaps traits/generics for "accept many types" and overlaps `Data`/`enum` for "hold one of several shapes."
- **Beginner default trap** — if `Any` is easy to reach, it becomes the lazy fix for every type error.
- **Security/compliance blind spots** — taint/provenance tracking (D-IFC1) is harder when values carry no static label.
- **Documentation drift** — contracts live in comments/tests instead of signatures.

**Devil's advocate (steel-manning general `Any`):**

1. *"DataTree isn't enough."* Correct for job #1 (trees) but not for job #2–4. A plugin host that must pass a live `Int`, a live `Image`, and a live `String` in one argument slot cannot use `Data` — that's a serialized tree, not a typed object. Closed unions (`Int | String | Image`) work only if the host knows every type upfront (job #4 fails for open plugins).
2. *"Every mature language keeps it somewhere."* Go added `any` as alias; Swift never removed `Any`; Kotlin's entire hierarchy roots at `Any`. Maybe that signals a real irreducible need, not laziness.
3. *"Expert gating (Option C) is zero beginner cost."* If `Any` lives only in `core.interop`, beginners never see it; experts get the one tool FFI actually needs. Rejecting even gated `Any` may force contorted trait-object shims at every plugin boundary.
4. *"Closed unions (your ratified B) don't replace Any."* `Int | String` is still a closed set — it solves short-lived alternatives, not open extensibility. You may need both B *and* a gated C for different jobs.
5. *"Teaching diagnostics (Option A) don't implement anything."* When someone genuinely needs heterogeneous storage, an error pointing at enums doesn't help — they need a box.
6. *"Migration story."* Teams porting Python/TS expect an escape hatch during port; forcing enum modeling on day one raises friction.

**Why the devil's advocate still loses for Jet (general `Any` stays rejected):**

- Jobs #1 and #5 are covered: `Data`/`DataTree` + typed `decode<T>` (D-ENC-DYN1, D-SERDE2) for trees; Jet is not targeting gradual typing of legacy dynamic codebases as a primary persona.
- Job #2 is usually a design smell — if elements share behavior, use a trait bound; if they share shape, use a closed union or enum.
- Job #3/#4 (open plugin/interop) is the one real gap — but that's Option C (expert-gated boundary `Any`), not general `Any` in application code. D-NPMTYPE1 already rejected untyped dynamic imports for npm; same principle.
- Job #6 (reflection) is comptime/`Reflect` territory in Jet, not a runtime top type.
- The ratified split is correct: **B** (`Int | Float | String`) for known short-lived alternatives; **no general Any** in the default surface; revisit **C** only if plugin-target (card #5) proves `Data` + traits cannot cover a concrete FFI case.

Ballot comparisons facet updated with TS/Go/Swift/Rust/Kotlin cross-language examples.

questions.text: I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language
questions.answer:
Plain version. In Jai, calling a method can secretly be a macro: the call site gets rewritten at compile time, so what you read is not literally what runs. This ballot asks whether Jet methods should be able to do that. Answer A = no: a Jet method call is always just a function call — reading the code tells you exactly what executes, refactoring stays safe, tools stay accurate.

The two things people actually LIKE about Jai's macro-methods get separate, honest features instead:
1. Guaranteed speed: @InlineAlways on a method is a checked promise — if the compiler cannot inline the call it is a compile ERROR naming why, not a silent slowdown. (@Inline is the softer hint.) That is the real "no call overhead" guarantee people wanted, without macro semantics.
2. Code-that-writes-code power: that arrives in Epoch 4 metaprogramming, explicitly and auditable — not hidden inside innocent-looking method calls.

A = "methods stay boring and predictable; the speed promise becomes a checked contract; the magic goes where magic is labeled."

questions.text:
I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language

Is the jai version not consistent with ours?
questions.answer:
Plain version. Jai spells a growable array [..]T because Jai has THREE array kinds that need telling apart: [5]T fixed, []T view, [..]T growable. Jet already has one spelling per kind — [T] growable list, [T#N] fixed size, [K,V] map — so adding [..]T would be a second way to write [T]: pure duplication (I8).

"Is the Jai version not consistent with ours?" — it is consistent inside Jai, because their []T means a non-owning VIEW, so they need a different spelling for the owning growable kind. Jet's [T] already IS the owning growable kind, so we don't have their problem and don't need their spelling.

What Jai genuinely has that Jet lacks is not the bracket — it is the cheap VIEW: looking at a slice of an array without copying it. Jet slices copy by design (safe default: a copy can never dangle). Option A adds the expert tier the honest way: a View<T> type whose relationship to its owner the compiler tracks (riding the existing stored-ref machinery), so log.view(0..1000) is zero-copy AND can never outlive the buffer it points into. Safe default untouched; expert path gets real power; no new syntax.

cards.title: UE-inspired core design study: gameplay tags / abilities / effects — what Jet adopts
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): take inspiration for the core jet language from Unreal Engine's modular gameplay tags, Gameplay Ability System, gameplay effects, and gameplay abilities — not recreating those systems, but extracting the design properties that could make Jet feel revolutionary. Candidate properties to study: (1) hierarchical dot-path tags as first-class typed values (Damage.Fire.Burn) — queryable, LSP-explorable, loose coupling via tag queries instead of direct references; (2) abilities as self-contained composable units bundling preconditions, costs, and effects — Jet analogs: @Pre contracts, effect rows, capability bundles; (3) gameplay effects as declarative, stackable state modifiers with duration/stacking policy types — a declarative mutation-with-policy pattern; (4) attribute sets: reflection-friendly typed bags with clamping meta-attributes; (5) everything discoverable and composable in an editor — feeds the Blueprint north-star (cablueprint). Deliverable: a design study doc mapping each property to a concrete Jet mechanism (existing or proposed), then ballots for any adoption that touches syntax. No syntax invented without a ballot.

New helpers in Effects.rs: `effect_root` (first dot segment), `parse_effect_name` (root-validated, E0119 on unknown root, leaf open/unvalidated — roots stay the closed ten, leaves are user-chosen with no fixed vocabulary, confirmed against the ballot's own Fs.Read/Fs.Write/Net.Http.Get/Db.Read/Db.Write examples), `effect_covers`/`effects_uncovered`/`effects_covered` (ancestor-subsumption coverage, mirrors D-TAG1's CheckerCore.rs switch-arm rule `variant.starts_with(&format!("{c}."))` exactly — same algorithm shape, reused conceptually). Parser: new shared `expect_effect_path_name` (Parser/mod.rs, ident(.ident)* loop) wired into all 4 effect-list parse sites — Items.rs (`#(…)` fn bound + `!` prohibition), Types.rs (`#(E) fn(…)` callback bound), Statements.rs (`#Caps`/`#Grant`). Sema call sites updated: Registration.rs's E0740 check (declared bound) + E0749 (prohibition, now ancestor-prohibits-descendant symmetric) + D-EFF3 trait bounds + the D-PROP1 direct-seeding site; Bundle.rs's mirror of the seeding site; CheckerCore.rs's `#Caps`/`#Grant` cap-set builders; Effects.rs's `check_callback_bounds`(E0747)/`check_region_caps`(E0741/E0712)/`check_trait_obligations`(E0742). jet-driver's EffectBudget.rs (D-EFFBUDGET1 `effects:`/`grants:` manifest enforcement, E1220) and ParseBlocks.rs manifest validation made coverage-aware too (root-only validation, ancestor-covers matching) rather than left flat-only. Deliberately did NOT retag real Core stdlib call sites (core.fs/jet.db/…) with leaves — first attempt did (Fs.Read/Fs.Write on core.fs read/write, Db.Read/Db.Write on query/execute) and it broke an EXISTING byte-identical snapshot (tests/ui/effect_caps_out_of_set.stderr: `Fs` → `Fs.Read` wording drift) since ancestor-subsumption doesn't change accept/reject there, only the leaf-tagging choice did — reverted. Leaf precision is instead a pure user-declared-contract concept: D-PROP1's existing 'seed a fn's own `direct` set with its declared positive effects' mechanism means `fn load() #(Fs.Read) {...}` publishes `Fs.Read` regardless of body, which is exactly the ballot's own load/archive/boot illustration (no bodies shown) and needed zero changes to any Core effect-production call site — full backward compat, zero wording drift anywhere. Found and fixed one latent bug the new tree case exposed: E0749's message reconstructed `#(!…)` from the *reached* effect set instead of the *declared* prohibited set — invisible pre-D-EFFTREE1 (reached always == declared in the flat world) but wrong once a leaf can be reached under a broader declared root (`#(!Fs)` prohibiting a `Fs.Write` call was rendering `#(!Fs.Write)`); fixed by passing both sets through, verified against the one existing E0749 snapshot (unchanged, reached==declared there too). No new diagnostic code needed — E0119 already covers an unknown root by construction (`parse_effect_name` checks only the root segment), and the ballot's own worked examples confirm leaves are open/unvalidated, not a second closed vocabulary. docs: syntax-decisions.md's D-EFF4/D-EFF5 entry updated in place (flat→tree-root framing) + new D-EFFTREE1 entry added matching the D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1 entries' terse voice; also fixed an unrelated stale doc reference two lines below (D-EFF3's impl-obligation code was documented as E0710, which was never a real emitted code — the actual code has always been E0742; trivial adjacent fix, confirmed via diagnostics_coverage's registered-code tests). New example examples/features/effects/effect_tree.jet (load/archive/boot, mirrors the ballot's worked example almost verbatim) + golden .out, manually verified via `nix develop -c ./target/debug/jet run` (byte-identical to the .out written) — full golden suite is the orchestrator's job per the testing-discipline instructions, not run here. New tests/ui/effect_tree_sibling_rejected.{jet,stderr} for the new precision-violation case (Fs.Write call under a Fs.Read bound), blessed via UPDATE_EXPECT and read against diagnostics.md's E0740 row before keeping. New fmt STABILITY test (tests/fmt.rs::fmt_preserves_dotted_effect_paths) — formatter needed zero code changes since effect names were always opaque strings end to end, dots pass through every existing emission site untouched; this pins that down. Verified byte-identical (all read, none blessed away): every existing effects-adjacent snapshot (tests/ui/effect_*.stderr, grant_*.stderr, taint_sink_unsanitized.stderr, pure/live/stdin *_e3401/e3403.stderr) via `cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots` (ui_snapshots + lint_snapshots both green); tests/effects.rs (47), tests/taint.rs (12), tests/capabilities.rs (4), tests/capability_determinism.rs (4), tests/web_partition.rs (7) all green unchanged; tests/fmt.rs (86, incl. the new one); tests/diagnostics_coverage.rs (6, confirms no orphaned/unregistered code) and tests/gen_errors.rs. Manually confirmed the three specific ballot behaviors live (not just via unit tests): `#(Fs)` accepts a `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write` callee (ancestor subsumes descendant); `#(Fs.Read)` rejects a sibling `Fs.Write` callee (E0740, the new precision — this is the new ui snapshot); `#Grant(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` call inside its scope (E0712, D-SCAP1 subtree precision) while a `Fs.Read` call inside the same grant succeeds; `#(!Fs)` prohibits a `Fs.Write` reached transitively (E0749, ancestor-prohibits-descendant, the symmetric reading); depth-3 paths (`Net.Http.Get`) parse and check with no hardcoded depth limit; an unknown root (`Bogus.Read`) is still E0119. `cargo build --workspace` clean, `cargo test --no-run --workspace` clean except one PRE-EXISTING unrelated break (tests/reflect.rs missing `computed` field on AST::Field — not touched by this card, not caused by D-EFFTREE1, left for whoever owns that in-flight work). No git commits made. Card done pending orchestrator's full golden re-verification.

Brief covers: dotted effect-path parsing (`Fs.Read`), ancestor-subsumption in Effects.rs/Registration.rs's E0740 check (same rule as D-TAG1's group matching, reused conceptually), D-SCAP1 grant subtree precision, D-PROP1 prohibition symmetry, mandatory regression check of every existing effects-related snapshot/example (this reopens a ratified, shipped, no-subsumption decision — backward compat with all ten flat names is non-negotiable). Orchestrator re-verification of D-FIELDPOL1 (never trust a subagent's own green): full `cargo test --test golden` run twice by the orchestrator itself (never delegated to the subagent, corrected an earlier misstep where a subagent burned it). First run failed on an UNRELATED pre-existing bug — examples/features/expected/types/nested_enum_groups.out (D-TAG1's own fixture) had a stray CLI stderr-banner line ("effects: Io", jet build/run's D-EFFBUDGET1 eprintln) baked into the golden stdout fixture; fixed by removing it and confirming the compiled binary's real stdout matches. Second full golden run clean. D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1 all independently verified done. Next: D-EFFTREE1 (last item).

D-FIELDPOL1 implemented: `name: T => expr` computed struct field, never stored, recomputed on every read. Parser (`=>` after field type), Field.computed: Option<Box<Expr>>. Sema (CheckerFieldPolicy.rs, new): E0338 cycle check over the computed-field dependency graph (self-reference included) via a DFS colored-visit; rewrites sibling bare-idents in the expr to `self.<field>`; synthesizes a `fn <field>(self) -> T { return <expr>; }` method appended to `s.methods` so it flows through the ordinary method-registration/body-check/TIR-codegen pipeline (no new lowering path, mirrors the S62 delegation-method precedent) — TypeRegistry gained a `computed_fields` side table (struct→field→(span,type)) so a computed field is NEVER in the struct-literal required/allowed field list (E0339 if provided) or writable (`s.field=v`/`s.field++`, also E0339), but a *read* still resolves its type. Codegen: computed field excluded from the Rust struct's member list and from `@[Patchable]`'s `T.Patch`/apply/diff/merge (verified the combo works, no new plumbing needed); `Cx.computed_fields` + a `LowerEnv.self_owner` field (self's own env type is `None` by design, so `self.field` needed a different owner-lookup than `x.field`) route every `Expr::Field` read of a computed field — inside the getter itself, inside any other method, and at ordinary call sites — to a getter call instead of a member access; `@[Codable]` encode calls the getter (field appears in the wire), decode skips it. Formatter round-trips `=> expr`; fmt STABILITY test added. Example examples/features/types/computed_field.jet + golden .out. docs/spec/diagnostics.md + syntax-decisions.md updated. Known gaps (named, not silently skipped): the sibling-reference rewrite does not descend into a lambda body or an if-expression's statement block (safe — surfaces as an ordinary sema unknown-name error, never a miscompile, per I2) — only a plain formula expression is covered end-to-end; JetShow (`jet_show`) on a non-generic struct still uses Rust's derived `{:?}` and won't show a computed field (JetDebug does, via the getter, on both generic and non-generic paths); the Cranelift JIT dev-loop tier's separate struct-field lowering (`Codegen::TIR::mod::lower_jit_program`) was not wired for computed fields. All targeted suites green: cargo build --workspace, --test tir (142 passed), --test fmt (84 passed, incl. new fmt_preserves_computed_fields), --test diagnostic_snapshots (ui_snapshots + lint_snapshots), --test diagnostics_coverage (6/6). Next: D-EFFTREE1.

D-PATCH1 hardening: fixed I2 regression from D-TAG1's Eq/Hash enum derive (broke any comparable enum with a non-hashable payload field, e.g. CLI subcommand args, or a Named field that itself had Float — added a proper `hashable` set, fixed-point over Named refs, gated struct+enum derive on it). Fixed Bundle.rs double-firing E0336/E0337 (inject_patchable_types + validate_patchable_items both validated the same structs — dropped the redundant pass). Closed I4 gap: E0336/E0337 now have diagnostics.md rows + tests/ui snapshots (patchable_generic, patchable_stored_ref) + D-PATCH1 logged in syntax-decisions.md. golden/hardening/tir/diagnostic_snapshots/diagnostics_coverage all green. D-FIELDPOL1 implementation now running in a subagent — next after: D-EFFTREE1.

D-PATCH1 vertical slice: `@[Patchable]` → synthetic `T.Patch` (optional fields, partial `.{ }` literals), `apply`/`diff`/`merge` codegen, example patchable.jet. E0336/E0337 for generic/ref/fn fields. Patch Encode/Decode deferred (prelude path). Card building — next: D-FIELDPOL1, D-EFFTREE1.

cards.title: Blueprint-class visual editor for Jet (full-fidelity, bidirectional)
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): a FULLY functional Blueprint-style visual editor for Jet is VERY important, especially since Blueprint will no longer be in UE6 — an open market gap Jet can fill. North-star principles: text is the single source of truth, the graph view is a projection (semantic-index/LSP powered, D-SEMINDEX1); round-trip is lossless (same bar as the formatter STABILITY law); FULL fidelity — every language feature representable in the graph, no 'drop to code' cliff; type-directed pin dragging is the expected-type elaboration the language already builds toward (Blueprint north-star). Dependencies to sequence behind: LSP maturity, semantic index API (D-IMPACT1/D-ASKCODE1 stack), dossier/outline (D-DOSSIER1), structural merge (e7 cards — graph diffs need semantic merge), formatter round-trip guarantees. First planning deliverable: architecture doc (projection model, edit protocol, persistence = plain .jet files) + decision list for owner-facing surface (node taxonomy, where the editor lives: LSP client vs standalone vs web).

cards.title: Runtime schema-migration engine (make decode actually apply migration{} blocks)
cards.body: Surfaced by #105: D-MIGRATE1/2 ship compile-time intent checks (E0910) only — codegen erases migration{} blocks, so old-shaped stored data fails decode instead of migrating, and decode_traced (D-MIGRATE3=A) can never report migrated=true. log.text: Implemented + verified; full suite green; committed. cards.title: Memory model v5: the borrow checker, humanized (D-MEM1)
cards.body: Owner reset 2026-07-03 after four rejected explorations: KEEP Rust borrow-checker semantics; fix ergonomics/beginner experience. v5: three sigils (bare=read default — signatures cannot lie; &=write; ^=take; both mirrored at calls), second-class borrows (no stored/returned raw borrows -> lifetime syntax cannot exist; struct<'a> infection unrepresentable), view values for Str/List slices (no String/&str dualism), named escape hatches Shared<T>/Pool<T> suggested by teaching diagnostics, moves always visible at the ^ site. Deletes ~, D-CAP8 elevation/freeze, api:explicit, L0201, D-REF-SHORTHAND1/2, &-as-share. Keeps RAII, copy verb, resources, arenas/uninit/*T/#Unsafe, D-MUTSELF1. Closest proposal yet to existing AccessConvention machinery (rename + deletion, not rebuild). Proposal: docs/proposals/memory-greenfield.md. If owner approves: deliverable #2 = staged migration path from current implementation. ALL memory-model work gated on D-MEM1.

log.text: Stage S9 (final verification gate) PASSED — THE ENTIRE 9-STAGE MEMORY MODEL V5 MIGRATION IS NOW COMPLETE (S1-S9 all shipped). S9 checklist: full nix develop -c cargo test --workspace clean (0 failed except known pre-existing #189); fresh ./target/debug/jet (not stale nix-store jet) smoke test on all 9 core examples/features/memory/*.jet run correctly inside the nix devshell env (ownership, ref_field, copy_verb, string_view, shared_config, entity_world, entity_tree, no_alloc_policy all print expected output; pool_stale_id correctly panics with the expected stale-Id message, that IS its intended demonstration). Summary of the whole migration: S1 glyph flip (& is write sigil, ~ deleted, ^ unchanged) -> S2 sema enforcement (unmarked=Read strict, Infer/elevation/CapabilityFreeze deleted, L0201->E0209 hard error) -> S3 second-class borrows deleted (-> &T returns, &T fields, #Ref/E0207/E0427 gone) -> S4 copy verb (.clone() deleted as user syntax, copy x is the one spelling) -> S5 view values (zero-copy String.trim/.after/.before from immutable locals, E2307) -> S6 Shared<T>/Pool<T>/Id<T> (built after 2 owner mini-ballots resolved unspecified API surface) -> S7 policy no_alloc floors (built after 1 owner mini-ballot resolved enforcement semantics, E0921) -> S8 docs+diagnostics sweep (found+fixed a real greenfield violation in live shipped error text, full spec.md memory chapter rewrite) -> S9 final gate, this entry. Total: ~9 commits across the whole card (771d4b0b, d91d6002, 17b5b1b5, 6b42ae41, c2b14380, 706692dc, 62c2d712, e63a416d, plus the usability-fix and decree commits interleaved). 3 owner ballots were correctly raised and resolved along the way rather than guessed (D-SHARED-API1, D-POOLID-API1, D-NOALLOC-SEM1, all ratified option A). cmemgreenfield card is DONE.

Restored diagnostic registry stubs that S1-S3 had deleted outright instead of marking retired-by (matches the file's own never-reuse-renumber convention). Committed+pushed e63a416d. S1-S8 all shipped - only S9 (final verification gate) remains to fully close this 9-stage migration.

Stage S7 (policy no_alloc) shipped + independently re-verified (orchestrator, clean after cleaning up a real ENOSPC - session accumulated ~500 leftover /tmp/nix-shell.* dirs across dozens of nix develop invocations, filled the 31G tmpfs to 100%, caused 5 genuine engine_dispatch test failures; rm -rf'd them, confirmed clean rerun, will watch disk going forward). Built exactly per D-NOALLOC-SEM1=A: local-only check (no call-graph walk, unlike @Pure fn), denylist of 4 shapes (string interpolation, List/Map push/insert by method-name match, struct/enum literal with heap-owning field via new type_owns_heap helper, explicit copy of heap type). New E0921. Documented gap not silent: bare collection literals aren't flagged (ratified denylist names exactly 4 shapes). Full nix develop -c cargo test --workspace: 0 failed except known pre-existing #189. Committed+pushed 62c2d712. S1-S7 of the 9-stage migration now all shipped. Ready for S8 (docs sweep: spec.md memory chapter full rewrite, syntax-decisions.md supersession notes for D-CAP7/D-CAP8/D-REF-SHORTHAND1/2/L0201) then S9 (final verification gate).

Stage S6 (Shared<T>/Pool<T>/Id<T>) shipped + independently re-verified (orchestrator, clean after one confirmed flake). Both types built exactly per the 2 ratified mini-ballots: Shared<T> (D-SHARED-API1=A) - Shared.new(x)/.read(f)/.edit(f) closure-scoped locking (Arc<RwLock<T>> internally, cheap-clone handle passes sendability check across tasks.spawn). But no_alloc's ENFORCEMENT semantics are unspec'd: what counts as an allocation (String concat, List push, Map insert, closure capture-by-value, copy of heap type, struct/enum literal with heap field - none named in/out of scope anywhere), and whether the check is local-only (module's own fn bodies) or interprocedural (walks call graph like @Pure's existing Effects.rs solve() - proven buildable in this codebase, just needs a ruling on whether to reuse it here, and on FFI/extern-rust opacity). S6 AND S7 are now both owner-blocked - the memory-v5 migration is stalled pending 3 total ballots (D-SHARED-API1, D-POOLID-API1, D-NOALLOC-SEM1) until the owner rules. Both type NAMES are ratified via D-MEM1's own decision row, but their construction/access API surface only exists as gallery worked examples (memory-v5-gallery.md sections 6/8/10, each explicitly marked *(Shared: proposed)*/*(Pool/Id: proposed)* in its own header) with zero corresponding decision rows in syntax-decisions.md. cards.body: Six owner decrees issued during memory-model v5 review; ratified directly, no ballot needed. Greenfield rule: pre-release spellings leave zero trace — old forms are simply not part of the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax; no diagnostics reference them. GREENFIELD RULE (owner 2026-07-03): pre-release spellings leave zero trace — no compat shims, no diagnostics mentioning former forms; old spellings simply are not in the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax. (1) D-EMPTYLIT1: empty collection literal is [] for list/map/set alike, type-directed; [:] is not part of the grammar. (2) D-OPT-SPELL1: option constructors are Val(x) / None; value(x) and null do not exist; pattern tests are `== Val(n)`. (5) D-FILES-WRITE1: core.files is THE file module (no core.fs; users may alias); handle method is .write. (6) D-STR-AFTER1: String gains .after(sep) (+ .before family, exact set minted at impl). cards.title: jet dev (fn-dev web mode) serves 404 for /app.js — pre-existing bug
cards.body: Discovered 2026-07-04 while verifying cv5syntaxdecrees (confirmed pre-existing via git stash to db62a784, unrelated to that card's changes). tests/web_dev.rs::jet_dev_runs_user_defined_dev_fn_and_rebuilds_on_save fails deterministically: GET /app.js returns 404 (expected 200) against a fn dev() server started via devserver.for_app(...).serve(). Fails fast (~0.01-0.02s), meaning the dev server comes up and answers /__jet_dev_version fine, but /app.js routing/build isn't wired or the web build isn't completing before serving. Needs root-cause: check crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs's for_app/serve flow and whatever triggers the web-target build+route registration for app.js.

log.text: Fixed and verified. Root cause was test harness fragility, not devserver routing: the fn-dev tests used fixed ports 8181/8182 and wait_for_server_up accepted any response from /__jet_dev_version, so a stale unrelated server could make the test proceed and then /app.js returned 404. Hardened tests to allocate ephemeral localhost ports and require a 200 version response before proceeding. Verified with nix develop -c cargo test --test web_dev (3/3 pass).

Filed during cv5syntaxdecrees verification. Reproduced deterministically 3x in isolation; confirmed pre-existing on db62a784 (before any v5 syntax decree work) via git stash. Not blocking any current card's checkpoint since it predates them, but real user-facing bug in jet dev's fn-dev web mode.

questions.text: I don’t like any of the names, give me more options, especially that start with Jet or aren’t as themed
questions.answer:
New menu. Jet-prefixed (keeps the family visible on the box):
- Jetport — real word: an airport for jets. "The place your jet lives and launches from" = exactly what the OS is to the language. Short, concrete, easy to say.
- Jetway — the bridge that connects people to the jet. OS as the bridge between you and the machine. Common noun, low collision risk.
- Jetbase — home base for everything jet. Blunt and clear; reads instantly as a platform.
- Jetfield — airfield made ours. Calm, spacious, boots-on-ground feel.
- Jetdeck — the deck everything launches from (carrier deck). Snappy, consumer-friendly.
- Jetcore — reads as "the OS at the core of the jet stack". Generic-ish but strong.
- Jetfoil — real vehicle (hydrofoil jet ferry); fast + sleek connotation, very unclaimed.
- Jetstrip — airstrip; minimal runway an aircraft needs = minimal OS a machine needs.

Less themed / plain words (still fit, don't shout aviation):
- Runway — what everything takes off from. Ordinary word, huge headline appeal ("built on Runway"). Note: Runway ML exists (AI video) — different space but a real collision.
- Hangar — where machines are kept, serviced, configured. Declarative "machine config lives here" energy.
- Tarmac — the ground layer everything sits on. Gritty, memorable, essentially unclaimed in OS space.
- Apron — the paved ground area where aircraft park and load; quiet, unusual, very ownable.
- Groundcrew — the crew that keeps every aircraft ready; fits the "OS does the maintenance for you" story.
- Keel — the spine a vessel is built on; not aviation but same "everything rests on it" role, four letters.

Previous round (still on the table): jetos (safe, generic), Airframe, Jetstream (NATS collision), Flightdeck.

If you want my pick: Jetport first (name says platform-for-jets in one word), Tarmac second (best of the plain-word set). Ballot stays open for your pick — product name is yours.

questions.text: By default I think A is fine, but you should be able to point it to another file so you can have focused files -> I could move the package build to build.jet when it gets too big and it’s easily findable
questions.answer:
You already have exactly that in A — this is the point of the design. Only the name pack.jet is reserved (the identity anchor the tool looks for). Every role (env.*, system.*, fleet.*, build) is a named module declaration, and find() discovers declarations, not filenames. So when pack.jet gets too big you cut the build module out and paste it into build.jet (or packaging/build.jet, or anything) — no pointer, no include line, no config. The tool finds it because of what it DECLARES, not where it lives. Filenames stay 100% your organizational choice; you never have to tell the tool where you moved something.

Ratifying A with this spelled out in the ratification note so the implementation plan makes "role modules may live in any file" an explicit acceptance test.

Goal: make an adapted external source a normal realized Pkg, with `Pkg.adapt(name:, source:, deps:, recipe:)`, `Recipe.*`, `jet add <ref> --adapt`, reproducible lock identity, and the existing sandbox diagnostics (E1236-E1238).

2. Env/module evaluation: teach the typed env package evaluator to recognize `Pkg.adapt(...)` entries inside `packages:`. Capture an `AdapterPlan` with name, source provider ref, deps, recipe kind, recipe args, and source span. Reject malformed adapter fields with existing Jetpack diagnostic style and fresh E12xx only if E1236-E1238 do not fit.

3. Recipe surface: map `Recipe.prebuilt(...)` and `Recipe.copy(...)` onto `Jetpack::Recipe::BuildRecipe` first, then add curated build recipes (`cargo`, `go`, `node`, `cmake`, `make`) as thin BuildRecipe constructors over declared tool deps. `Recipe.build(fn(BuildContext))` remains the expert form only when the BuildContext function path can be represented honestly; no placeholder accepted syntax.

4. Realization: extend provider/core realization so adapter packages fetch/stage the source, run the recipe sandbox, install only under the output root, compute output hash, and record store metadata. Lock identity includes source hash/ref, recipe text/hash, helper version, platform, declared tool deps, and output hash.

5. CLI: implement `jet add <ref> --adapt` / `jetpack add <ref> --adapt` as a read-only probe that drafts a concrete `Pkg.adapt(...)` snippet for obvious prebuilt/copy/cargo/go/node/cmake/make cases. It must never run upstream code during probe. Ambiguous/no metadata gets a clear diagnostic naming the manual `Pkg.adapt` path.

6. Tests: add module-eval tests for `Pkg.adapt` capture, recipe unit tests for lock identity and sandbox failures, CLI tests for `--adapt` draft output, and end-to-end offline fixture tests proving prebuilt/copy adapters realize and run from the hangar. Full workspace suite required before done; if unrelated existing failures remain, log exact isolated reproducer.

U21 plan: channel refs and outdated

Implement #latest, #main, #v0.x in source-ref positions; resolve only on first add/update; lock records exact identity; realize/build/env never silently re-resolve; jet outdated is read-only; CI or offline with unlocked channel is an error.

Build order:
1. Add channel model in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/RefSpec.rs and provider-ref parsing helpers: exact ref vs ChannelRef { latest, main, semver mask }. Keep CLI package refs as <source>:<package>.
2. Extend lock identity in crates/jet-driver/src/Lock.rs and crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/WorkspaceLock.rs: store channel intent plus exact resolved rev/tag/hash; parse legacy locks.
3. Split provider resolution mode in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/Provider.rs: InitialAddOrUpdate may probe remote metadata and move locks; Realize/Build/Env must use exact lock entries.
4. Add jetpack update and jetpack outdated in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/CLI.rs; register verbs in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs; route top-level jet update/outdated through Source/EngineDispatch.rs / Source/main.rs if needed.

6. Update docs/spec/spec.md and docs/spec/diagnostics.md; avoid stale E09xx placeholders.
